en/ai-llm/00-start-here/01-overview.title: Start from zero: what LLM integration actually is
en/ai-llm/00-start-here/01-overview.summary: Integrating an LLM means calling a probabilistic text model as a service and engineering around its limits — finite context window, per-token pricing, and outputs that can hallucinate. This is the map and the eight words the rest of the track assumes you already know.

en/ai-llm/01-prompt-caching/01-overview.title: Prompt caching: how a stable prefix cuts input cost 10x
en/ai-llm/01-prompt-caching/01-overview.summary: Prompt caching reuses an exact token-for-token prefix at ~0.1x the input price. Any byte that shifts that prefix — a timestamp, a reordered tool — invalidates the whole cache and silently 10x''''s your bill.

en/ai-llm/02-tool-calls/01-overview.title: Tool calls: the round-trip loop, schema validation, and the guard against runaway agents
en/ai-llm/02-tool-calls/01-overview.summary: Tool calling turns a model into a function caller, but the model only emits a request — you execute it. Every call is a full extra round trip, the arguments can be hallucinated, and an unguarded loop will burn tokens forever.

en/ai-llm/03-rag-architecture/01-overvie.summary: RAG is a retrieval problem wearing a generation costume. Chunk size, top-k, reranking, and context order each move recall and cost — and a retrieval miss makes the model confidently invent the answer instead of saying it doesn''''t know.

en/ai-llm/04-streaming/01-overview.summary: Streaming trades total generation time for time-to-first-token. SSE emits delta events you accumulate; tool-call args arrive as partial JSON you can''''t parse until done. The classic prod kill: a buffering proxy holds the whole response and streaming silently dies.

en/ai-llm/06-agents/01-overview.summary: An LLM agent is a while-loop that calls the model, runs a tool, appends the result, and calls the model again. The danger is the loop that won''''t stop and the history that won''''t stop growing — both bill you per token.

en/algorithms/01-thinking-complexity/01-.title: What is an algorithm?
en/algorithms/01-thinking-complexity/01-.summary: An algorithm is a finite list of unambiguous steps that turns an input into an output.

en/algorithms/01-thinking-complexity/02-.title: Is the algorithm correct?
en/algorithms/01-thinking-complexity/02-.summary: Correctness means the algorithm produces the right output for every valid input, not just the ones you tested. Use loop invariants to reason about correctness.

en/algorithms/01-thinking-complexity/03-.title: Counting the steps
en/algorithms/01-thinking-complexity/03-.summary: The cost of an algorithm is how many basic operations it performs. Count the steps for a given input size n, and see how the count grows as n grows.

en/algorithms/01-thinking-complexity/04-.title: Big-O notation
en/algorithms/01-thinking-complexity/04-.summary: Big-O describes how an algorithm''''s cost grows as input size increases. Learn to read O(1), O(n), O(n²), and why we drop constants and small terms.

en/algorithms/01-thinking-complexity/05-.title: The complexity classes
en/algorithms/01-thinking-complexity/05-.summary: Not all algorithms are created equal. Learn the seven Big-O classes you will meet again and again, from O(1) constant time to O(n!) factorial time, and when each is practical.

en/algorithms/01-thinking-complexity/06-.title: Time and space
en/algorithms/01-thinking-complexity/06-.summary: Until now, complexity meant time. But every algorithm also costs memory. Learn to measure space complexity — how much extra memory an algorithm uses — and the deliberate tradeoff between time and space.

en/algorithms/01-thinking-complexity/07-.title: Reading the constraints
en/algorithms/01-thinking-complexity/07-.summary: Before solving a problem, look at the input limits. Learn the rule of thumb (10⁸ operations per second), the standard mapping from input size to required complexity, and how to use constraints to eliminate impossible approaches.

en/algorithms/01-thinking-complexity/pro.title: Thinking & complexity: predict then measure
en/algorithms/01-thinking-complexity/pro.summary: Hands-on project — implement algorithms of different complexity classes, benchmark them across growing input sizes, and confirm the measured growth matches the predicted Big-O.

en/algorithms/01-thinking-complexity/qui.title: Thinking & complexity: multiple-choice review
en/algorithms/01-thinking-complexity/qui.summary: Multiple-choice synthesis across the complexity unit — dominant terms, Big-O classes, the time-space tradeoff, and reading constraints to pick an approach.

en/algorithms/01-thinking-complexity/qui.title: Thinking & complexity: code reading

en/algorithms/01-thinking-complexity/qui.title: Thinking & complexity: free-recall review

en/algorithms/02-arrays-strings/01-the-a.title: The array
en/algorithms/02-arrays-strings/01-the-a.summary: An array is a row of boxes in memory, each holding one value. Because the boxes are contiguous, you can jump to any box in O(1) time. Understand this one fact, and you unlock the cost of every array operation: read/write O(1), search O(n), insert in the middle O(n).

en/algorithms/02-arrays-strings/02-trave.title: Traversing an array
en/algorithms/02-arrays-strings/02-trave.summary: Traversing means visiting every element in an array, and it is the single most common operation you will perform. Learn the loop shapes, patterns (accumulate, find, transform, test), early exit, and backwards traversal.

en/algorithms/02-arrays-strings/03-two-p.title: Two pointers
en/algorithms/02-arrays-strings/03-two-p.summary: Keep two indices into the array and move them under a rule. Transforms O(n²) nested-loop problems into O(n) single-pass solutions. Two shapes: opposite-ends (start at both ends, move toward each other) and same-direction (both start front, one runs ahead).

en/algorithms/02-arrays-strings/04-slidi.title: The sliding window
en/algorithms/02-arrays-strings/04-slidi.summary: A window [left, right] slides across an array. Instead of recomputing a property for every subarray (O(n²)), you slide and update in O(1) per step for O(n) total. Two shapes: fixed-size (length k) and variable-size (grow/shrink based on condition).

en/algorithms/02-arrays-strings/05-prefi.title: Prefix sums
en/algorithms/02-arrays-strings/05-prefi.summary: Precompute a prefix array once. Then any range-sum query costs O(1) by subtraction instead of O(n) by traversal. Trade O(n) memory and setup for instant answers.

en/algorithms/02-arrays-strings/06-in-pl.title: Working in place
en/algorithms/02-arrays-strings/06-in-pl.summary: Modify an array without building a new one. Use O(1) extra space by overwriting cells in place: swap two elements, use a write pointer to compact an array, or reverse using two opposite-end pointers. In-place saves memory but destroys the original input.

en/algorithms/02-arrays-strings/07-strin.title: Strings are arrays
en/algorithms/02-arrays-strings/07-strin.summary: A string is a sequence of characters — algorithmically, an array. Indexing is O(1), but strings are immutable. The Unit 02 patterns work on strings; just avoid building one with repeated `+=` in a loop, a hidden O(n²) trap.

en/algorithms/02-arrays-strings/drill.title: Arrays & strings: interview drill

en/algorithms/03-sorting-search/01-why-s.title: Why sort?
en/algorithms/03-sorting-search/01-why-s.summary: Sorting is preprocessing: spend O(n log n) once to unlock O(log n) binary search, O(n) duplicate detection, O(n) median finding, and O(n) closest-pair detection. Learn when the cost is worth it.

en/algorithms/03-sorting-search/02-simpl.title: Simple sorts
en/algorithms/03-sorting-search/02-simpl.summary: Selection sort, insertion sort, and bubble sort run in O(n²) time. Selection sort always scans the whole rest of array to find the minimum. Insertion sort adapts: O(n) on nearly sorted input. All are in-place and educational; real systems use O(n log n) algorithms.

en/algorithms/03-sorting-search/03-merge.title: Merge sort
en/algorithms/03-sorting-search/03-merge.summary: Merge sort divides the array, recursively sorts each half, then merges them in O(n) time. The result: O(n log n) always. It is stable and not in-place, using O(n) extra memory. First taste of divide and conquer.

en/algorithms/03-sorting-search/04-quick.title: Quicksort
en/algorithms/03-sorting-search/04-quick.summary: Quicksort partitions the array around a pivot, then recursively sorts left and right. O(n log n) average, O(n²) worst case on bad pivots. In-place with O(log n) stack space. Not stable. Faster than merge sort in practice.

en/algorithms/03-sorting-search/05-binar.title: Binary search
en/algorithms/03-sorting-search/05-binar.summary: Binary search finds a value in a sorted array in O(log n) by repeatedly halving the search range. The precondition: the array must be sorted. The idea: keep bounds [lo, hi], check the middle element, discard half the range, repeat.

en/algorithms/03-sorting-search/06-binar.title: Binary search on the answer
en/algorithms/03-sorting-search/06-binar.summary: Binary search is not only for finding a value in a sorted array—it works on any sorted space. Search over possible answers when you can ask ''''is this answer feasible?'''' and the answer is monotonic: false, false, …, false, then true, true, …

en/algorithms/04-recursion-backtracking/.title: What is recursion?
en/algorithms/04-recursion-backtracking/.summary: A function that calls itself to solve a smaller version of the same problem. Two mandatory parts: the base case (stop here) and the recursive case (shrink and call yourself).

en/algorithms/04-recursion-backtracking/.title: The call stack
en/algorithms/04-recursion-backtracking/.summary: Every function call gets a stack frame holding its parameters and local variables. Recursive calls stack up; the deepest recursion uses O(n) stack space and can overflow if n is too large.

en/algorithms/04-recursion-backtracking/.title: The complexity of recursion
en/algorithms/04-recursion-backtracking/.summary: To find the Big-O of a recursive function, draw the recursion tree: each node is a call, and the cost is the number of nodes times the work per node. A function that calls itself once per level is O(n); a function that branches into two calls per level is O(2ⁿ).

en/algorithms/04-recursion-backtracking/.title: Backtracking
en/algorithms/04-recursion-backtracking/.summary: Backtracking systematically explores all candidate solutions by building them step by step. At each step, you make a choice, recurse, then undo the choice before trying the next. If a partial solution violates a constraint, prune that branch and skip the rest.

en/algorithms/04-recursion-backtracking/.title: Subsets and permutations
en/algorithms/04-recursion-backtracking/.summary: Two classic backtracking problems: generate every subset of n items (2ⁿ total) by choosing include/exclude at each step, or generate every ordering (n! total) by choosing which unused item goes next. Both apply the same template with different choices.

en/algorithms/04-recursion-backtracking/.title: Combinations
en/algorithms/04-recursion-backtracking/.summary: Generate every way to choose k items from n items, where order does not matter. Use the start index trick: walk items in fixed order and at each step choose to include or skip, never revisiting earlier items. Leads to C(n,k) = n! / (k!(n-k)!) combinations.

en/algorithms/05-hashing/01-hash-maps-an.title: Hash maps and hash sets
en/algorithms/05-hashing/01-hash-maps-an.summary: A hash set answers ''''is X present?'''' in O(1) time. A hash map stores key–value pairs and looks up by key in O(1). Both trade memory for speed using a hash function to jump straight to the answer.

en/algorithms/05-hashing/02-frequency-co.title: Frequency counting
en/algorithms/05-hashing/02-frequency-co.summary: Count how many times each value appears using a hash map: one O(n) pass builds a frequency tally. Solve anagrams, find duplicates, and group by count.

en/algorithms/05-hashing/03-the-seen-pat.title: The ''''seen'''' pattern
en/algorithms/05-hashing/03-the-seen-pat.summary: Keep a hash set of values you have seen. For each new element, check the set in O(1), then add it. One pass solves what O(n²) brute force once required.

en/algorithms/05-hashing/04-grouping.title: Grouping with a hash map
en/algorithms/05-hashing/04-grouping.summary: Partition a collection by computing a group key for each item. Store items in a list under their key: map[key].push(item). One O(n) pass groups everything; the heart is key design.

en/algorithms/05-hashing/05-collisions-a.title: Collisions and the real cost of hashing
en/algorithms/05-hashing/05-collisions-a.summary: A hash table achieves O(1) average lookup only when keys spread evenly across buckets. Collisions degrade performance, but chaining, load factor management, and rehashing keep average time O(1). Worst case is O(n) with a bad hash function.

en/algorithms/05-hashing/drill.summary: Timed arrays-and-hashing problems from the NeetCode-150, with progressive hints — solve each cold, then narrate the complexity.

en/algorithms/05-hashing/quiz-choice.summary: Multiple-choice synthesis across the hashing unit: hash functions, collisions, chaining, load factor, amortized resize, and the patterns built on hash maps and sets.

en/algorithms/06-lists-stacks-queues/01-.title: The linked list
en/algorithms/06-lists-stacks-queues/01-.summary: A linked list is a sequence of nodes. Each node holds a value and a pointer to the next node. Unlike an array (contiguous memory), a linked list uses scattered memory—the cost of indexing is O(n), but inserting at the head is O(1).

en/algorithms/06-lists-stacks-queues/02-.title: Pointer manipulation on linked lists
en/algorithms/06-lists-stacks-queues/02-.summary: Insert a node into a linked list, delete a node, and reverse the list using pointer updates. Learn the dummy-head (sentinel) pattern to eliminate edge cases and write cleaner code.

en/algorithms/06-lists-stacks-queues/03-.title: Fast and slow pointers
en/algorithms/06-lists-stacks-queues/03-.summary: Use two pointers advancing at different speeds to find the middle of a list, detect cycles (Floyd''''s tortoise-and-hare), and prove that the pointers must meet inside any cycle. A technique that solves hard linked-list problems with O(1) space.

en/algorithms/06-lists-stacks-queues/04-.title: The stack
en/algorithms/06-lists-stacks-queues/04-.summary: A stack is a LIFO container where you push elements on top and pop them from the top. Both operations run in O(1) constant time. Stacks model the undo/redo history, expression parsing, and any situation where the last thing added must be the first thing removed.

en/algorithms/06-lists-stacks-queues/05-.title: Queues and deques
en/algorithms/06-lists-stacks-queues/05-.summary: A queue: FIFO container where you enqueue at the rear, dequeue from the front. Both O(1) with proper implementation. A deque extends this to support O(1) at both ends, used in BFS and any situation requiring fairness.

en/algorithms/06-lists-stacks-queues/06-.title: The monotonic stack
en/algorithms/06-lists-stacks-queues/06-.summary: A stack kept in sorted order (increasing or decreasing) by removing elements that violate the invariant before pushing. The canonical application: find the next greater element to the right of each item in O(n) time, not O(n²).

en/algorithms/06-lists-stacks-queues/dri.title: Lists, stacks & queues: interview drill
en/algorithms/06-lists-stacks-queues/dri.summary: Timed linked-list and stack problems from the NeetCode-150, with progressive hints — solve each cold, then narrate the complexity.

en/algorithms/06-lists-stacks-queues/qui.summary: Multiple-choice synthesis across the unit: linked-list cost model, pointer manipulation, LIFO/FIFO discipline, deque implementation, and the monotonic-stack amortized argument.

en/algorithms/07-trees/01-the-binary-tre.title: The binary tree
en/algorithms/07-trees/01-the-binary-tre.summary: A tree is nodes in hierarchy: root at top, each pointing to children below. Binary tree restricts each node to at most 2 children (left, right). Trees fit recursion naturally - visit the node, then recursively process its left and right subtrees.

en/algorithms/07-trees/02-traversals.title: Tree traversals
en/algorithms/07-trees/02-traversals.summary: Three ways to visit nodes in a tree: pre-order (node, left, right), in-order (left, node, right), post-order (left, right, node). Each as a recursive function, each solving different problems based on whether you need ancestor context, sorted output, or child results.

en/algorithms/07-trees/03-level-order-tr.title: Level-order traversal (BFS)
en/algorithms/07-trees/03-level-order-tr.summary: Visit nodes level by level from top to bottom, left to right, using a queue. The breadth-first alternative to depth-first recursion. Why queues work for level-order, the basic loop, and the key variant: track queue size at level start to process nodes by depth.

en/algorithms/07-trees/04-recursion-on-t.title: Recursion on trees
en/algorithms/07-trees/04-recursion-on-t.summary: Solve tree problems by asking the same question of both subtrees, then combining their answers with the current node''''s value. The base case is an empty subtree. Two worked examples: computing height and counting nodes. The mental model: return rich information up; recurse down

en/algorithms/07-trees/05-binary-search-.title: Binary search trees
en/algorithms/07-trees/05-binary-search-.summary: A binary tree where every value in the left subtree is less than the node and the right is greater. This ordering invariant makes search and insertion O(h). In-order traversal yields sorted order. Height ranges from O(log n) for balanced to O(n) for degenerate trees.

en/algorithms/07-trees/06-tree-dp.title: Tree dynamic programming
en/algorithms/07-trees/06-tree-dp.summary: Return one piece of information up (height), track another in a side variable (diameter). Each node solves a subproblem and contributes to a global answer. Core idea: a single DFS pass, two pieces of information.

en/algorithms/07-trees/drill.title: Trees: interview drill
en/algorithms/07-trees/drill.summary: Timed tree and trie problems from the NeetCode-150, with progressive hints — solve each cold, then narrate the complexity.

en/algorithms/07-trees/quiz-choice.title: Trees: multiple-choice review
en/algorithms/07-trees/quiz-choice.summary: Multiple-choice synthesis across the trees unit — node structure, traversal choice, the BST invariant, balance and height, BFS vs DFS, and the tree-DP pattern.

en/algorithms/07-trees/quiz-short.title: Trees: free-recall review
en/algorithms/07-trees/quiz-short.summary: Free-recall prompts across the trees unit — recursive structure, the three DFS orders, the BST invariant and balance, BFS, and the tree-DP pattern. Answer first, then reveal.

en/algorithms/08-heaps/01-the-heap.title: The heap
en/algorithms/08-heaps/01-the-heap.summary: A complete binary tree where every parent is ≤ (or ≥) its children—enabling O(1) root access. Stored as a flat array with no pointers: for node at index i, parent is at ⌊(i−1)∕2⌋, left child at 2i+1, right child at 2i+2. Structure, not operations.

en/algorithms/08-heaps/02-heap-operation.title: Heap operations
en/algorithms/08-heaps/02-heap-operation.summary: Push, pop, and build-heap: how to mutate a heap while keeping the heap property. Sift-up and sift-down restore order. Build-heap turns any array into a heap in O(n) time—not O(n log n).

en/algorithms/08-heaps/03-priority-queue.title: Priority queues
en/algorithms/08-heaps/03-priority-queue.summary: Priority queue ADT: always extract the highest-priority element. Binary heap implementation: insert and extractMin O(log n), peek O(1). Uses: scheduling, Dijkstra, event merging. Key insight: ADT is the contract; heap is one way to keep it.

en/algorithms/08-heaps/04-top-k.title: Top-K and the k-th largest element
en/algorithms/08-heaps/04-top-k.summary: Find the k largest (or k smallest) elements efficiently using a size-k heap. Key insight: to find k largest, keep a min-heap of size k—push each element, evict the min when heap exceeds k. Result: O(n log k) time, O(k) space. Beats sorting O(n log n) when k is small.

en/algorithms/08-heaps/05-k-way-merge.title: K-way merge and merging sorted lists
en/algorithms/08-heaps/05-k-way-merge.summary: Merge k sorted lists using a min-heap. Store each list''''s head in a min-heap, pop the smallest, append to output, push the next element. Time O(n log k), space O(k). Beats naive O(nk) approach.

en/algorithms/08-heaps/drill.title: Heaps & priority queues: interview drill
en/algorithms/08-heaps/drill.summary: Timed heap and priority-queue problems from the NeetCode-150, with progressive hints — solve each cold, then narrate the complexity.

en/algorithms/08-heaps/quiz-choice.title: Heaps: multiple-choice review
en/algorithms/08-heaps/quiz-choice.summary: Multiple-choice synthesis across the heaps unit: the heap invariant, O(n) build-heap, the PQ contract, and choosing the right heap for top-k and k-way merge.

en/algorithms/08-heaps/quiz-code.summary: Read real heap code and predict behaviour: a sift-up bug, the build-heap loop bound, the top-k size-k heap, and the heapify complexity argument.

en/algorithms/09-graphs/01-graph-represe.title: Graph representations
en/algorithms/09-graphs/01-graph-represe.summary: A graph is vertices (nodes) + edges. Undirected vs directed. Weighted vs unweighted. Two main representations: adjacency list (O(V+E) space, iterate neighbors in O(degree)) and adjacency matrix (O(V²) space, check ''''edge u-v exists?'''' in O(1)). Tradeoff table.

en/algorithms/09-graphs/02-depth-first-s.title: Depth-first search (DFS)
en/algorithms/09-graphs/02-depth-first-s.summary: A graph traversal algorithm that explores as far as possible along each branch before backtracking. The crucial difference from trees: the visited set prevents infinite loops on cyclic graphs. Recursive and iterative approaches. O(V+E) time, O(V) space.

en/algorithms/09-graphs/03-breadth-first.title: Breadth-first search (BFS)
en/algorithms/09-graphs/03-breadth-first.summary: Explores a graph level by level using a queue (not a stack). Visited set prevents cycles. Mark on enqueue. Time O(V+E), space O(V). BFS finds shortest paths (fewest edges) in unweighted graphs.

en/algorithms/09-graphs/04-connected-com.title: Connected components: count islands and flood fill
en/algorithms/09-graphs/04-connected-com.summary: A connected component is a maximal set of mutually reachable vertices in an undirected graph. Loop over every vertex, launch BFS/DFS from each unvisited one, increment a counter. The grid ''''number of islands'''' is the same flood-fill idea. O(V+E); grid O(rows*cols).

en/algorithms/09-graphs/05-topological-s.title: Topological sort: ordering a DAG with Kahn and DFS
en/algorithms/09-graphs/05-topological-s.summary: A topological order lists every vertex of a DAG before all vertices it points to. It exists only for an acyclic graph. Kahn''''s algorithm peels off in-degree-0 vertices with a queue; the DFS variant reverses post-order. Both run in O(V+E) time, O(V) space, and detect cycles.

en/algorithms/09-graphs/06-shortest-path.title: Unweighted shortest path with BFS
en/algorithms/09-graphs/06-shortest-path.summary: BFS finds the shortest path (fewest edges) from a source to every reachable vertex in an unweighted graph: it visits vertices in non-decreasing distance order. Track dist[] and parent[] to rebuild a concrete path. O(V+E) time, O(V) space. Weighted graphs need Dijkstra.

en/algorithms/09-graphs/07-dijkstra.title: Dijkstra''''s algorithm: weighted shortest paths
en/algorithms/09-graphs/07-dijkstra.summary: Dijkstra finds shortest paths from a source on graphs with non-negative edge weights. A min-heap keyed by tentative distance pops the closest unsettled vertex, settles it, then relaxes its edges. Lazy deletion replaces decrease-key. O((V+E) log V). Negatives need Bellman-Ford.

en/algorithms/09-graphs/08-union-find.title: Union-Find (Disjoint Set Union): path compression and union by rank
en/algorithms/09-graphs/08-union-find.summary: DSU keeps a partition via a parent[] forest. find(x) returns a set''''s root; union(a,b) merges roots. Union by rank keeps trees shallow; path compression flattens them. Together: amortized O(alpha(n)), near-constant. Powers dynamic connectivity, cycle detection, Kruskal''''s MST

en/algorithms/10-dynamic-programming/01-.title: What is dynamic programming?
en/algorithms/10-dynamic-programming/01-.summary: DP solves a problem by combining answers to overlapping subproblems, storing each answer once. Two required properties: overlapping subproblems and optimal substructure. It turns exponential recursion (like naive Fibonacci) into linear.

en/algorithms/10-dynamic-programming/02-.title: Memoization: top-down DP, cache the recursion
en/algorithms/10-dynamic-programming/02-.summary: Memoization is DP top-down: take the natural recursion and add a cache keyed by the subproblem arguments. Check the cache before computing, store after. It computes each distinct state once, turning exponential fib into O(n) time and O(n) space (states times work per state).

en/algorithms/10-dynamic-programming/03-.title: Tabulation: bottom-up DP, the table
en/algorithms/10-dynamic-programming/03-.summary: Tabulation is DP bottom-up: build a dp array, fill base cases, then loop from small states up to the goal so every cell reads cells already filled. No recursion, no stack. Same O(n) time as memoization, and a rolling window can drop fib to O(1) space.

en/algorithms/10-dynamic-programming/04-.title: One-dimensional DP: house robber, climbing stairs, decode ways
en/algorithms/10-dynamic-programming/04-.summary: The 1D DP pattern: state is a single position i and dp[i] depends on a few earlier cells. House Robber is max(dp[i-1], dp[i-2]+nums[i]); Climbing Stairs is Fibonacci dp[i]=dp[i-1]+dp[i-2]; Decode Ways counts decodings with zero edge cases. O(n) time, O(1) space with rolling.

en/algorithms/10-dynamic-programming/05-.title: Two-dimensional DP: grid paths, LCS, edit distance
en/algorithms/10-dynamic-programming/05-.summary: When a subproblem needs two indices, the state is dp[i][j] and the cache is a 2D table. Fill row by row from a base row and column; read the answer at the bottom-right. Three classics: grid paths, LCS, edit distance. Time O(m*n), space O(m*n) shrinkable to O(min(m,n)).

en/algorithms/10-dynamic-programming/06-.title: 0/1 knapsack and subset sum: maximize value within a weight capacity
en/algorithms/10-dynamic-programming/06-.summary: 0/1 knapsack: items with weight+value, cap W, maximize value take each item 0 or 1 times. State dp[i][w] = max(skip, take if it fits). Subset sum is the boolean special case. The 1D rolling form runs capacity downward to avoid reusing an item. Time O(n*W), pseudo-polynomial.

en/algorithms/10-dynamic-programming/07-.title: Longest increasing subsequence: O(n^2) DP and the O(n log n) tails trick
en/algorithms/10-dynamic-programming/07-.summary: LIS is the longest strictly-increasing subsequence (not contiguous). The O(n^2) DP: dp[i] = 1 + max(dp[j]) over j<i with nums[j]<nums[i]. The O(n log n) trick keeps a tails array and binary-searches each value; the tails LENGTH is the answer, not its contents.

en/algorithms/10-dynamic-programming/08-.title: Interval DP: matrix chain and the last-action split
en/algorithms/10-dynamic-programming/08-.summary: Interval DP solves dp[i][j] over a subinterval [i..j] by picking a split k inside it and combining sub-intervals. Iterate by increasing length so smaller intervals are ready. Matrix chain: dp[i][j]=min over k of dp[i][k]+dp[k+1][j]+p[i-1]*p[k]*p[j]. Time O(n^3), space O(n^2).

en/algorithms/11-greedy/01-what-is-greed.title: What is a greedy algorithm? Local choice vs DP
en/algorithms/11-greedy/01-what-is-greed.summary: A greedy algorithm takes the locally-best choice and never reconsiders. Fast (usually O(n log n), dominated by a sort) but only correct with the greedy-choice property plus optimal substructure. Coin change {1,3,4} for 6 shows it losing: 4+1+1 = 3 coins vs optimal 3+3 = 2.

en/algorithms/11-greedy/02-the-exchange-.title: The Exchange Argument: proving a greedy choice is safe
en/algorithms/11-greedy/02-the-exchange-.summary: A greedy algorithm is only correct if its choice is safe. The exchange argument proves it: take any optimal solution, swap it one step toward the greedy choice without making it worse, and conclude a greedy-aligned optimum exists. When no such swap works, greedy is unsafe.

en/algorithms/11-greedy/03-interval-sche.title: Interval scheduling: activity selection and merging intervals
en/algorithms/11-greedy/03-interval-sche.summary: Two interval greedies. To pick the most non-overlapping intervals, sort by earliest finish time and take each that starts after the last taken finishes. To merge overlaps, sort by start and sweep. Both are O(n log n), dominated by the sort; shortest-duration is a wrong greedy.

en/algorithms/11-greedy/04-classic-greed.title: Classic greedy: jump game and gas station
en/algorithms/11-greedy/04-classic-greed.summary: Two famous greedy problems, both O(n). Jump Game tracks the FARTHEST reachable index in one sweep: you reach the end unless an index passes the frontier. Gas Station is circular: a trip exists iff total gas >= total cost, found by resetting the start when the tank goes negative.

en/algorithms/11-greedy/drill.summary: Timed greedy and interval problems from the NeetCode-150, with progressive hints — solve each cold, then narrate why the greedy choice is optimal.

en/algorithms/12-toolbox/01-bit-manipula.title: Bit manipulation: masks, shifts, and the n & (n-1) trick
en/algorithms/12-toolbox/01-bit-manipula.summary: Six bitwise operators plus a one-bit mask give O(1) idioms to test, set, clear, and toggle bits. Power-of-two is n & (n-1) == 0; popcount is Brian Kernighan's n &= n-1 loop, O(set bits). In JS, bitwise ops are 32-bit signed, so use >>> for unsigned.

en/apis/00-start-here/01-overview.title: Start from zero: what an API actually is
en/apis/00-start-here/01-overview.summary: An API is a contract two programs use to talk. This is the from-zero map and the eight words the rest of the track assumes you already know before the senior units begin.

en/apis/01-rest-modeling/01-overview.title: Modeling REST resources: nouns the client needs, not your verbs or tables
en/apis/01-rest-modeling/01-overview.summary: A REST API is a model of resources a client cares about. The two failures that hurt in prod: turning actions into verb endpoints, and mirroring your DB tables so every schema change breaks every client.

en/apis/02-status-codes-real/01-overview.summary: A status code is a contract three machines read before any human does: caches, dashboards, and retry logic. Getting the class wrong — or hiding errors in a 200 body — corrupts all three at once.

en/apis/03-pagination/01-overview.title: Pagination at scale: why OFFSET dies and keyset cursors survive
en/apis/03-pagination/01-overview.summary: OFFSET makes the database scan and throw away every row before your page, so deep pages slow linearly and drift when rows shift. Keyset cursors seek straight to the next page on an indexed key and stay flat.

en/apis/03-pagination/project.title: Pagination: migrate an offset feed to keyset
en/apis/03-pagination/project.summary: Hands-on project — build an offset list endpoint, reproduce its deep-page slowness and write-drift, then migrate it to a keyset cursor API and prove the fix with before/after numbers.

en/apis/03-pagination/quiz-choice.title: Pagination: multiple-choice review
en/apis/03-pagination/quiz-choice.summary: Multiple-choice synthesis across the pagination unit: offset-vs-keyset cost, page drift under writes, stable ordering, opaque cursors, and the hidden count tax.

en/apis/03-pagination/quiz-code.title: Pagination: SQL and code reading
en/apis/03-pagination/quiz-code.summary: Read real SQL, an EXPLAIN line, and a cursor handler, then predict the pagination behaviour and pick the highest-leverage fix.

en/apis/03-pagination/quiz-short.summary: Free-recall prompts across the pagination unit. Answer each in your own words first, then reveal the model answer and compare.

en/apis/04-openapi/01-overview.title: OpenAPI: making the contract the source of truth, not the docs
en/apis/04-openapi/01-overview.summary: OpenAPI only pays off when the spec is enforced — generating clients, validating requests, and failing CI on breaking diffs. A spec nobody checks is just docs that lie.

en/apis/04-openapi/project.title: OpenAPI: make the contract load-bearing
en/apis/04-openapi/project.summary: Hands-on project — make an OpenAPI spec the enforced source of truth for a small API: generate a client, validate at the edge, and gate breaking changes in CI.

en/apis/04-openapi/quiz-choice.summary: Multiple-choice synthesis across the OpenAPI unit — spec-first vs code-first, contract drift, breaking-change gates, codegen, validation, and the 3.1 schema shift.

en/apis/04-openapi/quiz-code.summary: Read real OpenAPI YAML fragments, a oasdiff verdict, and a generated client, then pick the highest-leverage fix to keep the contract honest.

en/apis/04-openapi/quiz-short.summary: Free-recall prompts across the OpenAPI unit. Answer each in your own words first, then reveal the model answer and compare.

en/apis/05-grpc-protobuf/01-overview.title: gRPC and Protobuf: the binary contract and what it costs you
en/apis/05-grpc-protobuf/01-overview.summary: gRPC trades JSON''''s human-readable payloads for a schema-bound binary wire format that is 4-10x faster and far smaller — but the field numbers become a contract you can never break, and the browser can''''t speak it without a proxy.

en/apis/05-grpc-protobuf/project.title: gRPC and Protobuf: build a contract that survives evolution
en/apis/05-grpc-protobuf/project.summary: Hands-on project — design a gRPC service, evolve its schema across two incompatible versions without breaking live peers, add a streaming RPC, and prove deadline propagation under failure.

en/apis/05-grpc-protobuf/quiz-choice.title: gRPC and Protobuf: multiple-choice review
en/apis/05-grpc-protobuf/quiz-choice.summary: Multiple-choice synthesis across the gRPC/Protobuf unit — field-number compatibility, schema evolution, streaming shapes, deadlines, and the gRPC-vs-REST edge decision.

en/apis/05-grpc-protobuf/quiz-short.summary: Free-recall prompts across the gRPC/Protobuf unit — wire format, field-number discipline, compatibility, streaming, deadlines, and the edge decision. Answer first, then reveal.

en/apis/06-graphql-n-plus-one/01-why-gra.title: Why GraphQL gets N+1
en/apis/06-graphql-n-plus-one/01-why-gra.summary: GraphQL''''s independent-resolver model hands the client flexibility and hands the server an accidental query storm — one HTTP request turns into hundreds of DB calls.

en/apis/06-graphql-n-plus-one/02-dataloa.title: DataLoader mechanics: tick-boundary batching
en/apis/06-graphql-n-plus-one/02-dataloa.summary: DataLoader waits for the current event-loop tick to finish, then fires one batched query for every key queued across all resolvers — turning N per-item SQL calls into one.

en/apis/06-graphql-n-plus-one/03-batch-f.title: Batch function contracts: ordering, shapes, errors
en/apis/06-graphql-n-plus-one/03-batch-f.summary: The batchLoadFn must return values in the same order as the input keys, handle missing rows and per-key errors explicitly, and support one-to-one, one-to-many, and count shapes.

en/apis/06-graphql-n-plus-one/04-federat.title: Federation and lookahead: batching beyond DataLoader
en/apis/06-graphql-n-plus-one/04-federat.summary: Apollo Federation gives you cross-subgraph batching for free via _entities; you still owe the intra-subgraph DataLoader. Lookahead joins collapse multi-level nesting at the cost of resolver isolation.

en/apis/06-graphql-n-plus-one/05-query-c.title: Query complexity defences: depth, cost, persisted queries
en/apis/06-graphql-n-plus-one/05-query-c.summary: DataLoader fixes database trips. Depth limits, complexity scoring, persisted queries, and alias caps stop attackers from sending query shapes that kill the server before any resolver fires.

en/apis/06-graphql-n-plus-one/06-graphql.title: Senior GraphQL API: scheduling contract, tenant isolation, observability
en/apis/06-graphql-n-plus-one/06-graphql.summary: DataLoader''''s exact scheduling semantics, tenant-safe per-request scoping, APQ vs trusted documents, multiplicative complexity scoring, alias-bomb anatomy, and the minimum-viable observability dashboard.

en/apis/06-graphql-n-plus-one/project.title: GraphQL N+1: batch and harden an API
en/apis/06-graphql-n-plus-one/project.summary: Hands-on project — build a GraphQL API that exhibits N+1, prove it with resolver/SQL counts, batch it with DataLoader, harden it against query-shape attacks, and verify with before/after numbers.

en/apis/06-graphql-n-plus-one/quiz-choic.summary: Multiple-choice synthesis across the GraphQL N+1 unit — resolver isolation, DataLoader scope, batch contracts, federation, and query-shape defences.

en/apis/06-graphql-n-plus-one/quiz-short.summary: Free-recall prompts across the GraphQL N+1 unit. Answer each in your own words first, then reveal the model answer and compare.

en/apis/07-rate-limiting/01-overview.title: Rate limiting: algorithms, the boundary burst, and the Redis counter
en/apis/07-rate-limiting/01-overview.summary: Fixed window is cheap but leaks a 2x burst at the boundary; token bucket smooths it. The real production lesson is that a per-node in-memory limiter multiplies your limit by N behind a load balancer — the counter has to live in Redis.

en/apis/07-rate-limiting/project.title: Rate limiting: build a distributed limiter that actually holds
en/apis/07-rate-limiting/project.summary: Hands-on project — build a distributed, atomic token-bucket limiter in Redis, prove it holds the real limit across multiple nodes, and ship a correct 429 contract.

en/apis/07-rate-limiting/quiz-choice.title: Rate limiting: multiple-choice review
en/apis/07-rate-limiting/quiz-choice.summary: Multiple-choice synthesis across the rate-limiting unit — algorithm tradeoffs, the boundary burst, distributed counters, atomicity, and the 429 contract.

en/apis/07-rate-limiting/quiz-code.title: Rate limiting: code and snippet reading
en/apis/07-rate-limiting/quiz-code.summary: Read real limiter snippets — a token-bucket refill, a Redis INCR race, a sliding-window counter, a sorted-set log — and pick the behaviour or the highest-leverage fix.

en/apis/07-rate-limiting/quiz-short.title: Rate limiting: free-recall review
en/apis/07-rate-limiting/quiz-short.summary: Free-recall prompts across the rate-limiting unit. Answer each from memory first, then reveal the model answer and compare.

en/apis/08-putting-it-together/01-overvi.title: Designing and reviewing a public API end to end
en/apis/08-putting-it-together/01-overvi.summary: Every API decision is connected: bad resource modeling forces status-code abuse, which makes clients retry wrong, which a missing contract hides, which breaks silently, which a missing rate limit turns into an outage. This is the senior''''s end-to-end review.

en/apis/08-putting-it-together/project.title: APIs: design and build a production API
en/apis/08-putting-it-together/project.summary: Capstone project — design and build a small production-grade public API end to end: noun-modeled resources, an honest status-code retry contract, cursor pagination, a spec-first OpenAPI contract with a CI break diff, and rate limiting.
