en/apis/08-putting-it-together/quiz-choi.summary: Multiple-choice synthesis across the APIs track — resource modeling, the status-code retry contract, cursor pagination, OpenAPI break diffs, gRPC-vs-REST, and rate-limit headers as one connected design.

en/apis/08-putting-it-together/quiz-code.title: APIs: contract and response reading
en/apis/08-putting-it-together/quiz-code.summary: Read real API contracts, responses, a pagination query, and rate-limit headers, then pick the senior call — the highest-leverage fix or the correct interpretation.

en/apis/08-putting-it-together/quiz-shor.title: APIs: free-recall review
en/apis/08-putting-it-together/quiz-shor.summary: Free-recall prompts spanning the APIs track. Answer each in your own words first, then reveal the model answer and compare against the senior end-to-end review.

en/architecture-patterns/00-start-here/0.title: What architecture actually is
en/architecture-patterns/00-start-here/0.summary: Architecture is the set of decisions that are expensive to change — not diagrams, not patterns. Design and architecture occupy different cost horizons. 'Best practice' is a category error: context determines fit, not a pattern name.

en/architecture-patterns/00-start-here/0.title: Fitness and tradeoffs
en/architecture-patterns/00-start-here/0.summary: No best architecture — only fit or unfit structures. The -ilities (maintainability, deployability, testability) compete: optimizing one costs another. Introduces the B2B order/billing platform used throughout the track.

en/architecture-patterns/01-coupling-and.title: Coupling forms
en/architecture-patterns/01-coupling-and.summary: Afferent and efferent coupling measure dependency flow in and out of a module. The classic coupling ladder runs content→common→control→stamp→data. Looser coupling is not always better — the right level depends on the forces.

en/architecture-patterns/01-coupling-and.title: Cohesion
en/architecture-patterns/01-coupling-and.summary: Cohesion measures module focus: do its parts change for the same reason? Functional cohesion is the goal; coincidental is an accident. LCOM signals disconnected clusters. Cohesion is the counterweight that stops over-decoupling from fragmenting a module.

en/architecture-patterns/01-coupling-and.title: Connascence
en/architecture-patterns/01-coupling-and.summary: Connascence unifies coupling and cohesion into one vocabulary. Static connascence is compile-time dependency; dynamic is runtime. Strength, locality, and degree tell you how costly the dependency is and which refactors reduce it most.

en/architecture-patterns/02-dependency-d.title: The dependency rule
en/architecture-patterns/02-dependency-d.summary: Source-code dependencies must point toward stable abstractions. When concrete modules depend on other concrete modules, changes cascade upward. The dependency rule breaks that rigidity by separating flow-of-control from flow-of-source-dependency.

en/architecture-patterns/02-dependency-d.title: Dependency inversion
en/architecture-patterns/02-dependency-d.summary: DIP: high-level modules should not depend on low-level modules — both depend on abstractions. The key insight: the consumer, not the provider, owns the interface. This is the mechanism behind hexagonal and clean architecture boundaries.

en/architecture-patterns/02-dependency-d.title: Acyclic and stable abstractions
en/architecture-patterns/02-dependency-d.summary: ADP, SDP, and SAP extend the dependency rule to the full component graph. ADP: no cycles. SDP: depend toward stability. SAP: stable components must be abstract. Together they define the main sequence and the zones of pain and uselessness.

en/architecture-patterns/03-layered-arch.title: N-tier layered architecture
en/architecture-patterns/03-layered-arch.summary: Layered architecture divides code into horizontal tiers — presentation, application, domain, infrastructure — each depending only on the layer below. It buys replaceability and testability but creates a sinkhole when layers merely pass data through without adding value.

en/architecture-patterns/03-layered-arch.title: Anemic vs rich domain model
en/architecture-patterns/03-layered-arch.summary: An anemic domain model puts all behavior in services and leaves domain objects as pure data bags. It is a recognized anti-pattern for complex domains because it destroys encapsulation and lets invariants drift. For simple CRUD it is often the pragmatic choice.

en/architecture-patterns/03-layered-arch.title: Where layering leaks
en/architecture-patterns/03-layered-arch.summary: Layered architecture leaks through three failure modes: the transaction-script trap (procedures, not layers), layer-skipping (presentation reaches into infrastructure), and the fat service god object. Each leak is a force that motivated hexagonal and clean architecture.

en/architecture-patterns/04-hexagonal/01.title: Ports and adapters
en/architecture-patterns/04-hexagonal/01.summary: In hexagonal architecture, a port is a domain-owned interface — the application defines it, not the infrastructure. An adapter is any component that implements or calls a port. This symmetry makes HTTP, CLI, and the database all 'just adapters' plugged into the domain's boundary.

en/architecture-patterns/04-hexagonal/02.title: Driving and driven sides
en/architecture-patterns/04-hexagonal/02.summary: The hexagon has two sides: driving (left) where actors initiate — HTTP, CLI, tests — and driven (right) where the application reaches out — database, payment, email. Both sides communicate through ports owned by the domain. The domain sits at the center, isolated from both.

en/architecture-patterns/04-hexagonal/03.title: Testing at the boundary
en/architecture-patterns/04-hexagonal/03.summary: Hexagonal architecture makes the domain trivially testable: drive through the primary port, substitute in-memory fakes at secondary ports, and the entire domain runs without a database or HTTP server. This structural property defines the test pyramid hexagonal teams actually use.

en/architecture-patterns/05-clean-and-on.title: The concentric dependency rule
en/architecture-patterns/05-clean-and-on.summary: Clean and Onion architecture arrange layers as concentric circles. The one absolute rule: source-code dependencies point inward only, toward higher-level policy. This generalizes hexagonal's two-sided inversion to any number of rings.

en/architecture-patterns/05-clean-and-on.title: Use cases and interactors
en/architecture-patterns/05-clean-and-on.summary: The Use Cases ring orchestrates entities to achieve one application goal. An interactor is the class that implements a use case: it receives a request model, calls entities, and returns a response model — never a framework type.

en/architecture-patterns/05-clean-and-on.title: The entity core and the cost
en/architecture-patterns/05-clean-and-on.summary: The Entities ring is the most stable code in the system — pure business rules with no dependencies. Clean Architecture's real cost is the mapping and indirection tax it charges on every ring boundary. That cost only pays off in specific circumstances.

en/architecture-patterns/06-domain-drive.title: Bounded contexts
en/architecture-patterns/06-domain-drive.summary: A bounded context is the explicit boundary within which a domain model is consistent. The same word — Order, Customer, Product — means a different model in each context. Bounded contexts are the primary unit of decomposition in DDD.

en/architecture-patterns/06-domain-drive.title: Ubiquitous language
en/architecture-patterns/06-domain-drive.summary: The ubiquitous language is the shared vocabulary of developers and domain experts within one bounded context. The model IS the language: naming drift signals a wrong boundary or a missing concept.

en/architecture-patterns/06-domain-drive.title: Aggregates and invariants
en/architecture-patterns/06-domain-drive.summary: An aggregate is a transactional consistency boundary. The aggregate root is the only external entry point. One transaction modifies one aggregate. Size aggregates by the invariant they enforce, not by the data graph — small is the right default.

en/architecture-patterns/06-domain-drive.title: Context mapping
en/architecture-patterns/06-domain-drive.summary: A context map documents how bounded contexts integrate. The patterns — Shared Kernel, Customer/Supplier, Conformist, ACL, Open Host Service — describe team relationships and translation strategies, not just API shapes.

en/architecture-patterns/07-cqrs/01-comm.title: Command-query split
en/architecture-patterns/07-cqrs/01-comm.summary: One model optimized for writes and another for reads — CQS principle scaled to architecture. Commands express intent and may be rejected; queries have no side effects. The split begins with two object models, not two databases.

en/architecture-patterns/07-cqrs/02-read.title: Read models and projections
en/architecture-patterns/07-cqrs/02-read.summary: Denormalized read models are built by projecting write-side state changes. The projection creates a sync problem: the read model can be stale. Bounding staleness is a design choice — synchronous projection is consistent but slower; asynchronous is fast but eventually consistent.

en/architecture-patterns/07-cqrs/03-when.title: When CQRS is overkill
en/architecture-patterns/07-cqrs/03-when.summary: CQRS buys structural separation at real cost: two models, eventual consistency, projection infra. It pays off only where read/write asymmetry is genuine. Most CRUD does not qualify. CQRS and event sourcing are independent — conflating them doubles the cost.

en/architecture-patterns/08-event-sourci.title: Events as the source of truth
en/architecture-patterns/08-event-sourci.summary: Event sourcing stores state as an append-only log of immutable facts. Current state is not stored directly — it is derived by folding (reducing) the event log. Events record what happened and why, not just the resulting after-image.

en/architecture-patterns/08-event-sourci.title: Projections, replay, and snapshots
en/architecture-patterns/08-event-sourci.summary: Read models in event sourcing are built by replaying the event log through a projection. Replay enables rebuild-on-demand and temporal queries. Snapshots bound replay cost. Event versioning and upcasting keep old events readable as the schema evolves.

en/architecture-patterns/08-event-sourci.title: The traps
en/architecture-patterns/08-event-sourci.summary: Event sourcing's immutability and eventual consistency are features on paper and constraints in production — schema evolution, GDPR erasure, bad events, and projection lag all require deliberate structural answers. Knowing when not to event-source is as important as knowing how.

en/architecture-patterns/09-event-driven.title: Choreography vs orchestration
en/architecture-patterns/09-event-driven.summary: Choreography lets services react to events with no central coordinator — the flow is implicit. Orchestration uses a central process-manager that explicitly directs each step. The real tradeoff is coupling vs visibility.

en/architecture-patterns/09-event-driven.title: Sagas
en/architecture-patterns/09-event-driven.summary: A saga coordinates a business process across services using local transactions and compensating actions — not a distributed 2PC lock. Compensation is not rollback: it appends a corrective action. Sagas accept visible intermediate states.

en/architecture-patterns/09-event-driven.title: Eventual consistency as a design choice
en/architecture-patterns/09-event-driven.summary: Designing for eventual consistency means solving the dual-write problem with the transactional outbox, making consumers idempotent, and accepting that read-your-writes requires explicit design. Consistency is a structural decision, not an afterthought.

en/architecture-patterns/10-decompositio.title: The Modular Monolith
en/architecture-patterns/10-decompositio.summary: A modular monolith enforces hard seams between features inside a single deployable. Package-by-feature, not by layer. Clean modules are the prerequisite for any future extraction — you earn the right to split.

en/architecture-patterns/10-decompositio.title: Monolith to Services
en/architecture-patterns/10-decompositio.summary: Decompose along bounded-context seams using the strangler fig: incrementally route features to new services while shrinking the monolith. Each service owns its data — no shared database.

en/architecture-patterns/10-decompositio.title: The Distributed Monolith
en/architecture-patterns/10-decompositio.summary: Services that deploy in lockstep, call each other synchronously across N hops, and share a database are a distributed monolith: every operational cost of distribution with none of the autonomy. The dual-write problem and temporal coupling are its defining symptoms.

en/architecture-patterns/11-evolution-an.title: Architecture Decision Records
en/architecture-patterns/11-evolution-an.summary: An ADR captures one architectural decision — context, forces, the choice, and consequences — so future engineers know WHY, not just what was decided. Lightweight, version-controlled, and superseded rather than deleted.

en/architecture-patterns/11-evolution-an.title: Fitness Functions and Evolutionary Architecture
en/architecture-patterns/11-evolution-an.summary: A fitness function is an automated test that an architectural property still holds. Fitness functions let architecture evolve incrementally under protection — the wrong-way detector that fails the build before a violation reaches production.

en/architecture-patterns/11-evolution-an.title: Tradeoff Analysis
en/architecture-patterns/11-evolution-an.summary: ATAM-lite: sensitivity points, tradeoff points, and risks — the vocabulary for reasoning about competing -ilities under real constraints. The closing synthesis: every pattern in this track is an answer to a tradeoff, and there is no best architecture, only fit-for-forces.

en/aws/00-start-here/01-what-aws-is.title: What AWS actually is
en/aws/00-start-here/01-what-aws-is.summary: AWS is a global utility-computing platform — on-demand compute, storage, networking, and managed services billed per use. This lesson maps the service categories and core vocabulary the rest of the track assumes.

en/aws/01-core-model/01-regions-and-az.title: Regions and availability zones
en/aws/01-core-model/01-regions-and-az.summary: AWS infrastructure is a hierarchy of failure-and-latency domains — Regions are isolated geographic areas, Availability Zones are independent datacenters inside one. Architect across ≥2 AZs or a single-AZ outage takes you down.

en/aws/01-core-model/02-iam-and-shared-r.title: IAM and the shared-responsibility model
en/aws/01-core-model/02-iam-and-shared-r.summary: AWS secures the cloud; you secure what's in it — and the dividing line moves by service. IAM is how you draw your half: identities, JSON policies, and an evaluation rule where explicit deny always wins over allow over implicit deny.

en/aws/01-core-model/03-billing-and-cost.title: Billing and cost basics
en/aws/01-core-model/03-billing-and-cost.summary: AWS bills pay-per-use across compute, storage, and data transfer — and egress is the silent killer. Match the workload to On-Demand, Reserved/Savings Plans, or Spot, and read the bill as an architecture signal.

en/aws/02-compute-and-deploy/01-compute-.title: Compute options: EC2, ECS/Fargate, Lambda, App Runner
en/aws/02-compute-and-deploy/01-compute-.summary: AWS compute is a spectrum from most-control/most-ops to least — EC2, ECS-on-EC2, Fargate, Lambda, App Runner. Pick by workload shape, not by hype, and price in the traps each tier hides.

en/aws/02-compute-and-deploy/02-deploy-a.title: Deploy a container end to end
en/aws/02-compute-and-deploy/02-deploy-a.summary: Build the image, push it to ECR, then run it — either an ECS/Fargate service behind an ALB or a managed App Runner service. The senior details are the two roles, the health check, and the arm64/amd64 trap.

en/aws/02-compute-and-deploy/03-lambda-e.title: Lambda in depth: cold starts, concurrency, and event sources
en/aws/02-compute-and-deploy/03-lambda-e.summary: A Lambda invocation has an INIT phase (cold start) then INVOKE, and reused environments mean clients belong at module scope. Account concurrency caps at a default 1000; reserved concurrency guarantees and limits, and a runaway function throttles everyone. Source sets retries.

en/aws/02-compute-and-deploy/04-autoscal.title: Autoscaling and load balancing: ALB, NLB, and target tracking
en/aws/02-compute-and-deploy/04-autoscal.summary: ALB routes layer 7; NLB is layer 4 for raw TCP and static IP. Health checks pick who gets traffic; deregistration delay drains in-flight on scale-in. Autoscaling is reactive — headroom, request-count signals, and warm capacity beat the scale-out lag that returns 5xx in a spike.

en/aws/02-compute-and-deploy/05-ecs-inte.title: ECS internals: task lifecycle, awsvpc networking, capacity providers
en/aws/02-compute-and-deploy/05-ecs-inte.summary: A task definition is the immutable blueprint, a task is a running instance, a service reconciles N of them. Tasks march through a lifecycle; awsvpc gives each its own ENI (a finite resource); capacity providers pick Fargate vs EC2; and stoppedReason tells you why a task died.

en/aws/03-storage/01-s3-object-storage.title: S3 object storage: classes, lifecycle, presigned URLs, durability
en/aws/03-storage/01-s3-object-storage.summary: S3 is a flat object store: buckets, keys, storage classes with retrieval/min-duration tradeoffs, lifecycle policies, presigned URLs, 11-nines durability (not availability), and strong consistency. Pick the class by access pattern, not by hope.

en/aws/03-storage/02-block-and-file.title: Block and file storage: EBS, EFS, and instance store
en/aws/03-storage/02-block-and-file.summary: EBS, EFS, and instance store are three attachment models, not three speeds. EBS is single-AZ block for one instance; EFS is multi-AZ NFS many instances share; instance store is ephemeral local NVMe you can lose. Pick by attachment and durability, not raw IOPS.

en/aws/03-storage/03-databases.title: Managed databases: RDS, Aurora, and DynamoDB
en/aws/03-storage/03-databases.summary: Managed relational (RDS/Aurora) versus managed NoSQL (DynamoDB). RDS hands off patching, backups, and failover but keeps you owning schema and a vertical ceiling; DynamoDB trades joins for single-digit-ms at any scale — if you design keys to dodge hot partitions.

en/aws/04-networking/01-vpc-and-subnets.title: VPC and subnets: CIDR, routing, and the NAT egress trap
en/aws/04-networking/01-vpc-and-subnets.summary: A VPC is an isolated virtual network you define by CIDR; subnets carve it per-AZ, and "public" vs "private" is decided by routing, not a flag. Master IGW, NAT, and gateway endpoints — or eat a five-figure egress bill.

en/aws/04-networking/02-security-groups-.title: Security groups and network ACLs: two filters, two state models
en/aws/04-networking/02-security-groups-.summary: AWS gives you two packet filters: security groups (instance-level, stateful, allow-only, SG-referencing) and network ACLs (subnet-level, stateless, ordered, deny-capable). Stateful vs stateless is the distinction that bites — open ephemeral return ports or watch responses vanish.

en/aws/04-networking/03-dns-and-cdn.title: DNS and CDN: Route 53, CloudFront, and ACM at the edge
en/aws/04-networking/03-dns-and-cdn.summary: Route 53 + CloudFront + ACM are the edge of the request path. ALIAS at the apex, the right routing policy and TTL, an OAC-locked origin, and a us-east-1 cert turn four moving parts into one fast, fail-over-ready front door.

en/aws/05-observability/01-cloudwatch.title: CloudWatch: metrics, logs, alarms, and the bill
en/aws/05-observability/01-cloudwatch.summary: CloudWatch is the default AWS telemetry plane: metrics, logs, alarms. The two traps are never-expire log retention (a silent bill) and alarming on average instead of p99. Spend ingest deliberately.

en/aws/05-observability/02-tracing-and-e.title: Distributed tracing and event-driven plumbing: X-Ray and EventBridge
en/aws/05-observability/02-tracing-and-e.summary: Metrics and logs tell you a box is sick; distributed tracing tells you which hop is slow, and EventBridge decouples the hops. Sample traces and bound log cardinality or observability bills you twice.

en/aws/05-observability/03-slos-and-aler.title: SLOs, error budgets, and alerts that don't cry wolf
en/aws/05-observability/03-slos-and-aler.summary: An SLI is a good/valid ratio, an SLO its target, the error budget 1−SLO — 99.9% is ~43 min/month. Page on symptoms users feel (burn rate, p99) not causes (CPU); composite alarms and treat-missing-as-breaching kill the noise that trains on-call to ignore the pager.

en/aws/05-observability/04-logs-at-scale.title: Logs at scale: Logs Insights, subscription pipelines, and the bill
en/aws/05-observability/04-logs-at-scale.summary: Operating logs at scale: Logs Insights queries are billed per GB scanned, so narrow the window; structured JSON makes logs queryable; subscription filters ship events to Lambda/Firehose/OpenSearch; and ingest — not storage — is the bill a DEBUG flag can 10-100x overnight.

en/aws/05-observability/05-opentelemetry.title: OpenTelemetry on AWS: unified signals and the cardinality trap
en/aws/05-observability/05-opentelemetry.summary: OpenTelemetry instruments traces, metrics, and logs once and exports anywhere; ADOT is the AWS Collector. The senior trap is cardinality — a user_id in a metric label is one time series per user, which melts the backend and the bill.

en/aws/06-iac/01-cloudformation-and-cdk.title: Infrastructure as code on AWS: CloudFormation and CDK
en/aws/06-iac/01-cloudformation-and-cdk.summary: CloudFormation is AWS-native declarative IaC: a template defines resources, a stack is a deployed instance, and change sets preview adds/modifies/replacements. CDK writes infra in a real language and synthesizes to CloudFormation — same stacks, change sets, drift underneath.

en/aws/06-iac/02-terraform-on-aws.title: Terraform on AWS: providers, state, and the remote backend
en/aws/06-iac/02-terraform-on-aws.summary: Terraform is cloud-agnostic IaC over HCL: the AWS provider maps resources to AWS APIs, but unlike CloudFormation you own a state file. Master remote backends, locking, and reading a plan, or state corruption and silent replaces will own you.

en/aws/06-iac/03-terraform-state-operati.title: Terraform state operations: import, move, and the destroy-by-rename trap
en/aws/06-iac/03-terraform-state-operati.summary: State maps config to real resource IDs and is authoritative: a refactor that renames a resource without a moved block tells Terraform to destroy prod and recreate it empty. Master import, state mv, state rm, and state splitting, and treat state as a secret.

en/aws/06-iac/04-modules-and-multi-accou.title: Modules and multi-account: composition, environments, blast radius
en/aws/06-iac/04-modules-and-multi-accou.summary: IaC at scale is composition plus isolation: versioned modules give a contracted building block, but over-abstraction makes a god-module where one change ripples everywhere. Promote the same code with per-env inputs; account-per-env under Organizations is the real blast boundary.

en/aws/06-iac/05-iac-pipelines-and-polic.title: IaC pipelines: plan-on-PR, policy-as-code, and drift
en/aws/06-iac/05-iac-pipelines-and-polic.summary: Running IaC safely is a pipeline, not a command: plan on PR (the diff is the review), env-gated apply, keyless OIDC auth, policy-as-code to block bad infra pre-apply, plus scheduled drift detection and state locking.

en/aws/07-cost-and-security/01-cost-opti.title: Cost optimization: purchase options, egress, idle waste, and visibility
en/aws/07-cost-and-security/01-cost-opti.summary: Cost is an architecture property. The biggest levers, in order: commit baseline compute to Savings Plans/Spot, kill idle waste, and stop paying for egress and NAT you did not need. Cost Explorer, Budgets, and activated tags give you the visibility to do it.

en/aws/07-cost-and-security/02-iam-deep-.title: IAM evaluation deep dive, KMS envelope encryption, and Secrets Manager
en/aws/07-cost-and-security/02-iam-deep-.summary: IAM resolves in a fixed order: default deny, an explicit allow grants, an explicit deny wins; boundaries and SCPs cap the ceiling, conditions scope each statement. Prefer roles+STS over long-lived keys, stop the confused deputy with ExternalId, encrypt with KMS envelope keys.

en/aws/07-cost-and-security/03-data-prot.title: Data protection: S3 public-access, encryption, and the breach class
en/aws/07-cost-and-security/03-data-prot.summary: The canonical cloud breach is a misconfigured public S3 bucket, not broken crypto. Block Public Access is the account-wide override; bucket policies beat ACLs; SSE-KMS adds an audit trail and revocation; deny non-TLS and unencrypted uploads; keep presigned URLs short and scoped.

en/aws/07-cost-and-security/04-threat-de.title: Threat detection and audit: CloudTrail, GuardDuty, Config, Security Hub
en/aws/07-cost-and-security/04-threat-de.summary: Lesson 02 prevented; this detects and responds. CloudTrail is the audit spine, GuardDuty flags active threats, Config catches misconfig drift, Security Hub aggregates — then EventBridge routes to automated response. No CloudTrail, no forensics after a breach.

en/aws/07-cost-and-security/05-cost-gove.title: Cost governance: budgets, anomaly alerts, and the surprise bill
en/aws/07-cost-and-security/05-cost-gove.summary: The AWS bill arrives a month after the spend, so a runaway resource burns silently for weeks. Governance beats optimization: Budgets and Anomaly Detection turn the delay into a same-day signal, allocation tags assign an owner, SCP guardrails stop spend before it starts.

en/aws/08-putting-it-together/01-capston.title: Capstone: a secure, resilient three-tier architecture end to end
en/aws/08-putting-it-together/01-capston.summary: The capstone: wire storage, networking, compute, data, security, observability, IaC, and cost into one secure, resilient three-tier web app — Route 53 to CloudFront to ALB to Fargate to RDS Multi-AZ and S3 — and trace the request path plus every trust boundary it crosses.

en/backend/00-start-here/01-overview.title: Start from zero: what a backend actually is
en/backend/00-start-here/01-overview.summary: A backend is the program that answers requests on a server — the half of the web you never see. This is the from-zero map and the eight words Unit 01 and every unit after it assumes you already know.

en/backend/01-request-lifecycle/01-overv.title: The journey of a request: seven stops from socket to response
en/backend/01-request-lifecycle/01-overv.summary: Every HTTP request makes the same trip — accept, parse, route, middleware, handle, serialize, drain. Knowing the map tells you where latency, failure, and security each hide.

en/backend/01-request-lifecycle/02-accep.title: Accept and parse: from kernel queue to a typed request
en/backend/01-request-lifecycle/02-accep.summary: Before your code runs, the kernel completes the handshake into a bounded accept queue, and the server turns raw bytes into a request line, headers, and body — each step with a hard limit you can overflow.

en/backend/01-request-lifecycle/03-routi.title: Routing and middleware: choosing what runs, and in what order
en/backend/01-request-lifecycle/03-routi.summary: Routing maps one request to one handler; the middleware chain decides what runs around it. Order is not cosmetic — it determines whether auth, body limits, and compression actually protect you.

en/backend/01-request-lifecycle/04-handl.title: Handler and response: from business logic to bytes on the wire
en/backend/01-request-lifecycle/04-handl.summary: The handler runs your logic, then the result is serialized, framed with a status and headers, and written to the socket. Serialization cost and keep-alive reuse decide how much that final stretch costs.

en/backend/01-request-lifecycle/05-strea.title: Streaming and backpressure: when the client reads slower than you write
en/backend/01-request-lifecycle/05-strea.summary: A response is not done when the handler returns — it is done when the bytes drain. If the client reads slower than the server writes and backpressure is ignored, the response buffers in RAM until the process dies.

en/backend/01-request-lifecycle/06-timeo.title: Timeouts and tail latency: budgets, deadlines, and the fan-out trap
en/backend/01-request-lifecycle/06-timeo.summary: Every hop needs a timeout, and timeouts must compose into a request-wide budget. At scale the tail dominates: fan out to enough services and the slowest one decides almost every user''''s latency.

en/backend/01-request-lifecycle/project.title: Request lifecycle: instrument and harden a service
en/backend/01-request-lifecycle/project.summary: Hands-on project — build a small HTTP service, instrument all seven stops, then deliberately trigger and fix one failure at each stop, proving every fix with before/after numbers.

en/backend/01-request-lifecycle/quiz-cho.title: Request lifecycle: multiple-choice review
en/backend/01-request-lifecycle/quiz-cho.summary: Multiple-choice synthesis across the request lifecycle — accept queues, middleware order as a security boundary, serialization cost, backpressure, and tail amplification under fan-out.

en/backend/01-request-lifecycle/quiz-cod.title: Request lifecycle: code reading
en/backend/01-request-lifecycle/quiz-cod.summary: Read real handler, middleware, streaming, and deadline-propagation snippets, predict the lifecycle failure, and pick the highest-leverage fix a senior would make first.

en/backend/01-request-lifecycle/quiz-sho.title: Request lifecycle: free-recall review
en/backend/01-request-lifecycle/quiz-sho.summary: Free-recall prompts across the request lifecycle. Answer each in your own words first, then reveal the model answer and compare against the unit's mechanisms.

en/backend/02-middleware-di/01-overview.title: Middleware and DI: the two patterns that shape every backend
en/backend/02-middleware-di/01-overview.summary: Two patterns sit underneath every framework: middleware intercepts each request in order, and dependency injection wires services once at startup. One controls what runs around your code; the other controls what your code can reach and how you test it.

en/backend/02-middleware-di/02-writing-m.title: Writing middleware: signatures, next(), and the three framework models
en/backend/02-middleware-di/02-writing-m.summary: A middleware is a function with a contract: read the request, optionally act, then call next() or terminate. The contract differs across Express, Koa, and Fastify — and the most common production bugs come from breaking it in the same three ways.

en/backend/02-middleware-di/03-inversion.title: Inversion of control: how dependencies reach a class
en/backend/02-middleware-di/03-inversion.summary: A class that constructs its own collaborators is welded to them. Inversion of control hands a class what it needs from the outside — and the choice between constructor injection, a service locator, and in-class `new` decides how testable and honest your code is.

en/backend/02-middleware-di/04-di-scopes.title: DI scopes and lifecycles: singleton, request, transient
en/backend/02-middleware-di/04-di-scopes.summary: A wired object has a lifetime: created once, once per request, or once per injection. Choosing wrong is two opposite bugs — a singleton holding per-request state leaks data between users, while request scope quietly recreates half your graph on every call.

en/backend/02-middleware-di/05-testing-a.title: DI as a testing seam: fakes, mocks, and the boundary that matters
en/backend/02-middleware-di/05-testing-a.summary: The whole point of injecting dependencies is the seam it creates: a place to substitute a test double. But there are two doubles with opposite purposes, and the most common testing failure is mocking everything until the test asserts the implementation instead of the behavior.

en/backend/02-middleware-di/06-di-in-pro.title: DI containers in production: resolution graphs, circular deps, and when not to
en/backend/02-middleware-di/06-di-in-pro.summary: A container is a graph resolver: it topologically sorts dependencies and instantiates them once. The sharp edges — circular deps it cannot order, eager startup that surfaces config bugs at boot, and a real cost meaning not every app needs one.

en/backend/02-middleware-di/project.title: Middleware and DI: wire a testable service
en/backend/02-middleware-di/project.summary: Hands-on project — build a small service with a correct middleware pipeline and an injected, composition-rooted object graph, then prove the seam, scopes, and ordering with tests and a load run.

en/backend/02-middleware-di/quiz-choice.title: Middleware and DI: multiple-choice review
en/backend/02-middleware-di/quiz-choice.summary: Multiple-choice synthesis across the middleware and DI unit — the two axes, the middleware contract, injection scopes, the testing seam, and container resolution.

en/backend/02-middleware-di/quiz-code.title: Middleware and DI: code and config reading
en/backend/02-middleware-di/quiz-code.summary: Read real Express and NestJS snippets — a middleware ordering bug, a singleton holding request state, a request-scope bubbling cost, and a dependency cycle — and pick the highest-leverage fix.

en/backend/02-middleware-di/quiz-short.title: Middleware and DI: free-recall review
en/backend/02-middleware-di/quiz-short.summary: Free-recall prompts across the middleware and DI unit. Answer each from memory first, then reveal the model answer and compare.

en/backend/03-async-blocking/01-overview.title: Blocking vs non-blocking I/O: two ways to wait
en/backend/03-async-blocking/01-overview.summary: A server spends most of its life waiting on I/O. Blocking I/O parks a whole thread on each wait, so concurrency costs memory; non-blocking I/O hands the wait to the kernel and lets one thread juggle thousands of sockets through an event loop.

en/backend/03-async-blocking/02-the-even.title: The event loop: one thread, ordered phases
en/backend/03-async-blocking/02-the-even.summary: The event loop is one thread running queued callbacks in fixed phases — timers, poll, check, close — and draining a higher-priority microtask queue between each. That order explains setTimeout vs setImmediate vs Promise, and why the concurrency is cooperative.

en/backend/03-async-blocking/03-what-blo.title: What blocks the loop: CPU work and sync calls
en/backend/03-async-blocking/03-what-blo.summary: Cooperative concurrency has one fatal failure mode: any synchronous work on the loop thread freezes every connection at once. Sync file reads, JSON.parse on big payloads, sync crypto, and catastrophic regexes are the usual culprits; event-loop lag reveals it first.

en/backend/03-async-blocking/04-offloadi.title: Offloading CPU work: worker threads and the libuv pool
en/backend/03-async-blocking/04-offloadi.summary: Two thread pools hide behind the single loop, and confusing them wastes weeks. The libuv pool runs native I/O like fs and crypto, never your JavaScript; CPU-bound JS needs worker threads or chunking, each carrying its own cost — message-copy overhead, partitioning complexity.

en/backend/03-async-blocking/05-backpres.title: Backpressure and bounded concurrency
en/backend/03-async-blocking/05-backpres.summary: Async makes it easy to start more work than the system can finish, and the loop will not stop you. Backpressure lets a fast producer feel a slow consumer; bounded concurrency caps how many run at once. Without them, unbounded fan-out becomes OOM and overloaded downstreams.

en/backend/03-async-blocking/06-throughp.title: Throughput under load: tail latency and saturation
en/backend/03-async-blocking/06-throughp.summary: Under load the average lies. Queueing theory says latency stays flat until ~70–80% utilization, then explodes nonlinearly, and one slow span at the head delays everything behind it. One loop is one core, so watch the tail and event-loop utilization, not the mean.

en/backend/03-async-blocking/project.title: Async vs blocking: unfreeze the loop
en/backend/03-async-blocking/project.summary: Hands-on project — build a service that blocks its own event loop, instrument the lag, then offload CPU, bound the fan-out, and prove the tail recovered with before/after numbers.

en/backend/03-async-blocking/quiz-choice.title: Async vs blocking: multiple-choice review
en/backend/03-async-blocking/quiz-choice.summary: Multiple-choice synthesis across the async/blocking unit — I/O models, the event-loop schedule, what blocks it, offloading CPU work, bounded concurrency, and tail latency under load.

en/backend/03-async-blocking/quiz-code.title: Async vs blocking: code and trace reading
en/backend/03-async-blocking/quiz-code.summary: Read real Node handlers and a perf signal, predict how each interacts with the event loop, and pick the fix a senior engineer reaches for first.

en/backend/03-async-blocking/quiz-short.title: Async vs blocking: free-recall review
en/backend/03-async-blocking/quiz-short.summary: Free-recall prompts across the async/blocking unit. Answer each from memory first, then reveal the model answer and compare.

en/backend/04-pooling/01-overview.title: Why pool: the cost of creating a connection
en/backend/04-pooling/01-overview.summary: Opening a database connection is not cheap — TCP, TLS, and auth cost milliseconds and the server allocates a whole backend process. A pool creates a small set of connections once and lends them out, so requests pay setup cost almost never instead of every time.

en/backend/04-pooling/02-pool-sizing.title: Pool sizing: why bigger is not faster
en/backend/04-pooling/02-pool-sizing.summary: The instinct is to raise the pool size until the database stops being the bottleneck — but past a small number throughput drops, because a connection is a real backend process competing for cores, locks, and memory. The right size is a small formula, not a big guess.

en/backend/04-pooling/03-acquisition-and.title: Acquisition and timeouts: the wait queue is the real latency dial
en/backend/04-pooling/03-acquisition-and.summary: When every connection is busy, a request does not fail — it waits in a queue. The acquisition timeout decides how long it waits before giving up, and that one number is the difference between failing fast and a pile-up that takes the whole service down.

en/backend/04-pooling/04-health-and-life.title: Connection lifecycle: stale connections and how to age them out
en/backend/04-pooling/04-health-and-life.summary: A pooled connection is reused for hours, which is the whole point — but the database, firewalls, and load balancers all reserve the right to kill it underneath you. Without max-lifetime, idle eviction, and validation, the pool happily hands out dead connections.

en/backend/04-pooling/05-pool-exhaustion.title: Pool exhaustion: leaks, and why a bigger pool won''''t save you
en/backend/04-pooling/05-pool-exhaustion.summary: The most common pool outage is not under-sizing — it is a leak, where code borrows a connection and never returns it. Each leak permanently shrinks the pool until nothing is left, and the instinct to enlarge the pool only delays the same failure.

en/backend/04-pooling/06-pooling-distrib.title: Pooling at scale: many instances, one database, and PgBouncer
en/backend/04-pooling/06-pooling-distrib.summary: One pool against one database is solved. The hard version is N application instances each with their own pool, all colliding against a single max_connections — where the math overflows and a transaction-level multiplexer becomes mandatory, with sharp tradeoffs.

en/backend/04-pooling/project.title: Pooling: diagnose and tame an exhausted pool
en/backend/04-pooling/project.summary: Hands-on project — instrument a pool, drive it into starvation, exhaust it with a planted leak, then size it, bound the wait, plug the leak, and prove each fix with before/after pool metrics.

en/backend/04-pooling/quiz-choice.title: Pooling: multiple-choice review
en/backend/04-pooling/quiz-choice.summary: Multiple-choice synthesis across the pooling unit — sizing math, acquisition timeouts, stale connections, leaks vs exhaustion, and fan-in against max_connections.

en/backend/04-pooling/quiz-code.title: Pooling: code and config reading
en/backend/04-pooling/quiz-code.summary: Read real pool config, handler code, and a Postgres log line, predict the failure, and pick the highest-leverage fix — sizing math, a leak, an idle-in-transaction hold, and a timeout config.

en/backend/04-pooling/quiz-short.title: Pooling: free-recall review
en/backend/04-pooling/quiz-short.summary: Free-recall prompts across the pooling unit. Answer each in your own words first, then reveal the model answer and compare.

en/backend/05-idempotency-retries/01-why.title: Why idempotency: making retries safe
en/backend/05-idempotency-retries/01-why.summary: A network can swallow the server''''s response. Without an idempotency key the client has no way to retry safely — every duplicate POST may fire the side effect twice.

en/backend/05-idempotency-retries/02-ser.title: Server-side state machine: four states of an idempotency key
en/backend/05-idempotency-retries/02-ser.summary: When a request arrives with an Idempotency-Key the server moves through four states: new, in-flight, replay, and mismatch. The request fingerprint catches reused keys with changed intent.

en/backend/05-idempotency-retries/03-ret.title: Retry strategies: backoff, jitter, and thundering herd
en/backend/05-idempotency-retries/03-ret.summary: Exponential backoff without jitter creates synchronized retry storms. Full jitter spreads retries across time. Retry-After and retry budgets prevent recovering services from being re-killed.

en/backend/05-idempotency-retries/04-out.title: Outbox and inbox: effectively-once across the dual-write boundary
en/backend/05-idempotency-retries/04-out.summary: Direct dual-write to DB + Kafka breaks in either order. The outbox pattern writes the event inside the DB transaction; the inbox pattern deduplicates on the consumer side. Together they give effectively-once delivery.

en/backend/05-idempotency-retries/05-con.title: Concurrency and cache architecture for idempotency at scale
en/backend/05-idempotency-retries/05-con.summary: Naive SELECT-then-INSERT is not atomic. Postgres ON CONFLICT or advisory locks prevent race conditions. At high throughput, a Redis Cluster hot-path with Postgres cold-path fallback is the production pattern.

en/backend/05-idempotency-retries/06-ide.title: Observability, production failures, and global-scale design
en/backend/05-idempotency-retries/06-ide.summary: Minimum viable idempotency dashboard, production failure stories from Stripe/Knight Capital/AWS S3/GitHub, cross-protocol patterns, and a global-anycast design exercise.

en/backend/05-idempotency-retries/projec.title: Idempotency and retries: build an effectively-once payment path
en/backend/05-idempotency-retries/projec.summary: Hands-on project — build an effectively-once payment path: idempotent POST, jittered retrying client, outbox + inbox to a consumer, then prove no duplicate side effect under crash and concurrency injection.

en/backend/05-idempotency-retries/quiz-c.title: Idempotency and retries: multiple-choice review
en/backend/05-idempotency-retries/quiz-c.summary: Multiple-choice synthesis across the idempotency + retries unit — keys, the four-state machine, jittered backoff, outbox/inbox, concurrency races, and production failure modes.

en/backend/05-idempotency-retries/quiz-c.title: Idempotency and retries: code and query reading
en/backend/05-idempotency-retries/quiz-c.summary: Read real idempotency, retry, and inbox snippets, predict their behaviour under concurrency or failure, and pick the highest-leverage fix.

en/backend/05-idempotency-retries/quiz-s.title: Idempotency and retries: free-recall review
en/backend/05-idempotency-retries/quiz-s.summary: Free-recall prompts across the idempotency + retries unit. Answer each from memory first, then reveal the model answer and compare.

en/backend/06-circuit-breakers/01-overvi.title: Why a circuit breaker: a slow dependency takes down the caller
en/backend/06-circuit-breakers/01-overvi.summary: A dependency rarely fails cleanly — it gets slow, and a slow dependency is more dangerous than a dead one because every caller waits, occupying a thread until the whole service starves. A circuit breaker fast-fails calls to a sick dependency so the caller stops waiting.

en/backend/06-circuit-breakers/02-the-st.title: The state machine: closed, open, half-open
en/backend/06-circuit-breakers/02-the-st.summary: A circuit breaker is a three-state machine: closed passes calls and counts failures, open rejects every call instantly for a cooldown, half-open lets a few trial calls test recovery. The cooldown timer is the recovery dial; half-open stops a recovering service being flooded.

en/backend/06-circuit-breakers/03-thresh.title: What trips it: failure rate, windows, and a volume floor
en/backend/06-circuit-breakers/03-thresh.summary: A breaker should not trip on a single failure or stay closed through a meltdown. What trips it is a failure rate over a sliding window, gated by a minimum-volume floor so it ignores noise — and a slow call counted as a failure, because slow is the state that hurts.

en/backend/06-circuit-breakers/04-bulkhe.title: Bulkheads: isolating failure domains
en/backend/06-circuit-breakers/04-bulkhe.summary: A breaker reacts after failures accumulate, but a shared thread pool can be drained by one slow dependency before it trips. A bulkhead caps concurrency per dependency so one sick downstream can''''t take the whole budget — thread-pool vs semaphore isolation is a real tradeoff.

en/backend/06-circuit-breakers/05-fallba.title: Timeouts and fallbacks: what to return when it''''s open
en/backend/06-circuit-breakers/05-fallba.summary: A breaker only works if a timeout makes a hang look like a failure, and an open breaker only helps if the caller has an answer ready. The senior view: a timeout is the trigger, a fallback is the answer, graceful degradation should be rare, and load shedding is the last line.

en/backend/06-circuit-breakers/06-distri.title: At scale: per-instance state, retry storms, and coordinated shedding
en/backend/06-circuit-breakers/06-distri.summary: Everything so far assumed one process. Across many instances a breaker becomes a per-instance guess with no shared view, retries multiply into call amplification, half-open probes herd, and the only stable shedding is coordinated. Resilience as a fleet property.

en/backend/06-circuit-breakers/project.title: Circuit breakers: contain a cascading failure
en/backend/06-circuit-breakers/project.summary: Hands-on project — build a service that cascades when a dependency slows, then add a breaker, bulkhead, timeout, and fallback until one sick downstream no longer takes the whole service down, proving each step with numbers.

en/backend/06-circuit-breakers/quiz-choi.title: Circuit breakers: multiple-choice review
en/backend/06-circuit-breakers/quiz-choi.summary: Multiple-choice synthesis across the circuit-breaker unit — fast-fail, the three-state machine, trip thresholds, bulkheads, fallbacks, and fleet-scale failure modes.

en/backend/06-circuit-breakers/quiz-code.title: Circuit breakers: code and config reading
en/backend/06-circuit-breakers/quiz-code.summary: Read real breaker config and call-site code, predict the state transitions and trip behaviour, and pick the fix a senior engineer would make first.

en/backend/06-circuit-breakers/quiz-shor.title: Circuit breakers: free-recall review
en/backend/06-circuit-breakers/quiz-shor.summary: Free-recall prompts across the circuit-breaker unit. Answer each in your own words first, then reveal the model answer and compare.

en/backend/07-graceful-shutdown/01-overv.title: Why graceful shutdown: the abrupt kill drops in-flight work
en/backend/07-graceful-shutdown/01-overv.summary: A process rarely gets to finish on its own terms — an orchestrator sends a kill signal on every deploy. An abrupt exit drops in-flight requests and resets live connections; graceful shutdown stops accepting new work, drains what is running, then exits cleanly.

en/backend/07-graceful-shutdown/02-signa.title: Signals and the grace period: SIGTERM, SIGKILL, and PID 1
en/backend/07-graceful-shutdown/02-signa.summary: Shutdown is a contract with the orchestrator: a preStop hook, then SIGTERM to PID 1, then a grace period (Kubernetes default 30s), then an unstoppable SIGKILL. The grace period is a hard deadline, and the classic bug is a process that never receives the signal at all.

en/backend/07-graceful-shutdown/03-the-d.title: The deregistration race: stop routing before you stop accepting
en/backend/07-graceful-shutdown/03-the-d.summary: The subtle bug is a race: SIGTERM and endpoint removal fire in parallel, but propagation delay means the load balancer keeps routing to a pod that has already started shutting down. The fix is to fail readiness first and wait out the delay before closing the listener.

en/backend/07-graceful-shutdown/04-drain.title: Draining and shutdown order: reverse the dependency graph
en/backend/07-graceful-shutdown/04-drain.summary: Draining is more than server.close(): keep-alive sockets must be closed deliberately, and resources must close in reverse dependency order — HTTP server first, datastores last — or in-flight requests hit a closed pool. A guardian timeout force-exits if the drain hangs.

en/backend/07-graceful-shutdown/05-in-fl.title: In-flight work: long requests, background jobs, and the deadline
en/backend/07-graceful-shutdown/05-in-fl.summary: The grace period is a budget, and long requests or background jobs may not fit. The senior question is what to do with work that won''''t finish: reject it cleanly, or requeue it — and requeue is only safe when the consumer is idempotent, tying back to the idempotency unit.

en/backend/07-graceful-shutdown/06-zero-.title: Zero-downtime deploys: graceful shutdown as a fleet property
en/backend/07-graceful-shutdown/06-zero-.summary: Across a rolling deploy, graceful shutdown becomes a fleet property: deregister before terminate, bring new pods to ready before old ones drain, size the deregistration delay to real p99, and jitter connection close so a fleet of clients doesn''''t reconnect in one thundering spi

en/backend/07-graceful-shutdown/project.title: Graceful shutdown: zero request loss on deploy
en/backend/07-graceful-shutdown/project.summary: Hands-on project — build a service that drops requests on deploy, then make it shut down gracefully and prove zero request loss across a rolling deploy with before/after numbers.

en/backend/07-graceful-shutdown/quiz-cho.title: Graceful shutdown: multiple-choice review
en/backend/07-graceful-shutdown/quiz-cho.summary: Multiple-choice synthesis across the graceful-shutdown unit — signals, the deregistration race, drain ordering, requeue safety, the deadline budget, and fleet-level zero-downtime deploys.

en/backend/07-graceful-shutdown/quiz-cod.title: Graceful shutdown: code and config reading
en/backend/07-graceful-shutdown/quiz-cod.summary: Read real shutdown handlers, a Kubernetes pod spec, and a drain sequence, predict the failure, and pick the highest-leverage fix a senior engineer would make first.

en/backend/07-graceful-shutdown/quiz-sho.title: Graceful shutdown: free-recall review
en/backend/07-graceful-shutdown/quiz-sho.summary: Free-recall prompts across the graceful-shutdown unit. Answer each in your own words first, then reveal the model answer and compare.

en/backend/08-putting-it-together/01-ove.title: Putting it together: the backend is a system, not a stack
en/backend/08-putting-it-together/01-ove.summary: The track taught seven concerns one at a time; production runs them at once. This capstone reframes them as one system: each unit was a single failure mode in isolation, but a real service faces them composed, where the hard bugs live in the interactions, not any one mechanism.

en/backend/08-putting-it-together/02-tra.title: Tracing one request: every unit on a single code path
en/backend/08-putting-it-together/02-tra.summary: Follow one request and the seven units line up as layers: lifecycle accepts and parses, middleware and DI wire dependencies, async I/O and a pool carry the downstream call, a breaker guards it, an idempotency key makes the write retry-safe, and shutdown waits for it.

en/backend/08-putting-it-together/03-whe.title: When failures compose: the cascade no single unit could show you
en/backend/08-putting-it-together/03-whe.summary: The dangerous outages are compositions, not single faults: a slow dependency exhausts the pool, retries amplify load into a storm, the breaker trips, and a deploy''''s drain races the in-flight job that must be idempotent. Senior work is seeing cross-products before they cascade.

en/backend/08-putting-it-together/04-see.title: Seeing the system: RED metrics, the p99 tail, and breaker state
en/backend/08-putting-it-together/04-see.summary: A backend you can''''t observe is one you can''''t operate. This lesson ties the mechanisms to telemetry: rate, errors, and duration (RED), the p99 tail behind the mean, pool saturation and queue depth, breaker transitions, and the error budget that gates shipping against reliabi

en/backend/08-putting-it-together/05-the.title: The service under overload: load shedding and graceful degradation
en/backend/08-putting-it-together/05-the.summary: Every mechanism is also a load-control knob, and overload is where they combine: pool and concurrency caps bound work in flight, timeouts and breakers cut losses, and load shedding rejects excess early with backpressure — so the service degrades gracefully instead of collapsing.

en/backend/08-putting-it-together/06-pro.title: Production readiness: the launch checklist that is the whole track
en/backend/08-putting-it-together/06-pro.summary: The capstone turns the track into a readiness review: a checklist where each unit is a launch gate — signals and PID 1 correct, pools sized to the dependency, retries idempotent, breakers and timeouts tuned, shutdown clean, telemetry wired — the model for service launch.

en/backend/08-putting-it-together/projec.title: Putting it together: build a resilient backend service
en/backend/08-putting-it-together/projec.summary: Capstone build — a resilient backend service combining a bounded pool, idempotent retries, a circuit breaker, graceful shutdown, and edge load shedding, proven to degrade gracefully under a fault-injected load test.

en/backend/08-putting-it-together/quiz-c.title: Putting it together: multiple-choice review
en/backend/08-putting-it-together/quiz-c.summary: Cross-track synthesis MCQs for the backend capstone: composition over addition, the latency cascade, nested timeout budgets, goodput vs throughput, the p99 tail, and readiness as a checklist.

en/backend/08-putting-it-together/quiz-c.title: Putting it together: code and incident reading
en/backend/08-putting-it-together/quiz-c.summary: Read real backend snippets — a blocked event loop, an unbounded pool acquire, a non-atomic idempotency check, and a breaker with no timeout — and pick the fix a senior would make first.

en/backend/08-putting-it-together/quiz-s.title: Putting it together: free-recall review
en/backend/08-putting-it-together/quiz-s.summary: Free-recall prompts spanning the backend track — composition vs addition, the nested timeout budget, the metastable cascade, goodput vs throughput, RED and the p99 tail, and readiness as a checklist.

en/base-cs/01-what-a-computer-is/01-bits.title: Bits and binary
en/base-cs/01-what-a-computer-is/01-bits.summary: A bit is the smallest unit of data: a single two-state signal. Hardware uses exactly two states because two levels are the most reliable to distinguish despite electrical noise.

en/base-cs/01-what-a-computer-is/02-coun.title: Counting in binary
en/base-cs/01-what-a-computer-is/02-coun.summary: A row of bits encodes a number through place value: each position is worth twice the one to its right. Understanding this doubling principle lets you read and write binary numbers and convert between binary and decimal.

en/base-cs/01-what-a-computer-is/03-enco.title: Encoding the world
en/base-cs/01-what-a-computer-is/03-enco.summary: The same bit pattern can mean a number, a letter, a colour, or a sound. The meaning lives in the encoding — the agreed rule that assigns meaning to bits. Without knowing which encoding was used, a bit pattern is meaningless noise.

en/base-cs/01-what-a-computer-is/04-bool.title: Boolean logic
en/base-cs/01-what-a-computer-is/04-bool.summary: A bit can be read as a truth value: 1 is true, 0 is false. Three operations — AND, OR, NOT — define how to combine truth values. Together they are complete: any true/false rule, no matter how complex, can be built from these three operations alone.

en/base-cs/01-what-a-computer-is/05-logi.title: Logic gates
en/base-cs/01-what-a-computer-is/05-logi.summary: A logic gate is hardware that physically performs one boolean operation. AND, OR, and NOT gates turn abstract truth tables into real silicon. Gates compose into circuits, and circuits compose into arithmetic: a binary adder is just a network of gates.

en/base-cs/01-what-a-computer-is/project.title: What a computer is: build a bits-to-arithmetic toolkit
en/base-cs/01-what-a-computer-is/project.summary: Build a tiny 'bits to arithmetic' toolkit by hand and in code: convert numbers, decode an encoding, and simulate gates up to a half-adder.

en/base-cs/01-what-a-computer-is/quiz-ch.title: What a computer is: multiple-choice review
en/base-cs/01-what-a-computer-is/quiz-ch.summary: Multiple-choice synthesis across the unit: why two states win, place value, encodings, boolean completeness, and gates building arithmetic.

en/base-cs/01-what-a-computer-is/quiz-co.title: What a computer is: read patterns and circuits
en/base-cs/01-what-a-computer-is/quiz-co.summary: Read bit patterns, ASCII bytes, a boolean expression, and a half-adder trace, then predict the result the way the unit taught you to.

en/base-cs/01-what-a-computer-is/quiz-sh.title: What a computer is: free-recall review
en/base-cs/01-what-a-computer-is/quiz-sh.summary: Free-recall prompts across the unit — say the full answer from memory, then reveal the model answer and compare.

en/base-cs/02-memory/01-addressable-cell.title: Addressable cells
en/base-cs/02-memory/01-addressable-cell.summary: Memory is one long row of numbered storage cells. The address is the cell''''s number; the value is what sits in the cell. The CPU asks for a cell by giving its address.

en/base-cs/02-memory/02-the-byte.title: The byte
en/base-cs/02-memory/02-the-byte.summary: The byte (8 bits) is the standard addressable unit of memory. Memory is byte-addressed: each address names one byte, not one bit. Word sizes group multiple bytes for arithmetic.

en/base-cs/02-memory/03-value-vs-address.title: Value vs. address
en/base-cs/02-memory/03-value-vs-address.summary: An address says which cell; a value says what is stored there. A value can itself be an address — that is the idea behind a pointer or reference. ''''Read the value at address X'''' is the operation that connects the two.

en/base-cs/02-memory/04-stack-and-heap.title: Stack and heap
en/base-cs/02-memory/04-stack-and-heap.summary: The address space is divided into regions. The stack grows and shrinks as functions run (last-in-first-out). The heap holds long-lived data. Both are regions of the same physical memory.

en/base-cs/02-memory/project.title: Memory: build a tiny memory simulator
en/base-cs/02-memory/project.summary: Build a tiny byte-addressed memory simulator with read, write, and dereference, then use it to model a pointer chain and a stack-vs-heap scenario.

en/base-cs/02-memory/quiz-choice.title: Memory: multiple-choice review
en/base-cs/02-memory/quiz-choice.summary: Multiple-choice synthesis across the memory unit: addresses vs values, byte-addressing, pointers and dereferencing, and stack vs heap lifetimes.

en/base-cs/02-memory/quiz-code.title: Memory: diagram and trace reading
en/base-cs/02-memory/quiz-code.summary: Read memory diagrams and small snippets, do address arithmetic, trace a pointer dereference, and decide stack vs heap placement.

en/base-cs/02-memory/quiz-short.title: Memory: free-recall review
en/base-cs/02-memory/quiz-short.summary: Free-recall prompts across the memory unit. Answer each from memory first, then reveal the model answer and compare.

en/base-cs/03-the-processor/01-the-instr.title: The instruction
en/base-cs/03-the-processor/01-the-instr.summary: An instruction is the smallest command the CPU can carry out. Every instruction names an operation (what to do) and its operands (what to do it to). The full set of instructions a CPU understands is its instruction set.

en/base-cs/03-the-processor/02-fetch-dec.title: Fetch–Decode–Execute
en/base-cs/03-the-processor/02-fetch-dec.summary: The CPU runs one loop forever: fetch the next instruction from memory, decode what it means, execute it, then advance the program counter and repeat. Every program ever run on any CPU is this loop.

en/base-cs/03-the-processor/03-registers.title: Registers
en/base-cs/03-the-processor/03-registers.summary: Registers are a small set of named, ultra-fast storage slots physically inside the CPU. The CPU does its actual arithmetic and logic on values held in registers, not in main memory. The program counter is itself a register.

en/base-cs/03-the-processor/04-machine-c.title: Machine code
en/base-cs/03-the-processor/04-machine-c.summary: Instructions are bits stored in memory, indistinguishable from data. The program counter walks through them. A program is data the CPU happens to execute — this is the stored-program (von Neumann) idea.

en/base-cs/03-the-processor/05-a-toy-cpu.title: A toy CPU
en/base-cs/03-the-processor/05-a-toy-cpu.summary: Put it all together: a toy CPU with two registers and a four-instruction set. Walk a small program — load two numbers, add them, store the result — through the fetch–decode–execute loop step by step.

en/base-cs/03-the-processor/project.title: The processor: build a CPU simulator
en/base-cs/03-the-processor/project.summary: Build a working software simulator of the toy CPU — registers, program counter, memory, and a fetch-decode-execute loop — then run a real machine-code program through it.

en/base-cs/03-the-processor/quiz-choice.title: The processor: multiple-choice review
en/base-cs/03-the-processor/quiz-choice.summary: Multiple-choice synthesis across the processor unit: instructions, the fetch-decode-execute loop, the program counter, registers, machine code, and the stored-program idea.

en/base-cs/03-the-processor/quiz-code.title: The processor: trace and decode
en/base-cs/03-the-processor/quiz-code.summary: Trace small programs in the toy instruction set, predict register and program-counter state, decode a machine-code word, and count clock cycles.

en/base-cs/03-the-processor/quiz-short.title: The processor: free-recall review
en/base-cs/03-the-processor/quiz-short.summary: Free-recall prompts across the processor unit. Answer each from memory first, then reveal the model answer and compare.

en/base-cs/04-machine-code-to-language/0.title: The assembler idea
en/base-cs/04-machine-code-to-language/0.summary: Assembly language gives each machine instruction a short human-readable mnemonic. The assembler is a program that translates assembly text to the binary machine code the CPU runs — one mnemonic per instruction, essentially one-to-one.

en/base-cs/04-machine-code-to-language/0.title: Why high-level languages
en/base-cs/04-machine-code-to-language/0.summary: Assembly is readable but still CPU-specific and verbose. A high-level language lets one statement stand for many machine instructions, is portable across different CPUs, and is far more productive. Abstraction is the point.

en/base-cs/04-machine-code-to-language/0.title: Compilation vs interpretation
en/base-cs/04-machine-code-to-language/0.summary: Two strategies to run high-level code. A compiler translates the whole program to machine code ahead of time. An interpreter reads and carries out the program statement by statement at run time. Each strategy has tradeoffs in speed, startup, and portability. JIT combines both.

en/base-cs/04-machine-code-to-language/0.title: The runtime
en/base-cs/04-machine-code-to-language/0.summary: A program never runs alone. The runtime is the support code and machinery that runs alongside your program: memory management and garbage collection, the call-stack machinery, the standard library, and the interpreter or virtual machine itself. Your code sits on top of all of it.

en/base-cs/04-machine-code-to-language/0.title: From source to running program
en/base-cs/04-machine-code-to-language/0.summary: Tie everything together: trace the full pipeline end to end — source text you write → translation (assemble, compile, or interpret) → machine instructions → loaded into memory → the CPU''''s fetch-decode-execute loop runs them.

en/base-cs/04-machine-code-to-language/p.title: From machine code to a language: trace a program down the ladder
en/base-cs/04-machine-code-to-language/p.summary: Hands-on project — take one tiny program, run it through the assembly, compiled, interpreted, and JIT paths, and document the layers, the one-to-one vs many-to-one mapping, and the full source-to-execution pipeline with evidence.

en/base-cs/04-machine-code-to-language/q.title: From machine code to a language: multiple-choice review
en/base-cs/04-machine-code-to-language/q.summary: Multiple-choice synthesis across the unit: the assembler's one-to-one rule, why high-level languages exist, compile vs interpret vs JIT tradeoffs, the runtime, and the full source-to-execution pipeline.

en/base-cs/04-machine-code-to-language/q.title: From machine code to a language: code and mapping reading
en/base-cs/04-machine-code-to-language/q.summary: Read assembly and high-level snippets, trace a source-to-machine-code mapping, and tell compilation from interpretation from JIT by what each one produces and when.

en/base-cs/04-machine-code-to-language/q.title: From machine code to a language: free-recall review
en/base-cs/04-machine-code-to-language/q.summary: Free-recall prompts across the unit. Answer each in your own words first, then reveal the model answer and compare.

en/base-cs/05-values-and-types/01-what-a.title: What a value is
en/base-cs/05-values-and-types/01-what-a.summary: A value is a fixed pattern of bits sitting in memory cells. The bits themselves carry no inherent meaning; meaning only arises when something decides how to read them.

en/base-cs/05-values-and-types/02-types-.title: Types interpret bits
en/base-cs/05-values-and-types/02-types-.summary: A type is the rule that says how to read a bit pattern. The same bits can be a number, a character, or a colour depending on which type rule applies. Encoding the world built this; now we name the mechanism.

en/base-cs/05-values-and-types/03-primit.title: Primitive types
en/base-cs/05-values-and-types/03-primit.summary: JavaScript/TypeScript has five primitive value categories you meet in everyday code: number, string, boolean, null, and undefined. The typeof operator reports which interpretation rule the runtime is applying to a value.

en/base-cs/05-values-and-types/04-why-ty.title: Why types exist
en/base-cs/05-values-and-types/04-why-ty.summary: Types catch ''''read these bits the wrong way'''' mistakes. Static typing catches them at compile time; dynamic typing catches them at run time. Both serve the same fundamental purpose: preventing misinterpretation.

en/base-cs/05-values-and-types/project.title: Values and types: build a value inspector
en/base-cs/05-values-and-types/project.summary: Hands-on project — build a small value inspector that stores bytes once and decodes them under several type rules, then demonstrates JS number precision and coercion with evidence.

en/base-cs/05-values-and-types/quiz-choi.title: Values and types: multiple-choice review
en/base-cs/05-values-and-types/quiz-choi.summary: Multiple-choice synthesis across the unit: bits carry no meaning, a type is the reading rule, the same bits decode differently, and what type errors actually are.

en/base-cs/05-values-and-types/quiz-code.title: Values and types: code reading
en/base-cs/05-values-and-types/quiz-code.summary: Read four short JS snippets and predict what the runtime actually does: float rounding, the safe-integer limit, silent coercion, and the typeof null quirk.

en/base-cs/05-values-and-types/quiz-shor.title: Values and types: free-recall review
en/base-cs/05-values-and-types/quiz-shor.summary: Free-recall prompts across the unit. Answer each from memory first, then open the model answer and compare what you missed.

en/base-cs/06-variables-and-state/01-a-v.title: A variable is a named cell
en/base-cs/06-variables-and-state/01-a-v.summary: A variable is a human-readable name permanently bound to a memory cell. The name is a label; the cell holds the value. Declaring a variable reserves the cell and gives it a name — they are different things.

en/base-cs/06-variables-and-state/02-ass.title: Assignment
en/base-cs/06-variables-and-state/02-ass.summary: Assignment is a store operation: the runtime evaluates the right-hand side, then writes the result into the cell bound to the variable on the left. The previous value is gone. The name stays; only the cell''''s contents change.

en/base-cs/06-variables-and-state/03-mut.title: Mutation and state
en/base-cs/06-variables-and-state/03-mut.summary: State is the set of values currently held across all live variables. Mutation is changing a value in place over time. ''''State'''' is the word for it because the collection of cell contents defines what the program currently is — its condition at this instant.

en/base-cs/06-variables-and-state/04-ref.title: References vs values
en/base-cs/06-variables-and-state/04-ref.summary: Primitive values are copied when assigned; objects and arrays are shared by reference. Two variables can be bound to the same object — aliasing. Understanding what sits in the cell (a value or a pointer) clarifies why mutations through one name affect what another name sees.

en/base-cs/06-variables-and-state/projec.title: Variables and state: build a state container
en/base-cs/06-variables-and-state/projec.summary: Build a tiny state container and a snapshot-history tool, then deliberately trigger and fix an aliasing bug — proving every claim by tracing the cells.

en/base-cs/06-variables-and-state/quiz-c.title: Variables and state: multiple-choice review
en/base-cs/06-variables-and-state/quiz-c.summary: Multiple-choice synthesis across the variables unit — binding vs value, assignment as a store, mutation and state, copy vs reference semantics, and aliasing traps.

en/base-cs/06-variables-and-state/quiz-c.title: Variables and state: code reading
en/base-cs/06-variables-and-state/quiz-c.summary: Read short TypeScript snippets — aliasing, copy vs reference, scope shadowing, and a swap — and predict exactly what value each variable holds and why.

en/base-cs/06-variables-and-state/quiz-s.title: Variables and state: free-recall review
en/base-cs/06-variables-and-state/quiz-s.summary: Free-recall prompts across the variables unit — answer each from memory first, then reveal the model answer and compare.

en/base-cs/07-control-flow/01-what-flow-.title: What flow means
en/base-cs/07-control-flow/01-what-flow-.summary: Execution flow is the order in which a CPU runs instructions. By default it runs straight down: the program counter advances one instruction at a time. Every deviation — a branch, a loop — is the CPU changing where the program counter points next.

en/base-cs/07-control-flow/02-conditiona.title: Conditionals as branches
en/base-cs/07-control-flow/02-conditiona.summary: An if statement is a conditional jump at the machine level. A compare instruction sets a flag in the CPU; a conditional jump reads that flag and either falls through or jumps to an alternate address. if/else is two destinations for the program counter.

en/base-cs/07-control-flow/03-loops-as-r.title: Loops as repeated jumps
en/base-cs/07-control-flow/03-loops-as-r.summary: A loop is a backward jump: run the body, test a condition, and if the condition is still true jump back to the top. while and for compile to the same backward-jump pattern. A loop is infinite when the jump-back is unconditional or the test never becomes false.

en/base-cs/07-control-flow/04-tracing-a-.title: Tracing a program
en/base-cs/07-control-flow/04-tracing-a-.summary: Step through a TypeScript program that combines a conditional and a loop. Follow the program counter and variable state on each iteration to see exactly how if and while behave together at the instruction level.

en/base-cs/07-control-flow/project.title: Control flow: build a jump machine
en/base-cs/07-control-flow/project.summary: Build a tiny instruction interpreter that runs a program counter over a list of instructions with conditional and backward jumps, then prove your model by tracing real branches and loops through it.

en/base-cs/07-control-flow/quiz-choice.title: Control flow: multiple-choice review
en/base-cs/07-control-flow/quiz-choice.summary: Multiple-choice synthesis across the control-flow unit: the program counter, conditional jumps and flags, fall-through, backward jumps, and why loops repeat or run forever.

en/base-cs/07-control-flow/quiz-code.title: Control flow: trace the code
en/base-cs/07-control-flow/quiz-code.summary: Read four small programs and trace them by hand: predict loop counts and outputs, spot an off-by-one boundary, and reason about short-circuit evaluation as chained conditional jumps.

en/base-cs/07-control-flow/quiz-short.title: Control flow: free-recall review
en/base-cs/07-control-flow/quiz-short.summary: Free-recall prompts across the control-flow unit. Answer each from memory first, then reveal the model answer and compare.

en/base-cs/08-functions-and-the-call-sta.title: What a function is
en/base-cs/08-functions-and-the-call-sta.summary: A function is a named block of instructions the CPU can jump to and return from. Naming a block makes it reusable and gives its purpose a single word.

en/base-cs/08-functions-and-the-call-sta.title: The call stack
en/base-cs/08-functions-and-the-call-sta.summary: Each function call pushes a stack frame (return address + locals) onto the stack. Returning pops it. At any moment the stack holds exactly the frames of all active calls.

en/base-cs/08-functions-and-the-call-sta.title: Parameters and return values
en/base-cs/08-functions-and-the-call-sta.summary: Parameters are values copied into the new frame before the function body runs. The return value is handed back to the caller when RET fires. Both pass data through the stack frame boundary.

en/base-cs/08-functions-and-the-call-sta.title: Scope
en/base-cs/08-functions-and-the-call-sta.summary: Scope is which names are visible at a given point in the code. Locals live in their frame and vanish when it pops. The lifetime of a name is tied directly to the lifetime of its frame.

en/base-cs/08-functions-and-the-call-sta.title: Recursion preview
en/base-cs/08-functions-and-the-call-sta.summary: A recursive function calls itself. Each call is just another frame on the stack. The base case stops the descent. Without a base case, the stack overflows.

en/base-cs/09-data-in-memory/01-arrays-a.title: Arrays as contiguous cells
en/base-cs/09-data-in-memory/01-arrays-a.summary: An array is a run of equal-size cells placed back-to-back in memory. Because every element has the same type, every cell is the same size, and the whole array occupies one unbroken block of addresses.

en/base-cs/09-data-in-memory/02-indexing.title: Indexing and offsets
en/base-cs/09-data-in-memory/02-indexing.summary: Reaching arr[i] is fast because the address of element i is a single arithmetic step: base_address + i x element_size. arr[0] is the first element because its offset is zero. Any element is one multiply and one add away — constant time.

en/base-cs/09-data-in-memory/03-objects-.title: Objects as key-value
en/base-cs/09-data-in-memory/03-objects-.summary: An object is a set of named fields: each key names a slot that holds a value. Where an array reaches an element by a numeric position, an object reaches a value by its name.

en/base-cs/09-data-in-memory/04-collecti.title: Collections in memory
en/base-cs/09-data-in-memory/04-collecti.summary: An array of numbers is contiguous values. But an array or object of objects is really a run of cells holding references — addresses that point elsewhere. Nested data is a graph of cells linked by references.

en/base-cs/09-data-in-memory/project.title: Data in memory: build a memory-layout model
en/base-cs/09-data-in-memory/project.summary: Hands-on project — build a tiny memory model that lays out arrays and objects as cells, computes element addresses by hand, and shows where values end and references begin.

en/base-cs/09-data-in-memory/quiz-choice.summary: Multiple-choice synthesis across the data-in-memory unit: contiguous layout, index arithmetic, named-field objects, and how references let a fixed-shape container hold variable-shape data.
