en/base-cs/09-data-in-memory/quiz-short.summary: Free-recall prompts across the data-in-memory unit. Answer each in your own words first, then reveal the model answer and compare.

en/base-cs/10-abstraction/01-what-abstra.title: What abstraction is
en/base-cs/10-abstraction/01-what-abstra.summary: Abstraction is hiding detail behind a name so you can use a thing without knowing how it works. A function call and a variable name are abstractions you have already met: the interface is what you use, the implementation is the hidden how.

en/base-cs/10-abstraction/02-bundling-da.title: Bundling data and behaviour
en/base-cs/10-abstraction/02-bundling-da.summary: An object can hold operations alongside its data. A function stored as a field of an object is a method; it works on that object''''s own fields. The bundle exposes operations and hides the field layout behind them.

en/base-cs/10-abstraction/03-modules.title: Modules
en/base-cs/10-abstraction/03-modules.summary: A module groups related code behind a boundary. It exposes a public interface — the names it marks as exports — and keeps everything else private. The boundary stops one part of a program from reaching into another.

en/base-cs/10-abstraction/04-why-abstrac.title: Why abstraction exists
en/base-cs/10-abstraction/04-why-abstrac.summary: Abstraction manages complexity by stacking layers: each layer lets you reason without holding the one below in your head. The whole track is such a stack. The tradeoff: abstractions leak — the layer below shows through when it fails or runs slow.

en/base-cs/10-abstraction/project.title: Abstraction: build a leak-proof-then-leaky module
en/base-cs/10-abstraction/project.summary: Build a small stack data structure as an encapsulated module with a fixed public interface, swap its hidden implementation without touching callers, then deliberately make it leak and document the leak.

en/base-cs/10-abstraction/quiz-choice.title: Abstraction: multiple-choice review
en/base-cs/10-abstraction/quiz-choice.summary: Multiple-choice synthesis across the abstraction unit — interface vs implementation, encapsulation, module boundaries, namespacing, and why every non-trivial abstraction leaks.

en/base-cs/10-abstraction/quiz-short.title: Abstraction: free-recall review
en/base-cs/10-abstraction/quiz-short.summary: Free-recall prompts across the abstraction unit. Answer each in your own words first, then reveal the model answer and compare.

en/base-cs/11-when-a-program-fails/01-er.title: Errors vs exceptions
en/base-cs/11-when-a-program-fails/01-er.summary: An error is a condition the program cannot handle in normal flow. An exception is the mechanism: when an error is raised, normal control flow stops and the runtime unwinds the call stack searching for a handler.

en/base-cs/11-when-a-program-fails/02-th.title: The stack trace
en/base-cs/11-when-a-program-fails/02-th.summary: A stack trace is the snapshot of the call stack at the moment an exception is raised — the list of frames from where it threw down to the program entry. Read top-down, it shows what threw and through what chain of calls.

en/base-cs/11-when-a-program-fails/03-un.title: Undefined behaviour
en/base-cs/11-when-a-program-fails/03-un.summary: A defined error is detected and reported — the machine raises an exception. Undefined behaviour gives no guaranteed result: reading past an array end, integer overflow, relying on undefined. No error is raised; the program continues with garbage.

en/base-cs/11-when-a-program-fails/04-de.title: Debugging as reasoning
en/base-cs/11-when-a-program-fails/04-de.summary: Debugging is not guessing. The machine is deterministic — fetch-decode-execute always does the same thing for the same state. Debugging is forming a hypothesis about which step diverged from expected, then testing it: narrow the range, read the trace, check state.

en/base-cs/11-when-a-program-fails/proje.title: When a program fails: hunt two bugs by reasoning
en/base-cs/11-when-a-program-fails/proje.summary: Hands-on project: build a small buggy program, drive it into one loud crash and one silent wrong answer, then locate each cause by reasoning and prove the fix.

en/base-cs/11-when-a-program-fails/quiz-.summary: Multiple-choice synthesis across the failure unit: error vs exception, stack unwinding, reading a trace, undefined behaviour, and debugging as reasoning.

en/base-cs/11-when-a-program-fails/quiz-.title: When a program fails: code and trace reading

en/base-cs/11-when-a-program-fails/quiz-.title: When a program fails: free-recall review
en/base-cs/11-when-a-program-fails/quiz-.summary: Free-recall prompts across the failure unit. Answer each in your own words first, then reveal the model answer and compare.

en/base-cs/12-time-and-concurrency/01-wh.title: Why async exists
en/base-cs/12-time-and-concurrency/01-wh.summary: A CPU runs an instruction in roughly a nanosecond, but a disk or network answers in milliseconds — millions of cycles. Async exists so the CPU does other useful work during that gap instead of sitting idle.

en/base-cs/12-time-and-concurrency/02-bl.title: Blocking vs non-blocking
en/base-cs/12-time-and-concurrency/02-bl.summary: A blocking call does not return until the work is done — its stack frame is stuck waiting. A non-blocking call returns immediately and delivers the result later through a callback: a function handed over to be run when the answer is ready.

en/base-cs/12-time-and-concurrency/03-th.title: The event loop
en/base-cs/12-time-and-concurrency/03-th.summary: The event loop is a queue of pending callbacks plus a loop that, whenever the call stack is empty, takes the next callback off the queue and runs it. It is why synchronous code finishes before any callback runs.

en/base-cs/12-time-and-concurrency/04-co.title: Concurrency vs parallelism
en/base-cs/12-time-and-concurrency/04-co.summary: Concurrency is interleaving many tasks on one core — they take turns, one runs at a time. Parallelism is many tasks literally running at the same instant on multiple cores. Concurrency is about structure; parallelism is about execution.

en/base-cs/12-time-and-concurrency/proje.title: Time and concurrency: reproduce and fix a race
en/base-cs/12-time-and-concurrency/proje.summary: Hands-on project — build a shared counter, run it across many threads to reproduce a lost-update race, then fix it with a lock and prove correctness with before/after counts.

en/base-cs/12-time-and-concurrency/quiz-.summary: Multiple-choice synthesis across the time-and-concurrency unit — async, blocking vs non-blocking, the event loop, concurrency vs parallelism, and the race conditions that appear once tasks share state.

en/browser/00-start-here/01-overview.title: Start from zero: what a browser actually does
en/browser/00-start-here/01-overview.summary: When a browser opens a page it downloads HTML, builds the DOM, applies CSS, runs JavaScript on a single main thread, and paints pixels. This is the zero-level map and the eight words the rest of the browser track assumes you already know.

en/browser/01-event-loop/02-queues-and-s.title: Tasks, microtasks, and scheduler.yield()
en/browser/01-event-loop/02-queues-and-s.summary: The HTML spec''''s processing model — task sources, the 5-step iteration, how input lands on the loop, and how to yield without breaking rendering.

en/browser/01-event-loop/03-timer-accura.title: Timer accuracy, throttling, and idle work
en/browser/01-event-loop/03-timer-accura.summary: Why setTimeout(fn, 100) rarely fires at 100 ms — three throttling layers, background-tab coalescing, requestIdleCallback, and Promise combinator semantics.

en/browser/01-event-loop/04-microtask-st.title: Microtask starvation, Long Tasks, and LoAF
en/browser/01-event-loop/04-microtask-st.summary: The starvation failure mode, how to detect it in production with PerformanceLongTaskTiming and LoAF, and scheduler.yield() / scheduler.postTask() as the cure.

en/browser/01-event-loop/05-node-differe.title: Node.js event loop: phases, nextTick, and loop lag
en/browser/01-event-loop/05-node-differe.summary: How Node''''s libuv-driven six-phase loop differs from the browser loop — process.nextTick priority, setImmediate vs setTimeout(0), blocking the Node loop, and measuring event-loop lag.

en/browser/02-render-pipeline/06-layout-.summary: How reading geometry after writing styles forces an immediate layout flush, what N forced layouts per frame look like in DevTools, and the two-pass batch fix.

en/browser/02-render-pipeline/07-beginma.summary: How the Chromium two-thread handshake works, why CSS animations on transform/opacity survive a blocked main thread, and what happens when GPU memory is exhausted.

en/browser/02-render-pipeline/08-observa.summary: LoAF and INP in production telemetry, off-main-thread scroll, display locking, reduced-motion, Web Workers, Service Workers, CI testing, and the complete render-pipeline attack surface.

en/browser/03-v8-internals/01-what-v8-is.title: What V8 is and why performance varies 100×
en/browser/03-v8-internals/01-what-v8-is.summary: V8 turns JS source into machine code through four compilation tiers — the same function can run 100× faster or slower depending on whether V8 can keep it on the hot path.

en/browser/03-v8-internals/02-jit-pipeli.title: V8''''s four-tier JIT pipeline and profile-guided tiering
en/browser/03-v8-internals/02-jit-pipeli.summary: How Ignition, Sparkplug, Maglev, and TurboFan cooperate — compile costs, runtime speeds, the FeedbackVector, and operational levers for keeping code on the fast tier.

en/browser/03-v8-internals/03-hidden-cla.title: Hidden classes, transition trees, and memory layout
en/browser/03-v8-internals/03-hidden-cla.summary: How V8 tracks object shapes via hidden classes, why property-addition order matters, in-object vs out-of-object slots, array element kinds, and the dictionary-mode trap.

en/browser/03-v8-internals/04-inline-cac.title: Inline caches, IC states, and deoptimization
en/browser/03-v8-internals/04-inline-cac.summary: How V8''''s per-call-site inline caches track hidden classes, the monomorphic/polymorphic/megamorphic state machine, deoptimization triggers, and the FadedExample of a hidden-class transition breaking a hot IC.

en/browser/03-v8-internals/05-gc-orinoco.title: Orinoco GC: parallel scavenger, concurrent marking, and write barriers
en/browser/03-v8-internals/05-gc-orinoco.summary: How V8''''s Orinoco garbage collector separates young and old generation, runs minor GC in parallel, moves major GC marking to a background thread, and uses write barriers to stay correct while JS executes.

en/browser/03-v8-internals/06-turbofan-a.title: TurboFan''''s speculative engine and the deopt-loop trap
en/browser/03-v8-internals/06-turbofan-a.summary: TurboFan''''s sea-of-nodes IR, escape analysis, polymorphic inlining, speculative guards, the FeedbackVector in depth, Sparkplug''''s non-optimising pass, and diagnosing deopt-loops with --trace-deopt.

en/browser/04-workers/01-what-workers-ar.title: What workers are and why they exist
en/browser/04-workers/01-what-workers-ar.summary: Workers run JavaScript off the main thread — web workers compute, service workers proxy the network, each with a hard boundary the DOM cannot cross.

en/browser/04-workers/02-web-worker-mech.title: Web worker mechanics: dedicated, shared, and OffscreenCanvas
en/browser/04-workers/02-web-worker-mech.summary: Dedicated vs shared vs module workers, the OffscreenCanvas escape hatch, and why the worker script URL must be same-origin.

en/browser/04-workers/03-structured-clon.title: Structured clone and transferables
en/browser/04-workers/03-structured-clon.summary: postMessage deep-copies data via structured clone at ~1 ms/MB — transferables move ArrayBuffers in O(1) by handing ownership to the receiving thread.

en/browser/04-workers/04-service-worker-.title: Service worker lifecycle and cache strategies
en/browser/04-workers/04-service-worker-.summary: Register → install → waiting → activate → fetch: the lifecycle that enables offline apps, instant repeat loads, and the waiting-state trap that surprises everyone the first time.

en/browser/04-workers/05-shared-array-bu.title: SharedArrayBuffer, Atomics, and cross-origin isolation
en/browser/04-workers/05-shared-array-bu.summary: SAB is real shared memory between threads, gated behind COOP + COEP; Atomics prevents data races; the relaxed memory model means atomic operations are the only safe ordering guarantee.

en/browser/04-workers/06-service-worker-.title: Service worker edge cases: version skew, durability, and navigation traps
en/browser/04-workers/06-service-worker-.summary: Version skew from content-unhashed assets, the kill-and-restart durability trap, and why a broken navigation-intercepting service worker is a stop-the-deploy incident.

en/browser/04-workers/07-worker-pools-an.title: Worker pools, Comlink, and production observability
en/browser/04-workers/07-worker-pools-an.summary: Pool N workers sized to hardwareConcurrency − 1, dispatch jobs via a priority queue with backpressure, wrap with Comlink for ergonomics — but postMessage task-hops still cost, and every worker thread needs its own telemetry.

en/browser/05-react-fiber/01-reconciler-.title: What the reconciler does: render vs commit
en/browser/05-react-fiber/01-reconciler-.summary: React splits every update into an interruptible render phase that computes the diff and an atomic commit phase that applies DOM mutations — the gap between them is where both performance wins and bugs live.

en/browser/05-react-fiber/02-fiber-data-.title: The fiber object and the double-buffer tree
en/browser/05-react-fiber/02-fiber-data-.summary: A fiber is a plain JS object — one per component — holding state, hooks, and tree pointers. The linked-list structure is what makes rendering interruptible, and the two-tree double buffer is what makes interruption free.

en/browser/05-react-fiber/03-render-and-.title: Render phase purity and commit phase sub-steps
en/browser/05-react-fiber/03-render-and-.summary: Render must be pure because React 18 may replay it; commit is synchronous, atomic, and has three sub-steps — before-mutation, mutation, and layout — each with specific APIs and failure modes.

en/browser/05-react-fiber/04-reconciliat.title: Reconciliation: diffing heuristics and the key trap
en/browser/05-react-fiber/04-reconciliat.summary: React reduces O(n³) tree diffing to O(n) with two heuristics — same type keeps state, different type destroys it. Keys identify list items across renders: index keys silently corrupt uncontrolled state on reorder.

en/browser/05-react-fiber/05-lanes-and-t.title: Priority lanes, time-slicing, and useTransition
en/browser/05-react-fiber/05-lanes-and-t.summary: React 18 assigns every update a lane (priority bucket). Time-slicing breaks render work into 5 ms slices. useTransition and useDeferredValue put expensive updates in the transition lane so keystrokes can interrupt them.

en/browser/05-react-fiber/06-bailout-and.title: Bailout, memoisation, and tearing
en/browser/05-react-fiber/06-bailout-and.summary: React bails out of re-running a component if props and state are unchanged by reference. Referential stability (useMemo, useCallback, React.memo) is what enables the bailout. useSyncExternalStore prevents concurrent-render tearing.

en/browser/05-react-fiber/07-profiler-an.title: React Profiler, the Compiler, and production observability
en/browser/05-react-fiber/07-profiler-an.summary: The React DevTools Profiler exposes why each fiber re-rendered and how long it took. The React Compiler automates memoisation. Pairing Profiler with LoAF entries closes the loop from user-reported lag to the exact line of code.

en/browser/07-core-web-vitals/01-what-vi.summary: Three field metrics real Chrome users generate on every visit — and why all the other performance work in this pillar ultimately rolls up into these three numbers.

en/browser/07-core-web-vitals/02-lcp-mec.title: LCP: four phases, one dominant cost
en/browser/07-core-web-vitals/02-lcp-mec.summary: Largest Contentful Paint decomposes into TTFB, resource load delay, resource load time, and render delay — diagnosing and fixing the right phase is the whole game.

en/browser/07-core-web-vitals/03-inp-mec.title: INP: input delay, processing, presentation
en/browser/07-core-web-vitals/03-inp-mec.summary: Interaction to Next Paint decomposes into three parts — and early-only poor INP points straight at the hydration long task, not the event handlers.

en/browser/07-core-web-vitals/04-cls-cau.title: CLS: why layout shifts happen and how to stop them
en/browser/07-core-web-vitals/04-cls-cau.summary: Cumulative Layout Shift scores the worst burst of unexpected movement — un-sized images, late ads, font swaps, dynamically injected banners — and the fix is always the same: reserve space before the bytes arrive.

en/browser/07-core-web-vitals/05-lab-vs-.title: Lab vs field: why the two disagree and how to use each
en/browser/07-core-web-vitals/05-lab-vs-.summary: Lighthouse is a lab tool — reproducible, great for debugging. CrUX is field data from real Chrome users — and only the field drives Search ranking. Knowing which to trust for which question ends the confusion.

en/browser/07-core-web-vitals/06-tradeof.title: Metric tradeoffs, RUM attribution, and the CI+field loop
en/browser/07-core-web-vitals/06-tradeof.summary: The three vitals share a budget — a fix for one can break another. Complete production observability needs web-vitals RUM for the field verdict and a throttled CI gate for regressions — neither alone is enough.

en/browser/08-putting-it-together/01-the.summary: A page load is a relay race across network, parse, paint, and hydration stages — one slow runner makes every later runner late, and the user only sees the finish line.

en/caching/00-start-here/01-overview.summary: A cache is a fast nearby copy of expensive-to-get data. This is the from-zero map and the eight words the rest of the caching track assumes you already know.

en/caching/01-layers/01-overview.title: Caching layers: from L1 to CDN, and where the wrong layer bites
en/caching/01-layers/01-overview.summary: Every layer from CPU cache to CDN trades latency for distance and cost. Caching at the wrong layer, double-caching, or fronting a fast origin with a slow cache all make systems worse, not faster.

en/caching/02-invalidation/01-overview.summary: TTL, event-driven purge, write-through, write-behind, write-around — each trades freshness for a different failure. The senior trap is the cache-aside delete that a concurrent reader silently repopulates with the value you just overwrote.

en/caching/03-stampede/01-what-is-stampe.title: What is a cache stampede and why it makes things worse
en/caching/03-stampede/01-what-is-stampe.summary: A single TTL expiry under concurrent traffic forces every waiting request to rebuild the cache at once, turning the cache into a weapon against its own database.

en/caching/03-stampede/02-lock-and-singl.title: Lock and single-flight: bounding concurrent rebuilds
en/caching/03-stampede/02-lock-and-singl.summary: A Redis SETNX lock serialises rebuilds across the fleet; in-process single-flight collapses the per-node herd to one Promise at zero network cost. Use both layers in sequence.

en/caching/03-stampede/03-xfetch-probabi.title: XFetch: coordination-free probabilistic early expiration
en/caching/03-stampede/03-xfetch-probabi.summary: Vattani et al.''''s XFetch algorithm refreshes the cache before TTL fires using a probabilistic decision rule — no locks, no coordination, expected exactly one early refresh per TTL window regardless of fleet size.

en/caching/03-stampede/04-stale-while-re.title: Stale-while-revalidate and CDN request coalescing
en/caching/03-stampede/04-stale-while-re.summary: RFC 5861''''s stale-while-revalidate directive returns the stale cached value immediately while refreshing in the background — eliminating the wait entirely. CDNs extend this with request coalescing that forwards exactly one origin fetch per cache miss.

en/caching/03-stampede/05-detection-and-.title: Detecting stampedes and designing TTL for production
en/caching/03-stampede/05-detection-and-.summary: The observability fingerprint of a cache stampede, minimum-viable dashboard metrics, TTL jitter to spread boundaries, negative caching, and pre-warming strategies to survive cache-cold restarts.

en/caching/03-stampede/06-stampede-senio.title: Metastable failure, fencing tokens, and production postmortems
en/caching/03-stampede/06-stampede-senio.summary: How an unmitigated stampede pushes a system into a self-sustaining retry storm it cannot escape, the fencing token fix for lock TTL races, four production stampede postmortems, and a three-tier global cache design exercise.

en/caching/04-etag/01-overview.title: ETags and conditional requests: 304 saves the bytes, not the round-trip
en/caching/04-etag/01-overview.summary: The server fingerprints a resource into an ETag; the client revalidates with If-None-Match and gets a 304 with an empty body when nothing changed. The classic prod failure is an ETag that differs per node, so no client ever sees a 304.

en/caching/05-cache-control/01-overview.title: Cache-Control: the header that programs every cache in the chain
en/caching/05-cache-control/01-overview.summary: no-cache does not disable caching, private can still leak into a CDN, and a missing s-maxage hands your CDN the wrong TTL. The directives tell browser, proxy, and CDN exactly how to behave — and the defaults are traps.

en/caching/06-swr/01-overview.title: Stale-while-revalidate: serve stale now, refresh in the background
en/caching/06-swr/01-overview.summary: SWR decouples freshness from latency at two layers — the HTTP Cache-Control directive and the client data-fetching model. You trade bounded staleness for an erased p99 revalidation spike, because no request ever blocks on the origin.

en/caching/07-dogpile/01-overview.title: Dogpile effect: the concurrency collision at the instant a hot key expires
en/caching/07-dogpile/01-overview.summary: When a hot key expires, every in-flight request misses at the same instant and recomputes the same value in parallel — one expensive query becomes N. Single-flight locks, XFetch early expiry, and TTL jitter break the collision.

en/caching/08-putting-it-together/01-ove.summary: A multi-layer cache is only as correct as the way its layers compose. This capstone is the senior framework: which layer owns which data, how TTLs cascade, where a purge propagates, and how each layer fails open under origin loss.
