en/ci-cd/00-start-here/01-what-cicd-is.title: What CI/CD actually is
en/ci-cd/00-start-here/01-what-cicd-is.summary: CI builds and tests every push on a clean machine so integration breaks surface in minutes. CD keeps that artifact always releasable: continuous delivery ships on a button, continuous deployment auto-ships every green commit.

en/ci-cd/01-pipelines/01-github-actions-.title: GitHub Actions: workflows, jobs, steps
en/ci-cd/01-pipelines/01-github-actions-.summary: A workflow is a YAML file under .github/workflows triggered by on: events. It holds jobs that run in parallel on fresh runner VMs; each job has steps that either use an action or run a shell command.

en/ci-cd/01-pipelines/02-caching-and-mat.title: Caching, matrix builds and artifacts
en/ci-cd/01-pipelines/02-caching-and-mat.summary: Cache keyed on a lockfile hash restores dependencies across runs; a matrix fans one job across versions and OSes in parallel; artifacts hand build output between jobs. A stale key is worse than no cache.

en/ci-cd/01-pipelines/03-secrets-and-env.title: Secrets, environments and OIDC
en/ci-cd/01-pipelines/03-secrets-and-env.summary: CI credentials live as masked secrets, scoped by environment with protection rules. Forks get no secrets by default — and OIDC retires long-lived cloud keys for a short-lived signed token the cloud exchanges for temporary credentials.

en/ci-cd/02-testing-in-ci/01-test-pyrami.title: The test pyramid and required checks
en/ci-cd/02-testing-in-ci/01-test-pyrami.summary: Shape the suite as a pyramid — many fast unit tests, fewer integration, a thin e2e cap — then make only the fast, reliable checks block a merge via branch protection. Invert either and the gate turns slow, flaky, and untrustworthy.

en/ci-cd/02-testing-in-ci/02-vitest-jest.title: Vitest/Jest unit + Playwright e2e in CI
en/ci-cd/02-testing-in-ci/02-vitest-jest.summary: Unit tests (Vitest/Jest) must be fast, isolated, and deterministic — run vitest run, not watch, and mock the boundaries. Playwright e2e drives a real headless browser with auto-waiting locators, sharded across runners, and uploads a trace on failure.

en/ci-cd/02-testing-in-ci/03-contract-an.title: Contract testing and taming flaky tests
en/ci-cd/02-testing-in-ci/03-contract-an.summary: Independently deployed services break each other through APIs; consumer-driven contracts catch it before deploy without a shared integration env. And flaky tests rot trust until green stops meaning "safe to merge" — make them deterministic, not retried.

en/ci-cd/03-delivery-and-deploy/01-cd-st.title: Continuous delivery vs deployment, and release strategies
en/ci-cd/03-delivery-and-deploy/01-cd-st.summary: Continuous delivery keeps a release-ready artifact and a human clicks deploy; continuous deployment auto-ships every green commit. Then pick a rollout: blue-green, canary, rolling, or flag-gated — each with its own rollback speed, infra cost, and DB compatibility trap.

en/ci-cd/03-delivery-and-deploy/02-envir.title: Environments, approvals, and rollback
en/ci-cd/03-delivery-and-deploy/02-envir.summary: A GitHub environment is a deploy gate. Required reviewers, wait timers, and branch rules pause the prod job; env-scoped secrets stay locked until approval. And when a deploy goes bad, roll-forward often beats rollback once a migration has run.

en/ci-cd/03-delivery-and-deploy/03-build.title: Build once, promote many: immutable artifacts
en/ci-cd/03-delivery-and-deploy/03-build.summary: Build once, pin the artifact by its sha256 digest, and promote that exact digest through staging to prod with config injected at runtime. Rebuilding per environment ships different bytes — "works in staging, breaks in prod" with no diff to explain it.

en/ci-cd/04-release-automation/01-semver.title: SemVer, conventional commits, and automated changelogs
en/ci-cd/04-release-automation/01-semver.summary: SemVer encodes a contract — MAJOR breaks consumers, MINOR adds compatibly, PATCH fixes compatibly. Conventional commits make that intent machine-readable so tools compute the bump and generate the changelog. Forget to mark a break and it ships as a MINOR.

en/ci-cd/04-release-automation/02-taggin.title: Tagging and publishing releases from CI
en/ci-cd/04-release-automation/02-taggin.summary: A pushed tag is the trigger that turns a commit into a published release. Gate the workflow on a v*.*.* tag, scope the token least-privilege with a permissions block, and publish with provenance — so a leaked PAT or a publish-on-every-push never ships.

en/ci-cd/04-release-automation/03-progre.title: Progressive delivery: canary, blue-green and flags
en/ci-cd/04-release-automation/03-progre.summary: Deploying code is not releasing it. Decouple them: ship dark, then expose gradually — canary at 1-5% with metric-gated auto-rollback, blue-green for instant flip-back, feature flags as a redeploy-free kill switch. Contain the blast radius instead of betting on staging.

en/ci-cd/04-release-automation/04-safe-m.title: Safe schema migrations and rollback
en/ci-cd/04-release-automation/04-safe-m.summary: Code rolls back in seconds; a database does not. A destructive migration that shipped with the deploy makes rollback impossible. Split every schema change into expand/contract across releases so old and new code both work, additive before deploy, destructive after.

en/ci-cd/04-release-automation/05-artifa.title: Build once, promote everywhere: artifacts and environments
en/ci-cd/04-release-automation/05-artifa.summary: Build the artifact exactly once and promote that same immutable, digest-pinned image through dev to staging to prod — never rebuild per environment. A rebuild from the same commit is not the same artifact; config is injected at runtime, and prod is gated behind approval.

en/ci-cd/05-supply-chain/01-sbom-and-pro.title: SBOM, build provenance, and signing: prove what you ship
en/ci-cd/05-supply-chain/01-sbom-and-pro.summary: An SBOM inventories every dependency so you answer "are we affected by CVE-X?" in minutes; provenance and SLSA prove who built the artifact and how; cosign keyless signing plus an attestation, verified at deploy, is what turns all of it from paperwork into a gate.

en/ci-cd/05-supply-chain/02-dependency-a.title: Dependency and secret hygiene: hardening CI itself
en/ci-cd/05-supply-chain/02-dependency-a.summary: The CI runner holds every secret you give it, so harden CI itself: pin actions by full commit SHA (a tag can be moved to malicious code), scan and block leaked credentials at push, set permissions to least-privilege, and prefer short-lived OIDC creds over stored keys.

en/ci-cd/05-supply-chain/03-dependency-c.title: Dependency confusion and typosquatting
en/ci-cd/05-supply-chain/03-dependency-c.summary: Two name-resolution attacks that turn your install step into RCE: dependency confusion (a public package shares your internal name at a higher version) and typosquatting (a near-miss of a popular name). Pin the scope to your registry, install with npm ci, block scripts.

en/ci-cd/05-supply-chain/04-pipeline-sec.title: Pipeline security and poisoned builds
en/ci-cd/05-supply-chain/04-pipeline-sec.summary: The CI runner holds every secret and can tamper with the artifact, so threat-model it. Poisoned Pipeline Execution runs attacker code with your privileges — classically via pull_request_target running a fork PR. Isolate untrusted builds, default-deny the token, use OIDC.

en/ci-cd/05-supply-chain/05-verifying-pr.title: Verifying provenance and policy gates
en/ci-cd/05-supply-chain/05-verifying-pr.summary: L01 signed images and produced SLSA provenance — but a signature nobody checks protects nothing. The enforcement half: verify signature + provenance + builder/source identity at the deploy boundary via an admission controller, fail closed, as policy-as-code.

en/ci-cd/06-scaling-ci/01-monorepo-and-a.title: Monorepo CI: affected-only builds and remote caching
en/ci-cd/06-scaling-ci/01-monorepo-and-a.summary: In a large monorepo, "build & test everything on every PR" stops scaling. Run only the affected subset from the git diff, restore prior outputs from a content-hashed remote cache, and shard what's left — but a cache key that misses an input ships a stale build.

en/ci-cd/06-scaling-ci/02-pipeline-perfo.title: Pipeline performance: caching, parallelism, fail-fast
en/ci-cd/06-scaling-ci/02-pipeline-perfo.summary: Make one pipeline fast and cheap. Cache deps on a lockfile hash with restore-keys fallback, run the cheapest checks first behind needs, fan out only where it pays, quarantine flaky tests, and watch that parallelism doesn't just buy idle runner minutes.

en/ci-cd/06-scaling-ci/03-test-sharding-.title: Test sharding and flaky-test quarantine
en/ci-cd/06-scaling-ci/03-test-sharding-.summary: Scaling the test suite has two failure modes: a serial suite that gates every merge, and flaky tests that compound to keep CI red most of the time. Shard by timing data, not file count; detect flakes on retry and quarantine them off the gate — never make global retry the policy.

en/ci-cd/06-scaling-ci/04-runner-infrast.title: Runner infrastructure and CI cost at scale
en/ci-cd/06-scaling-ci/04-runner-infrast.summary: The CI bill is only half the cost: queue time multiplied by engineer-hours is the other half. Run ephemeral runners (clean room per job), autoscale to the queue, put them on spot to cut the bill 60-90%, right-size, and watch p95 queue time, not just job duration.

en/ci-cd/06-scaling-ci/05-merge-queues-a.title: Merge queues and keeping main green
en/ci-cd/06-scaling-ci/05-merge-queues-a.summary: Required PR checks test stale main, so two independently green PRs can break main via a logical conflict git never sees. A merge queue speculatively builds main + queued PRs before landing, batches for throughput, and bisects to eject the culprit — main green by construction.

en/ci-cd/07-putting-it-together/01-capst.title: Capstone: design a complete CI/CD pipeline end to end
en/ci-cd/07-putting-it-together/01-capst.summary: A production pipeline is one chain — PR checks gate merge, the artifact is built once with an SBOM and a signed provenance attestation, then the same digest is promoted staging → canary → prod with metric-gated rollback. Skip any link and the chain breaks.

en/ci-cd/08-workflows-deep/01-events-and.title: Events and triggers: what fires a workflow, and the pull_request_target trap
en/ci-cd/08-workflows-deep/01-events-and.summary: A workflow is event-driven: the `on:` block, filters, and concurrency decide what runs and what gets cancelled. pull_request runs untrusted code without secrets; pull_request_target runs trusted code with secrets against a fork — the classic exfiltration hole.

en/ci-cd/08-workflows-deep/02-contexts-a.title: Contexts and expressions: the data model, and script injection via github.event
en/ci-cd/08-workflows-deep/02-contexts-a.summary: Contexts (`github`, `env`, `secrets`, `needs`, `matrix`) are the workflow's data model; expressions in `${{ }}` filter, branch, and compute. Interpolating attacker-controlled `github.event` text straight into `run:` is remote code execution.

en/ci-cd/08-workflows-deep/03-jobs-matri.title: Jobs, matrix, and reuse: the DAG, fan-out limits, and reusable-workflow nesting
en/ci-cd/08-workflows-deep/03-jobs-matri.summary: Jobs form a DAG via `needs`; a matrix fans one job into many legs with `max-parallel` and `fail-fast` governing cost. Reusable workflows (`workflow_call`) factor pipelines into callable units — bounded at 4 levels of nesting and 20 unique called files.

en/ci-cd/08-workflows-deep/04-artifacts-.title: Artifacts and caching: passing files between jobs, and the cache that never hits
en/ci-cd/08-workflows-deep/04-artifacts-.summary: Artifacts move files between jobs and out of a run (90-day default retention); cache speeds repeat runs via a restore key. The classic failure: a cache key that omits the lockfile hash so it never invalidates, or never hits across the 10 GB / 7-day eviction window.

en/ci-cd/09-actions-authoring/01-composi.title: Composite actions: bundling steps with zero runtime overhead
en/ci-cd/09-actions-authoring/01-composi.summary: A composite action packages a sequence of steps into one reusable action.yml with no separate runtime — it runs inline on the host runner in milliseconds, but inherits the runner shell and shares the filesystem instead of isolating dependencies.

en/ci-cd/09-actions-authoring/02-javascr.title: JavaScript actions: the node20 runtime, the toolkit, and the ncc bundle
en/ci-cd/09-actions-authoring/02-javascr.summary: A JavaScript action runs as a node20 process on the runner with the @actions/toolkit for inputs, outputs, and the GitHub API. Its dependencies must be committed — bundled with ncc into one file — because runners do not run npm install for an action.

en/ci-cd/09-actions-authoring/03-docker-.title: Docker actions: total environment control at the cost of Linux-only and image overhead
en/ci-cd/09-actions-authoring/03-docker-.summary: A Docker action packages its entire environment in a container — any language, any system dependency — but runs only on Linux runners and pays a 30-90s image pull or build per run, versus a composite or JS action measured in milliseconds.

en/ci-cd/10-security-and-oidc/01-github-.title: The GITHUB_TOKEN: default permissions, least privilege, and why read-all is a footgun
en/ci-cd/10-security-and-oidc/01-github-.summary: Every job gets an auto-minted GITHUB_TOKEN whose default scope can be write-all to the repo. Scope it per-job with permissions, drop to contents:read, and elevate only the one job that needs it.

en/ci-cd/10-security-and-oidc/02-oidc-to.title: OIDC to the cloud: short-lived tokens instead of long-lived AWS keys, and pinning the sub claim
en/ci-cd/10-security-and-oidc/02-oidc-to.summary: OIDC lets a job mint a short-lived (~1h) cloud token via AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity instead of storing a forever AWS key. The trust policy must pin the sub claim or any repo can assume your role.

en/ci-cd/10-security-and-oidc/03-injecti.title: Untrusted input in CI: script injection via interpolated context and the pull_request_target pwn-request
en/ci-cd/10-security-and-oidc/03-injecti.summary: Interpolating attacker-controlled context like github.event.issue.title into a run step is shell injection. pull_request_target runs with secrets and a write token — checking out PR head there is the pwn-request.

en/ci-cd/11-runners-and-scale/01-hosted-.title: Hosted vs self-hosted runners: the spec, the bill, and the public-repo trap
en/ci-cd/11-runners-and-scale/01-hosted-.summary: GitHub-hosted runners are 4 vCPU / 16 GB, billed per minute (~$0.008/min Linux at 1x), with larger runners costing a vCPU multiple. Self-hosted runners are free of compute minutes but cost you machines, maintenance, and — on public repos — a code-execution attack surface.

en/ci-cd/11-runners-and-scale/02-autosca.title: Autoscaling with Actions Runner Controller: ephemeral pods that scale to the queue
en/ci-cd/11-runners-and-scale/02-autosca.summary: Actions Runner Controller (ARC) runs self-hosted runners as ephemeral Kubernetes pods. A runner scale set scales pods up to maxRunners, each servicing one job, giving hosted-like isolation on your cluster with capacity that tracks the job queue instead of a fixed pool.

en/ci-cd/11-runners-and-scale/03-cache-a.title: Cache and cost strategy: restore-keys hierarchy, the 10 GB eviction wall, and Docker layer cache
en/ci-cd/11-runners-and-scale/03-cache-a.summary: GitHub Actions cache gives each repo a 10 GB store with LRU eviction. A precise key plus broad restore-keys turns a cold cache warm; Docker layer caching via the gha backend caches build layers, but an oversized cache that evicts itself can cost more than no cache at all.

en/ci-cd/12-release-engineering/01-versi.title: Versioning and tags: semver, conventional commits, and the immutable release ref
en/ci-cd/12-release-engineering/01-versi.summary: Semver encodes a compatibility contract: major breaks, minor adds, patch fixes. Conventional commits let CI derive the bump automatically. An annotated, immutable git tag plus a content digest is the auditable ref a release points at — and the thing rollback re-deploys.

en/ci-cd/12-release-engineering/02-chang.title: Changelogs and releases: generated notes, PR labels, and the human-facing record
en/ci-cd/12-release-engineering/02-chang.summary: A changelog is the human-readable diff between two tags. Generate it from conventional commits or PR labels so it cannot drift from what shipped, attach it to an immutable GitHub Release tied to the tag and artifact, and the record becomes the auditable answer to what changed.

en/ci-cd/12-release-engineering/03-envir.title: Environments and gates: required reviewers, wait timers, and branch protection
en/ci-cd/12-release-engineering/03-envir.summary: A GitHub Environment scopes secrets and wraps a deploy job in protection rules: required reviewers force human approval, a wait timer creates a soak window, and deployment-branch rules plus branch protection ensure only reviewed code from main can ever reach production.

en/ci-cd/12-release-engineering/04-capst.title: Capstone: reading a real deploy.yml as a release-engineering case study
en/ci-cd/12-release-engineering/04-capst.summary: Read one real deploy workflow end to end — concurrency cancel-in-progress, a single artifact-free build-deploy job, cache-keyed state, a ~12-minute build — and judge it against the release-engineering bar: versioning, changelog, gates, and reversibility. Critique, not recall.

en/cli/01-the-shell/01-what-is-a-termina.title: What is a terminal?
en/cli/01-the-shell/01-what-is-a-termina.summary: A terminal emulator is the window; the shell is the program running inside it that reads your commands and executes them. The prompt is the shell's invitation to type.

en/cli/01-the-shell/02-the-prompt-and-co.title: The prompt and commands
en/cli/01-the-shell/02-the-prompt-and-co.summary: A shell command has three parts: the program name, optional flags that change behaviour, and arguments that say what to act on. Learning to read and compose this grammar unlocks every command-line tool.

en/cli/01-the-shell/03-where-am-i.title: Where am I?
en/cli/01-the-shell/03-where-am-i.summary: The filesystem is a tree of directories rooted at /. pwd prints your current position in that tree; cd moves you. Absolute paths start from /; relative paths start from where you are now.

en/cli/02-files-and-paths/01-paths-absol.title: Absolute and relative paths
en/cli/02-files-and-paths/01-paths-absol.summary: Every file on Linux has an address in the filesystem tree. Absolute paths start at / and are unambiguous from anywhere; relative paths start from the current working directory and are shorter but context-dependent. . is here, .. is parent, ~ is home.

en/cli/02-files-and-paths/02-making-and-.title: Making, copying, moving, and deleting
en/cli/02-files-and-paths/02-making-and-.summary: mkdir creates directories, cp copies files or directory trees, mv moves or renames them, rm deletes them permanently — there is no Trash. The rm -rf combination is the most dangerous command beginners encounter: it silently destroys entire directory trees with no undo.

en/cli/02-files-and-paths/03-reading-fil.title: Reading files
en/cli/02-files-and-paths/03-reading-fil.summary: cat dumps the entire file to stdout — useful for small files and piping. less is a pager for large files: scroll with arrow keys, search with /, quit with q. head and tail print the first or last N lines; tail -f follows a live log in real time.

en/cli/03-streams-and-pipes/01-stdin-std.title: stdin, stdout, and stderr
en/cli/03-streams-and-pipes/01-stdin-std.summary: Every process starts with three open file descriptors: stdin (fd 0) reads input, stdout (fd 1) writes normal output, stderr (fd 2) writes errors. Understanding these three streams is the foundation of shell pipelines.

en/cli/03-streams-and-pipes/02-redirecti.title: Redirection
en/cli/03-streams-and-pipes/02-redirecti.summary: Redirection rewires the standard streams before a command starts: > truncates stdout to a file, >> appends, < feeds a file into stdin, 2> captures stderr, and 2>&1 merges stderr into stdout. Order of operators matters.

en/cli/03-streams-and-pipes/03-pipes-and.title: Pipes and grep
en/cli/03-streams-and-pipes/03-pipes-and.summary: The pipe operator | connects the stdout of one process to the stdin of the next, running both simultaneously. grep filters lines by a pattern — matching lines pass through, non-matching lines are discarded.

en/cli/03-streams-and-pipes/04-counting-.title: Counting and slicing
en/cli/03-streams-and-pipes/04-counting-.summary: wc counts lines, words, and bytes; head and tail slice the top or bottom N lines; sort orders a stream; uniq -c collapses consecutive duplicates into a count. Together they form the classic frequency-analysis pipeline: sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head.

en/cli/04-finding-things/01-globs-and-wi.title: Globs and wildcards
en/cli/04-finding-things/01-globs-and-wi.summary: Globs are patterns the shell expands into matching filenames before any command sees them. * matches any string, ? matches one character, [...] matches a set, and {a,b} produces alternatives.

en/cli/04-finding-things/02-find.title: Finding files with find
en/cli/04-finding-things/02-find.summary: find searches a directory tree by name, type, size, or modification time. -exec runs a command on each result; -print0 with xargs -0 handles filenames with spaces safely.

en/cli/04-finding-things/03-grep-recursi.title: Searching content with grep
en/cli/04-finding-things/03-grep-recursi.summary: grep searches file contents for a pattern. -r searches a whole directory tree; -n shows line numbers; -i ignores case; -l lists only matching filenames; --include limits the search to specific file types.

en/cli/04-finding-things/04-which-and-ty.title: Locating commands with which and type
en/cli/04-finding-things/04-which-and-ty.summary: which, type, and command -v locate commands by searching $PATH and the shell's own lookup table. type also reveals whether a name is a builtin, function, or alias — which only finds external executables.

en/cli/05-permissions-and-users/01-rwx-a.title: rwx and chmod
en/cli/05-permissions-and-users/01-rwx-a.summary: Every Linux file carries nine permission bits — read, write, execute for user, group, and other. chmod sets them numerically (e.g. 640 = rw-r-----) or symbolically (u+x, go-w). Get these right and you control who can do what.

en/cli/05-permissions-and-users/02-owner.title: Ownership and chown
en/cli/05-permissions-and-users/02-owner.summary: Every Linux file has an owner (a user) and an owning group. The kernel checks ownership first to decide which rwx triplet applies. chown changes owner and group; chgrp changes group alone. Wrong ownership is the most common cause of unexpected permission denials.

en/cli/05-permissions-and-users/03-sudo-.title: sudo and root
en/cli/05-permissions-and-users/03-sudo-.summary: Root (uid 0) bypasses all file permission checks. sudo lets a normal user run a single command as root without becoming root permanently. The footguns: sudoing every command, chmod 777 as a fix, and recursive chown on the wrong path.

en/cli/06-text-processing/01-cut-and-fie.title: cut and fields
en/cli/06-text-processing/01-cut-and-fie.summary: cut slices columns from delimited text. -d sets the delimiter, -f selects fields by number or range, -c cuts by character position. Together they replace a full parser for simple structured logs and TSV files.

en/cli/06-text-processing/02-sort-and-un.title: sort and uniq
en/cli/06-text-processing/02-sort-and-un.summary: sort orders lines lexically or numerically; -k selects a sort key by field, -n sorts numerically, -r reverses. uniq -c counts consecutive identical lines. The idiom sort | uniq -c | sort -rn produces a frequency table sorted highest-first.

en/cli/06-text-processing/03-sed-substit.title: sed substitution
en/cli/06-text-processing/03-sed-substit.summary: sed processes text line by line. The s/old/new/g command substitutes a regex pattern with a replacement string. Address prefixes (line numbers, /regex/) restrict which lines are edited. -i rewrites files in-place — portability between GNU and BSD sed requires care.

en/cli/06-text-processing/04-awk-essenti.title: awk essentials
en/cli/06-text-processing/04-awk-essenti.summary: awk splits each line into fields $1..$NF. NR counts records; NF counts fields. Pattern/action pairs run selectively. BEGIN initializes state; END prints summaries. Use associative arrays for per-key counts and sums in one pass.

en/cli/07-processes-and-jobs/01-processe.title: Processes and ps
en/cli/07-processes-and-jobs/01-processe.summary: Every running program is a process with a PID and a PPID forming a tree rooted at init. ps aux and ps -ef give you two views of the process table: the first is user-centric, the second shows full command lines and parent relationships.

en/cli/07-processes-and-jobs/02-signals-.title: Signals and kill
en/cli/07-processes-and-jobs/02-signals-.summary: Signals are asynchronous notifications the kernel delivers to processes. SIGTERM (15) asks politely and can be caught; SIGKILL (9) cannot be caught or ignored and skips all cleanup. Reach for SIGTERM first — SIGKILL is the last resort.

en/cli/07-processes-and-jobs/03-jobs-and.title: Jobs and backgrounding
en/cli/07-processes-and-jobs/03-jobs-and.summary: Job control lets you suspend, background, and foreground processes within a shell session. nohup and disown protect long-running jobs from SIGHUP when the terminal closes — without them, backgrounding alone is not enough.

en/cli/07-processes-and-jobs/04-monitori.title: Monitoring resources
en/cli/07-processes-and-jobs/04-monitori.summary: top and htop give real-time per-process CPU and memory. Load average tells you how many processes are competing for CPU averaged over 1, 5, and 15 minutes. free shows RAM and swap usage in one line. Together these three answer: is the machine healthy right now?

en/cli/08-shell-scripting/01-variables-a.title: Variables and quoting
en/cli/08-shell-scripting/01-variables-a.summary: Variables in bash hold strings; quoting determines whether the shell expands, word-splits, or passes values literally. Unquoted variables are split on whitespace and glob-expanded — the source of most beginner script bugs.

en/cli/08-shell-scripting/02-conditional.title: Conditionals and exit codes
en/cli/08-shell-scripting/02-conditional.summary: Every command exits with a numeric code: 0 means success, non-zero means failure. $? holds the last exit code. [[ ]] is the modern bash test construct; && and || chain commands on success or failure.

en/cli/08-shell-scripting/03-loops-and-a.title: Loops and arguments
en/cli/08-shell-scripting/03-loops-and-a.summary: for iterates over a list; while iterates until a condition fails. $@ expands to all positional arguments as separate words; $* joins them. read processes stdin line by line. shift discards $1 and renumbers the rest.

en/cli/08-shell-scripting/04-robust-scri.title: Robust scripts
en/cli/08-shell-scripting/04-robust-scri.summary: set -euo pipefail turns bash into a fail-fast interpreter: -e exits on any error, -u treats unset variables as errors, -o pipefail catches failures inside pipelines. trap cleans up on exit. Functions with local variables prevent variable leakage.

en/cli/09-ssh-and-remote/01-ssh-basics.title: SSH basics
en/cli/09-ssh-and-remote/01-ssh-basics.summary: ssh opens an encrypted remote shell. The first-connect host-key prompt implements Trust On First Use (TOFU): accept it once, and SSH will alert you if the server identity ever changes. ~/.ssh/config maps aliases to real hosts, users, and ports.

en/cli/09-ssh-and-remote/02-key-authenti.title: Key authentication
en/cli/09-ssh-and-remote/02-key-authenti.summary: Key authentication replaces passwords with a cryptographic proof: the private key never leaves your machine; the server holds only the public key and verifies a signed challenge. ssh-agent caches the decrypted key so you type the passphrase once per session.

en/cli/09-ssh-and-remote/03-scp-and-rsyn.title: scp and rsync
en/cli/09-ssh-and-remote/03-scp-and-rsyn.summary: scp copies files over SSH. rsync -avz transfers only changed bytes and compresses in transit; rsync -a --delete mirrors a directory and removes remote files absent from the source — a footgun unless you verify with --dry-run first.

en/cli/09-ssh-and-remote/04-tmux-basics.title: tmux basics
en/cli/09-ssh-and-remote/04-tmux-basics.summary: tmux keeps processes running after SSH disconnects by hosting them inside a server process that survives terminal closure. Sessions contain windows; windows contain panes. Detach with C-b d, reattach with tmux attach — your work is exactly where you left it.

en/cli/10-putting-it-together/01-log-ana.title: Log analysis pipeline
en/cli/10-putting-it-together/01-log-ana.summary: Compose find, grep, cut, sort, uniq -c, and awk into a multi-stage pipeline that extracts real insight from access logs — top client IPs, status-code distribution, and error spikes — in a single shell one-liner.

en/cli/10-putting-it-together/02-a-maint.title: A maintenance script
en/cli/10-putting-it-together/02-a-maint.summary: A robust maintenance script uses set -euo pipefail to fail fast, a trap on EXIT for guaranteed cleanup, named functions for readability, and disciplined quoting throughout. These four habits together prevent the silent data-loss bugs that haunt naive scripts.

en/cli/10-putting-it-together/03-remote-.title: Remote ops capstone
en/cli/10-putting-it-together/03-remote-.summary: Tie ssh, rsync, and tmux into a complete remote-ops workflow: sync a directory to a remote server, start a long-running job in a detached tmux session, and reconnect to it later — surviving disconnects without losing work.

en/code-patterns/00-what-good-code-is/01.title: The cost of change
en/code-patterns/00-what-good-code-is/01.summary: Code is read and changed far more than it is written, so the dominant cost of software is the cost of changing it. "Good code" is not an aesthetic — it is code whose next change is cheap. This lesson defines the cost-of-change lens the whole track uses.

en/code-patterns/00-what-good-code-is/02.title: The maintainability triad
en/code-patterns/00-what-good-code-is/02.summary: "Good code" splits into three measurable, separable properties — readability (cost to understand), changeability (cost to safely modify), testability (cost to verify in isolation) — and seniors review code by naming which property each change improves or degrades.

en/code-patterns/00-what-good-code-is/03.title: Clean, not clever
en/code-patterns/00-what-good-code-is/03.summary: Clever code optimizes for the writer — fewest keystrokes, density, ego; clean code optimizes for the next reader and the next change. Cleverness is a tax every future reader pays, justified only by a measured hot-path reason and a comment. Clean means obvious, not fancy.

en/code-patterns/01-names/01-naming-as-d.title: Naming is a design act
en/code-patterns/01-names/01-naming-as-d.summary: A name compresses a concept's intent into a word, so the act of naming forces you to understand and bound that concept — which makes naming difficulty a direct signal about your design, not just your vocabulary.

en/code-patterns/01-names/02-intention-r.title: Intention-revealing names
en/code-patterns/01-names/02-intention-r.summary: A name should answer why this exists, what it does, and how it is used, so the code reads as its intent — name by concept not type, kill noise words, replace magic numbers with named constants, and encode units.

en/code-patterns/01-names/03-consistency.title: Consistency and scope
en/code-patterns/01-names/03-consistency.summary: Use one word per concept across the codebase — mixed synonyms are hidden coupling readers must decode — and let name length scale with scope: terse in tiny locals, descriptive at module boundaries.

en/code-patterns/02-functions-and-cohesi.title: Small functions, one job
en/code-patterns/02-functions-and-cohesi.summary: A function should do one thing — have one reason to change — at one level of abstraction; extracting the sub-intents and naming each step is the win, not hitting a line count, and over-extraction is as harmful as a god function.

en/code-patterns/02-functions-and-cohesi.title: One level of abstraction
en/code-patterns/02-functions-and-cohesi.summary: A function should operate at one level of abstraction — high-level policy reads as a narrative that calls the next level down (the stepdown rule), with low-level detail extracted behind names so the reader can skim the decision without context-switching every line.

en/code-patterns/02-functions-and-cohesi.title: Command/query separation
en/code-patterns/02-functions-and-cohesi.summary: A function should either DO something (a command, with an effect) or ANSWER something (a query, with no observable side effect) — not both; separating them makes queries safe to call freely and your code predictable and testable.

en/code-patterns/02-functions-and-cohesi.title: Arguments and side effects
en/code-patterns/02-functions-and-cohesi.summary: A function's parameter list and its hidden effects are honest signals of its cohesion — 0–2 arguments are ideal, flag and output arguments mean it does two jobs, and side effects buried behind an innocent name are the costliest lie a signature can tell.

en/code-patterns/03-comments-and-contrac.title: When comments lie
en/code-patterns/03-comments-and-contrac.summary: Comments are not executed, so they rot — and a confidently wrong comment is worse than none. Learn to delete the bad ones and keep the few that earn their place by explaining WHY the code is what it is, never WHAT it does.

en/code-patterns/03-comments-and-contrac.title: Self-documenting code
en/code-patterns/03-comments-and-contrac.summary: A comment that explains WHAT the code does is usually a name waiting to be extracted. Move the WHAT into structure — named functions and variables — and keep comments for the WHY code can't carry: rationale, constraints, links.

en/code-patterns/03-comments-and-contrac.title: Types and tests as documentation
en/code-patterns/03-comments-and-contrac.summary: Types and tests are executable, machine-checked documentation that cannot rot. A precise type encodes an invariant a comment can only assert: a discriminated union makes illegal states unrepresentable, a branded type stops unit mix-ups, and a named test pins behaviour as a spec.

en/code-patterns/04-srp/01-reasons-to-ch.title: One reason to change
en/code-patterns/04-srp/01-reasons-to-ch.summary: SRP is not 'do one thing'. A module should have one reason to change — be responsible to one actor whose changing requirements force edits. Merging actors (Finance + HR + DBA) into one class is the violation; split by actor.

en/code-patterns/04-srp/02-actors-and-ax.title: Actors and axes of change
en/code-patterns/04-srp/02-actors-and-ax.summary: A component often mixes three independent change axes — presentation policy, a business rule, persistence — each requested by a different actor. Group code by axis so one change touches one place. SRP attacks coupling across axes; over-splitting imagined axes costs indirection.

en/code-patterns/04-srp/03-splitting-wit.title: Splitting without shattering
en/code-patterns/04-srp/03-splitting-wit.summary: SRP has a sweet spot. Over-applied, it shatters one cohesive concept into a fog of tiny classes you must reassemble in your head — a god class in reverse. Split on real change boundaries (independent cadence, different actors); keep together what changes together.

en/code-patterns/05-ocp-lsp/01-open-clos.title: Open for extension, closed for modification
en/code-patterns/05-ocp-lsp/01-open-clos.summary: OCP means adding behavior by adding code — a new type or strategy — not by editing tested code. But you can only be closed against the one axis of variation you predict; guess wrong and you over-engineer. The skill is choosing which change to make cheap.

en/code-patterns/05-ocp-lsp/02-polymorph.title: Polymorphism over conditionals
en/code-patterns/05-ocp-lsp/02-polymorph.summary: When the same type-switch appears in many places, each new variant forces edits everywhere. Move per-case behaviour onto the types or a dispatch map so dispatch is one mechanism — but only when the switch is repeated and variants keep arriving.

en/code-patterns/05-ocp-lsp/03-liskov-su.title: Liskov substitution
en/code-patterns/05-ocp-lsp/03-liskov-su.summary: A subtype must be substitutable for its supertype without surprising callers. LSP is about behavioral contracts, not type compatibility — the compiler accepts the subclass; the runtime betrays it. The tell is `instanceof` special-casing at call sites.

en/code-patterns/05-ocp-lsp/04-contract-.title: Designing and honoring contracts
en/code-patterns/05-ocp-lsp/04-contract-.summary: Substitutability is behaviour, not shape: a type-correct implementation can still break callers. State contracts as pre/post/invariants, encode shape in types, and pin behaviour with one shared contract test run against every implementation so drift is caught.

en/code-patterns/06-isp-dip/01-interface.title: Interface segregation
en/code-patterns/06-isp-dip/01-interface.summary: A fat interface is a coupling magnet — one client's change forces recompile and retest on every other consumer. Segregate into role interfaces named for how each client uses the type, not per method, or the cure becomes a swarm of one-method noise.

en/code-patterns/06-isp-dip/02-dependenc.title: Dependency inversion
en/code-patterns/06-isp-dip/02-dependenc.summary: High-level policy must not depend on low-level detail; both depend on an abstraction the policy owns. Flip the arrow — OrderService → OrderRepository ← MySqlOrderRepository — so business logic is testable and infrastructure swappable.

en/code-patterns/06-isp-dip/03-ports-and.title: Ports and adapters
en/code-patterns/06-isp-dip/03-ports-and.summary: Hexagonal architecture scales DIP to whole systems — the domain owns the ports (interfaces it needs), infrastructure provides the adapters, and every dependency points inward. The domain is the stable center; I/O is replaceable at the edge. The structure must earn its cost.

en/code-patterns/06-isp-dip/04-dependenc.title: Dependency injection in TypeScript
en/code-patterns/06-isp-dip/04-dependenc.summary: DI wires abstractions to implementations. The coupling to kill is new ConcreteThing() inside a class. Use constructor injection, assemble the graph at a composition root, and keep the core pure and testable with fakes — reach for a container only when manual wiring hurts.

en/code-patterns/07-coupling-and-cohesio.title: Connascence
en/code-patterns/07-coupling-and-cohesio.summary: Connascence is a precise taxonomy of coupling — two components are connascent when changing one forces changing the other. Its two rules (prefer weaker, prefer more local) let you compare two designs' coupling objectively instead of by taste.

en/code-patterns/07-coupling-and-cohesio.title: The Law of Demeter
en/code-patterns/07-coupling-and-cohesio.summary: Law of Demeter — only talk to your immediate neighbours, never reach through a.getB().getC() chains. Train-wreck chains couple you to the whole object graph's shape; "tell, don't ask" moves behaviour to the data and shrinks the blast radius of structural change.

en/code-patterns/07-coupling-and-cohesio.title: Drawing module boundaries
en/code-patterns/07-coupling-and-cohesio.summary: Maximize cohesion inside a module, minimize coupling across. Afferent vs efferent coupling and the Stable-Dependencies Principle: depend toward stability. Package by feature, not by layer — package-by-layer scatters one feature's change across every folder.

en/code-patterns/08-smells-bloaters/01-l.title: Long method, large class
en/code-patterns/08-smells-bloaters/01-l.summary: Bloater smells — the long method and the large class — are cohesion decay: responsibilities pile up until no one can hold the unit in their head. Detect by signals, cure by extracting along responsibility seams, not at arbitrary line counts.

en/code-patterns/08-smells-bloaters/02-p.title: Primitive obsession & data clumps
en/code-patterns/08-smells-bloaters/02-p.summary: Modelling money, email, or a date range as a raw string or number scatters validation and rules across the codebase. The same fields always travelling together signal a missing concept. The cure is a value object — applied where there's an invariant, not as reflex ceremony.

en/code-patterns/08-smells-bloaters/03-d.title: Divergent change & shotgun surgery
en/code-patterns/08-smells-bloaters/03-d.summary: Divergent change and shotgun surgery are opposite SRP smells you read from git history, not from arguing about responsibilities. One module edited for many reasons means split it; one change touching many modules means consolidate it.

en/code-patterns/09-smells-couplers-disp.title: Feature envy & inappropriate intimacy
en/code-patterns/09-smells-couplers-disp.summary: Feature envy is behaviour living next to the wrong data; inappropriate intimacy is two classes reaching into each other's internals. Cure both by moving behaviour to the data it envies and restoring encapsulation — but don't relocate orchestration that legitimately spans objects.

en/code-patterns/09-smells-couplers-disp.title: Message chains & middle man
en/code-patterns/09-smells-couplers-disp.summary: Message chains couple a caller to a whole object graph; middle man is the over-correction that delegates everything and earns nothing. Hide delegate, remove middle man, and tell-don't-ask are the cures — but Demeter pulls both ways, so the senior call is balance, not zealotry.

en/code-patterns/09-smells-couplers-disp.title: Dead code & speculative generality
en/code-patterns/09-smells-couplers-disp.summary: Dead code and speculative generality are dispensable smells: unused params, unreachable branches, never-called functions, and "just in case" abstractions that cost reading and testing for zero benefit. Cure: delete fearlessly — git remembers, YAGNI re-adds when truly needed.

en/code-patterns/09-smells-couplers-disp.title: Type switches & refused bequest
en/code-patterns/09-smells-couplers-disp.summary: Two OO smells. A type-switch repeated in N places grows with every variant — the strongest signal for replace-conditional-with-polymorphism. Refused bequest, where a subclass no-ops inherited methods, means the is-a was false; cure it with delegation.

en/code-patterns/10-refactoring-safety-n.title: Characterization tests
en/code-patterns/10-refactoring-safety-n.summary: Before refactoring legacy code you don't fully understand, characterization tests pin its current behavior — even the wrong parts — so a refactor can't change behavior silently. They are the net that makes refactoring safe and the record of what the code actually does.

en/code-patterns/10-refactoring-safety-n.title: Seams
en/code-patterns/10-refactoring-safety-n.summary: A seam is a place where you can change a unit's behaviour without editing it there — by injecting a clock, repository, or parameter — so stubborn legacy code becomes testable through a small local change instead of a risky rewrite.

en/code-patterns/10-refactoring-safety-n.title: Core moves under green
en/code-patterns/10-refactoring-safety-n.summary: The catalog of small refactorings done under green tests, one at a time — extract, inline, rename, move, change declaration, encapsulate variable. The rhythm is tiny step, run tests, commit, repeat; never bundle a refactor with a behavior change.

en/code-patterns/11-refactoring-larger/0.title: Extract class
en/code-patterns/11-refactoring-larger/0.summary: A class that quietly grew a second responsibility — a data clump plus the behaviour around it — wants splitting. Extract Class is SRP done by refactoring: read the seam from the clump, then move fields and methods incrementally under green tests.

en/code-patterns/11-refactoring-larger/0.title: Replace conditional with polymorphism
en/code-patterns/11-refactoring-larger/0.summary: The larger move under tests: turn a sprawling, repeated type-switch into a polymorphic family one case at a time. Pin behaviour with tests, introduce the interface, migrate cases incrementally, delete the switch last — and only do it when the variation axis is real.

en/code-patterns/11-refactoring-larger/0.title: Introduce parameter object
en/code-patterns/11-refactoring-larger/0.summary: Replace a recurring data clump or long parameter list with a parameter object that names a real concept, so related behavior and validation gravitate to it and call sites get clearer — without it becoming a junk drawer.

en/code-patterns/11-refactoring-larger/0.title: Refactoring toward patterns
en/code-patterns/11-refactoring-larger/0.summary: Design patterns are destinations you refactor TOWARD when a smell demands them, not templates you impose up front. Duplicated construction pulls toward a Factory; a growing conditional toward Strategy or State. YAGNI stops you cargo-culting all 23 GoF patterns into a simple app.

en/code-patterns/12-heuristics-and-trade.title: DRY, KISS, YAGNI in tension
en/code-patterns/12-heuristics-and-trade.summary: DRY, KISS, and YAGNI are heuristics, not laws, and they pull against each other. DRY targets one source of knowledge — not identical-looking text. Two fragments that change for different reasons are not duplication, and DRY-ing them couples unrelated things.

en/code-patterns/12-heuristics-and-trade.title: The rule of three
en/code-patterns/12-heuristics-and-trade.summary: Don't abstract on the first or second occurrence — wait for the third, when the real axis of variation is finally visible. Abstracting early guesses the axis wrong and ossifies the wrong shape. The exception: obvious knowledge duplication, which you de-dupe immediately.

en/code-patterns/12-heuristics-and-trade.title: The wrong abstraction
en/code-patterns/12-heuristics-and-trade.summary: Duplication is cheaper than the wrong abstraction. A premature shared method grows a flag per caller until it is a tangle. The fix is to inline it back, then re-derive the right abstraction from the now-visible differences.

en/code-patterns/13-antipatterns-and-deb.title: God object & anemic domain model
en/code-patterns/13-antipatterns-and-deb.summary: Two structural anti-patterns pull in opposite directions: the god object knows and does everything, while the anemic model has data classes with no behavior at all. The fix for one must not become the other — move behavior to its data, spread across cohesive objects.

en/code-patterns/13-antipatterns-and-deb.title: The technical debt quadrant
en/code-patterns/13-antipatterns-and-deb.summary: Fowler's debt quadrant splits shortcuts by intent: deliberate vs inadvertent, prudent vs reckless. Not all debt is bad — prudent deliberate debt is a financing tool. The real hazards are reckless debt and untracked debt that compounds invisibly.

en/code-patterns/13-antipatterns-and-deb.title: Legacy code & the boy-scout rule
en/code-patterns/13-antipatterns-and-deb.summary: Legacy = code without tests (Feathers). Change it safely with the algorithm: find a seam, pin behaviour with characterization tests, then change and refactor under that net. Boy-scout incrementally; resist the rewrite and the gold-plating that balloons the diff.

en/code-patterns/14-capstone/01-smell-in.title: Capstone I: the smell inventory
en/code-patterns/14-capstone/01-smell-in.summary: Before you touch a messy module, diagnose it: name each smell with the track vocabulary, locate it, and rank by change-cost. A prioritized inventory tied to likely changes — not a cleanup urge — is what lets you prove the refactor improved anything.

en/code-patterns/14-capstone/02-incremen.title: Capstone II: the incremental refactor
en/code-patterns/14-capstone/02-incremen.summary: Execute the part-1 refactor end to end. Net the module in characterization tests, then make one small reversible move per commit under green — extract, value objects, polymorphism for the payment switch, a persistence port — never sneaking a behavior change into a refactor.

en/code-patterns/14-capstone/03-measure-.title: Capstone III: measure before and after
en/code-patterns/14-capstone/03-measure-.summary: The refactor paid off only if the target changes are now cheap. Measure before vs after — edits per change, coupling, test seams, cohesion — against unit 00s cost-of-change lens, and know when good-enough beats endless gold-plating. The track closes here.

en/data-engineering/00-start-here/01-ove.title: Start from zero: what data engineering actually is
en/data-engineering/00-start-here/01-ove.summary: Data engineering is the discipline of moving and reshaping data from where apps produce it to where analysts can query it. This is the from-zero map and the eight words the rest of the track assumes you already know.

en/data-engineering/01-oltp-vs-olap/01-o.title: OLTP vs OLAP: the workload split that defines data engineering
en/data-engineering/01-oltp-vs-olap/01-o.summary: Row-store OLTP and column-store OLAP optimize opposite shapes: tiny indexed writes vs huge scans. Running analytics on the prod replica is the classic outage — the fix is a separate columnar store fed by ETL/CDC.

en/data-engineering/01-oltp-vs-olap/proj.title: OLTP vs OLAP: split the workload
en/data-engineering/01-oltp-vs-olap/proj.summary: Hands-on project — reproduce the analytics-on-OLTP outage, then split the workload into a columnar store fed by CDC/ETL and prove the fix with before/after numbers.

en/data-engineering/01-oltp-vs-olap/quiz.title: OLTP vs OLAP: multiple-choice review
en/data-engineering/01-oltp-vs-olap/quiz.summary: Multiple-choice synthesis across the OLTP vs OLAP unit — row vs column layout, column pruning, compression, vectorization, the replica-analytics outage, and when to split stores.

en/data-engineering/01-oltp-vs-olap/quiz.title: OLTP vs OLAP: query and plan reading
en/data-engineering/01-oltp-vs-olap/quiz.summary: Read real query plans, DDL, and pipeline config across the OLTP vs OLAP unit, predict scan cost on row vs column storage, and pick the highest-leverage fix.

en/data-engineering/01-oltp-vs-olap/quiz.title: OLTP vs OLAP: free-recall review
en/data-engineering/01-oltp-vs-olap/quiz.summary: Free-recall prompts across the OLTP vs OLAP unit. Answer each in your own words first, then reveal the model answer and compare.

en/data-engineering/02-elt-vs-etl/01-ove.title: ELT vs ETL: where the Transform runs, and why the industry flipped
en/data-engineering/02-elt-vs-etl/01-ove.summary: ETL transforms before load in a separate engine; ELT loads raw into the warehouse and transforms in SQL. Cheap columnar compute and split storage/compute flipped the default — and moved the cost onto the warehouse bill.

en/data-engineering/02-elt-vs-etl/projec.title: ELT vs ETL: build a replayable, idempotent pipeline
en/data-engineering/02-elt-vs-etl/projec.summary: Hands-on project — build a small ELT pipeline with a medallion layout, make it incremental and idempotent, prove a retry does not duplicate, and run a restartable backfill with before/after cost numbers.

en/data-engineering/02-elt-vs-etl/quiz-c.title: ELT vs ETL: multiple-choice review
en/data-engineering/02-elt-vs-etl/quiz-c.summary: Multiple-choice synthesis across the ELT-vs-ETL unit: where the Transform runs, replayability, warehouse cost, idempotency, and the medallion contract.

en/data-engineering/02-elt-vs-etl/quiz-c.title: ELT vs ETL: model and config reading
en/data-engineering/02-elt-vs-etl/quiz-c.summary: Read real dbt model configs and a Snowflake bill signature, predict the pipeline behaviour — idempotency, incremental load, backfill — and pick the highest-leverage fix.

en/data-engineering/02-elt-vs-etl/quiz-s.title: ELT vs ETL: free-recall review
en/data-engineering/02-elt-vs-etl/quiz-s.summary: Free-recall prompts across the ELT-vs-ETL unit. Answer each in your own words first, then reveal the model answer and compare.

en/data-engineering/03-parquet/01-overvi.title: Parquet: why analytics stores columns, not rows
en/data-engineering/03-parquet/01-overvi.summary: Parquet is columnar, self-describing, and carries per-row-group min/max stats in its footer — so a filter can skip whole row groups and read only the columns it needs. CSV must parse every byte. The senior traps are small files, wrong row-group size, and dictionary blowup.

en/data-engineering/03-parquet/project.title: Parquet: build a query-efficient lake table
en/data-engineering/03-parquet/project.summary: Hands-on project — convert a CSV dataset to Parquet, lay it out for pushdown and pruning, then prove with before/after numbers that filtered queries read a fraction of the bytes.

en/data-engineering/03-parquet/quiz-choi.title: Parquet: multiple-choice review
en/data-engineering/03-parquet/quiz-choi.summary: Multiple-choice synthesis across the Parquet unit — columnar layout, footer stats and pushdown, encoding vs compression, row-group sizing, and the small-files trap.

en/data-engineering/03-parquet/quiz-code.title: Parquet: code and config reading
en/data-engineering/03-parquet/quiz-code.summary: Read real PyArrow/DuckDB read paths and a writer config, predict the I/O and GC of bytes scanned, and pick the highest-leverage fix for pushdown, sizing, and projection.

en/data-engineering/03-parquet/quiz-shor.title: Parquet: free-recall review
en/data-engineering/03-parquet/quiz-shor.summary: Free-recall prompts across the Parquet unit — columnar layout, footer pushdown, encoding vs compression, row-group sizing, schema evolution, and table formats.

en/data-engineering/04-materialized-view.title: Materialized views: trading staleness and storage for read latency
en/data-engineering/04-materialized-view.summary: A materialized view stores the result of an expensive query instead of recomputing it each read. The real decision is refresh: full recompute locks readers, incremental needs an extension, and a stale refresh silently serves wrong aggregates.

en/data-engineering/04-materialized-view.title: Materialized views: own the refresh
en/data-engineering/04-materialized-view.summary: Hands-on project — build a slow aggregate dashboard, materialize it, compare full-CONCURRENTLY vs pg_ivm refresh under load, bound the staleness window, and prove the tradeoffs with before/after numbers.

en/data-engineering/04-materialized-view.title: Materialized views: multiple-choice review
en/data-engineering/04-materialized-view.summary: Multiple-choice synthesis across the materialized-views unit — refresh strategy, CONCURRENTLY's hidden costs, incremental maintenance tradeoffs, staleness ownership, and streaming MVs.

en/data-engineering/04-materialized-view.title: Materialized views: SQL and refresh reading
en/data-engineering/04-materialized-view.summary: Read real SQL — REFRESH CONCURRENTLY setup, pg_ivm immv creation, and a staleness-window check — and pick the behaviour or the highest-leverage fix a senior would make first.

en/data-engineering/04-materialized-view.title: Materialized views: free-recall review
en/data-engineering/04-materialized-view.summary: Free-recall prompts across the materialized-views unit. Answer each from memory first, then reveal the model answer and compare.

en/data-engineering/05-event-sourcing/01.title: Event sourcing: the append-only log as source of truth
en/data-engineering/05-event-sourcing/01.summary: Store the immutable stream of state-changing events, not the current state — current state is a left-fold over the log. You buy audit, time-travel, and replay; you pay in versioning, GDPR, snapshots, and eventual consistency.

en/data-engineering/05-event-sourcing/pr.title: Event sourcing: build an auditable ledger
en/data-engineering/05-event-sourcing/pr.summary: Hands-on project — build a small event-sourced service with an append-only store, a rebuildable CQRS projection, snapshots, an upcaster, and crypto-shredding, and prove each property.

en/data-engineering/05-event-sourcing/qu.title: Event sourcing: multiple-choice review
en/data-engineering/05-event-sourcing/qu.summary: Multiple-choice synthesis across event sourcing — log as source of truth, projections and CQRS, replay, snapshots, event versioning, and GDPR on an immutable log.

en/data-engineering/05-event-sourcing/qu.title: Event sourcing: code reading
en/data-engineering/05-event-sourcing/qu.summary: Read real event-sourcing snippets — a projection rebuild, a snapshot-aware load, and an upcaster — predict the behaviour, and pick the senior fix.

en/data-engineering/05-event-sourcing/qu.title: Event sourcing: free-recall review
en/data-engineering/05-event-sourcing/qu.summary: Free-recall prompts across event sourcing. Answer each in your own words first, then reveal the model answer and compare against the senior bar.

en/data-engineering/06-search/01-overvie.title: Full-text search: inverted indexes, analysis, and why ranking beats matching
en/data-engineering/06-search/01-overvie.summary: LIKE ''''%term%'''' scans every row and ignores relevance. Full-text search flips the problem: an inverted index finds candidate docs in milliseconds, an analysis pipeline normalizes text, and BM25 ranks by usefulness, not just presence.

en/data-engineering/06-search/project.title: Full-text search: build and migrate a search index
en/data-engineering/06-search/project.summary: Hands-on project — build real full-text search over a document corpus, prove relevance against judged queries, and migrate an analyzer change behind a read alias with zero downtime.

en/data-engineering/06-search/quiz-choic.title: Full-text search: multiple-choice review
en/data-engineering/06-search/quiz-choic.summary: Multiple-choice synthesis across the search unit — inverted index, analyzer parity, BM25 tuning, GIN vs GiST, near-real-time refresh, and zero-downtime reindex.

en/data-engineering/06-search/quiz-code.title: Full-text search: code and query reading
en/data-engineering/06-search/quiz-code.summary: Read real index-build code, an analyzer pipeline, a BM25 scoring sketch, and a Postgres tsvector query, then predict the behaviour and pick the highest-leverage fix.

en/data-engineering/06-search/quiz-short.title: Full-text search: free-recall review
en/data-engineering/06-search/quiz-short.summary: Free-recall prompts across the search unit. Answer each in your own words first, then reveal the model answer and compare against the unit's spine.

en/data-engineering/07-vectors/01-overvi.title: Vector search: the recall–latency–memory triangle behind RAG
en/data-engineering/07-vectors/01-overvi.summary: Semantic search ranks embeddings by distance, but exact kNN is O(N·d) and dies at scale. ANN indexes like HNSW buy speed by trading recall — and the wrong ef param drops recall silently while every query still returns ten rows.

en/data-engineering/07-vectors/project.title: Vector search: catch the silent recall drop
en/data-engineering/07-vectors/project.summary: Hands-on project — build a pgvector RAG search, expose its silent recall drop with an exact baseline, then tune ef_search, fix post-filtering, and add hybrid search, proving each step with recall numbers.

en/data-engineering/07-vectors/quiz-choi.title: Vector search: multiple-choice review
en/data-engineering/07-vectors/quiz-choi.summary: Multiple-choice synthesis across the vector-search unit — recall vs latency, HNSW vs IVF-PQ, distance metrics, post-filtering, and the silent-recall failure mode.

en/data-engineering/07-vectors/quiz-code.title: Vector search: code and query reading
en/data-engineering/07-vectors/quiz-code.summary: Read real pgvector DDL and queries — predict the recall/latency behaviour and pick the highest-leverage fix for HNSW params, distance operators, and filtered search.

en/data-engineering/07-vectors/quiz-shor.title: Vector search: free-recall review
en/data-engineering/07-vectors/quiz-shor.summary: Free-recall prompts across the vector-search unit — answer each from memory first, then reveal the model answer and compare.

en/data-engineering/08-putting-it-togeth.title: Putting it together: the system breaks at the seams, not the stores
en/data-engineering/08-putting-it-togeth.summary: Trace one product through OLTP, warehouse, dbt, MVs, an event log, search, and a vector index. Each store is correct; the system drifts where two correct stores meet — so consistency, freshness, and lineage are end-to-end properties you design.

en/data-engineering/08-putting-it-togeth.title: Data platform: design ingest to serving
en/data-engineering/08-putting-it-togeth.summary: Capstone project — design and build a small data platform from ingest to serving, choosing the right store, format, and index per workload, and prove the seams hold.

en/databases/00-start-here/01-overview.title: Start from zero: what a database actually is
en/databases/00-start-here/01-overview.summary: A database is durable, queryable, structured storage — the memory your app writes to that survives restarts. This is the from-zero map and the eight words every senior unit assumes you already know.

en/databases/01-relational-model/01-what.title: What a relation is: tables, rows, keys, and constraints
en/databases/01-relational-model/01-what.summary: The core vocabulary of the relational model — relations, tuples, candidate keys, and why declarative constraints are the model''''s enduring win.

en/databases/01-relational-model/02-cons.title: Constraints, keys, and Postgres data types
en/databases/01-relational-model/02-cons.summary: The five constraint kinds in depth, surrogate vs natural keys, SQL''''s gap from relational algebra, and how picking the narrowest Postgres type is itself a constraint.

en/databases/01-relational-model/03-norm.title: Normal forms, denormalization, and why schemas stick
en/databases/01-relational-model/03-norm.summary: 1NF through BCNF in plain terms, when to deliberately denormalize, the ORM traps that quietly break schema discipline, and naming conventions that pay back across years.

en/databases/01-relational-model/04-json.title: JSONB, arrays, and when a side table wins
en/databases/01-relational-model/04-json.summary: When JSONB and typed arrays are the right choice, GIN vs expression B-tree index strategies, FK at scale, generated STORED columns, and the relational-shortcut pattern that keeps the schema honest.

en/databases/01-relational-model/05-heap.title: Heap storage, TOAST, and column alignment
en/databases/01-relational-model/05-heap.summary: How Postgres stores rows in 8KB pages, what TOAST does to wide values, why column declaration order affects storage size, and how to pick Postgres data types at the byte level.

en/databases/01-relational-model/06-sche.title: Schema integrity: deferral, versioning, and production failure modes
en/databases/01-relational-model/06-sche.summary: Temporal invariants and state-transition enforcement, constraint deferral for complex transactions, schema-as-code with expand-then-contract, and the five failure modes that recur across production schemas.

en/databases/01-relational-model/07-rela.title: Relational vs document, wide-column, graph, and key-value
en/databases/01-relational-model/07-rela.summary: The precise conditions where each data model wins, why Postgres covers more ground than its ''''relational'''' label suggests, the pgsql vs MySQL defaults that matter for schema design, and a design exercise for multi-tenant schema.

en/databases/01-relational-model/project.title: Relational model: design and migrate a multi-tenant schema
en/databases/01-relational-model/project.summary: Design, harden, and migrate a multi-tenant marketplace schema — keys, constraints, normalization, JSONB-vs-side-table calls, RLS isolation, and a zero-downtime column change proven end to end.

en/databases/01-relational-model/quiz-ch.title: Relational model: multiple-choice review
en/databases/01-relational-model/quiz-ch.summary: Multiple-choice synthesis across the relational-model unit: keys, normal forms, JSONB vs side tables, FK at scale, TOAST storage, and zero-downtime schema change.

en/databases/01-relational-model/quiz-sh.title: Relational model: free-recall review
en/databases/01-relational-model/quiz-sh.summary: Free-recall prompts across the relational-model unit. Answer each in your own words first, then reveal the model answer and compare.

en/databases/02-indexes/01-index-anatomy.title: What an index is and how it speeds up queries
en/databases/02-indexes/01-index-anatomy.summary: An index is a sorted copy of column values that lets Postgres skip full table scans. Every index trades write speed and storage for read speed.

en/databases/02-indexes/02-leading-colum.title: The leading-column rule and composite index design
en/databases/02-indexes/02-leading-colum.summary: A multi-column B-tree is sorted by its first column first. Queries that skip the leading column cannot use it. Designing composites around this rule is the central skill in Postgres index engineering.

en/databases/02-indexes/03-partial-expre.title: Partial, expression, and covering indexes
en/databases/02-indexes/03-partial-expre.summary: Three index modifiers that change what a B-tree costs and what it can answer: partial restricts to a row subset, expression indexes a derived value, INCLUDE adds projection columns without affecting the sort key.

en/databases/02-indexes/04-index-types.title: Index types: GIN, GiST, BRIN, Hash, Bloom, and HOT updates
en/databases/02-indexes/04-index-types.summary: Beyond B-tree: when GIN, GiST, BRIN, Hash, and Bloom are the right tool, how HOT updates reduce index write overhead, why fillfactor matters, and why fresh statistics matter more than the index itself.

en/databases/02-indexes/05-index-only-sc.title: Index-only scans, the Visibility Map, and INCLUDE
en/databases/02-indexes/05-index-only-sc.summary: Index-only scans return data straight from the index without touching the heap — but only when the Visibility Map confirms row visibility. This lesson covers the VM, VACUUM, autovacuum tuning, and the INCLUDE clause for covering indexes.

en/databases/02-indexes/06-production-fa.title: Production failure modes and the index audit playbook
en/databases/02-indexes/06-production-fa.summary: The seven most common index failures in production — missing FK index, type coercion, stale stats, bloat, wrong composite order, JSONB cardinality bomb — plus the quarterly audit playbook and per-environment index strategy.

en/databases/02-indexes/07-index-design-.title: Index design exercise: full-text search strategy
en/databases/02-indexes/07-index-design-.summary: A synthesis exercise: choose the right index strategy for a full-text search feature, evaluate tradeoffs between GIN tsvector, pg_trgm, Elasticsearch, and pgvector HNSW, and design indexes for a complete ticketing system.

en/databases/02-indexes/project.title: Indexes: design and audit a real index set
en/databases/02-indexes/project.summary: Hands-on project — design, deploy, and audit the index set for a realistic multi-tenant table, proving every choice with EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) before/after numbers.

en/databases/02-indexes/quiz-choice.title: Indexes: multiple-choice review
en/databases/02-indexes/quiz-choice.summary: Multiple-choice synthesis across the indexes unit — leading-column rule, partial and covering indexes, index-only scans and the Visibility Map, index-type selection, and production failure modes.

en/databases/02-indexes/quiz-short.title: Indexes: free-recall review
en/databases/02-indexes/quiz-short.summary: Free-recall prompts across the indexes unit — answer each in your own words first, then reveal the model answer and compare.

en/databases/03-execution-plans/01-expla.title: EXPLAIN and execution plans: what the planner decides and why
en/databases/03-execution-plans/01-expla.summary: An execution plan is the tree of operations Postgres picks for a query. EXPLAIN shows the plan; EXPLAIN ANALYZE runs it and shows real timings. Rows-estimated vs rows-actual is the most diagnostic number in the output.

en/databases/03-execution-plans/02-scan-.title: Scan types: Seq, Index, Bitmap, Index-Only
en/databases/03-execution-plans/02-scan-.summary: Postgres picks among four scan types based on selectivity and I/O cost. Reading the cost line tells you what the planner assumed and whether BUFFERS confirms it.

en/databases/03-execution-plans/03-join-.title: Join algorithms and the row-estimate cascade
en/databases/03-execution-plans/03-join-.summary: Postgres picks Nested Loop, Hash Join, or Merge Join based on row estimates. When the outer side is underestimated by 1000×, Nested Loop blows up — the algorithm is the symptom, the bad row estimate is the cause.

en/databases/03-execution-plans/04-stati.title: pg_statistic, ANALYZE, and production observability
en/databases/03-execution-plans/04-stati.summary: The planner''''s row estimates come from pg_statistic: MCV lists, histograms, correlation, and n_distinct. ANALYZE keeps them fresh. auto_explain and pg_stat_statements together tell you which queries are slow and why.

en/databases/03-execution-plans/05-exten.title: Extended statistics: fixing correlated-column estimate failures
en/databases/03-execution-plans/05-exten.summary: By default the planner assumes columns are independent. CREATE STATISTICS teaches it about functional dependencies, multi-column n_distinct, and MCV combinations — eliminating the largest class of row-estimate failures.

en/databases/03-execution-plans/06-plan-.title: Plan cache, cost-constant tuning, and planner internals
en/databases/03-execution-plans/06-plan-.summary: Prepared statements switch to a generic plan after 5 executions — a trap for skewed parameters. SSD systems need random_page_cost = 1.1. GEQO handles large joins. JIT helps CPU-bound queries. Each mechanism has a specific failure mode and fix.

en/databases/03-execution-plans/07-plan-.title: Production failure modes and plan stability
en/databases/03-execution-plans/07-plan-.summary: Eight real failure modes — stale stats, generic-plan trap, correlated columns, SSD mis-tuning, JIT overhead, work_mem spill, random_page_cost drift, and plan flips — plus the operational strategy to detect and prevent plan regressions across deploys.

en/databases/03-execution-plans/project.title: Execution plans: diagnose and stabilise a slow query
en/databases/03-execution-plans/project.summary: Hands-on project — provoke a correlated-column row-estimate blowup in a real Postgres, diagnose it from EXPLAIN ANALYZE, fix the cause, and prove plan stability with before/after evidence.

en/databases/03-execution-plans/quiz-cho.summary: Multiple-choice synthesis across the execution-plans unit — reading EXPLAIN ANALYZE, scan and join choice, the row-estimate cascade, extended statistics, and the generic-plan trap.
