en/databases/03-execution-plans/quiz-sho.summary: Free-recall prompts across the execution-plans unit. Answer each from memory first, then reveal the model answer and compare against what the seven lessons taught.

en/databases/04-mvcc-isolation/01-mvcc-b.title: MVCC: why readers and writers never wait for each other
en/databases/04-mvcc-isolation/01-mvcc-b.summary: MVCC keeps every row''''s history so each transaction sees a stable snapshot without locking the rows other people are touching.

en/databases/04-mvcc-isolation/02-row-ve.title: Row versions and snapshots: the on-disk mechanics
en/databases/04-mvcc-isolation/02-row-ve.summary: Every Postgres tuple carries a 23-byte header with xmin/xmax; a snapshot is three numbers that decide which versions are visible — this is the entire mechanism.

en/databases/04-mvcc-isolation/03-hot-up.title: HOT updates and isolation levels: what you gain and what you pay
en/databases/04-mvcc-isolation/03-hot-up.summary: HOT updates cut index write cost by up to 70% when conditions are right; the four isolation levels decide which concurrency anomalies the database prevents vs leaves to the application.

en/databases/04-mvcc-isolation/04-vacuum.title: Vacuum and bloat: keeping the storage tax bounded
en/databases/04-mvcc-isolation/04-vacuum.summary: Autovacuum reclaims dead tuple slots but cannot shrink the file; a long transaction or orphan replication slot pins everything it touched. Understanding the mechanics is the difference between 20 GB and 200 GB tables.

en/databases/04-mvcc-isolation/05-clog-x.title: CLOG, XID wraparound, and MultiXact: deep visibility internals
en/databases/04-mvcc-isolation/05-clog-x.summary: HeapTupleSatisfiesMVCC walks infomask bits before touching CLOG; 32-bit XIDs wrap at 2 billion and freeze at 200 million; shared row locks use a separate MultiXactId with its own wraparound clock.

en/databases/04-mvcc-isolation/06-ssi-an.title: SSI internals and production autovacuum tuning
en/databases/04-mvcc-isolation/06-ssi-an.summary: SSI detects write skew via predicate locks and rw-antidependency cycles; production autovacuum needs per-table overrides, cost_delay=0 on NVMe, and a separate replica analytics policy to keep bloat bounded.

en/databases/04-mvcc-isolation/07-real-w.title: Real-world MVCC failures, deployment patterns, and distributed snapshots
en/databases/04-mvcc-isolation/07-real-w.summary: Long transactions, orphan replication slots, pg_repack, pgbouncer SET LOCAL, idle_in_transaction_session_timeout, Postgres version history 8.3–18, and how distributed systems extend or replace single-node MVCC.

en/databases/04-mvcc-isolation/project.title: MVCC and isolation: diagnose bloat and a write-skew anomaly
en/databases/04-mvcc-isolation/project.summary: Hands-on project — reproduce MVCC bloat and a write-skew anomaly on a real Postgres, diagnose the oldest-xmin pin, fix isolation and autovacuum, and prove it with before/after numbers.

en/databases/04-mvcc-isolation/quiz-choi.title: MVCC and isolation: multiple-choice review
en/databases/04-mvcc-isolation/quiz-choi.summary: Multiple-choice synthesis across the MVCC unit — snapshot visibility, isolation-level tradeoffs, write skew vs lost update, bloat pinning, and XID wraparound.

en/databases/04-mvcc-isolation/quiz-shor.title: MVCC and isolation: free-recall review
en/databases/04-mvcc-isolation/quiz-shor.summary: Free-recall prompts across the MVCC unit — visibility math, isolation anomalies, HOT, oldest xmin and bloat, SSI. Answer from memory first, then reveal.

en/databases/05-pooling/01-why-pools-exi.title: Connection pools: amortising the cost of a Postgres backend
en/databases/05-pooling/01-why-pools-exi.summary: Every Postgres connection forks a heavyweight OS process; a pool caches a small set of open connections so queries never pay the setup cost again.

en/databases/05-pooling/02-pgbouncer-mod.title: PgBouncer session, transaction, and statement modes
en/databases/05-pooling/02-pgbouncer-mod.summary: Transaction mode gives 10–100× multiplexing but breaks SET, LISTEN, SQL PREPARE, and session-level advisory locks; each has a transaction-mode-safe equivalent.

en/databases/05-pooling/03-pool-sizing-m.title: Pool sizing: the (cores × 2) + spindles formula and the two-layer stack
en/databases/05-pooling/03-pool-sizing-m.summary: Postgres throughput peaks at (cores × 2) + spindle-count active backends; client-pool size per worker follows concurrent-requests × db-calls × avg-ms / budget-ms; the layered math keeps both in bounds.

en/databases/05-pooling/04-pool-exhausti.title: Pool exhaustion and idle-in-transaction: the 3 AM failure mode
en/databases/05-pooling/04-pool-exhausti.summary: Pool exhaustion is almost always a hold-time problem, not a sizing problem; idle-in-transaction is the silent killer that drains a pool in seconds and also blocks VACUUM.

en/databases/05-pooling/05-transaction-m.title: Migrating to transaction mode: rollout playbook and PgBouncer 1.21 prepared statements
en/databases/05-pooling/05-transaction-m.summary: A five-step transaction-mode rollout — audit, size, tune GUCs, canary, observe — plus the 2024 PgBouncer 1.21 breakthrough that unblocked prepared statements in transaction mode.

en/databases/05-pooling/06-postgres-proc.title: The Postgres process model and why raising max_connections degrades throughput
en/databases/05-pooling/06-postgres-proc.summary: Each Postgres connection forks a backend via the postmaster; throughput peaks at (cores × 2) active processes and drops non-linearly past that — raising max_connections without a pooler is almost always the wrong fix.

en/databases/05-pooling/07-pooler-landsc.title: Pooler landscape 2026, serverless connection storms, and the full failure-mode taxonomy
en/databases/05-pooling/07-pooler-landsc.summary: PgBouncer vs Odyssey vs PgCat vs Supavisor — when to reach for each; serverless cold-start connection storms; the eight failure modes and how to detect each one.

en/databases/05-pooling/project.title: Connection pooling: tame an exhausted pool
en/databases/05-pooling/project.summary: Hands-on project — front a Postgres service with PgBouncer in transaction mode, induce and diagnose pool exhaustion from idle-in-transaction, then prove the fix with before/after numbers.

en/databases/05-pooling/quiz-choice.title: Connection pooling: multiple-choice review
en/databases/05-pooling/quiz-choice.summary: Multiple-choice synthesis across the pooling unit: process model, PgBouncer modes, sizing math, exhaustion vs idle-in-transaction, and pooler selection.

en/databases/05-pooling/quiz-short.title: Connection pooling: free-recall review
en/databases/05-pooling/quiz-short.summary: Free-recall prompts across the pooling unit. Answer each in your own words first, then reveal the model answer and compare.

en/databases/06-migrations/01-what-a-mig.title: What a schema migration is and why it replaces ad-hoc DDL
en/databases/06-migrations/01-what-a-mig.summary: A migration is a versioned, ordered SQL script that changes the database schema in lock-step with the application code that depends on it.

en/databases/06-migrations/02-add-column.title: ADD COLUMN: instant in PG 11+ vs rewrite in older Postgres
en/databases/06-migrations/02-add-column.summary: A constant default makes ADD COLUMN instant on any table size since PG 11; volatile defaults and NOT NULL without backfill still rewrite or block.

en/databases/06-migrations/03-lock-queue.title: The lock-queue failure mode: why instant DDL can freeze the database
en/databases/06-migrations/03-lock-queue.summary: A waiting ALTER TABLE blocks every subsequent SELECT on the table — a FIFO lock queue turns one slow query into a full-table outage.

en/databases/06-migrations/04-safe-ddl-p.title: Safe DDL patterns: NOT VALID, CONCURRENTLY, and unsafe-op fixes
en/databases/06-migrations/04-safe-ddl-p.summary: Every unsafe DDL has a safe multi-step equivalent; the discipline is to know the mapping and use it instead of the textbook one-liner.

en/databases/06-migrations/05-expand-con.title: Expand-contract: zero-downtime for breaking schema changes
en/databases/06-migrations/05-expand-con.summary: Any breaking change — rename, drop, type-change — decomposes into an expand (add) phase and a contract (remove) phase, each independently deployable and reversible.

en/databases/06-migrations/06-advisory-l.title: Advisory locks, migration tools, and deploy coordination
en/databases/06-migrations/06-advisory-l.summary: pg_advisory_lock serialises concurrent migration runners; migration tool choice (Atlas, pgroll, Prisma, Drizzle) determines how much safety is automated vs manual.

en/databases/06-migrations/07-migration-.title: Migration failure taxonomy and production discipline
en/databases/06-migrations/07-migration-.summary: Nine named failure modes — lock-queue freeze, INVALID index, WAL flood, schema drift — each with a detection signal and a durable fix.

en/databases/06-migrations/project.title: Schema migrations: a zero-downtime column rename under load
en/databases/06-migrations/project.summary: Hands-on project: rename a column zero-downtime via expand-contract on a loaded Postgres table, proving lock-safety, a batched backfill, and both-version compatibility with evidence at every step.

en/databases/06-migrations/quiz-choice.title: Schema migrations: multiple-choice review
en/databases/06-migrations/quiz-choice.summary: Multiple-choice synthesis across the migrations unit: lock-queue freeze, ADD COLUMN rewrite, NOT VALID/VALIDATE, expand-contract, backfill WAL flood, and deploy order.

en/databases/06-migrations/quiz-short.title: Schema migrations: free-recall review
en/databases/06-migrations/quiz-short.summary: Free-recall prompts across the migrations unit. Answer each in your own words first, then reveal the model answer and compare.

en/databases/07-sharding/01-why-sharding.title: Why sharding exists: the single-Postgres ceiling
en/databases/07-sharding/01-why-sharding.summary: Every Postgres instance has hard CPU, storage, and throughput ceilings; sharding is the only path past them — but it multiplies every operational task by the shard count.

en/databases/07-sharding/02-shard-key-se.title: Shard-key selection: hash, range, list, and directory strategies
en/databases/07-sharding/02-shard-key-se.summary: A good shard key has four properties — selectivity, uniform distribution, stability, and availability at routing time. Hash, range, list, and directory strategies each trade different failure modes.

en/databases/07-sharding/03-partitioning.title: Partitioning vs sharding: same word, two different things
en/databases/07-sharding/03-partitioning.summary: Partitioning is single-instance query pruning and retention management; sharding is multi-instance throughput scaling. They are complementary and typically composed in production.

en/databases/07-sharding/04-colocation-a.title: Co-location and Citus: the invariant that makes sharding usable
en/databases/07-sharding/04-colocation-a.summary: Co-location — same shard key means same worker — keeps tenant-scoped joins single-node. Citus''''s table types (distributed, reference, local) and query planner make the difference between single-shard and fan-out queries explicit.

en/databases/07-sharding/05-hot-shard-fa.title: The hot-shard failure mode: detection, isolation, and durable policy
en/databases/07-sharding/05-hot-shard-fa.summary: Hash sharding produces hot shards on skewed key distributions. Citus''''s isolate_tenant_to_new_shard() is the production mitigation; skew monitoring and a tenant-tier policy are the durable fix.

en/databases/07-sharding/06-schema-based.title: Schema-based sharding and multi-tenancy alternatives
en/databases/07-sharding/06-schema-based.summary: Citus 12 schema-based sharding, database-per-tenant, application-level routing, and RLS are four valid multi-tenancy architectures — each with a specific tenant count and isolation-requirement range.

en/databases/07-sharding/07-resharding-a.title: Online resharding, 2PC, and the operational cost of sharding
en/databases/07-sharding/07-resharding-a.summary: Citus 11.1+ online rebalancing uses logical replication for sub-second shard-move pauses. Two-phase commit is necessary for cross-shard transactions but carries stuck-transaction risk. Every operational task multiplies by shard count.

en/databases/07-sharding/project.title: Sharding: provoke and tame a hot shard
en/databases/07-sharding/project.summary: Hands-on project — stand up a Citus cluster, provoke a hot shard on a power-law tenant, isolate it online, and prove the fix with before/after skew and latency numbers.

en/databases/07-sharding/quiz-choice.title: Sharding: multiple-choice review
en/databases/07-sharding/quiz-choice.summary: Multiple-choice synthesis across the sharding unit — shard-key choice, partitioning vs sharding, co-location, hot shards, cross-shard transactions, and online resharding.

en/databases/07-sharding/quiz-short.title: Sharding: free-recall review
en/databases/07-sharding/quiz-short.summary: Free-recall prompts across the sharding unit. Answer each in your own words first, then reveal the model answer and compare.

en/databases/08-putting-it-together-db/p.title: Database track: design and tune a production schema
en/databases/08-putting-it-together-db/p.summary: Capstone: design and tune a production PostgreSQL schema end to end — model, index, read a plan, pick isolation, size the pool, plan a zero-downtime migration, and decide if and when to shard, each with evidence.

en/databases/08-putting-it-together-db/q.title: Database track: multiple-choice synthesis
en/databases/08-putting-it-together-db/q.summary: Cross-track synthesis MCQs: connect schema, indexes, plans, MVCC, pooling, migrations, and sharding into the one decision tree that takes a product from MVP to a sharded cluster.

en/databases/08-putting-it-together-db/q.title: Database track: free-recall synthesis
en/databases/08-putting-it-together-db/q.summary: Free-recall prompts spanning the database track — schema, indexes, plans, MVCC, pooling, migrations, sharding. Answer from memory first, then reveal and compare.

en/databases/08-putting-it-together-db/0.title: The seven acts: from CREATE TABLE to Citus
en/databases/08-putting-it-together-db/0.summary: A single product grows from a 1-table MVP to a 1-billion-row Citus cluster through seven moments of database failure — each one names the trigger, the symptom, and the lever that resolves it.

en/databases/08-putting-it-together-db/0.title: Acts 1–3 in depth: schema, indexes, and planner statistics
en/databases/08-putting-it-together-db/0.summary: The first three acts compound irreversibly — a wrong type is a multi-day migration at 100M rows, the leading-column rule is the most violated principle in the wild, and stale statistics make the planner choose the wrong plan 1000× slower.

en/databases/08-putting-it-together-db/0.title: Acts 4–6 in depth: MVCC bloat, connection pooling, and safe migrations
en/databases/08-putting-it-together-db/0.summary: One long transaction can grow a 200 MB table to 80 GB. A cold-start pod surge can turn 4 ms queries into 4 s timeouts. A single ALTER TABLE can freeze production for eight minutes. All three failures share a root cause: resource starvation from an unbounded operation.

en/databases/08-putting-it-together-db/0.title: Act 7 in depth: sharding, co-location, and the seven-tier tradeoff cascade
en/databases/08-putting-it-together-db/0.summary: Sharding is the last resort — chosen when single-Postgres limits are measured and proven. The shard key is irreversible, co-location determines which joins stay local, and the tradeoff cascade shows why skipping any earlier act makes sharding harder.

en/databases/08-putting-it-together-db/0.title: Observability, anti-patterns, and production triage
en/databases/08-putting-it-together-db/0.summary: USE + RED maps which lever to pull; pg_stat_statements, pg_stat_activity, and pg_stat_user_tables are the eyes. An inherited Postgres at 200M rows, 600 backends, and 40 GB bloat has a three-week triage order — the seven-act model doubles as an emergency protocol.

en/deployment/00-start-here/01-overview.title: Start from zero: what deployment actually is
en/deployment/00-start-here/01-overview.summary: Deployment is turning the code on your laptop into something that runs reliably for strangers on machines you will never touch. This is the from-zero map and the eight words the rest of the track assumes you already know.

en/deployment/01-image-layers/01-overvie.title: Image layers and the build cache: order is everything
en/deployment/01-image-layers/01-overvie.summary: An image is a stack of read-only layers, each Dockerfile step cached by its instruction plus input hash. Order steps least- to most-changing or every source edit reinstalls the world — and a deleted secret still lives in history.

en/deployment/01-image-layers/project.title: Image layers: optimise a real Dockerfile

en/deployment/06-lb-levels/01-overview.title: Load balancing L4 vs L7: what each layer can and can''''t see

An L7 balancer terminates the connection and reads HTTP, enabling path routing and retries at a CPU cost. Pick the wrong layer and path routing is simply impossible.

en/deployment/07-secrets-at-deploy/01-ov.title: Secrets at deploy: where they enter, where they leak
en/deployment/07-secrets-at-deploy/01-ov.summary: Secrets must enter at deploy/runtime, never baked into the image. A Kubernetes Secret is base64-encoded, not encrypted — anyone with read access or a leaked manifest reads it in one second.

en/deployment/08-putting-it-together/01-.summary: Each deploy stage is correct alone, yet the release breaks where two compose wrong: a rolling update with no readiness probe, a blue-green flip over an incompatible migration, an L4 LB that can''''t drain. en/deployment/09-docker-deep/01-containe.title: Container networking: bridges, DNS by name, and the localhost trap
en/deployment/09-docker-deep/01-containe.summary: Containers talk over network drivers — bridge by default. A user-defined bridge adds DNS by container name; the default bridge does not. Publish ports only for outside access, and never trust localhost inside a container.

en/deployment/09-docker-deep/02-volumes-.title: Volumes and persistence
en/deployment/09-docker-deep/02-volumes-.summary: A container's writable layer dies with the container, so persistent data needs a mount: a Docker-managed named volume for databases, a bind mount for dev source, tmpfs for in-memory secrets — each with its own lifecycle and traps.

en/deployment/09-docker-deep/03-image-se.title: Image security and scanning
en/deployment/09-docker-deep/03-image-se.summary: An image ships its whole filesystem as attack surface: minimise the base, drop to non-root, pin by digest, and scan in CI and over time — because a base CVE that was clean at build can turn critical while it sits in prod.

en/deployment/10-k8s-deep/01-services-an.title: Services and ingress
en/deployment/10-k8s-deep/01-services-an.summary: Pods are ephemeral with changing IPs, so you reach them through a Service: a stable virtual IP that load-balances over pods matching a label selector, with Ingress as the shared HTTP router in front. Selector mismatch means zero endpoints.

en/deployment/10-k8s-deep/02-config-and-.title: ConfigMaps and secrets
en/deployment/10-k8s-deep/02-config-and-.summary: Inject config and secrets at runtime, never bake them into the image. ConfigMaps and Secrets feed env vars or mounted files — but base64 is encoding, not encryption, so enable encryption-at-rest and RBAC.

en/deployment/10-k8s-deep/03-probes-and-.title: Probes and resource limits
en/deployment/10-k8s-deep/03-probes-and-.summary: Readiness gates traffic, liveness restarts, startup shields slow boots; requests schedule and limits cap — over-CPU throttles, over-memory is OOMKilled. Set them wrong and a healthy app CrashLoops or gets evicted.

en/deployment/10-k8s-deep/04-helm-intro.title: Helm: charts and values
en/deployment/10-k8s-deep/04-helm-intro.summary: Helm is the Kubernetes package manager. A chart templates manifests with Go-template placeholders; values override them per environment; and install/upgrade/rollback track a named, versioned release that raw kubectl apply never gives you.

en/distributed/00-start-here/01-overview.title: Start from zero: what a distributed system actually is
en/distributed/00-start-here/01-overview.summary: A distributed system is many computers cooperating as one, where the network and machines fail independently. This is the from-zero map and the eight words the rest of the track assumes you already know.

en/distributed/01-cap-practice/01-overvi.title: CAP in practice: consistency vs availability during inevitable partitions
en/distributed/01-cap-practice/01-overvi.summary: Network partitions are inevitable. The only choice you get is to trade off consistency (correctness) against availability (responsiveness) during partitions. PACELC maps this trade-off when the system is healthy, trading latency for consistency.

en/distributed/03-quorum/01-overview.title: Quorums: the R + W > N invariant and how it quietly breaks
en/distributed/03-quorum/01-overview.summary: A quorum is a tunable promise: if read replicas and write replicas overlap (R + W > N), a read sees the latest write. Sloppy quorums and W=1 trade that promise away — and that is where prod loses writes.

en/distributed/04-leader-election/01-ove.title: Leader election: one writer, terms, and the split-brain that fencing tokens stop
en/distributed/04-leader-election/01-ove.summary: A single leader serializes writes so a cluster avoids conflicts — but a GC pause or partition can leave two nodes both convinced they''''re leader. Terms, leases, and a monotonic fencing token are how production survives it.

en/distributed/05-clocks/01-overview.title: Time and ordering: why wall-clock timestamps lie
en/distributed/05-clocks/01-overview.summary: Across a fleet, wall clocks drift and jump backward on NTP sync, so ordering writes by client timestamp silently drops data. Logical clocks order events without trusting the wall; Spanner''''s TrueTime buys ordering with hardware and a deliberate wait.

en/distributed/06-sagas/01-overview.title: Sagas: long-lived transactions across services without 2PC
en/distributed/06-sagas/01-overview.summary: When a workflow spans flight, hotel, and car services, you cannot hold one ACID transaction across all of them. A saga is a chain of local commits, each with a compensating undo — buying availability at the cost of isolation.

en/docker/01-images-and-layers/01-what-i.title: What an image actually is: a config plus a stack of content-addressed layers, not a machine snapshot
en/docker/01-images-and-layers/01-what-i.summary: An image is not a tarball of a running machine — it is a JSON config plus an ordered list of content-addressed read-only layers. The config carries env, entrypoint and rootfs digests; the runtime stacks them and adds one writable layer. This kills the VM-snapshot model.

en/docker/01-images-and-layers/02-layers.title: Layers and content-addressing: diff_id vs descriptor digest, chain_id, and the gzip non-determinism trap
en/docker/01-images-and-layers/02-layers.summary: A layer has two sha256 identities — the diff_id over the uncompressed tar (drives chain_id and overlay dedup) and the descriptor digest over the compressed blob (drives pull). Confuse them and gzip non-determinism stores identical layers twice and shreds cross-runner cache.

en/docker/01-images-and-layers/03-the-oc.title: The OCI image spec: index, manifest, config and layers as a Merkle DAG of descriptors
en/docker/01-images-and-layers/03-the-oc.summary: The OCI Image Spec is the vendor-neutral standard that split from Docker schema2 in 2016. An image is a Merkle DAG of descriptors — index to manifests, manifest to config plus layers — each a mediaType, digest and size. Wrong media types make old registries say manifest unknown.

en/docker/01-images-and-layers/04-docker.title: Dockerfile mechanics: which instructions become layers, how the cache keys each step, and why order matters
en/docker/01-images-and-layers/04-docker.summary: Each Dockerfile instruction is either a filesystem layer (RUN, COPY, ADD) or a zero-byte config mutation (ENV, WORKDIR, CMD, …). The cache keys each step on parent state plus instruction text plus, for COPY/ADD, a file checksum. The first changed step busts every layer below it.

en/docker/02-runtime-internals/01-namesp.title: Namespaces: the kernel view a container is allowed to see
en/docker/02-runtime-internals/01-namesp.summary: A container is a normal process whose kernel-side view is fenced by namespaces. There are 8 types; runc unshares them via clone() flags. PID, mount, and network namespaces do the visible isolation work — and a forgotten PID namespace means nobody reaps zombies.

en/docker/02-runtime-internals/02-cgroup.title: Cgroups: the resource budget the kernel actually enforces
en/docker/02-runtime-internals/02-cgroup.summary: If namespaces decide what a container sees, cgroups decide what it can consume. cgroup v2 controllers meter CPU, memory, pids, and IO. memory.max is a hard wall — cross it and the kernel OOM-kills inside the cgroup; CPU is a quota, not a wall.

en/docker/02-runtime-internals/03-capabi.title: Capabilities and seccomp: why container root is a declawed root
en/docker/02-runtime-internals/03-capabi.summary: Container root is not host root. Capabilities split root's power into ~40 flags — Docker keeps ~14 and drops the rest. Seccomp filters the syscall table, blocking ~44 of 350+ by default. --privileged throws both away, and that is how escapes happen.

en/docker/02-runtime-internals/04-the-co.title: The container lifecycle: from docker run to a reaped exit
en/docker/02-runtime-internals/04-the-co.summary: A container's life is dockerd → containerd → shim → runc. runc sets up namespaces/cgroups, execs your binary, and exits — the shim stays as PID parent. Stop is SIGTERM, a 10 s grace, then SIGKILL; signals only reach PID 1 if it forwards them.

en/docker/03-networking/01-network-names.title: Network namespaces and bridges: what 'docker run' actually wires up
en/docker/03-networking/01-network-names.summary: A container's network is a Linux netns with its own interfaces and routes, joined to the host by a veth pair on the docker0 bridge, with iptables MASQUERADE NATing egress. Knowing the four primitives turns most networking bugs into a one-command diagnosis.

en/docker/03-networking/02-port-publishi.title: Publishing ports and the embedded DNS: DNAT, bind addresses, and 127.0.0.11
en/docker/03-networking/02-port-publishi.summary: Publishing a port installs an iptables DNAT rule rewriting host:port to container:port, scoped by the bind address. User-defined networks add an embedded DNS at 127.0.0.11 resolving names. Most 'works locally but not remotely' and 'name not found' bugs are these two, misread.

en/docker/03-networking/03-container-to-.title: Container-to-container: same host, cross host, and the overlay illusion
en/docker/03-networking/03-container-to-.summary: Containers on one user-defined bridge talk directly at L2; the default bridge lacks DNS. Across hosts, an overlay builds a virtual L2 over VXLAN with a distributed control plane — and the leaks (DNS scope, MTU overhead, hairpin NAT) are where multi-host networking actually fails.

en/docker/04-storage-and-volumes/01-the-.title: The writable layer: copy-on-write, the upperdir, and why container state evaporates
en/docker/04-storage-and-volumes/01-the-.summary: Every container gets a thin writable layer stacked over the read-only image via overlay2. Writes copy-up whole files from lowerdir to upperdir, the layer dies with the container, and unbounded writes (logs, temp files) silently fill the host disk.

en/docker/04-storage-and-volumes/02-volu.title: Volumes, bind mounts, and tmpfs: three ways to escape the writable layer
en/docker/04-storage-and-volumes/02-volu.summary: Named volumes are Docker-managed durable storage under /var/lib/docker/volumes; bind mounts paste a host path straight in; tmpfs lives in RAM. Each picks a different tradeoff in portability, UID semantics, and latency — and getting it wrong loses data or breaks writes.

en/docker/04-storage-and-volumes/03-stor.title: Storage drivers: overlay2, copy-up granularity, and the inode trap
en/docker/04-storage-and-volumes/03-stor.summary: The storage driver decides how image layers stack and how the writable layer copies up. overlay2 is the default; its file-level copy-up, inode pressure, and page-cache sharing are what let you diagnose a node whose disk reads full but du reads empty.

en/docker/05-buildkit-and-cache/01-build.title: BuildKit as a build graph: LLB, content-addressed cache keys, and why a build is a DAG not a script
en/docker/05-buildkit-and-cache/01-build.summary: BuildKit parses a Dockerfile into LLB — a content-addressed DAG of build operations, not a top-to-bottom script. Independent stages build in parallel, and cache hits are decided by the digests of an operation's inputs, not by line numbers.

en/docker/05-buildkit-and-cache/02-multi.title: Multi-stage builds: a fat builder, a thin runtime, and how COPY --from collapses 1.2 GB into 28 MB
en/docker/05-buildkit-and-cache/02-multi.summary: A multi-stage build compiles in a fat builder stage, then a thin runtime stage copies only the artifact. BuildKit builds just the final target and its deps, prunes unreferenced stages, and ships a 28 MB image instead of 1.2 GB — with toolchains and source absent from the layers.

en/docker/05-buildkit-and-cache/03-cache.title: Cache mounts and build secrets: --mount=type=cache keeps downloads warm, --mount=type=secret keeps tokens out of layers
en/docker/05-buildkit-and-cache/03-cache.summary: RUN --mount=type=cache persists a package cache across builds even on cache-miss layers, turning a cold npm/go/pip download warm. RUN --mount=type=secret feeds a credential to one command without writing it to a layer — the fix for the token ARG and ENV bake into image history.

en/docker/05-buildkit-and-cache/04-repro.title: Reproducible builds: SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH, digest-pinned bases, and why a churning layer digest breaks signing
en/docker/05-buildkit-and-cache/04-repro.summary: A reproducible build yields byte-identical layer digests from the same source on any machine. Embedded timestamps, unpinned base tags, and checkout mtimes break it — churning digests and undermining signing. SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH and digest-pinned bases are the levers.

en/docker/06-compose-and-local-dev/01-co.title: The Compose model: a project, a network, and services that find each other by name
en/docker/06-compose-and-local-dev/01-co.summary: Compose turns a multi-container topology into a declarative YAML file: a project namespace, a default network with DNS by service name, named volumes, and a desired-state convergence model. The file is the local environment, not a wiki of run commands.

en/docker/06-compose-and-local-dev/02-de.title: Startup order is not readiness: depends_on, healthchecks, and restart policies
en/docker/06-compose-and-local-dev/02-de.summary: depends_on without a healthcheck orders container starts, not readiness — the API races a database still replaying WAL. condition: service_healthy plus a healthcheck (interval, timeout, retries, start_period) gates on readiness; restart policy decides if a crash heals or hides.

en/docker/06-compose-and-local-dev/03-de.title: The dev loop: overrides, watch/sync, profiles, and not drifting from prod
en/docker/06-compose-and-local-dev/03-de.summary: A productive Compose dev loop layers a base file with an override for live reload (develop.watch sync/rebuild), gates optional services behind profiles, and treats the compose file as the contract that keeps dev from drifting away from prod.

en/docker/07-security/01-rootless-and-us.title: Rootless Docker and user namespaces: why container root is host root, and how to break the link
en/docker/07-security/01-rootless-and-us.summary: By default container UID 0 is host UID 0, so a bind-mount escape writes host files as root. User namespaces remap container root to an unprivileged /etc/subuid range; rootless Docker runs the daemon unprivileged, trading ~20-30% slirp4netns throughput for a smaller blast radius.

en/docker/07-security/02-image-scanning.title: Image scanning: why a fat base ships a CVE backlog, and what Trivy and Grype actually measure
en/docker/07-security/02-image-scanning.summary: A fat base (ubuntu/node) carries 300+ OS packages and a long CVE tail you never call; distroless drops that to single digits. Trivy and Grype match package versions against vuln databases — they find known CVEs in your SBOM, not exploitability, so the lever is shrinking the base.

en/docker/07-security/03-secrets-and-sup.title: Secrets and the supply chain: keeping secrets out of layers, and signing images so they cannot be swapped
en/docker/07-security/03-secrets-and-sup.summary: A secret in ENV or ARG leaks via docker inspect and bakes into a layer; build secret mounts keep it out. An unsigned image can be swapped at the registry; cosign signs the digest, records it in Rekor, and an admission gate refuses unsigned images — the SLSA build-to-admit chain.

en/docker/08-registries-and-distribution.title: The registry pull/push protocol: manifests, blobs, and content-addressed distribution
en/docker/08-registries-and-distribution.summary: A registry is a content-addressed blob store behind a small HTTP API. Pull resolves a tag to a manifest, fetches a config and layer blobs by sha256 digest; push uploads blobs (chunked or monolithic, or cross-repo mounted) then PUTs the manifest. Digests are the real identity.

en/docker/08-registries-and-distribution.title: Tags move, digests do not: pinning and signing for a verifiable supply chain
en/docker/08-registries-and-distribution.summary: Tags move, digests do not: a tag is a mutable label, a digest is the sha256 of the manifest and fixes the bytes. Signing (cosign) binds a claim to the digest, stored as a referring artifact. Deploy by digest and verify the signature, or you trust whatever the tag last pointed at.

en/docker/08-registries-and-distribution.title: Pull-through caches and mirrors: surviving rate limits without serving stale images
en/docker/08-registries-and-distribution.summary: A pull-through cache is a registry in proxy mode: it serves layer blobs locally and only fetches misses upstream. It collapses fleet bandwidth and dodges Docker Hub rate limits — but a moved tag can serve a stale manifest unless tag resolution stays authoritative.

en/docker/09-debugging-containers/01-exe.title: docker exec and inspect: joining a container's namespaces and reading the engine's ground truth
en/docker/09-debugging-containers/01-exe.summary: docker exec joins a running container's namespaces to give you a shell, but it runs as a sibling of PID 1 — not as PID 1 — so a healthy shell can hide a dead app. inspect reads the engine's truth: State.ExitCode where 137 is OOM-kill and 143 is SIGTERM.

en/docker/09-debugging-containers/02-log.title: docker logs and events: the rotation that eats your evidence and the daemon stream that kept it
en/docker/09-debugging-containers/02-log.summary: docker logs replays whatever the logging driver captured from stdout/stderr — the default json-file driver's max-size and max-file silently rotate old lines away. docker events is the daemon's real-time stream: the OOM kill and restart no app log recorded.

en/docker/09-debugging-containers/03-deb.title: Debugging distroless: no shell, no exec — bringing your own tools into another container's namespaces
en/docker/09-debugging-containers/03-deb.summary: A distroless image has no shell, so docker exec sh fails — nothing to exec into. Debug it from outside: an ephemeral debug container (docker debug / kubectl debug) sharing the target's namespaces with its own tools, or read the filesystem at /proc/PID/root.

en/docker/10-production-patterns/01-reso.title: Resource limits and OOM: cgroup ceilings, exit 137, and runtimes that ignore them
en/docker/10-production-patterns/01-reso.summary: A container with no memory limit can OOM the whole node, and a runtime that ignores cgroup limits OOMs itself. --memory sets the cgroup ceiling, exit 137 is the OOM kill, and cgroup-aware runtimes (GOMEMLIMIT, MaxRAMPercentage) keep the heap under it.

en/docker/10-production-patterns/02-heal.title: Health and lifecycle: honest probes, the SIGTERM grace window, and preStop
en/docker/10-production-patterns/02-heal.summary: A health check that pings a port while the app is wedged is worse than none. Honest health means liveness, readiness and startup are distinct, and the SIGTERM → grace → SIGKILL lifecycle with a preStop hook is what makes a rollout drop zero requests.

en/docker/10-production-patterns/03-imag.title: Image slimming: multi-stage, distroless, and layers that pull in seconds
en/docker/10-production-patterns/03-imag.summary: A 1.2 GB image slows every pull, every deploy and every scaler scale-up, and ships a full shell as attack surface. Multi-stage builds plus a distroless or scratch final stage cut it to ~25 MB, shrink the CVE count, and order layers so a code change rebuilds in seconds.

en/docker/10-production-patterns/04-caps.title: Capstone: a mini-PaaS — registry, build, run, health, and zero-downtime rollout
en/docker/10-production-patterns/04-caps.summary: A mini-PaaS ties the whole track together: a registry pins immutable digests, the build ships slim distroless artifacts, run enforces resource limits, honest health gates traffic, and a rolling deploy with maxUnavailable and preStop swaps versions with zero dropped requests.

en/engineering-practice/00-start-here/01.title: Start from zero: what engineering practice actually is
en/engineering-practice/00-start-here/01.summary: Engineering practice is the collection of team habits — commits, tests, CI, review, refactoring, and deploy cadence — that let you change code safely and repeatedly. This is the from-zero map and the eight words the rest of the track assumes you know.

en/engineering-practice/01-tdd-property/.title: Red-green-refactor is a design loop, not a testing ritual
en/engineering-practice/01-tdd-property/.summary: Writing the test first is design pressure, not coverage hygiene. You call your own API before it exists, so a bad interface shows up in seconds instead of after fifteen call sites. The payoff lives in the refactor step teams skip under deadline.

en/engineering-practice/01-tdd-property/.title: Test doubles: London vs Detroit, and the over-mocking trap
en/engineering-practice/01-tdd-property/.summary: Mockist (London) tests assert interactions; classicist (Detroit) tests assert state with real collaborators. Mock the boundaries — network, clock, payment — and use real objects inside. Over-mocking couples tests to call structure: they break on refactor and stay green on bugs.

en/engineering-practice/01-tdd-property/.title: Property-based testing: invariants over examples, with shrinking
en/engineering-practice/01-tdd-property/.summary: Example tests only check the cases you thought of. Property tests assert an invariant over generated input — round-trip, oracle, metamorphic — and shrink failures to a minimal counterexample, finding the .005-class bugs no human enumerates.

en/engineering-practice/01-tdd-property/.title: When TDD pays off and when it actively hurts
en/engineering-practice/01-tdd-property/.summary: TDD''''s return scales with how stable the spec is and how long the code lives. On exploratory spikes and fast-moving UI it taxes you 15–22% to lock in a design you''''re about to throw away. The senior move is spike-then-rebuild, not test-induced design damage.

en/engineering-practice/01-tdd-property/.title: Mutation testing: the honest metric for test quality
en/engineering-practice/01-tdd-property/.summary: Line coverage tells you a line ran, not that a test would notice if it broke. Mutation testing injects bugs and checks your suite kills them — you can hit 100% coverage with a 67% mutation score. Survived mutants are the assertions you''''re missing, at a real CPU cost.

en/engineering-practice/01-tdd-property/.title: TDD: build a suite that would notice the bug
en/engineering-practice/01-tdd-property/.summary: Hands-on project — drive a small domain module test-first, harden it with the boundary rule and a property test, then prove suite quality with a mutation score, not coverage.

en/engineering-practice/01-tdd-property/.title: TDD: multiple-choice review
en/engineering-practice/01-tdd-property/.summary: Multiple-choice synthesis across the TDD unit — design pressure, the boundary rule for doubles, property shapes, the spec-stability tradeoff, and mutation score as the honest metric.

en/engineering-practice/01-tdd-property/.title: TDD: code and test reading
en/engineering-practice/01-tdd-property/.summary: Read real test code — a first failing test, a fragile mock-heavy test, a property, and a surviving mutant — and pick the fix or diagnosis a senior makes first.

en/engineering-practice/01-tdd-property/.summary: Free-recall prompts across the TDD unit. Answer each in your own words first, then reveal the model answer and compare.

en/engineering-practice/02-contract-test.title: The integration-testing dilemma
en/engineering-practice/02-contract-test.summary: Spinning every service up together works for two services and collapses for twenty: e2e is slow, flaky on any hop, and grows ~N² so teams mute it and catch nothing. The test pyramid breaks at the service boundary, where unit tests mock the very thing that breaks.

en/engineering-practice/02-contract-test.title: Consumer-driven contracts: the consumer states the truth
en/engineering-practice/02-contract-test.summary: A consumer-driven contract is an executable spec generated from a passing consumer test, not a hand-kept doc. The consumer declares what it needs against a mock, producing a pact file of interactions published to a broker. The provider is told what to honour, not left to guess.

en/engineering-practice/02-contract-test.title: Provider verification and the broker: replaying the consumer''''s expectations against the real service
en/engineering-practice/02-contract-test.summary: The consumer published a pact; now the provider must replay every recorded interaction and prove each one holds. Provider states set up the data so an interaction is satisfiable. The broker stores pacts plus results and, via webhooks, decouples the two CI pipelines.

en/engineering-practice/02-contract-test.title: can-i-deploy and contract versioning: the deployment-safety gate
en/engineering-practice/02-contract-test.summary: A verified pact proves two versions agree, not that this consumer is safe against what''''s running now. Version pacts by git SHA, record what''''s deployed where, and gate deploys on can-i-deploy — it reads the matrix for your version against the provider actually in the target

en/engineering-practice/02-contract-test.title: Evolving contracts safely and the limits of contract testing
en/engineering-practice/02-contract-test.summary: Break a provider safely with expand-then-contract, let pending and WIP pacts absorb new expectations without failing the build, and know the hard limits: contracts test shape not business logic, need known consumers, and never replace a few real e2e smoke tests.

en/engineering-practice/02-contract-test.title: Contract testing: build the gate and survive a breaking change
en/engineering-practice/02-contract-test.summary: Hands-on project — stand up a consumer/provider pair with a broker, gate deploys on can-i-deploy, then catch and safely ship a breaking field rename via expand-then-contract.

en/engineering-practice/02-contract-test.title: Contract testing: multiple-choice review
en/engineering-practice/02-contract-test.summary: Multiple-choice synthesis across the contract-testing unit — why e2e collapses, consumer-driven recording, provider verification, the deploy gate, and the hard limits.

en/engineering-practice/02-contract-test.title: Contract testing: code and contract reading
en/engineering-practice/02-contract-test.summary: Read real Pact consumer tests, a provider verification setup, and a contract-break diff, then predict the behaviour and pick the highest-leverage fix.

en/engineering-practice/02-contract-test.title: Contract testing: free-recall review
en/engineering-practice/02-contract-test.summary: Free-recall prompts across the contract-testing unit. Answer each in your own words first, then reveal the model answer and compare.

en/engineering-practice/03-code-review/0.title: Code review: what humans catch, what tooling should, and why latency is the real cost
en/engineering-practice/03-code-review/0.summary: Review exists to catch design and intent, not style — automate style. The dominant cost is latency: a PR waiting a day blocks the author. And defect detection collapses past a few hundred lines, so big diffs get rubber-stamped.

en/engineering-practice/03-code-review/0.title: PR size sets review latency and detection at once
en/engineering-practice/03-code-review/0.summary: Big PRs don''''t get more scrutiny — they get less, because attention is a fixed budget. Detection peaks at 200-400 LOC and collapses past it, while large diffs sit longest waiting for a free hour. Small PRs are the one lever that cuts latency and raises quality together.

en/engineering-practice/03-code-review/0.title: Giving and receiving review without the friction
en/engineering-practice/03-code-review/0.summary: A review comment that doesn''''t say its severity or its fix is a guess the author has to decode. Tag blocker vs nit, make it actionable, attack the code not the person. And the author''''s annotations do more for defects than any reviewer — preparation finds bugs before review s

en/engineering-practice/03-code-review/0.title: Automate the mechanical, reserve humans for judgement
en/engineering-practice/03-code-review/0.summary: Every deterministic check a human performs in review is wasted senior attention. Push format, lint, types, and security scanning into a blocking CI gate that runs before review, so the human budget lands on design, intent, and correctness — the things no tool can decide.

en/engineering-practice/03-code-review/0.title: Review anti-patterns and scaling review across an org
en/engineering-practice/03-code-review/0.summary: Rubber-stamps, bikeshedding, the bottleneck reviewer, and the metric trap all fail the same way: review stops being about design. Scaling fixes route ownership, time-box pickup, balance load, and sometimes move review continuous (pairing) or post-commit on a high-trust base.

en/engineering-practice/03-code-review/p.title: Code review: redesign a review process
en/engineering-practice/03-code-review/p.summary: Hands-on project — redesign a real repo's code-review process: add a blocking pre-review gate, a small-PR norm, a severity-tagged comment convention, and latency/outcome metrics, then prove the change with before/after numbers.

en/engineering-practice/03-code-review/q.title: Code review: multiple-choice review
en/engineering-practice/03-code-review/q.summary: Multiple-choice synthesis across the code-review unit — what humans catch vs tooling, PR size and latency, feedback that triages, scaling the queue, and the anti-patterns that invert review's purpose.

en/engineering-practice/03-code-review/q.title: Code review: reading diffs and comments
en/engineering-practice/03-code-review/q.summary: Read real diffs, a PR description, and review comments — spot the design bug a reviewer must catch, judge a PR's reviewability, and rewrite a comment so it states severity and a fix.

en/engineering-practice/03-code-review/q.title: Code review: free-recall review
en/engineering-practice/03-code-review/q.summary: Free-recall prompts across the code-review unit — what review is for, why PR size sets latency and detection, how to make feedback triageable, and how to scale the queue. Answer first, then reveal.

en/engineering-practice/04-trunk-based/0.title: Integration frequency is the lever
en/engineering-practice/04-trunk-based/0.summary: Merge cost is set by how far trunk drifted since you forked, and drift compounds as everyone keeps committing. Integrating daily doesn''''t avoid conflicts — it keeps each one small enough to resolve in minutes with full context, before it becomes a big-bang nobody can review.

en/engineering-practice/04-trunk-based/0.title: Short-lived branches vs gitflow
en/engineering-practice/04-trunk-based/0.summary: Trunk-based means short-lived branches — three or fewer, gone within a day, no integration phase — not no branches. Gitflow suits scheduled shrink-wrapped releases but institutionalizes drift for continuous deploy. Big refactors stay on trunk via branch by abstraction.

en/engineering-practice/04-trunk-based/0.title: Feature flags decouple deploy from release
en/engineering-practice/04-trunk-based/0.summary: Daily integration of long features needs deploy and release split apart. A flag ships unfinished work to production dark — integrated but unreachable — so release is a runtime ramp you can roll back in seconds. Flag types differ in lifetime: release, ops, experiment, permission.

en/engineering-practice/04-trunk-based/0.title: The green-trunk gate is the whole bargain
en/engineering-practice/04-trunk-based/0.summary: A shared trunk means one break halts everyone, so trunk-based needs a fast, blocking CI gate. At scale a naive pre-merge gate races itself, so teams adopt merge queues that test against the projected trunk — but one FIFO queue bottlenecks past ~20-30 devs.

en/engineering-practice/04-trunk-based/0.title: Flag debt and rollout discipline
en/engineering-practice/04-trunk-based/0.summary: Trunk-based trades branch debt for flag debt: a release flag left on after rollout is a long-lived branch hiding in an if, and N stale flags make 2^N untested configs. The discipline that makes it pay off is cleanup — delete the branch on merge, the flag on rollout.

en/engineering-practice/04-trunk-based/p.title: Trunk-based: run one full cycle
en/engineering-practice/04-trunk-based/p.summary: Hands-on project — take a repo through one full trunk-based cycle: ship an unfinished feature dark behind a flag, do a branch-by-abstraction swap, gate trunk green, ramp with a kill switch, and clean up the flag.

en/engineering-practice/04-trunk-based/q.summary: Multiple-choice synthesis across the trunk-based unit — drift, short-lived branches, feature flags, the green CI gate, merge queues at scale, and flag debt.

en/engineering-practice/04-trunk-based/q.summary: Read real diffs and a CI config, predict the trunk-based behaviour, and pick the highest-leverage fix — flag wrapping, branch by abstraction, and the green gate.

en/engineering-practice/05-feature-flags.title: Feature flags: decoupling deploy from release without drowning in flag debt
en/engineering-practice/05-feature-flags.summary: Flags ship code dark and release by toggle, buying gradual rollout and instant kill-switch. The senior cost: every flag is a live branch in prod, and a forgotten one took $440M from Knight Capital in 45 minutes.

en/engineering-practice/06-postmortems/0.title: Blameless postmortems: turning outages into systems you fix, not people you blame
en/engineering-practice/06-postmortems/0.summary: Blame makes people hide incidents, so you lose the learning. A blameless postmortem treats failure as data: timeline, impact, contributing factors (not one root cause), and owned action items that actually ship.

en/engineering-practice/06-postmortems/p.title: Postmortems: write and review a blameless retro
en/engineering-practice/06-postmortems/p.summary: Hands-on project — take a real or seeded incident, write a blameless postmortem end to end, then run a review pass that catches blame language, single-root-cause collapse, and untrackable action items.

en/engineering-practice/06-postmortems/q.title: Postmortems: multiple-choice review
en/engineering-practice/06-postmortems/q.summary: Multiple-choice synthesis across the postmortems unit — blameless culture, contributing factors vs single root cause, action-item quality, the five-whys critique, and learning culture.

en/engineering-practice/06-postmortems/q.title: Postmortems: artifact reading and critique
en/engineering-practice/06-postmortems/q.summary: Read real incident timelines, log lines, action-item lists, and a bad postmortem draft, then pick the senior critique or the highest-leverage fix.

en/engineering-practice/08-debugger-mast.title: Breakpoints and watchpoints: how INT3, the four debug registers, and conditional eval actually work
en/engineering-practice/08-debugger-mast.summary: A breakpoint is either a 0xCC byte patched into code or one of four hardware debug registers. Conditional breakpoints evaluate on every hit and can run 1000x slower. Watchpoints trap a memory address. Optimized builds reorder and inline, breaking line stepping.

en/engineering-practice/08-debugger-mast.title: Core dumps and post-mortem: ulimit, core_pattern, build-id matching, and unwinding a SIGSEGV after the fact

Dumps reach gigabytes. gdb matches the dump to symbols by build-id; a mismatched build gives a garbage stack — the classic works-in-dev, cores-in-prod trap.

en/engineering-practice/08-debugger-mast.title: Production debugging with no repro: perf, eBPF, flame graphs, and why ptrace stops the world
en/engineering-practice/08-debugger-mast.summary: A wedged prod process has no repro and you cannot stop it. Sampling tools — perf, eBPF/bpftrace, async-profiler — observe at 1-5% overhead without halting; a ptrace attach stops the process. USDT probes and flame graphs locate the hot path on a live, untouched service.

en/git/01-version-control-and-the-git-mo.title: Why version control?
en/git/01-version-control-and-the-git-mo.summary: A version control system records a project's full history — what changed, when, by whom, and why — so you can roll back to any earlier state. Copying folders by hand loses authorship, parallel work, and recovery; version control is what fixes all three.

en/git/01-version-control-and-the-git-mo.title: Snapshots, not diffs
en/git/01-version-control-and-the-git-mo.summary: Git stores each commit as a full snapshot of the project tree, not as a chain of diffs. A commit points to a tree, the tree points to blobs, and unchanged files reuse the same content-addressed blob — so snapshots are cheap. A diff is computed on demand, never stored.

en/git/01-version-control-and-the-git-mo.title: The three areas
en/git/01-version-control-and-the-git-mo.summary: Every change sits in one of three areas: the working tree (files you edit), the staging area/index (the proposed next commit), and the repository (history in .git). git add stages, git commit writes the index and moves HEAD, git status maps where each change is.

en/git/01-version-control-and-the-git-mo.title: Install and first repo
en/git/01-version-control-and-the-git-mo.summary: Install git, verify it, then set a one-time identity with git config --global user.name and user.email so every commit has an author. Then start a repo two ways: git init creates an empty .git in place, git clone copies an existing repo with its full history.

en/git/02-recording-changes/01-add-commi.title: The core loop — add, commit, status
en/git/02-recording-changes/01-add-commi.summary: The core git loop is edit then stage then commit. git status shows tracked vs untracked files; git add picks exactly what goes into the next commit; git commit -m records it. Learn the staging area, git add . vs explicit paths, and the -am shortcut and its caveat.

en/git/02-recording-changes/02-reading-d.title: Reading diffs and the log
en/git/02-recording-changes/02-reading-d.summary: git diff shows working tree vs index; git diff --staged shows index vs HEAD; git diff HEAD shows everything since the last commit. Learn to read a unified diff hunk — the @@ header and the +/- lines — and to browse history with git log, --oneline, --graph, and git show.

en/git/02-recording-changes/03-gitignore.title: Ignoring files with .gitignore
en/git/02-recording-changes/03-gitignore.summary: A .gitignore file lists glob patterns for paths git should leave untracked. Learn anchoring, directory and negation rules, the ** wildcard, and the key gotcha: gitignore only affects UNTRACKED files — an already-tracked file needs git rm --cached to stop being committed.

en/git/02-recording-changes/04-good-comm.title: What makes a good commit
en/git/02-recording-changes/04-good-comm.summary: A good commit is atomic — one logical change that stands on its own — with a clear message: an imperative-mood subject under ~50 chars, a blank line, then a body explaining why. Learn Conventional Commits (type(scope): subject) and how to split noisy work into clean commits.

en/git/03-branches-and-merging/01-branch.title: Branches are pointers
en/git/03-branches-and-merging/01-branch.summary: A git branch is just a 41-byte file under .git/refs/heads/ — a movable pointer to one commit. HEAD points at the current branch. That is why creating a branch is O(1) and cheap, unlike systems that copy whole working directories.

en/git/03-branches-and-merging/02-create.title: Create and switch branches
en/git/03-branches-and-merging/02-create.summary: git switch moves HEAD between branches and git switch -c creates one in a single step. git branch creates without switching, -d/-D delete, -m renames, -vv lists with tracking. Uncommitted changes can block a switch; checking out a commit detaches HEAD.

en/git/03-branches-and-merging/03-mergin.title: Merging and fast-forward
en/git/03-branches-and-merging/03-mergin.summary: git merge folds another branch into the current one. If the current branch has not moved, git fast-forwards the pointer with no merge commit. If both diverged, a three-way merge from their common-ancestor merge base creates a commit with two parents. --no-ff forces it.

en/git/03-branches-and-merging/04-merge-.title: Resolving merge conflicts
en/git/03-branches-and-merging/04-merge-.summary: A merge conflict happens when both branches change the same lines. Git writes conflict markers into the file (HEAD vs incoming), leaving the merge paused. You edit to the final content, delete the markers, git add, then commit. git merge --abort backs out the whole merge.

en/git/04-undo-and-rewrite-history/01-re.title: Restore and reset
en/git/04-undo-and-rewrite-history/01-re.summary: git restore discards working-tree edits or unstages files; git reset moves HEAD and can reset the index and working tree. Its three modes — soft, mixed, hard — differ in how far the reset reaches, and --hard is the one that permanently destroys uncommitted work.

en/git/04-undo-and-rewrite-history/02-re.title: Revert — the safe undo
en/git/04-undo-and-rewrite-history/02-re.summary: git revert undoes a commit by adding a NEW commit that inverts it, leaving history intact — so it is safe on shared, pushed branches where reset is not. Reverting a merge needs -m 1 to pick the mainline parent, and --no-commit lets you batch several reverts.

en/git/04-undo-and-rewrite-history/03-re.title: Reflog and recovery
en/git/04-undo-and-rewrite-history/03-re.summary: git reflog records every move of HEAD locally — commits, resets, checkouts, rebases — so you can find and recover work after a bad reset --hard or a deleted branch. Entries expire after about 90 days; git fsck --lost-found finds dangling commits as a last resort.

en/git/04-undo-and-rewrite-history/04-am.title: Amend and interactive rebase
en/git/04-undo-and-rewrite-history/04-am.summary: git commit --amend rewrites the last commit (new SHA); git rebase -i HEAD~N opens a todo list to reword, edit, squash, fixup, drop, or reorder commits before a PR. Both rewrite history — so the golden rule is: never rewrite commits others have already pulled.

en/git/04-undo-and-rewrite-history/05-ch.title: Changing commit author and dates
en/git/04-undo-and-rewrite-history/05-ch.summary: A commit has an author and a committer, each with its own date. Fix the last with --amend --author or --reset-author; set dates via GIT_AUTHOR_DATE or --date; rewrite many with rebase --exec or git filter-repo. A .mailmap fixes displayed names without rewriting history.

en/git/05-remotes-and-collaboration/01-r.title: Remotes explained
en/git/05-remotes-and-collaboration/01-r.summary: A remote is a named reference to another copy of the repo, usually called origin. Remote-tracking branches like origin/main are read-only local mirrors updated only by git fetch. The key distinction: your local main versus origin/main, your last-known snapshot of the remote.

en/git/05-remotes-and-collaboration/02-p.title: Push and pull
en/git/05-remotes-and-collaboration/02-p.summary: git push sends local commits to the remote; git pull is fetch plus integrate. Set the upstream once with push -u origin branch, then bare push and pull work. git branch -vv shows tracking. A push is rejected as non-fast-forward when the remote has commits you lack — pull first.

en/git/05-remotes-and-collaboration/03-f.title: Fetch and integrate
en/git/05-remotes-and-collaboration/03-f.summary: git fetch only updates origin/*, never your work. Then choose how to integrate: pull (merge) makes merge bubbles, pull --rebase replays your commits for a linear history, pull --ff-only refuses to merge when diverged. Merge keeps the true history; rebase keeps it linear.

en/git/05-remotes-and-collaboration/04-f.title: Force-push safely
en/git/05-remotes-and-collaboration/04-f.summary: After rebasing or amending, a normal push is rejected as non-fast-forward. git push --force overwrites the remote and can erase teammates' commits. git push --force-with-lease is safer: it refuses if the remote moved since your last fetch. Never force shared branches like main.

en/git/05-remotes-and-collaboration/05-p.title: Pull requests
en/git/05-remotes-and-collaboration/05-p.summary: A pull request is a platform workflow on top of git: push a feature branch, open a PR, get review and CI checks, then merge. PRs offer three merge strategies — merge commit, squash-and-merge, rebase-and-merge. Review plus CI is the gate before code reaches main.

en/git/06-team-workflows/01-why-a-workfl.title: Why a branching workflow?
en/git/06-team-workflows/01-why-a-workfl.summary: A branching workflow is a team's contract for how code goes from idea to production: which branches exist, what is protected, how releases and hotfixes happen. Four axes — branch count, branch lifetime, release cadence, integration timing — separate the three models.

en/git/06-team-workflows/02-git-flow.title: Git-flow
en/git/06-team-workflows/02-git-flow.summary: Git-flow keeps two long-lived branches — main (released) and develop (integration) — plus short-lived feature/, release/, and hotfix/ branches. It excels at versioned releases and multiple live versions, but its many branches make it heavy for CD; legacy for web apps.

en/git/06-team-workflows/03-github-flow.title: GitHub flow
en/git/06-team-workflows/03-github-flow.summary: GitHub flow keeps ONE long-lived branch — main, always deployable — plus short-lived feature branches: open a pull request, pass CI and review, merge, deploy. No develop, no release branches. Fast for CD web apps, but assumes strong CI, quick review, and feature flags.

en/git/06-team-workflows/04-trunk-based-.title: Trunk-based development
en/git/06-team-workflows/04-trunk-based-.summary: Trunk-based development: everyone integrates to one trunk (main) via very short-lived branches, with incomplete features hidden behind feature flags, not long branches. Needs heavy CI and flags; release branches cut from trunk give versioning. How big orgs avoid merge hell.

en/git/06-team-workflows/05-choosing-a-w.title: Choosing a workflow
en/git/06-team-workflows/05-choosing-a-w.summary: How to pick a branching workflow: weigh release model (continuous vs versioned), team size, CI maturity, feature-flag infrastructure, and repo structure. Web app + CD + small team to GitHub flow; large org to trunk-based; versioned library, desktop, or firmware to git-flow.

en/git/07-daily-power-tools/01-stash.title: Stashing work in progress
en/git/07-daily-power-tools/01-stash.summary: git stash shelves uncommitted tracked changes and gives you a clean tree, so you can switch branches mid-work. pop reapplies and drops the entry; apply reapplies but keeps it. Stashes form a stack you list and drop — but they are local-only and easy to forget.

en/git/07-daily-power-tools/02-cherry-pi.title: Cherry-picking a single commit
en/git/07-daily-power-tools/02-cherry-pi.summary: git cherry-pick replays the change introduced by one commit onto your current branch as a brand-new commit with a new SHA. It is the backport tool — grab one fix without merging a whole branch. Resolve conflicts with --continue/--abort; beware duplicates when you later merge.

en/git/07-daily-power-tools/03-tags-and-.title: Tags and releases
en/git/07-daily-power-tools/03-tags-and-.summary: Tags name a fixed point in history, usually a release. A lightweight tag is just a pointer; an annotated tag (git tag -a) is a real object with tagger, date, and message — use it for releases. Tags are NOT pushed by default; send them with git push --tags. Version with semver.

en/git/07-daily-power-tools/04-worktrees.title: Multiple working trees
en/git/07-daily-power-tools/04-worktrees.summary: git worktree add checks out a second working tree from one repository, sharing a single .git object store. Run a long build or review a PR on branch B while you keep editing branch A — no stash, no second clone. A branch cannot be checked out in two worktrees at once.

en/git/07-daily-power-tools/05-aliases-a.title: Aliases and config
en/git/07-daily-power-tools/05-aliases-a.summary: git config tunes git to your hands. Aliases shorten commands (alias.co checkout, a graph-log alias, shell aliases with !). Settings like pull.rebase and push.autoSetupRemote remove daily friction. Config has three scopes — system, global, local — and the most specific wins.

en/git/08-under-the-hood/01-objects.title: The object store — blobs, trees, commits, tags
en/git/08-under-the-hood/01-objects.summary: Git stores everything as four content-addressed object types: blob (file bytes), tree (a directory), commit (one tree plus parents and metadata), and tag. An object's name is the SHA of its content, so identical content is stored once. Inspect with git cat-file.

en/git/08-under-the-hood/02-refs-and-hea.title: Refs and HEAD — how names point at commits
en/git/08-under-the-hood/02-refs-and-hea.summary: Refs are human names for commit hashes: a branch under refs/heads is a file holding one SHA, tags and remotes live alongside. HEAD is a symbolic ref pointing at the current branch (attached) or straight at a SHA (detached). Committing moves the branch ref and HEAD follows.

en/git/08-under-the-hood/03-how-merge-an.title: How merge and rebase actually work
en/git/08-under-the-hood/03-how-merge-an.summary: Merge finds the lowest common ancestor (merge base), does a three-way merge of base/ours/theirs, and writes one commit with two parents — true history. Rebase replays your commits onto a new base as brand-new SHAs — linear history, rewritten. Same result tree, different graph.

en/git/08-under-the-hood/04-hooks.title: Git hooks — scripts that gate your workflow
en/git/08-under-the-hood/04-hooks.summary: Git hooks are scripts in .git/hooks that fire on events: pre-commit (lint), commit-msg (message format), pre-push (tests), plus server-side pre-receive. A non-zero exit aborts the operation. Hooks are not committed, so teams share them with husky or lefthook.

en/git/08-under-the-hood/05-rerere.title: rerere — reuse recorded conflict resolutions
en/git/08-under-the-hood/05-rerere.summary: rerere (REuse REcorded REsolution) records how you resolved a conflict and auto-replays it when the same conflict reappears — a big win for long-lived branches rebased repeatedly. Enable with rerere.enabled true; resolutions live in .git/rr-cache. Review what it auto-applies.

en/git/09-scaling-and-rescue/01-large-re.title: Working with very large repos
en/git/09-scaling-and-rescue/01-large-re.summary: A full clone downloads every object from every commit. Shallow clone (--depth 1) truncates history for fast CI; partial clone (--filter=blob:none) fetches blobs on demand; sparse-checkout populates only part of a monorepo working tree. Each trades a different cost.

en/git/09-scaling-and-rescue/02-submodul.title: Submodules and subtrees
en/git/09-scaling-and-rescue/02-submodul.summary: A submodule stores a pinned pointer (gitlink) to one external commit via .gitmodules; a subtree merges the external code into your tree. Submodules stay light but track a commit, not a branch; subtrees are simpler for consumers but bulk up history.

en/git/09-scaling-and-rescue/03-rewritin.title: Rewriting an entire repository's history
en/git/09-scaling-and-rescue/03-rewritin.summary: An old committed secret lives in every clone. git filter-repo rewrites all history to strip a path (--path X --invert-paths) or replace text. Every commit hash changes, so you force-push and re-clone everywhere — and a leaked secret must still be rotated: it is already public.

en/git/09-scaling-and-rescue/04-signing-.title: Signing commits and trust
en/git/09-scaling-and-rescue/04-signing-.summary: Anyone can set any author name and email on a commit, so the author field proves nothing. Signing a commit or tag with a GPG or SSH key proves who made it. git commit -S and git log --show-signature verify authorship; the host shows a Verified badge once your key is registered.

en/git/09-scaling-and-rescue/05-disaster.title: Disaster recovery
en/git/09-scaling-and-rescue/05-disaster.summary: When a reset, rebase, or branch delete seems to destroy work, escalate calmly: git reflog finds moved tips, git fsck --lost-found surfaces dangling objects, git cat-file -p inspects them. Aggressive git gc prunes unreachable objects. The only true loss is never-committed work.

en/git/10-putting-it-together/01-a-day-i.title: A day in a real team
en/git/10-putting-it-together/01-a-day-i.summary: The full daily loop on a trunk-based team, end to end: branch off main, make atomic commits, rebase onto origin/main to stay current, push and open a PR, address review with fixup and force-with-lease, then squash-merge and sync. Every earlier unit clicks into one workflow.

en/git/10-putting-it-together/02-inciden.title: Incident: a bad merge
en/git/10-putting-it-together/02-inciden.summary: A bad merge lands on main and CI goes red. Worked under pressure: diagnose with log --graph and show, then revert the merge with -m 1 (never reset shared history), and recover force-pushed commits via reflog from a clone or the server. Revert vs reset, decided under fire.

en/git/10-putting-it-together/03-git-int.title: Git interview fluency
en/git/10-putting-it-together/03-git-int.summary: The mental models a senior git interview really tests, each framed as what they probe plus the one-sentence answer: merge vs rebase, reset vs revert, what HEAD is, reflog recovery, force-with-lease, snapshot-not-diff storage. The whole track, distilled to recall-ready fluency.

en/go/01-language-core/01-types-and-stru.title: Types and structs: value semantics, zero values, and the slice header
en/go/01-language-core/01-types-and-stru.summary: Go copies structs by default — a pointer is an explicit opt-in, and zero values like sync.Mutex work uninitialized. Embedding is composition, not inheritance. A slice is a 24-byte header over a shared array: append within cap silently aliases, past cap it reallocates.

en/go/01-language-core/02-error-handling.title: Errors are values: wrapping, sentinels, and the if err != nil discipline
en/go/01-language-core/02-error-handling.summary: Go errors are plain values: handle every err or discard it on purpose. Wrap with %w so errors.Is/As survive layering — == breaks the moment anyone wraps. Pick sentinel, typed, or opaque errors by how much callers must couple. panic is for bugs; swallowed errors detonate far away.

en/go/01-language-core/03-interfaces.title: Interfaces: implicit satisfaction, the typed-nil trap, and what indirection costs
en/go/01-language-core/03-interfaces.summary: Go interfaces are satisfied implicitly and stored as a (type, value) pair — which is why a nil *T returned as error makes err != nil true, the classic prod bug. Keep interfaces small, accept interfaces and return structs; dispatch blocks inlining and forces heap escapes.

en/go/02-concurrency/01-goroutines-and-s.title: Goroutines and the scheduler: cheap stacks, GMP, and the leaks that outlive requests
en/go/02-concurrency/01-goroutines-and-s.summary: Goroutines start at ~2 KB and grow on demand; the GMP scheduler multiplexes them onto OS threads with work stealing and, since 1.14, async preemption. GOMAXPROCS caps parallelism. The classic failure is the leak: goroutines blocked forever on a channel, found via pprof.

en/go/02-concurrency/02-channels.title: Channels: synchronization points, bounded queues, and the deadlocks between them
en/go/02-concurrency/02-channels.summary: An unbuffered channel is a synchronization point; a buffered one is a bounded queue. Axioms: nil blocks forever, closed reads zero values, send on closed panics. select, fan-out/fan-in, worker pools, context through pipelines — and the deadlock from a forgotten close.

en/go/02-concurrency/03-sync-and-races.title: The Go memory model, data races, and the -race detector
en/go/02-concurrency/03-sync-and-races.summary: Go guarantees behavior only for race-free programs: happens-before comes from channels, mutexes, atomics. Any data race is undefined behavior; benign races do not exist. Run -race in CI (2–20x slower, 5–10x memory). Mutexes guard state; channels transfer ownership.

en/go/03-http-services/01-servers-and-ro.title: net/http as the framework: Handler, the 1.22 ServeMux, and routing without dependencies
en/go/03-http-services/01-servers-and-ro.summary: http.Handler is one method and HandlerFunc adapts plain functions. Since Go 1.22 ServeMux routes by method and {id} wildcards with most-specific-wins precedence and panics on conflicts at registration. For most services the stdlib mux is the framework.

en/go/03-http-services/02-middleware-pat.title: Middleware patterns: chaining, ordering, context, and the ResponseWriter wrapping traps
en/go/03-http-services/02-middleware-pat.summary: Middleware is func(http.Handler) http.Handler composed outside-in: logging outside recovery outside auth. Request-scoped data rides the context with unexported typed keys. Wrapping ResponseWriter to capture status risks double WriteHeader and silently losing Flusher and Hijacker.

en/go/03-http-services/03-timeouts-and-l.title: Timeouts and limits: the zero values that hold connections forever
en/go/03-http-services/03-timeouts-and-l.summary: http.Server ships with zero timeouts: ReadHeader, Read, Write, and Idle all default to infinite, so one slowloris client exhausts connections. Set them, add per-request context deadlines, configure Transport timeouts on outbound clients, and cap bodies with MaxBytesReader.

en/go/03-http-services/04-graceful-shutd.title: Graceful shutdown: Shutdown(ctx), SIGTERM wiring, and why deploys still drop requests
en/go/03-http-services/04-graceful-shutd.summary: Shutdown(ctx) closes listeners, stops accepting, and drains in-flight requests until the context deadline; signal.NotifyContext wires SIGTERM to it. It does not cover hijacked conns or websockets, and in k8s you flip readiness and wait out endpoint propagation before draining.

en/go/04-testing-and-tooling/01-table-te.title: Table tests and subtests: cases as data, t.Run, and why Go ships no assert library
en/go/04-testing-and-tooling/01-table-te.summary: Table tests turn cases into a slice of anonymous structs: one loop, t.Run gives each row a name to filter with -run and parallelize. Failures read as got/want with cmp.Diff; t.Helper keeps traces honest; golden files cover big outputs. No assert in the stdlib — on purpose.

en/go/04-testing-and-tooling/02-fuzzing-.title: Fuzzing and benchmarks: coverage-guided inputs, b.Loop, and benchstat honesty
en/go/04-testing-and-tooling/02-fuzzing-.summary: Native fuzzing mutates inputs coverage-guided from seeds and minimizes crashers into testdata/fuzz as permanent regressions — finding what tables cannot. Benchmarks: b.Loop (1.24) over b.N, ns/op and allocs/op via b.ReportAllocs, benchstat over -count=10 runs for honesty.

en/go/04-testing-and-tooling/03-mocks-fa.title: Mocks, fakes, and interfaces: test doubles without testing the double
en/go/04-testing-and-tooling/03-mocks-fa.summary: Test doubles the Go way: consumers define small interfaces, hand-written fakes beat interaction-asserting mock frameworks, httptest covers the HTTP edge in-process or via a real listener, testcontainers earns its 1–3 s where SQL is the logic. Over-mocking tests the mock.

en/go/04-testing-and-tooling/04-modules-.title: Modules and tooling: MVS, go.sum, workspaces, and the CI toolchain
en/go/04-testing-and-tooling/04-modules-.summary: go.mod requires are minimums and MVS picks the maximum of them — deterministic, no solver, no surprise upgrades; go.sum is a checksum ledger, not a lockfile. replace works only in the main module; go.work wires multi-module dev. CI: vet, staticcheck, -race, drift checks.

en/go/05-generics-and-design/01-type-par.title: Type parameters and constraints: type sets, inference limits, and GCShape stenciling
en/go/05-generics-and-design/01-type-par.summary: Type parameters with constraints as type sets: ~T approximation, unions, comparable. Where inference works and where it stops. Instantiation via GCShape stenciling — value types get their own machine code, all pointer types share one instance plus a runtime dictionary.

en/go/05-generics-and-design/02-when-gen.title: When generics, when interfaces: the decision senior reviewers actually make
en/go/05-generics-and-design/02-when-gen.summary: Interfaces for behaviour, generics for data structures and algorithms over them. The slices/maps packages as the canon, the anti-patterns — generic everything, method-only constraints — and honest performance: value-shape devirtualization vs gcshape dictionaries.

en/go/05-generics-and-design/03-package-.title: Package design: names as API, internal/, dependency direction, and the cycle that blocks your hotfix
en/go/05-generics-and-design/03-package-.summary: Package boundaries as API design: the package name is the prefix of every export, internal/ as the visibility tool, accept interfaces and return structs, why util/common rot, and how cyclic-import pressure exposes a wrong dependency direction — with a refactoring case study.

en/go/05-generics-and-design/04-errors-a.title: Errors as API: sentinels, types, the Is/As contract, and the %w that leaks your internals
en/go/05-generics-and-design/04-errors-a.summary: Errors are part of your public API: sentinel vs typed vs opaque, the errors.Is/As contract you promise, wrapping discipline at package boundaries — %w exports the whole chain — and keeping errors stable across versions so consumers never have to parse text.

en/go/06-runtime-and-performance/01-memo.title: Memory and escape analysis: who decides stack vs heap, and what an allocation really costs
