en/go/06-runtime-and-performance/01-memo.summary: Escape analysis decides stack vs heap at compile time: values that outlive their frame, feed interfaces, or get captured by reference escape. Read -gcflags=-m, know that stacks grow by copy, and remember the real cost of an allocation is GC pressure, not the ~25 ns malloc.

en/go/06-runtime-and-performance/02-gc-m.title: GC mechanics and tuning: tri-color mark-sweep, the pacer, GOGC and GOMEMLIMIT without myths
en/go/06-runtime-and-performance/02-gc-m.summary: Go runs a concurrent tri-color mark-sweep GC with write barriers and two sub-ms STW pauses. GOGC trades heap headroom for cycle frequency; GOMEMLIMIT adds a soft ceiling that can death-spiral near the limit. No compaction, no generations — deliberate choices, not gaps.

en/go/06-runtime-and-performance/03-ppro.title: pprof end to end: CPU, heap, goroutine and mutex profiles from a live service to the leak
en/go/06-runtime-and-performance/03-ppro.summary: net/http/pprof turns a prod service into a self-reporting lab: CPU at 100 Hz, heap inuse vs alloc, goroutine, mutex and block profiles. Read flamegraphs by width, diff heap snapshots with -base to corner leaks, and keep continuous profiling for incidents you did not predict.

en/go/06-runtime-and-performance/04-benc.title: Benchmarking real services: percentiles, coordinated omission, and the optimization loop
en/go/06-runtime-and-performance/04-benc.summary: Microbenchmarks do not predict service latency. Load-test open-loop at a fixed arrival rate, read p99/p999 instead of averages, beware coordinated omission, profile under load, and gate CI on benchstat deltas across many runs — a single noisy run proves nothing.

en/go/07-production-patterns/01-context-.title: Context discipline: cancellation, deadlines, and values that flow down the call chain
en/go/07-production-patterns/01-context-.summary: Context carries cancellation, deadlines and request-scoped values down every call chain: ctx first arg, derive with WithTimeout and defer cancel or you leak timers. Cancellation is cooperative — code must check ctx.Done(). Values carry metadata, never dependencies.

en/go/07-production-patterns/02-configur.title: Configuration without magic: env, flags, files, and a typed Config that fails at boot
en/go/07-production-patterns/02-configur.summary: Parse configuration once at startup into a typed, eagerly validated Config: defaults, then file, then env, then flags. Fail at boot, not at 3am request time. Secrets get a redacting String method; hot reload is complexity most services should trade for a restart.

en/go/07-production-patterns/03-structur.title: Structured logging with slog: handlers, attrs, levels, and the price of every line
en/go/07-production-patterns/03-structur.summary: slog separates API from output: Logger feeds Records to a Handler that writes JSON or text. Typed Attrs avoid boxing, LogValuer redacts secrets, With(request_id) scopes loggers per request. Levels are a contract: Error pages someone. About 1 µs per line — hot loops pay.

en/go/07-production-patterns/04-retries-.title: Retries and resilience: jittered backoff, retry budgets, and circuit breakers
en/go/07-production-patterns/04-retries-.summary: Retry only idempotent work, with exponential backoff plus full jitter to break synchronized herds. Cap retries with a budget or they amplify outages 3x at the worst moment. Per-attempt timeouts live under one overall deadline; circuit breakers stop hammering a downed peer.

en/go/08-data-access/01-database-sql-and.title: database/sql is a pool: knobs, sizing math, and the rows.Close leak that starves it
en/go/08-data-access/01-database-sql-and.summary: sql.DB is a lazy connection pool: Open dials nothing, Ping verifies. Four knobs bound it, each preventing a real outage — unbounded conns melt Postgres, infinite lifetime pins dead failover targets. Size pools against max_connections across all pods, and close every Rows.

en/go/08-data-access/02-transactions-and.title: Transactions pin connections: isolation levels from Go, and retrying 40001 and 40P01
en/go/08-data-access/02-transactions-and.summary: A Tx pins one connection from Begin to Commit — slow work inside a transaction starves the pool. BeginTx asks for isolation; Postgres gives read committed by default, snapshots, and serializable that obliges a 40001 retry loop. Deadlocks return 40P01 — retry the victim.

en/go/08-data-access/03-sqlc-and-wrapper.title: sqlc and the wrapper spectrum: typed SQL codegen, query builders, and honest ORM tradeoffs
en/go/08-data-access/03-sqlc-and-wrapper.summary: Raw database/sql means boilerplate and scan bugs; sqlc generates typed Go from real SQL with compile-time column checks; builders cover dynamic WHERE; ORMs trade explicitness for magic. The generated Querier interface enables test fakes.

en/go/09-grpc-and-apis/01-grpc-and-proto.title: gRPC and protobuf: the compiled contract, HTTP/2 transport, and the balancer that ignored your new pods
en/go/09-grpc-and-apis/01-grpc-and-proto.summary: A .proto file compiles into client and server stubs; field tags, not names, are the wire contract, and tags 1-15 encode in one byte. HTTP/2 multiplexes every RPC over one connection — so an L4 balancer pins all load to one backend — and deadlines propagate across hops natively.

en/go/09-grpc-and-apis/02-contract-versi.title: Contract versioning: evolve by addition, reserve dead tags, let buf breaking guard the wire
en/go/09-grpc-and-apis/02-contract-versi.summary: Protobuf evolves by addition: new fields with new tags deploy in any order because unknown fields are skipped and absent fields read as defaults. Changing or reusing a tag silently corrupts decoded data — reserved retires tags, buf breaking gates CI, a v2 package forks the rest.

en/go/09-grpc-and-apis/03-gateways-and-r.title: Gateways and REST: google.api.http annotations, transcoding limits, gRPC-Web, and the ConnectRPC alternative
en/go/09-grpc-and-apis/03-gateways-and-r.summary: grpc-gateway compiles google.api.http annotations into a proxy translating JSON REST to protobuf RPCs — the internal-gRPC, public-REST topology. Streaming and error mapping are rough edges, browsers need a proxy for trailers, ConnectRPC collapses the stack into plain HTTP.

en/go/10-advanced-concurrency/01-errgrou.title: errgroup as structured concurrency: scoped goroutines, first-error cancellation, and SetLimit
en/go/10-advanced-concurrency/01-errgrou.summary: errgroup scopes goroutines to a region: Go starts children, Wait joins all and returns the first error, WithContext cancels siblings cooperatively — every child must watch ctx.Done. SetLimit adds bounded parallelism; raw WaitGroup offers neither errors nor cancellation.

en/go/10-advanced-concurrency/02-pipelin.title: Pipelines under cancellation: guarded sends, closing discipline, and the canonical goroutine leak
en/go/10-advanced-concurrency/02-pipelin.summary: Pipeline stages connect by channels; every send must select on ctx.Done or the goroutine leaks the moment downstream stops reading. Only the sender closes; fan-in closes after a WaitGroup. Buffers absorb jitter, not imbalance. Stage depth gauges make leaks visible.

en/go/10-advanced-concurrency/03-semapho.title: Semaphores and backpressure: bounding work at every boundary before the queue becomes the outage
en/go/10-advanced-concurrency/03-semapho.summary: Bound concurrency with a buffered-channel semaphore or semaphore.Weighted; when full, block or reject the producer — an unbounded queue is deferred OOM plus latency hiding. Size limits with Little's law (L = λW), align with the DB pool, prefer 503 + Retry-After to melting.

en/go/10-advanced-concurrency/04-deadloc.title: Deadlock postmortems: lock-order inversion, channel-under-mutex, and reading the goroutine dump
en/go/10-advanced-concurrency/04-deadloc.summary: Three deadlock shapes: lock-order inversion, channel send under a mutex, WaitGroup.Add racing Wait. The runtime panic fires only when every goroutine blocks; partial deadlocks show up as stack clusters in the goroutine profile. go test -race finds the racy cousins.

en/go/11-security-and-supply-chain/01-cr.title: Crypto from the stdlib, used correctly: argon2 for passwords, constant-time compares, and the GCM nonce invariant
en/go/11-security-and-supply-chain/01-cr.summary: Passwords get argon2id or bcrypt tuned to ~100ms, never bare sha256. Secrets compare with subtle.ConstantTimeCompare because early-exit equality leaks prefix length. Keys come from crypto/rand; AES-GCM lives or dies on nonce uniqueness — reuse leaks the auth key.

en/go/11-security-and-supply-chain/02-go.title: govulncheck and dependency hygiene: symbol reachability, go.sum integrity, and MVS without surprise upgrades
en/go/11-security-and-supply-chain/02-go.summary: govulncheck reports only vulns your code actually reaches through the call graph — often a 10:1 cut over image scanners. go.sum pins content hashes while go.mod selects versions, MVS never upgrades without an explicit bump, and nightly scans catch new CVEs in old code.

en/go/11-security-and-supply-chain/03-mi.title: Minimal container images for Go: the attack-surface ladder from ubuntu to scratch via multi-stage builds
en/go/11-security-and-supply-chain/03-mi.summary: Every binary in an image is a tool for an attacker after RCE. Multi-stage builds compile with the full toolchain, then COPY one static binary into scratch or distroless — no shell, no package manager, nothing for a scanner to flag. Add CA certs and a nonroot user.

en/go/12-deployment-and-ops/01-static-bi.title: Static binaries and cross-compilation: CGO_ENABLED=0, the missing ld-linux mystery, and build-flag discipline
en/go/12-deployment-and-ops/01-static-bi.summary: CGO_ENABLED=0 removes libc: no ld-linux interpreter, pure-Go DNS resolver, scratch-safe binary. GOOS/GOARCH cross-compiles without a C toolchain until cgo enters. -trimpath makes builds reproducible, -X injects versions, go version -m audits the provenance of any binary.

en/go/12-deployment-and-ops/02-container.title: Containers for Go: GOMAXPROCS vs CPU quota, GOMEMLIMIT vs OOM, and the multi-stage Dockerfile that caches right
en/go/12-deployment-and-ops/02-container.summary: The runtime defaults to host CPU count, so a 2-CPU-limit pod with GOMAXPROCS=64 throttles itself into p99 collapse; GOMEMLIMIT trades GC pressure for OOM-kills. Multi-stage builds with go mod download as its own layer turn the static binary into a tiny, cache-friendly image.

en/go/12-deployment-and-ops/03-healthche.title: Healthchecks and lifecycle: liveness vs readiness vs startup, and the shutdown sequence that drops zero requests
en/go/12-deployment-and-ops/03-healthche.summary: Liveness restarts, readiness routes, startup grants boot grace — checking dependencies in liveness turns a DB blip into a restart storm. Real readiness pings what the service needs, flips off first on SIGTERM, and the whole drain fits inside terminationGracePeriodSeconds.

en/go/13-systems-projects/01-cli-tools.title: CLI tools in Go: stdout is data, stderr is diagnostics, exit codes are the API
en/go/13-systems-projects/01-cli-tools.summary: The Unix contract for Go CLIs: stdout is data, stderr is diagnostics, exit codes are the machine API — 0 ok, 1 failure, 2 usage. Detect a TTY to pick human tables or --json, read stdin like a filter, clean temp files on ctrl-C via signal.NotifyContext, ship one static binary.

en/go/13-systems-projects/02-daemons-and.title: Daemons and signals: no fork dance, the SIGTERM contract, signal.NotifyContext as the one shutdown path
en/go/13-systems-projects/02-daemons-and.summary: Modern daemons never fork: systemd or the container runtime owns the lifecycle. SIGTERM means stop accepting and drain before TimeoutStopSec becomes SIGKILL, SIGHUP means atomic config reload, signal.NotifyContext unifies shutdown, and a second signal exits immediately.

en/go/13-systems-projects/03-os-integrat.title: OS integration: os/exec without injection, atomic rename, advisory locks, fsnotify, and go:embed
en/go/13-systems-projects/03-os-integrat.summary: os/exec with arg slices and CommandContext kills shell injection and hung children; ExitError carries the code. Files: O_EXCL lock files, atomic replace via temp plus fsync plus rename on one filesystem, advisory flock, fsnotify storms on editor saves, go:embed for one binary.

en/js-engine/00-start-here/01-what-an-en.title: What a JavaScript engine is
en/js-engine/00-start-here/01-what-an-en.summary: A JS engine turns source text into CPU work: parse, compile to bytecode, interpret, then JIT-optimise the hot parts — with a garbage collector reclaiming memory underneath. Engine vs runtime, and the map of this track.

en/js-engine/00-start-here/02-the-engine.title: The engine landscape: V8, JSC, SpiderMonkey
en/js-engine/00-start-here/02-the-engine.summary: The four engines that matter — V8, SpiderMonkey, JavaScriptCore, Hermes — share the same adaptive shape: interpreter plus tiered JIT plus GC. Why this track teaches V8, what transfers, and the terminology map across engines.

en/js-engine/01-how-js-runs/01-source-to.title: From source text to AST
en/js-engine/01-how-js-runs/01-source-to.summary: Before a line of code runs, V8 scans UTF-16 source into tokens and a recursive-descent parser builds an Abstract Syntax Tree. The AST is a transient intermediate form — fed to the bytecode generator, then discarded. Parse cost is linear in source bytes

en/js-engine/01-how-js-runs/02-lazy-pars.title: Lazy parsing and the pre-parser
en/js-engine/01-how-js-runs/02-lazy-pars.summary: V8 runs two parsers: the full parser that builds an AST and allocates scopes, and the PreParser that skims function bodies to find boundaries and early errors without building a tree. Functions are pre-parsed on first load and fully parsed only when first called

en/js-engine/01-how-js-runs/03-ignition-.title: Ignition and the bytecode
en/js-engine/01-how-js-runs/03-ignition-.summary: Ignition is V8's register-based bytecode interpreter. Bytecode is far more compact than machine code — its original motivation was memory, cutting V8's code memory roughly in half on mobile. A single accumulator plus a register file

en/js-engine/01-how-js-runs/04-interpret.title: Inside the interpreter loop
en/js-engine/01-how-js-runs/04-interpret.summary: Ignition runs bytecode with a dispatch loop: fetch the opcode, jump to its handler, do the work, advance the bytecode pointer, dispatch the next. The accumulator threads values between handlers, feedback slots fill in as types are observed

en/js-engine/02-values-and-memory/01-val.title: How V8 represents a value
en/js-engine/02-values-and-memory/01-val.summary: Every JS value is one 64-bit machine word that is either a tagged small integer (Smi) or a pointer to a heap object. This tagged-union word is the foundation: a HeapObject's first word points to its Map, and one low tag bit decides which path the engine takes.

en/js-engine/02-values-and-memory/02-smi.title: Smis, doubles, and HeapNumbers
en/js-engine/02-values-and-memory/02-smi.summary: A Smi is a 31-bit signed integer packed into a 64-bit word — arithmetic in one instruction, no allocation. Step outside the Smi range or use a fraction and the number becomes a heap-allocated HeapNumber holding a double. That transition is V8's classic deopt trigger

en/js-engine/02-values-and-memory/03-poi.title: Pointer tagging and pointer compression
en/js-engine/02-values-and-memory/03-poi.summary: The low tag bit distinguishes a Smi from a HeapObject pointer; the engine masks it to dereference. Pointer compression (V8 8.0, 2020) then stores those pointers as 32-bit offsets inside a 4GB cage, cutting heap size by roughly 40%

en/js-engine/02-values-and-memory/04-the.title: The V8 heap and object layout
en/js-engine/02-values-and-memory/04-the.summary: The V8 heap is split into spaces — new space (two semi-spaces, bump-pointer allocation), old space, large-object space, code space, read-only space. Allocation in new space is a pointer bump until the semi-space fills, triggering a Scavenge.

en/js-engine/02-values-and-memory/05-str.title: How V8 stores strings
en/js-engine/02-values-and-memory/05-str.summary: V8 represents strings as a tree of types: flat Seq strings (Latin1 or UTF-16), ConsString (O(1) concatenation node), SlicedString (O(1) substring that pins its parent), ThinString, and ExternalString. Internalised strings compare by pointer.

en/js-engine/03-hidden-classes/01-shapes.title: What a Map really is: opening the hidden class
en/js-engine/03-hidden-classes/01-shapes.summary: A V8 Map is a fixed-size HeapObject describing one object layout: instance size, a DescriptorArray (name → field index, representation, constness, attributes), elements kind, a back-pointer, and transitions. Objects with identical layout+history share it

en/js-engine/03-hidden-classes/02-shape-.title: Transition trees, deprecation, and migration
en/js-engine/03-hidden-classes/02-shape-.summary: Adding a property follows or creates a transition edge to a new Map; the tree branches by addition order, by elements-kind change, and by field-representation generalization. When a representation must widen across instances

en/js-engine/03-hidden-classes/03-proper.title: Fast properties, slow properties, and slack tracking
en/js-engine/03-hidden-classes/03-proper.summary: Three storage modes: in-object properties (inline in the body, single load), out-of-object fast properties (PropertyArray, +1 dereference), and dictionary mode (NameDictionary hashmap, ~50-100 cycles, set by deletes or too many props).

en/js-engine/03-hidden-classes/04-inline.title: Inline caches, deeply: feedback slots and handlers
en/js-engine/03-hidden-classes/04-inline.summary: An IC lives in a feedback-vector slot on the function; a load IC caches {map → handler}. A handler is a Smi-encoded field index for a simple in-object load, or a richer handler object for accessors, prototype, or dictionary loads.

en/js-engine/03-hidden-classes/05-mono-p.title: Monomorphic, polymorphic, megamorphic — and the stub cache
en/js-engine/03-hidden-classes/05-mono-p.summary: The IC state machine: uninitialized → premonomorphic → monomorphic (1 map) → polymorphic (2-4 maps, a scanned list) → megamorphic (≥5 maps, consult the global megamorphic stub cache, a hash probe far slower and JIT-hostile). Prototype ICs use validity cells.

en/js-engine/04-the-jit/01-tiers-and-war.title: Four tiers and how warm-up works
en/js-engine/04-the-jit/01-tiers-and-war.summary: V8 runs four execution tiers — Ignition, Sparkplug, Maglev, TurboFan — that trade compile cost for run speed. How invocation counts and loop back-edges drive tier-up, and why higher tiers compile concurrently on background threads.

en/js-engine/04-the-jit/02-type-feedback.title: Type feedback: the fuel for the optimiser
en/js-engine/04-the-jit/02-type-feedback.summary: An optimiser is useless without runtime type information. How the feedback vector records, per IC site, the maps, primitive-type lattice, call targets, and binary-op types the interpreter observes — and why garbage feedback produces generic code or no optimisation at all.

en/js-engine/04-the-jit/03-turbofan.title: TurboFan: the sea-of-nodes optimiser
en/js-engine/04-the-jit/03-turbofan.summary: TurboFan represents code as a sea-of-nodes graph — value, effect, and control edges — instead of a statement CFG, freeing the scheduler to place computation late. The full phase pipeline from bytecode and feedback to register allocation and code generation.

en/js-engine/04-the-jit/04-speculative-o.title: Speculation and guards
en/js-engine/04-the-jit/04-speculative-o.summary: TurboFan bakes optimistic assumptions from feedback into fast code, protected by cheap guards — CheckMaps, CheckSmi, CheckBounds, CheckString. How guards gate the fast path, how inlining fuses small callees

en/js-engine/04-the-jit/05-deoptimizatio.title: Deoptimization: falling off the cliff
en/js-engine/04-the-jit/05-deoptimizatio.summary: Deopt abandons optimised machine code and resumes in Ignition at the exact bytecode offset. Eager vs lazy deopt, the frame-translation mechanism that reconstructs the interpreter frame, the catastrophic deopt-loop, and the triggers and flags to diagnose it.

en/js-engine/04-the-jit/06-osr.title: On-Stack Replacement: swapping the frame mid-loop
en/js-engine/04-the-jit/06-osr.summary: A function called once but containing a long hot loop never returns to be re-entered, so normal tier-up can't speed it up. OSR swaps the executing frame in flight

en/js-engine/05-closures-scope/01-scope-.title: Scopes, contexts, and the scope chain
en/js-engine/05-closures-scope/01-scope-.summary: Lexical scoping is identifier resolution along a chain of scopes. V8 describes scopes at compile time with ScopeInfo and materialises only the captured ones at runtime as heap Context objects linked by outer pointers — most loads resolve to a fixed (depth, slot).

en/js-engine/05-closures-scope/02-closur.title: What a closure actually retains
en/js-engine/05-closures-scope/02-closur.summary: A closure is a function plus a pointer to its Context. That Context keeps every context-allocated variable alive — including ones the closure never reads — because sibling closures share one Context. The canonical closure leak, and how to break it.

en/js-engine/05-closures-scope/03-contex.title: When V8 allocates a Context (and what it costs)
en/js-engine/05-closures-scope/03-contex.summary: V8 allocates a Context only when an inner function captures a variable; otherwise variables stay in registers, free. A let loop whose body captures the binding allocates a fresh Context per iteration — real cost in hot loops. How to minimise captures.

en/js-engine/05-closures-scope/04-call-s.title: Closures, feedback vectors, and call-site polymorphism
en/js-engine/05-closures-scope/04-call-s.summary: Every closure instance has its own feedback vector but shares bytecode via SharedFunctionInfo. A call through a variable forms a call IC recording targets: monomorphic for one callee, megamorphic for many. A hot dispatcher fed many function identities can't be inlined.

en/js-engine/06-garbage-collection/01-wh.title: Why a GC, and reachability
en/js-engine/06-garbage-collection/01-wh.summary: You never free memory in JavaScript — you make objects unreachable. V8 uses a tracing GC: from a fixed set of roots it marks everything transitively reachable; the rest is garbage. Tracing vs reference counting, and why liveness is reachability.

en/js-engine/06-garbage-collection/02-ge.title: Generational GC and the Scavenger
en/js-engine/06-garbage-collection/02-ge.summary: Most objects die young, so V8 splits the heap by age. New space is two semi-spaces collected by the Scavenger using Cheney's copying algorithm: copy survivors, flip the spaces, promote two-time survivors to old space. Orinoco makes it parallel.

en/js-engine/06-garbage-collection/03-ma.title: Major GC: mark, sweep, compact
en/js-engine/06-garbage-collection/03-ma.summary: Old space is collected by mark-sweep-compact. Marking uses the tri-color abstraction (white/grey/black) and runs incrementally and concurrently to shrink the stop-the-world window; sweeping reclaims white objects into free lists

en/js-engine/06-garbage-collection/04-wr.title: Write barriers: the price of incremental and generational GC
en/js-engine/06-garbage-collection/04-wr.summary: Every pointer store into a heap object runs a write barrier. It serves two masters: a generational barrier records old→young pointers into a remembered set so minor GC need not scan old space

en/js-engine/06-garbage-collection/05-me.title: Leaks in a garbage-collected language
en/js-engine/06-garbage-collection/05-me.summary: A leak here is unintended retention: a live reference keeps a dead-in-spirit object reachable. A field guide to the real causes — timers, listeners, growing caches, closures pinning a Context, detached DOM, sliced strings, globals

en/js-engine/06-garbage-collection/06-me.title: Measuring the heap
en/js-engine/06-garbage-collection/06-me.summary: The tools that turn 'memory keeps climbing' into a named retainer: heap snapshots (shallow vs retained size, dominators, the three-snapshot diff), allocation timelines, process.memoryUsage(), --trace-gc, v8.getHeapStatistics(), --max-old-space-size

en/js-engine/07-async-deep/01-event-loop.title: The engine vs the loop
en/js-engine/07-async-deep/01-event-loop.summary: The engine has no event loop — the host (browser, Node via libuv) owns it. What the engine provides is the microtask queue and one operation: PerformMicrotaskCheckpoint. The host runs a task; on return the engine drains microtasks.

en/js-engine/07-async-deep/02-microtasks.title: Microtasks vs macrotasks: ordering
en/js-engine/07-async-deep/02-microtasks.summary: One macrotask runs per loop turn; the entire microtask queue drains after each macrotask and whenever the JS stack empties. A microtask that enqueues a microtask runs in the same drain — the root of starvation. Plus Node's process.nextTick ordering.

en/js-engine/07-async-deep/03-promise-in.title: Inside a Promise
en/js-engine/07-async-deep/03-promise-in.summary: A Promise is a settle-once state machine holding a state, a value, and a list of PromiseReaction records. .then registers reactions and returns a new promise; settling enqueues a PromiseReactionJob per reaction. Resolving with a thenable costs an extra tick.

en/js-engine/07-async-deep/04-async-awai.title: async/await, desugared
en/js-engine/07-async-deep/04-async-awai.summary: An async function returns a promise; await suspends it, wraps the operand via PromiseResolve, and resumes via a microtask when the operand settles — a generator plus a driver. V8 7.2 (2018) removed await's extra ticks for native promises

en/js-engine/08-measuring-optimizing/01-.title: Tracing optimization and deopt
en/js-engine/08-measuring-optimizing/01-.summary: The practitioner toolbox for watching V8 optimise and bail out: --trace-opt, --trace-deopt, --trace-ic, --print-bytecode, --allow-natives-syntax (%OptimizeFunctionOnNextCall, %GetOptimizationStatus), and node --prof / --cpu-prof. How to read a deopt line and name the cause.

en/js-engine/08-measuring-optimizing/02-.title: Monomorphism discipline
en/js-engine/08-measuring-optimizing/02-.summary: The actionable checklist that ties the track together: build objects with fields in a fixed order, never delete, keep arrays one element kind, pass consistently-shaped arguments to hot functions, keep numbers in Smi range, and avoid megamorphic dispatch

en/js-engine/08-measuring-optimizing/03-.title: Why your microbenchmark lies
en/js-engine/08-measuring-optimizing/03-.summary: The traps that make microbenchmarks report fantasy numbers: dead-code elimination, constant folding and hoisting, un-accounted JIT warm-up, OSR mid-measure, GC noise, console.log/try-catch deopts in the timed region, and micro-vs-macro mismatch

en/js-engine/08-measuring-optimizing/04-.title: Real-world wins
en/js-engine/08-measuring-optimizing/04-.summary: Five case studies that tie the whole track together: a JSON ingest path made megamorphic, a numeric pipeline boxed into HeapNumbers, GC churn from per-request allocation, a deopt loop from polymorphic args, and microtask starvation stalling a render — each as symptom

en/js-engine/09-putting-it-together/01-c.title: Capstone: optimize a hot path
en/js-engine/09-putting-it-together/01-c.summary: One slow request handler, every layer of the engine in play. Profile it, read the deopt and IC traces, fix the shape, the boxing, the GC churn, and the microtask stall — then prove the win. The whole track, applied to one function.

en/linux/01-what-is-linux/01-kernel-and-.title: Kernel and userland
en/linux/01-what-is-linux/01-kernel-and-.summary: The kernel runs in ring 0 and owns every CPU, memory page, and device. Your programs run in ring 3 and can only touch hardware by asking the kernel via a syscall — a deliberate, auditable crossing of the privilege boundary.

en/linux/01-what-is-linux/02-distributio.title: Distributions
en/linux/01-what-is-linux/02-distributio.summary: A Linux distro is the same kernel wrapped in different userland choices: GNU coreutils, a C library, a package manager, and defaults. Debian/Ubuntu, RHEL/Fedora, and Arch share the kernel but differ in package format, release cadence, and philosophy.

en/linux/01-what-is-linux/03-filesystem-.title: The filesystem hierarchy
en/linux/01-what-is-linux/03-filesystem-.summary: Linux has one filesystem tree rooted at /. The Filesystem Hierarchy Standard assigns a purpose to each top-level directory: /etc for config, /var for mutable state, /proc and /sys for live kernel data. Everything — including devices and kernel tunables — is a file.

en/linux/01-what-is-linux/04-proc-and-sy.title: procfs and sysfs
en/linux/01-what-is-linux/04-proc-and-sy.summary: /proc and /sys are virtual filesystems the kernel generates on demand in RAM — no bytes on disk. They expose live process tables, memory maps, CPU info, and hardware tunables as ordinary files you can cat, grep, and in /sys even write to change kernel behavior at runtime.

en/linux/02-boot-and-init/01-the-boot-se.title: The boot sequence
en/linux/02-boot-and-init/01-the-boot-se.summary: Linux boots in a strict chain: firmware → bootloader → kernel → initramfs → PID 1. Each stage hands control to the next with a specific handoff. Knowing where the chain breaks tells you exactly how to recover a box that will not boot.

en/linux/02-boot-and-init/02-grub.title: GRUB — the bootloader
en/linux/02-boot-and-init/02-grub.summary: GRUB is the bootloader on Debian/Ubuntu. Its config is generated from /etc/default/grub by update-grub. At boot you can edit the kernel command line to recover a broken system — adding init=/bin/bash or removing "quiet" unlocks the single most powerful recovery tool in Linux.

en/linux/02-boot-and-init/03-pid1-and-in.title: PID 1 and init
en/linux/02-boot-and-init/03-pid1-and-in.summary: PID 1 is the root of every process. It cannot be killed with SIGKILL — if it dies, the kernel panics. Its jobs: orphan reaping, service supervision, bringing the system to a target state. systemd replaced SysV init by making dependencies explicit and parallel.

en/linux/02-boot-and-init/04-targets-and.title: Targets and runlevels
en/linux/02-boot-and-init/04-targets-and.summary: systemd targets are named synchronization points that group units — multi-user.target is a normal server, graphical.target adds a desktop. rescue.target and emergency.target are recovery modes. systemctl isolate switches the running system to a different target immediately.

en/linux/03-systemd-and-services/01-unit.title: Units and systemctl
en/linux/03-systemd-and-services/01-unit.summary: systemd manages everything through units — typed objects with declared dependencies. systemctl is the tool to inspect, start, stop, enable, and disable them. Enabled means start at boot; active means running right now.

en/linux/03-systemd-and-services/02-writ.title: Writing a service unit file
en/linux/03-systemd-and-services/02-writ.summary: A systemd service unit has three sections: [Unit] for metadata and deps, [Service] for process config, [Install] for boot-time wiring. ExecStart, Type, Restart, User, and WorkingDirectory are the five knobs you will set on every service you write.

en/linux/03-systemd-and-services/03-depe.title: Dependencies and ordering
en/linux/03-systemd-and-services/03-depe.summary: Wants/Requires declare what must exist; After/Before declare what must come first. They are orthogonal — you can have ordering without dependency and dependency without ordering. Most bugs come from confusing the two.

en/linux/03-systemd-and-services/04-sock.title: Socket activation and custom targets
en/linux/03-systemd-and-services/04-sock.summary: Socket activation lets systemd hold a socket open while the service starts lazily on first connection — enabling zero-downtime restarts and faster boots. Custom targets group related services into a named synchronisation point you can activate, isolate, or depend on.

en/linux/04-package-management/01-apt-an.title: apt and repositories
en/linux/04-package-management/01-apt-an.summary: apt is the Debian package front-end. apt update refreshes the local index; apt upgrade installs newer versions; apt install fetches and wires up a package. Repositories are signed with GPG — installing from an unsigned repo is a security decision, not an option.

en/linux/04-package-management/02-dpkg-i.title: dpkg internals
en/linux/04-package-management/02-dpkg-i.summary: dpkg is the low-level engine under apt. A .deb file is a two-archive bundle: control.tar with metadata and maintainer scripts, data.tar with the actual files. dpkg -i/-l/-L/-S query and manipulate the local package database at /var/lib/dpkg.

en/linux/04-package-management/03-depend.title: Dependencies, holds, and pinning
en/linux/04-package-management/03-depend.summary: Debian packages declare Depends, Recommends, Suggests, and Conflicts. apt resolves the full dependency graph before touching disk. Holds freeze a package at its current version; pinning controls which repository version wins when multiple sources provide the same package.

en/linux/04-package-management/04-dnf-an.title: dnf and the RHEL side
en/linux/04-package-management/04-dnf-an.summary: RHEL/Fedora uses the same two-layer model as Debian: dnf is the front-end, rpm is the low-level engine. Repository config lives in /etc/yum.repos.d/. Every apt command has a dnf parallel — learning the mapping makes you effective on both distro families.

en/linux/05-users-groups-pam/01-passwd-a.title: passwd and shadow
en/linux/05-users-groups-pam/01-passwd-a.summary: Every Linux process runs as a UID. /etc/passwd maps UIDs to usernames and shells; /etc/shadow holds the actual password hash and aging policy. Understanding the split — and the hash format — is how you reason about identity and credential storage.

en/linux/05-users-groups-pam/02-permissi.title: permissions deeper
en/linux/05-users-groups-pam/02-permissi.summary: Beyond rwx: setuid makes a binary run as its owner; setgid on a directory forces group inheritance; sticky on /tmp stops users deleting others files. umask gates default permissions, and POSIX ACLs grant per-user access that the nine-bit model cannot express.

en/linux/05-users-groups-pam/03-sudo-and.title: sudo and privilege
en/linux/05-users-groups-pam/03-sudo-and.summary: sudo is a policy engine: sudoers rules decide who may run what command as whom. visudo is the only safe editor. NOPASSWD is a deliberate tradeoff. su swaps your entire identity; sudo elevates for a single command. Least privilege: grant exactly what is needed.

en/linux/05-users-groups-pam/04-pam-and-.title: PAM and login
en/linux/05-users-groups-pam/04-pam-and-.summary: PAM is the authentication middleware between programs (sshd, login, sudo) and the actual authentication mechanism. The stack has four groups: auth, account, password, session. Control flags (required/requisite/sufficient) determine whether a failure is fatal or skippable.

en/linux/06-filesystems-and-mounts/01-bl.title: Block devices and partitions
en/linux/06-filesystems-and-mounts/01-bl.summary: A block device is a disk exposed as a file in /dev. lsblk shows the tree of devices and partitions. A partition is just a byte range on the device — GPT and MBR are the two schemes that record where those ranges start and end.

en/linux/06-filesystems-and-mounts/02-fi.title: Filesystems
en/linux/06-filesystems-and-mounts/02-fi.summary: A filesystem maps filenames and directories onto disk blocks. ext4 is the safe default; xfs scales for large files; btrfs adds copy-on-write and snapshots. Inodes store metadata — and you can run out of inodes while the disk still has free space.

en/linux/06-filesystems-and-mounts/03-mo.title: Mounting
en/linux/06-filesystems-and-mounts/03-mo.summary: Mounting grafts a filesystem into the single Linux directory tree at a chosen path. Mount options like ro, noexec, and nosuid add security constraints. Bind mounts expose an existing directory at a second path. findmnt and /proc/mounts show what is mounted.

en/linux/06-filesystems-and-mounts/04-fs.title: fstab and boot mounts
en/linux/06-filesystems-and-mounts/04-fs.summary: /etc/fstab records which filesystems to mount at boot: device, mount point, fstype, options, dump, and pass. Use UUID not /dev names — device names shift when disks are added. A bad fstab line drops the system to emergency mode; nofail prevents this for non-critical mounts.

en/linux/07-storage-and-lvm/01-why-lvm.title: Why LVM
en/linux/07-storage-and-lvm/01-why-lvm.summary: LVM places three layers between raw disks and filesystems: physical volumes (PV) pool disk space, volume groups (VG) aggregate PVs, and logical volumes (LV) carve out named slices. This indirection lets you resize, span, and move data without repartitioning.

en/linux/07-storage-and-lvm/02-growing-a.title: Growing LVs and LVM snapshots
en/linux/07-storage-and-lvm/02-growing-a.summary: Growing an LV online requires lvextend (to grow the block device) then resize2fs or xfs_growfs (to grow the filesystem) — order matters. LVM snapshots are copy-on-write point-in-time views ideal for consistent backups. A snapshot that fills up silently becomes invalid.

en/linux/07-storage-and-lvm/03-raid-basi.title: RAID basics with mdadm
en/linux/07-storage-and-lvm/03-raid-basi.summary: mdadm manages Linux software RAID arrays. RAID 0 stripes for speed (zero redundancy), RAID 1 mirrors for safety, RAID 5/6 use parity to tolerate 1/2 disk failures, RAID 10 combines both. RAID is not a backup — it protects against hardware failure, not data loss.

en/linux/07-storage-and-lvm/04-disk-fail.title: Disk failure and RAID recovery
en/linux/07-storage-and-lvm/04-disk-fail.summary: When a disk fails in RAID 1/5, the array degrades but keeps running. Recovery is: spot the failure in /proc/mdstat, mark the disk failed, remove it, hot-add the replacement, and monitor the rebuild. The rebuild window is when second-failure risk is highest.

en/linux/08-processes-and-resources/01-p.title: Process lifecycle
en/linux/08-processes-and-resources/01-p.summary: Every Linux process is born via fork() (clone the parent) then exec() (replace with a new program). The parent must call wait() to reap the child; a child whose parent never waits becomes a zombie. Orphans are reparented to PID 1.

en/linux/08-processes-and-resources/02-s.title: Signals — deeper
en/linux/08-processes-and-resources/02-s.summary: Signals are asynchronous notifications the kernel delivers to a process. SIGTERM is catchable and asks for graceful shutdown; SIGKILL is uncatchable and forces immediate termination. A D-state process ignores even SIGKILL.

en/linux/08-processes-and-resources/03-c.title: cgroups and resource limits
en/linux/08-processes-and-resources/03-c.summary: cgroups v2 cap CPU and memory for groups of processes; systemd slices use MemoryMax and CPUQuota to set those caps. rlimits (ulimit) cap per-process resources. The two mechanisms are complementary: rlimits are per-process, cgroups are per-group.

en/linux/08-processes-and-resources/04-t.title: The OOM killer
en/linux/08-processes-and-resources/04-t.summary: When physical memory is exhausted the kernel OOM killer picks a victim by oom_score and kills it. oom_score_adj biases selection. A cgroup MemoryMax triggers a cgroup-local OOM before system memory runs out. The kill shows in dmesg and journalctl.

en/linux/09-networking/01-interfaces-and.title: Interfaces and ip
en/linux/09-networking/01-interfaces-and.summary: The iproute2 suite — ip addr, ip link, ss — replaced legacy ifconfig/netstat. Predictable interface names (ens3, enp2s0) survive reboots; loopback (lo) is always present. ss -tlnp shows what is listening and which process owns it.

en/linux/09-networking/02-routing.title: Routing
en/linux/09-networking/02-routing.summary: The routing table is the kernel data structure that decides which interface and next-hop a packet uses. ip route shows it, ip route get asks the kernel which route wins for a specific destination, and the default route (0.0.0.0/0) is the catch-all gateway.

en/linux/09-networking/03-dns-resolution.title: DNS resolution
en/linux/09-networking/03-dns-resolution.summary: Name resolution follows the nsswitch hosts: line — files then dns by default. /etc/hosts is checked first; /etc/resolv.conf (or systemd-resolved at 127.0.0.53) provides the DNS server. getent follows nsswitch; dig bypasses it and talks directly to a nameserver.

en/linux/09-networking/04-firewalls-nfta.title: Firewalls and nftables
en/linux/09-networking/04-firewalls-nfta.summary: nftables organises rules into tables and chains hooked into netfilter points (input, forward, output). A default-deny inbound policy drops everything unless explicitly permitted. firewalld is a higher-level manager over the same nftables kernel subsystem.

en/linux/10-logs-and-journald/01-journal.title: journald and journalctl
en/linux/10-logs-and-journald/01-journal.summary: journald is systemd's structured, indexed binary log store. journalctl queries it by unit (-u), priority (-p), boot (-b), and follows live with -f. Structured fields like _SYSTEMD_UNIT, PRIORITY, and _PID make filtering precise in a way plain-text logs never were.

en/linux/10-logs-and-journald/02-persist.title: Persistent journals and log rotation
en/linux/10-logs-and-journald/02-persist.summary: By default journald is volatile: logs vanish on reboot unless Storage=persistent is set in journald.conf. SystemMaxUse caps disk use. journalctl --vacuum-size/--vacuum-time trims old data. logrotate handles the plain-text logs apps still write to /var/log.

en/linux/10-logs-and-journald/03-syslog-.title: Syslog and rsyslog
en/linux/10-logs-and-journald/03-syslog-.summary: The syslog model classifies messages by facility (auth, cron, daemon…) cross severity (emerg…debug). rsyslog rules route by facility.severity to files or remote collectors. journald can forward to syslog via imjournal, bridging the structured and classic worlds.

en/linux/10-logs-and-journald/04-reading.title: Reading a failure from the logs
en/linux/10-logs-and-journald/04-reading.summary: When a service or boot fails, the operator workflow is: journalctl -u svc -b -p err, find the FIRST error not the last, correlate timestamps across units, and check systemctl status for the exit code. Chasing the last error is the most common log-reading mistake.

en/linux/11-scheduling/01-cron.title: cron and crontab
en/linux/11-scheduling/01-cron.summary: cron schedules commands with a five-field expression (minute hour dom month dow). User crontabs live under /var/spool/cron; system jobs in /etc/cron.d. The cron environment is minimal — bare PATH, no profile — which is the top source of "works in my shell, fails in cron".

en/linux/11-scheduling/02-systemd-timers.title: systemd timers
en/linux/11-scheduling/02-systemd-timers.summary: A systemd timer (.timer unit) activates a companion .service unit on a schedule. OnCalendar sets wall-clock events; OnBootSec/OnUnitActiveSec set monotonic intervals. Persistent=true catches up a missed run. systemctl list-timers shows all timers and next activation.

en/linux/11-scheduling/03-choosing-and-d.title: Choosing between cron and timers, and debugging missed jobs
en/linux/11-scheduling/03-choosing-and-d.summary: cron wins on portability and simplicity; systemd timers win on logging, dependency ordering, and catch-up. Debugging a missed job means checking: wrong user, minimal PATH, unescaped % in cron, timezone/DST shift, missing trailing newline, or timer not enabled.

en/linux/12-kernel-tuning/01-sysctl.title: Kernel parameters with sysctl
en/linux/12-kernel-tuning/01-sysctl.summary: The kernel exposes thousands of tunables under /proc/sys. sysctl -w sets them at runtime (lost on reboot); /etc/sysctl.d/*.conf makes them permanent. Key knobs: vm.swappiness, net.ipv4.ip_forward (required for routing and containers), fs.file-max.

en/linux/12-kernel-tuning/02-modules.title: Kernel modules — loading, inspecting, and blacklisting
en/linux/12-kernel-tuning/02-modules.summary: The kernel loads driver and feature support as modules instead of compiling everything in. lsmod/modinfo inspect loaded modules; modprobe loads with dependency resolution; rmmod unloads. Auto-load via /etc/modules-load.d; blacklist via /etc/modprobe.d.

en/linux/12-kernel-tuning/03-namespaces-.title: Namespaces and cgroups — the container primitives
en/linux/12-kernel-tuning/03-namespaces-.summary: Namespaces isolate global kernel resources per process group (pid, net, mnt, uts, ipc, user, cgroup). Combined with cgroups for resource limits and a root filesystem, they form the complete container primitive. No magic — this is where the Docker track picks up.

en/logic/01-propositional-logic/01-state.title: Statements and truth: what a proposition really is
en/logic/01-propositional-logic/01-state.summary: A proposition is a statement that is definitely true or definitely false — never both, never neither. 'x > 3' isn't one until x gets a value, and every if-condition in your code becomes one the moment it runs. Truthiness bugs begin exactly where strict truth values end.

en/logic/01-propositional-logic/02-and-o.title: AND, OR, NOT: truth tables, De Morgan, and the art of negating conditions
en/logic/01-propositional-logic/02-and-o.summary: AND, OR, NOT and XOR are fully defined by tiny truth tables. De Morgan's laws say how negation distributes — NOT (a AND b) becomes (NOT a) OR (NOT b) — and short-circuit evaluation is the truth table running at runtime. Most compound-condition bugs are De Morgan done wrong.

en/logic/01-propositional-logic/03-impli.title: Implication and equivalence: if-then, vacuous truth, and guard clauses
en/logic/01-propositional-logic/03-impli.summary: p → q is false in exactly one case: p true, q false. A false p makes the rule hold vacuously. Converse and inverse are NOT equivalent to it — the contrapositive is, and every guard clause and early return in your code is contrapositive reasoning in disguise.

en/logic/02-reasoning-and-proof/01-argum.title: Valid arguments: modus ponens, modus tollens, and the fallacies that fool debuggers
en/logic/02-reasoning-and-proof/01-argum.summary: A valid argument's form guarantees the conclusion whenever the premises hold; soundness adds true premises. Modus ponens and modus tollens are the two safe moves; affirming the consequent and denying the antecedent look similar — and are how debugging hunches go wrong.

en/logic/02-reasoning-and-proof/02-quant.title: Quantifiers: for-all, there-exists, and why 'all tests pass' can lie
en/logic/02-reasoning-and-proof/02-quant.summary: ∀ means every case, ∃ means at least one. Negation swaps them — not-all equals exists-a-counterexample — and quantifier order changes what a sentence promises. In code: .every() and .some(), where .every() on an empty array is true — 'all tests pass' can mean 'no tests ran'.

en/logic/02-reasoning-and-proof/03-induc.title: Induction and loop invariants: proving code correct for every n
en/logic/02-reasoning-and-proof/03-induc.summary: Induction proves a claim for every n from a base case plus a step that carries truth from n to n+1; strong induction lets the step lean on all smaller cases. A loop invariant is the same proof in code: true before the loop, preserved by each pass, at exit yielding correctness.

en/logic/03-sets-and-relations/01-sets-a.title: Sets and membership: in or not in
en/logic/03-sets-and-relations/01-sets-a.summary: A set stores one fact per value: in, or not in. No order, no duplicates, no counts — which is why new Set([1, 2, 2, 3]) has size 3 and deduplication is set semantics. Covers element vs subset, the empty set, infinite sets as rules, and types as sets of values.

en/logic/03-sets-and-relations/02-operat.title: Set operations and Venn diagrams: union, intersection, difference, complement
en/logic/03-sets-and-relations/02-operat.summary: Union, intersection, difference, complement — four operations that are OR, AND, NOT over membership. Venn diagrams map the regions, De Morgan flips union into intersection under complement, and inclusion-exclusion explains why 1200 + 300 subscribers may be only 1400 people.

en/logic/03-sets-and-relations/03-relati.title: Relations: ordered pairs and the grid of who relates to whom
en/logic/03-sets-and-relations/03-relati.summary: An ordered pair remembers order: (a, b) is not (b, a). The cartesian product A × B is the grid of every pair, and a relation is whichever subset of the grid holds. Foreign keys, === and follows graphs are relations — reflexive, symmetric, transitive tell them apart.

en/logic/03-sets-and-relations/04-equiva.title: Equivalence and order: classes, partitions, and what you can compare
en/logic/03-sets-and-relations/04-equiva.summary: Reflexive + symmetric + transitive = an equivalence relation, and every equivalence partitions a set into disjoint classes — the math behind hash buckets and dedup. Orders rank instead; partial orders allow incomparable pairs, which is how 1.2 vs 1.10 sorts wrong.

en/logic/04-proof-techniques/01-direct-a.title: Direct proof and the contrapositive: chaining implications, and when to flip them
en/logic/04-proof-techniques/01-direct-a.summary: A direct proof chains implications from premise to goal, each link justified: assume, manipulate, conclude. When that road is steep, flip to the contrapositive — ¬Q→¬P proves P→Q. Code review works the same way: you approve a function by chaining its guarantees.

en/logic/04-proof-techniques/02-contradi.title: Proof by contradiction: assume it is false, derive the impossible
en/logic/04-proof-techniques/02-contradi.summary: Proof by contradiction assumes the claim is false and derives something impossible, so the assumption falls. The irrationality of √2 and Euclid's primes both yield to it. Engineers use it daily: assume the loop never terminates, assume two users got the same id — impossible.

en/logic/04-proof-techniques/03-countere.title: Counterexamples and claims: who carries the burden of proof
en/logic/04-proof-techniques/03-countere.summary: Quantifier shape decides the burden of proof: a ∀-claim dies to one counterexample and is never proven by examples; an ∃-claim is proven by one witness. A failing test is a counterexample, edge values are where they hide, and a vague claim with no quantifier cannot be argued.

en/logic/05-recursion-and-recurrences/01.title: Recursive definitions: base cases, smaller selves, and the contract behind the leap of faith
en/logic/05-recursion-and-recurrences/01.summary: A recursive definition has two parts: base case(s) and a rule that builds n from a smaller self — 0! = 1, n! = n·(n-1)!. Lists, trees, and file systems are defined the same way. Two laws keep it honest: every call steps toward a base, and a base exists on every path.

en/logic/05-recursion-and-recurrences/02.title: Unrolling recurrences: linear and quadratic cost
en/logic/05-recursion-and-recurrences/02.summary: A recurrence counts the work of a recursion. T(n) = T(n-1) + 1 unrolls to n+1 (linear scan), T(n) = T(n-1) + n unrolls via Gauss to n(n+1)/2 (quadratic). Unroll 3-4 steps, spot the pattern, sum, sanity-check a small n.

en/logic/05-recursion-and-recurrences/03.title: Recurrence growth classes: logarithmic, n·log n, and exponential
en/logic/05-recursion-and-recurrences/03.summary: T(n) = T(n/2) + 1 halves to log₂ n steps (binary search). 2T(n/2) + n gives n·log n by the level-sum picture (merge sort). Two calls on n-1 and n-2 explode exponentially (fibonacci). The shape of the call tree — how fast it shrinks versus how wide it fans — decides the bill.

en/logic/05-recursion-and-recurrences/04.title: Recursion and induction: one structure, two sides — proving your code correct for all n
en/logic/05-recursion-and-recurrences/04.summary: Induction and recursion are one structure seen from two sides: a proof uses P(smaller), a function calls f(smaller). Prove sum(list) by trusting the tail, see the same proof living inside a loop as an invariant, and add a strictly decreasing measure to guarantee termination.

en/logic/06-combinatorial-reasoning/01-c.title: Counting principles: multiply the and-thens, add the eithers
en/logic/06-combinatorial-reasoning/01-c.summary: All counting stands on two laws: independent sequential choices multiply (4 shirts × 3 pants = 12 outfits), disjoint cases add (3 pastas + 4 pizzas = 7 dinners). Factorials, permutations, combinations and the size of your CI matrix are these two rules applied over and over.

en/logic/06-combinatorial-reasoning/02-p.title: The pigeonhole principle: guaranteed collisions, and the craft of choosing the holes
en/logic/06-combinatorial-reasoning/02-p.summary: Put n+1 items into n boxes and some box holds two — obvious to state, powerful because you design the boxes: months, remainders mod n, hash buckets. A 1000-bucket table holding 1001 keys collides by arithmetic, not bad luck — and collisions get likely long before guaranteed.

en/logic/06-combinatorial-reasoning/03-i.title: Invariants in practice: proving a goal unreachable without searching
en/logic/06-combinatorial-reasoning/03-i.summary: An invariant is a property no allowed move can change. Find one on which start and goal differ, and you have proved the goal unreachable — no simulation. The mutilated chessboard, sign-flip games, water jugs, loop invariants and conservation asserts all run on this one engine.

en/math/01-numbers/01-counting.title: Counting
en/math/01-numbers/01-counting.summary: What a number is before it is anything else: a way to count things.

en/math/01-numbers/02-comparing.title: Comparing numbers
en/math/01-numbers/02-comparing.summary: Which of two numbers is bigger — and how to write the answer with the > and < signs.

en/math/01-numbers/03-place-value.title: Place value
en/math/01-numbers/03-place-value.summary: Why 30 and 3 are different numbers even though the digit is the same — where a digit sits decides what it is worth.

en/math/01-numbers/04-the-number-line.title: The number line
en/math/01-numbers/04-the-number-line.summary: One straight line holds every number in order — with equal gaps that turn counting into movement you can see and point to.

en/math/01-numbers/project.title: Numbers: build a number line by hand
en/math/01-numbers/project.summary: Hands-on exploration: build a number line by hand, count and compare real groups of objects, and break numbers into their place values — proving each idea with your own drawings and counts.

en/math/01-numbers/quiz-choice.title: Numbers: multiple-choice review
en/math/01-numbers/quiz-choice.summary: Multiple-choice synthesis across the numbers unit: counting, comparing with the greater-than and less-than signs, place value, the role of zero, and the number line.

en/math/01-numbers/quiz-short.title: Numbers: free-recall review
en/math/01-numbers/quiz-short.summary: Free-recall prompts across the numbers unit. Answer each in your own words first, then reveal the model answer and compare.

en/math/02-operations/01-addition.title: Addition
en/math/02-operations/01-addition.summary: What it really means to add: joining two amounts into one total — and the place-value trick that lets you add numbers too big to count on your fingers.

en/math/02-operations/02-subtraction.title: Subtraction
en/math/02-operations/02-subtraction.summary: Taking away, and finding the gap between two numbers — two questions with one answer, the difference — plus the borrowing trick for larger numbers.

en/math/02-operations/03-multiplication.title: Multiplication
en/math/02-operations/03-multiplication.summary: Adding the same number again and again, made short — equal groups, the product, why order does not matter, and how to multiply larger numbers a place at a time.

en/math/02-operations/04-division.title: Division
en/math/02-operations/04-division.summary: Splitting an amount into equal groups — the two questions division answers, why it undoes multiplication, what a remainder is, and why you can never divide by zero.

en/math/02-operations/project.title: Four operations: plan a party by hand
en/math/02-operations/project.summary: Hands-on project — plan a party for a fixed number of people on paper, using all four operations and showing every step, then check each answer with its inverse.

en/math/02-operations/quiz-choice.title: Four operations: multiple-choice review
en/math/02-operations/quiz-choice.summary: Multiple-choice review across the four operations — carrying and borrowing, why order matters for some operations and not others, remainders, and dividing by zero.

en/math/02-operations/quiz-short.title: Four operations: free-recall review
en/math/02-operations/quiz-short.summary: Free-recall prompts across the four operations. Answer each in your own words first, then reveal the model answer and compare.

en/math/03-fractions/01-what-is-a-fracti.title: What is a fraction
en/math/03-fractions/01-what-is-a-fracti.summary: A fraction names a part of a whole — the bottom number says how many equal parts the whole is cut into, the top says how many you have.

en/math/03-fractions/02-equivalent-fract.title: Equivalent fractions
en/math/03-fractions/02-equivalent-fract.summary: The same amount can be written with different numbers — multiply or divide top and bottom by the same number, and the value never changes.

en/math/03-fractions/03-adding-fractions.title: Adding fractions
en/math/03-fractions/03-adding-fractions.summary: Add fractions with the same bottom number by adding the tops — and when the bottoms differ, make them match first with equivalent fractions.

en/math/03-fractions/04-decimals.title: Decimals
en/math/03-fractions/04-decimals.summary: A decimal is a fraction written with place value — the places after the dot are tenths, hundredths, and so on, each ten times smaller than the last.

en/math/03-fractions/05-percents.title: Percents
en/math/03-fractions/05-percents.summary: A percent is a fraction whose denominator is always 100 — one fixed scale that lets any two parts be compared, and converted freely to fractions and decimals.

en/math/03-fractions/project.title: Fractions: a three-way budget chart
en/math/03-fractions/project.summary: Hands-on project — split a real allowance into categories, then write every share three ways (fraction, decimal, percent) and prove the parts add up to the whole.

en/math/03-fractions/quiz-choice.title: Fractions: multiple-choice review
en/math/03-fractions/quiz-choice.summary: Multiple-choice synthesis across the fractions unit — equal parts, equivalence, adding with a common denominator, and moving between fractions, decimals, and percents.

en/math/03-fractions/quiz-short.title: Fractions: free-recall review
en/math/03-fractions/quiz-short.summary: Free-recall prompts across the fractions unit — say a full answer from memory first, then reveal the model answer and compare.

en/math/04-powers/01-exponents.title: Exponents
en/math/04-powers/01-exponents.summary: An exponent is shorthand for multiplying a number by itself again and again — and that repeated multiplication makes numbers grow startlingly fast.

en/math/04-powers/02-powers-of-ten.title: Powers of ten
en/math/04-powers/02-powers-of-ten.summary: Ten raised to a power is just a 1 followed by that many zeros — and this is exactly the engine behind place value and how we write large numbers.

en/math/04-powers/03-square-roots.title: Square roots
en/math/04-powers/03-square-roots.summary: Squaring asks what a number times itself comes to; the square root asks the question backwards — what number, squared, gives this?

en/math/04-powers/project.title: Powers and roots: build a reference card
en/math/04-powers/project.summary: Build a one-page powers-and-roots reference card by hand — a powers table, a powers-of-ten/scientific-form converter, and a perfect-squares-and-roots ladder — each entry verified.

en/math/04-powers/quiz-choice.title: Powers and roots: multiple-choice review
en/math/04-powers/quiz-choice.summary: Multiple-choice review across the powers unit — what an exponent counts, powers of ten and their zeros, the power 0, and square roots as the backwards question.

en/math/04-powers/quiz-short.title: Powers and roots: free-recall review
en/math/04-powers/quiz-short.summary: Free-recall prompts across the powers unit. Answer each in your own words first, then reveal the model answer and compare.

en/math/05-algebra/01-variables.title: Variables
en/math/05-algebra/01-variables.summary: A variable is a letter standing in for a number — one you have not found yet, or one that is allowed to change.

en/math/05-algebra/02-expressions.title: Expressions
en/math/05-algebra/02-expressions.summary: An expression combines numbers, variables, and operations into something with a value — evaluate it by substituting, simplify it by combining like terms.

en/math/05-algebra/03-equations.title: Equations
en/math/05-algebra/03-equations.summary: An equation says two things are equal; solving it means finding the variable''''s value — by doing the same move to both sides until the variable stands alone.

en/math/05-algebra/04-inequalities.title: Inequalities
en/math/05-algebra/04-inequalities.summary: An inequality compares with greater-than or less-than instead of equals — so its answer is not one number but a whole range of them.

en/math/05-algebra/project.title: Algebra: build a pocket-money rule
en/math/05-algebra/project.summary: Hands-on project — turn a real spending situation into a variable, an expression, an equation, and an inequality, then solve all three by hand and check every answer.

en/math/05-algebra/quiz-choice.title: Algebra: multiple-choice review
en/math/05-algebra/quiz-choice.summary: Multiple-choice synthesis across the algebra unit — variables, evaluating and simplifying expressions, solving equations by balance, and inequality ranges.

en/math/05-algebra/quiz-short.title: Algebra: free-recall review
en/math/05-algebra/quiz-short.summary: Free-recall prompts across the algebra unit — answer each in your own words first, then reveal the model answer and compare.

en/math/06-functions/01-what-is-a-functi.title: What is a function
en/math/06-functions/01-what-is-a-functi.summary: A function is a rule that takes an input and returns exactly one output — the same input always producing the same result.

en/math/06-functions/02-linear-functions.title: Linear functions
en/math/06-functions/02-linear-functions.summary: A linear function changes by the same amount with every step of the input — a steady rate plus a starting value, the most predictable function there is.

en/math/06-functions/03-graphs.title: Graphs
en/math/06-functions/03-graphs.summary: A graph turns a function into a picture — every input-output pair becomes a point on a grid, and a linear function''''s points form a straight line.

en/math/06-functions/project.title: Functions: model a real-world rate
en/math/06-functions/project.summary: Hands-on project — model a real situation as a linear function, build its table and graph, evaluate it, and read predictions straight off the picture.

en/math/06-functions/quiz-choice.title: Functions: multiple-choice review
en/math/06-functions/quiz-choice.summary: Multiple-choice synthesis across the functions unit: the one-output rule, function notation, evaluation, linear rate and starting value, and reading a graph.

en/math/06-functions/quiz-short.title: Functions: free-recall review
en/math/06-functions/quiz-short.summary: Free-recall prompts across the functions unit. Answer each in your own words first, then reveal the model answer and compare.

en/math/07-logic/01-true-and-false.title: True and false
en/math/07-logic/01-true-and-false.summary: A statement is a sentence that is definitely true or definitely false — and that single fixed truth value is what logic is built on.

en/math/07-logic/02-and-or-not.title: And, or, not
en/math/07-logic/02-and-or-not.summary: Three small words combine and flip statements — AND needs both, OR needs at least one, NOT reverses — and together they are the whole grammar of logic.

en/math/07-logic/03-sets.title: Sets
en/math/07-logic/03-sets.summary: A set is a collection of distinct things — and once you can ask what is in it, you can combine sets by union and intersection.

en/math/07-logic/project.title: Logic and sets: build a reasoning kit
en/math/07-logic/project.summary: Hands-on project: build a small truth-table-and-sets reference kit from everyday sentences, then use it to settle three real yes-or-no questions.

en/math/07-logic/quiz-choice.title: Logic and sets: multiple-choice review
en/math/07-logic/quiz-choice.summary: Multiple-choice synthesis across the logic-and-sets unit: statements and truth values, the AND/OR/NOT rules, and combining sets by union and intersection.

en/math/07-logic/quiz-short.title: Logic and sets: free-recall review
en/math/07-logic/quiz-short.summary: Free-recall prompts across the logic-and-sets unit: statements, the AND/OR/NOT rules, set membership, and union versus intersection. Answer first, then check.

en/math/08-growth/01-linear-vs-exponenti.title: Linear vs exponential
en/math/08-growth/01-linear-vs-exponenti.summary: Two ways to grow: add the same amount each step, or multiply by the same amount each step — and the second one always wins in the end.

en/math/08-growth/02-logarithms.title: Logarithms
en/math/08-growth/02-logarithms.summary: A logarithm runs an exponent backwards — it asks how many times you must multiply the base to reach a number, and so it measures explosive growth on a calm scale.

en/math/08-growth/project.title: Growth: the race and the ruler
en/math/08-growth/project.summary: Hands-on project — build a growth comparison by hand, watch exponential overtake linear, then use a logarithm to count the doublings and read the result back.

en/math/08-growth/quiz-choice.title: Growth: multiple-choice review
en/math/08-growth/quiz-choice.summary: Multiple-choice synthesis across the growth unit — telling adding from multiplying, why exponential overtakes linear, and reading a logarithm as the exponent that reverses it.

en/math/08-growth/quiz-short.title: Growth: free-recall review
en/math/08-growth/quiz-short.summary: Free-recall prompts across the growth unit. Answer each in your own words first, then reveal the model answer and compare.

en/math/09-combinatorics/01-counting-pri.title: The counting principle
en/math/09-combinatorics/01-counting-pri.summary: When you make several independent choices in a row, the number of possible outcomes is the choices multiplied together — count without ever listing.

en/math/09-combinatorics/02-permutations.title: Permutations
en/math/09-combinatorics/02-permutations.summary: A permutation is an arrangement where order matters — count it by multiplying the shrinking number of choices, which is exactly what a factorial does.

en/math/09-combinatorics/03-combinations.title: Combinations
en/math/09-combinatorics/03-combinations.summary: A combination is a selection where order does not matter — count it by taking the permutations and dividing out the orderings you no longer want to distinguish.

en/math/09-combinatorics/project.title: Combinatorics: build a counting handbook
en/math/09-combinatorics/project.summary: Hands-on project — build a one-page 'counting handbook' that solves real possibility-counting questions by choosing the right rule, showing the arithmetic, and proving the count is exact.

en/math/09-combinatorics/quiz-choice.title: Combinatorics: multiple-choice review
en/math/09-combinatorics/quiz-choice.summary: Multiple-choice synthesis across the combinatorics unit — the counting principle, permutations and factorials, combinations, and telling order-matters from order-does-not.

en/math/09-combinatorics/quiz-short.title: Combinatorics: free-recall review
en/math/09-combinatorics/quiz-short.summary: Free-recall prompts across the combinatorics unit. Answer each in your own words first, then reveal the model answer and compare.

en/math/10-probability/01-what-is-probab.title: What is probability
en/math/10-probability/01-what-is-probab.summary: Probability puts a number from 0 to 1 on how likely something is — and for equally likely outcomes, that number is favourable outcomes over total outcomes.

en/math/10-probability/02-combining-even.title: Combining events
en/math/10-probability/02-combining-even.summary: Probabilities combine with three moves: multiply for two independent events both happening, add for exclusive events, and subtract from 1 for an event not happening.

en/math/10-probability/project.title: Probability: predict and test a chance game
en/math/10-probability/project.summary: Hands-on project: predict the probabilities of a two-stage chance game using the unit's rules, then run the game many times and check whether the real counts match your predictions.

en/math/10-probability/quiz-choice.title: Probability: multiple-choice review
en/math/10-probability/quiz-choice.summary: Multiple-choice review across the probability unit: the 0-to-1 scale, favourable-over-total, multiplying for AND, adding for exclusive OR, the complement, and independent vs dependent events.

en/math/10-probability/quiz-short.title: Probability: free-recall review
en/math/10-probability/quiz-short.summary: Free-recall prompts across the probability unit. Answer each in your own words first, then reveal the model answer and compare.

en/nest/00-start-here/01-why-nest.title: Why NestJS, and the DI mental model
en/nest/00-start-here/01-why-nest.summary: NestJS adds structure to a bare Node backend: modules, controllers, providers — and dependency injection. You declare what a class needs in its constructor; the IoC container builds and injects it, so wiring is central and code stays testable.
prereqs: Comfortable with Node.js and TypeScript (classes, decorators, async/await)

en/nest/01-building-blocks/01-modules-co.title: Modules, controllers, providers
en/nest/01-building-blocks/01-modules-co.summary: NestJS is three building blocks: controllers route requests and stay thin, providers hold business logic and are injected, modules group them and gate visibility via imports/exports. Forget to export and DI cannot resolve the dependency.

en/nest/01-building-blocks/02-dependency.title: Dependency injection, scopes, custom providers
en/nest/01-building-blocks/02-dependency.summary: Nest registers providers under a token and reads constructor types to build the graph once at boot. Custom providers swap how a token resolves; scopes decide how many instances live and how far REQUEST contagion spreads.

en/nest/01-building-blocks/03-lifecycle-.title: Lifecycle hooks and graceful shutdown
en/nest/01-building-blocks/03-lifecycle-.summary: Nest fires lifecycle hooks bottom-up on init and reverse on shutdown — but shutdown hooks are OFF until you call enableShutdownHooks(). Skip it and SIGTERM kills the process instantly: pools severed mid-query, consumers never commit. Drain under 30s.

en/nest/01-building-blocks/04-dynamic-mo.title: Dynamic modules and async configuration
en/nest/01-building-blocks/04-dynamic-mo.summary: A static @Module has a fixed provider set; a dynamic module is a class whose static method returns a DynamicModule descriptor at runtime so the importer can pass config. forRoot once, forFeature per slice, register per import — and forRootAsync when config comes from a provider.

en/nest/01-building-blocks/05-request-pi.title: The request pipeline: middleware, guards, interceptors, pipes, filters
en/nest/01-building-blocks/05-request-pi.summary: The request runs middleware → guard → interceptor(pre) → pipe → handler → interceptor(post) → filter. Two senior traps: a guard sees the raw un-validated body (pipes run after it), and a hand-newed global enhancer is outside DI — bind via APP_GUARD to inject.

en/nest/02-validation-and-pipes/01-dto-v.title: DTOs, class-validator and pipes
en/nest/02-validation-and-pipes/01-dto-v.summary: A DTO is a runtime class whose class-validator decorators describe a valid request; ValidationPipe reads that metadata before the handler, rejects bad input with 400, strips unknown props, and coerces types — so the handler trusts its args.

en/nest/02-validation-and-pipes/02-guard.title: Guards, interceptors and exception filters
en/nest/02-validation-and-pipes/02-guard.summary: Nest's request lifecycle is fixed — middleware, guard, interceptor (pre), pipe, handler, interceptor (post), filter. Put auth in a guard, validation in a pipe, logging/transform in an interceptor, error shape in a filter.

en/nest/02-validation-and-pipes/03-custo.title: Custom pipes and the transformation stage
en/nest/02-validation-and-pipes/03-custo.summary: A pipe runs per-argument right before the handler and does two jobs: coerce and validate. The transform stage is where "42" becomes 42 and a plain body becomes a real DTO — and where enableImplicitConversion silently turns ?active=false into true.

en/nest/02-validation-and-pipes/04-valid.title: Whitelisting, nested validation and partial updates
en/nest/02-validation-and-pipes/04-valid.summary: Hardening ValidationPipe past the basics: whitelist strips undecorated fields to kill mass-assignment, but only as one layer; nested DTOs need @ValidateNested + @Type or validation silently no-ops; PATCH needs PartialType, not skipMissingProperties.

en/nest/02-validation-and-pipes/05-custo.title: Custom and async validators (and their traps)
en/nest/02-validation-and-pipes/05-custo.summary: Custom constraints: a @ValidatorConstraint class or a registerDecorator factory. Async DB validators hide traps — forgetting useContainer leaves injected repos undefined, and the read-then-write race means only a DB unique index, not the validator, guarantees uniqueness.

en/nest/03-config-and-modules/01-config-.title: The config module: typed, validated env
en/nest/03-config-and-modules/01-config-.summary: ConfigModule.forRoot wraps dotenv, validates env at boot with a schema (fail fast), and exposes a typed ConfigService. Use registerAs for namespaced config and inject it with ConfigType — never scatter process.env.

en/nest/03-config-and-modules/02-dynamic.title: Dynamic modules: forRoot, forRootAsync, forFeature
en/nest/03-config-and-modules/02-dynamic.summary: A DynamicModule returns its definition at runtime. forRoot configures once, forRootAsync pulls options from DI (ConfigService), forFeature registers per-consumer. Build one with an options token; ConfigurableModuleBuilder generates the boilerplate.

en/nest/03-config-and-modules/03-lifecyc.title: Lifecycle hooks and graceful shutdown
en/nest/03-config-and-modules/03-lifecyc.summary: Nest fires init hooks bottom-up (onModuleInit then onApplicationBootstrap) and shutdown hooks in reverse (onModuleDestroy, beforeApplicationShutdown, onApplicationShutdown) — but only if you call enableShutdownHooks() so it listens for SIGTERM.

en/nest/04-persistence/01-typeorm-or-pri.title: TypeORM or Prisma: integrating an ORM
en/nest/04-persistence/01-typeorm-or-pri.summary: TypeORM and Prisma both wire an ORM into Nest, but the type-safety source of truth differs: decorator @Entity classes registered through TypeOrmModule, or a schema.prisma that generates a client you wrap as a PrismaService.

en/nest/04-persistence/02-repositories-a.title: Repositories, transactions and the unit of work
en/nest/04-persistence/02-repositories-a.summary: A repository is bound to the default manager — calling an injected repo inside dataSource.transaction does NOT join the tx. Route every write through the SAME transactional EntityManager (manager.getRepository), or a partial commit leaves orphaned rows.

en/nest/04-persistence/03-data-modeling-.title: Data modeling pitfalls: N+1, lazy vs eager, request scope
en/nest/04-persistence/03-data-modeling-.summary: Three data-modeling traps that look fine in dev and burn p99 in prod: relations that quietly trigger N+1, lazy vs eager defaults that hide or force joins, and request-scoped providers that bubble up the whole graph. Load relations explicitly; reach for durable providers.

en/nest/05-auth/01-passport-and-jwt.title: Passport strategies and JWT auth
en/nest/05-auth/01-passport-and-jwt.summary: Passport gives Nest two strategies — LocalStrategy validates credentials on /login, JwtStrategy verifies a Bearer token on every protected route. A global JwtAuthGuard fails closed; @Public() opts routes out. A JWT is signed, not encrypted.

en/nest/05-auth/02-rbac-and-guards.title: RBAC: roles, guards and the Reflector
en/nest/05-auth/02-rbac-and-guards.summary: RBAC lives in a guard: a @Roles() decorator stamps metadata, a RolesGuard reads it via the Reflector. But a role guard cannot enforce "edit only your own post" — ownership needs the loaded record, so it belongs in a policy guard or the service.

en/nest/05-auth/03-refresh-tokens-and-ro.title: Refresh tokens, rotation and reuse detection
en/nest/05-auth/03-refresh-tokens-and-ro.summary: A JWT access token cannot be revoked before exp, so keep it short (~15 min) and pair it with a long-lived refresh token that rotates single-use. Reusing a consumed refresh token means two parties hold it — revoke the whole family and force re-auth.

en/nest/05-auth/04-sessions-vs-jwt-and-l.title: Sessions vs JWT, and why logout is hard
en/nest/05-auth/04-sessions-vs-jwt-and-l.summary: Sessions store auth server-side and revoke by deleting a row; a JWT carries its own claims and cannot be revoked before exp. That is why logout is hard with JWT — clearing the cookie does nothing to a stolen token. Mitigate with short TTL plus a denylist or per-user tokenVersion.

en/nest/05-auth/05-jwt-verification-pitf.title: JWT verification pitfalls: algorithms, claims and keys
en/nest/05-auth/05-jwt-verification-pitf.summary: A signature only proves integrity, not that a token is for you. The JWT header is attacker-controlled, so a verifier that trusts its alg/kid invites alg:none and HS256/RS256 key confusion. Pin an algorithms allowlist, validate aud/iss/exp, and key JWKS by kid.

en/nest/06-testing/01-unit-testing-provi.title: Unit testing providers with the testing module
en/nest/06-testing/01-unit-testing-provi.summary: Unit-test a Nest provider by building an isolated DI container with Test.createTestingModule, mocking every dependency at its boundary (the repository, the HTTP client) via useValue or overrideProvider, then asserting behavior with jest.fn().

en/nest/06-testing/02-e2e-testing.title: E2E testing with supertest
en/nest/06-testing/02-e2e-testing.summary: E2E tests boot the whole app (createTestingModule(AppModule), createNestApplication, app.init), then drive it with supertest against the real pipeline, a real test DB, and a real JWT or an overridden guard. Always app.close().

en/nest/06-testing/03-mocking-and-test-d.title: Mocking, test doubles and the over-mocking trap
en/nest/06-testing/03-mocking-and-test-d.summary: Stub returns canned data, mock verifies behaviour, fake is a working impl. Override Nest deps with overrideProvider, not jest.mock. The over-mocking trap: mock boundaries you do not own, fake or integrate what you do — else a green suite tests your assumptions, not your code.

en/nest/06-testing/04-integration-testin.title: Integration testing against a real database
en/nest/06-testing/04-integration-testin.summary: Mocks assert your assumptions; a real database asserts reality.
