Integration tests run code against a throwaway Postgres (Testcontainers) to catch constraints, cascades, and migration drift mocks can't — paid for with per-test rollback and seconds of runtime.

en/nest/06-testing/05-testing-async-and-.title: Testing async code and killing flaky tests
en/nest/06-testing/05-testing-async-and-.summary: Async tests fail when the assertion races the work it checks. Always await; replace the clock with fake timers (and flush microtasks); await handlers, never setTimeout(50). A flaky test is a bug report about non-determinism — fix the race, never retryTimes(3) it away.

en/nest/07-errors-and-observability/01-e.title: Exception filters and structured logging
en/nest/07-errors-and-observability/01-e.summary: One global @Catch() filter maps every throw to a consistent JSON error envelope with a requestId; a structured JSON logger plus an AsyncLocalStorage correlation id lets you trace one request across many log lines and services.

en/nest/07-errors-and-observability/02-h.title: Health checks and cross-cutting interceptors
en/nest/07-errors-and-observability/02-h.summary: @nestjs/terminus aggregates health indicators behind /health. The senior split: liveness must stay dependency-free (it triggers restarts), readiness checks deps and gates the LB. Layer TimeoutInterceptor + a metrics interceptor on top.

en/nest/07-errors-and-observability/03-d.title: Distributed tracing with OpenTelemetry
en/nest/07-errors-and-observability/03-d.summary: One request fans out across N services; per-service logs cannot tell you which hop is slow or where it broke. A trace stitches the request into one tree of spans via a shared traceId — if you propagate context across HTTP and async boundaries, and sample sanely.

en/nest/07-errors-and-observability/04-m.title: Metrics, percentiles and SLOs
en/nest/07-errors-and-observability/04-m.summary: Metrics are not logs or traces: they are cheap aggregates you alert on. Pick the right type (counter/gauge/histogram), measure the tail with p99 not the lying average, keep labels low-cardinality or Prometheus OOMs, and alert on SLO budget burn.

en/nest/07-errors-and-observability/05-e.title: Error tracking, correlation and alert fatigue
en/nest/07-errors-and-observability/05-e.summary: Logs, metrics, and traces are three haystacks until a shared traceId joins them. An error tracker groups by fingerprint and dedupes; scrub PII before egress; alert on error RATE not count, or the channel gets muted and the real outage hides in the noise.

en/nest/08-microservices-and-graphql/01-.title: Microservice transports: TCP, Redis, NATS, Kafka
en/nest/08-microservices-and-graphql/01-.summary: A Nest microservice listens on a swappable transporter, not HTTP. send/@MessagePattern is request–response; emit/@EventPattern is fire-and-forget. Pick the transport on delivery: TCP/Redis lose messages, RabbitMQ/Kafka redeliver — forcing idempotent consumers.

en/nest/08-microservices-and-graphql/02-.title: Code-first GraphQL, resolvers and DataLoader
en/nest/08-microservices-and-graphql/02-.summary: Code-first GraphQL generates the SDL from @ObjectType/@Resolver classes. Field resolvers create the N+1; a per-request DataLoader batches keys into one DB call. Harden prod with depth/complexity limits.

en/nest/08-microservices-and-graphql/03-.title: Message patterns and delivery semantics
en/nest/08-microservices-and-graphql/03-.summary: Two message patterns (send/request-response vs emit/event) and the delivery guarantee that actually ships: at-least-once. Exactly-once delivery is a myth; you get effectively-once only by making the consumer idempotent. Dedup by key, DLQ poison messages.

en/nest/08-microservices-and-graphql/04-.title: Sagas, compensations and the outbox pattern
en/nest/08-microservices-and-graphql/04-.summary: A business operation spanning service-owned databases can not use one ACID transaction, and 2PC is a fragile SPOF. Sagas chain local transactions with compensations; the transactional outbox commits state and event in one DB txn so a crash never loses the event.

en/nest/08-microservices-and-graphql/05-.title: GraphQL hardening: query cost, depth and federation
en/nest/08-microservices-and-graphql/05-.summary: A public GraphQL endpoint lets the client compose the query, so one request can fan out to millions of resolver and DB calls — a DoS vector REST does not have. Harden with depth limits, query-cost analysis, and persisted queries; scale ownership with Apollo Federation.

en/nest/09-putting-it-together/01-capsto.title: Capstone: a fully-typed, authed, tested API
en/nest/09-putting-it-together/01-capsto.summary: Tie the whole track together: feature modules over Controller -> Service -> Repository, a core module that binds the global guard/pipe/interceptor/filter, types enforced at the edges, and a production-readiness checklist that fails fast.

en/networking/00-start-here/01-overview.title: Start from zero: what a computer network actually is
en/networking/00-start-here/01-overview.summary: A network is machines exchanging packets. This lesson defines the eight terms every networking unit assumes — packet, IP address, port, protocol, client/server, router, DNS, latency/bandwidth — and traces one URL from your browser to a server.

en/networking/01-physical-link/01-bits-o.title: Bits on the wire
en/networking/01-physical-link/01-bits-o.summary: Voltage, photons, and radio waves carry every byte you send. The speed of light through a medium sets the latency floor nothing above can escape.

en/networking/01-physical-link/02-modula.title: Modulation and Shannon
en/networking/01-physical-link/02-modula.summary: PAM-5 on copper, photons through glass, OFDM over radio — every medium has its own encoding scheme. Shannon''''s theorem sets the absolute ceiling no engineering can exceed.

en/networking/01-physical-link/03-latenc.title: Latency math
en/networking/01-physical-link/03-latenc.summary: Geography, medium, and hops each add measurable delay. Knowing the numbers lets you distinguish bugs from physics — and design around the floor you cannot lower.

en/networking/01-physical-link/04-buffer.title: Bufferbloat and congestion
en/networking/01-physical-link/04-buffer.summary: Oversized buffers at the network edge trade packet drops for latency — a saturated link queues 100s of ms, breaking interactive apps while throughput numbers stay green.

en/networking/01-physical-link/05-the-da.title: The datacentre fabric
en/networking/01-physical-link/05-the-da.summary: Clos spine-leaf topology, RoCE for GPU clusters, 800G optics, kernel-bypass NICs, and the power-and-cooling ceiling — the physical layer at hyperscale.

en/networking/01-physical-link/06-the-ph.title: The physical frontier
en/networking/01-physical-link/06-the-ph.summary: Coherent optics, Wi-Fi 7, 5G-Advanced, hollow-core fibre — the physical layer keeps moving, but one mental model decodes every new link technology you will ever meet.

en/networking/01-physical-link/project.title: The physical link: audit and tame a real link
en/networking/01-physical-link/project.summary: Hands-on project — measure your own link's latency floor versus reality, expose bufferbloat under load, tame it with SQM, and prove the fix with before/after numbers.

en/networking/01-physical-link/quiz-choi.title: The physical link: multiple-choice review
en/networking/01-physical-link/quiz-choi.summary: Multiple-choice synthesis across the physical-link unit — latency floors, Shannon ceilings, bufferbloat, RoCE fabrics, and the frontier.

en/networking/01-physical-link/quiz-code.title: The physical link: code and trace reading
en/networking/01-physical-link/quiz-code.summary: Read a BDP calculation, an ethtool counter dump, an SQM shaping config, and a leaf oversubscription sum — then pick the read a senior engineer would make.

en/networking/01-physical-link/quiz-shor.title: The physical link: free-recall review
en/networking/01-physical-link/quiz-shor.summary: Free-recall prompts across the physical-link unit. Answer each in your own words first, then reveal the model answer and compare.

en/networking/02-ip-packet/01-the-ip-env.title: The IP envelope
en/networking/02-ip-packet/01-the-ip-env.summary: IP is the addressed envelope every chunk of Internet traffic travels inside — no router knows the full route, yet millions cooperate to deliver the packet.

en/networking/02-ip-packet/02-reading-th.title: Reading the IP header
en/networking/02-ip-packet/02-reading-th.summary: Every field in the IPv4 and IPv6 headers has a job: TTL prevents loops, DSCP marks priority, the protocol field hands the payload to the right L4 handler.

en/networking/02-ip-packet/03-routing-an.title: Routing and forwarding
en/networking/02-ip-packet/03-routing-an.summary: How routers decide where a packet goes next: longest-prefix match in the FIB, CIDR aggregation, BGP between autonomous systems, and ECMP across equal-cost paths.

en/networking/02-ip-packet/04-mtu-and-fr.title: MTU and fragmentation
en/networking/02-ip-packet/04-mtu-and-fr.summary: A packet larger than a link''''s MTU must be shrunk or split. IPv4 routers can fragment; IPv6 forbids it. PMTUD black holes happen when ICMP is blocked.

en/networking/02-ip-packet/05-nat-and-ad.title: NAT, addressing, and IPv6 deployment
en/networking/02-ip-packet/05-nat-and-ad.summary: NAT extended the IPv4 Internet past 4 billion addresses but broke end-to-end connectivity. IPv6, SLAAC, anycast, and dual-stack are the principled way forward.

en/networking/02-ip-packet/06-ip-securit.title: IP security and operations
en/networking/02-ip-packet/06-ip-securit.summary: IP spoofing, BGP hijacks, DDoS amplification, and RPKI — the attacks at the network layer, how they work, and what operators do to defend against them.

en/networking/02-ip-packet/project.title: IP packets: trace, decode, and fix a path-MTU black hole
en/networking/02-ip-packet/project.summary: Hands-on project — capture and decode real IP packets, map a path with traceroute, then reproduce and fix a PMTUD black hole, proving each step with evidence.

en/networking/02-ip-packet/quiz-choice.title: IP packets: multiple-choice review
en/networking/02-ip-packet/quiz-choice.summary: Multiple-choice synthesis across the IP-packet unit — header semantics, longest-prefix routing, MTU black holes, NAT traversal, and BGP/spoofing defences.

en/networking/02-ip-packet/quiz-code.title: IP packets: dump and trace reading
en/networking/02-ip-packet/quiz-code.summary: Read real packet dumps, route tables, and traceroute output; decode the header, predict the forwarding decision, and pick the highest-leverage fix.

en/networking/02-ip-packet/quiz-short.title: IP packets: free-recall review
en/networking/02-ip-packet/quiz-short.summary: Free-recall prompts across the IP-packet unit. Answer each from memory first, then reveal the model answer and compare.

en/networking/03-tcp-handshake/01-the-th.title: The three-way handshake
en/networking/03-tcp-handshake/01-the-th.summary: TCP turns two strangers on the network into a reliable two-way conversation — the handshake is the three-step ritual that starts it.

en/networking/03-tcp-handshake/02-sequen.title: Sequence numbers and connection state
en/networking/03-tcp-handshake/02-sequen.summary: How ISN randomisation hardens TCP against injection attacks, and the full state machine from CLOSED to TIME-WAIT.

en/networking/03-tcp-handshake/03-flow-a.title: Flow control and congestion control
en/networking/03-tcp-handshake/03-flow-a.summary: Sliding windows let the receiver pace the sender; slow start and CUBIC let TCP discover the network''''s capacity without overloading it.

en/networking/03-tcp-handshake/04-tcp-op.title: TCP options and common pathologies
en/networking/03-tcp-handshake/04-tcp-op.summary: The TCP header anatomy, Nagle+delayed-ACK stalls, ECN, keepalive, and the CLOSE-WAIT socket-leak trap every backend engineer eventually hits.

en/networking/03-tcp-handshake/05-syn-co.title: SYN cookies, TFO, and TIME-WAIT at scale
en/networking/03-tcp-handshake/05-syn-co.summary: How SYN cookies trade memory for CPU under flood, what TCP Fast Open saves and why deployment stalled, and how to fix TIME-WAIT exhaustion on a busy load balancer.

en/networking/03-tcp-handshake/06-bbr-an.title: BBR, production observability, and beyond TCP
en/networking/03-tcp-handshake/06-bbr-an.summary: BBR''''s bandwidth-RTT model sustains throughput on lossy paths where CUBIC collapses. Production ss/tcpdump/nstat output, RST semantics, MPTCP, kTLS, and TCP''''s relationship to QUIC.

en/networking/03-tcp-handshake/project.title: TCP handshake: measure and tame a connection-churn problem
en/networking/03-tcp-handshake/project.summary: Hands-on project — capture a real handshake, reproduce a per-request-connection latency and TIME-WAIT problem, then fix it with pooling and tuning and prove it with before/after numbers.

en/networking/03-tcp-handshake/quiz-choi.title: TCP handshake: multiple-choice review
en/networking/03-tcp-handshake/quiz-choi.summary: Multiple-choice synthesis across the TCP-handshake unit — RTT cost, ISN randomisation, SYN cookies, congestion control, Nagle stalls, and TIME-WAIT exhaustion.

en/networking/03-tcp-handshake/quiz-code.title: TCP handshake: trace and code reading
en/networking/03-tcp-handshake/quiz-code.summary: Read real tcpdump traces, ss output, and a connection-handling snippet, then predict the TCP behaviour and pick the highest-leverage fix.

en/networking/03-tcp-handshake/quiz-shor.title: TCP handshake: free-recall review
en/networking/03-tcp-handshake/quiz-shor.summary: Free-recall prompts across the TCP-handshake unit. Answer each in your own words first, then reveal the model answer and compare.

en/networking/04-dns-resolution/01-dns-w.title: DNS: what it does and why it exists
en/networking/04-dns-resolution/01-dns-w.summary: DNS turns human-friendly names into IP addresses through a hierarchy of servers — the phonebook the whole internet depends on.

en/networking/04-dns-resolution/02-the-r.title: The resolver walk: referrals, record types, and glue
en/networking/04-dns-resolution/02-the-r.summary: How a recursive resolver follows referrals from root to authoritative, what the DNS message sections mean, and why missing glue breaks everything.

en/networking/04-dns-resolution/03-ttl-a.title: TTL, caching, and DNS propagation
en/networking/04-dns-resolution/03-ttl-a.summary: TTL is permission, not a command — understanding its operational impact on freshness, load, and the myth of DNS propagation.

en/networking/04-dns-resolution/04-dnsse.title: DNSSEC: chain of trust and validation failure
en/networking/04-dns-resolution/04-dnsse.summary: How DNSSEC signs every RRset from root to leaf, what breaks when the DS-KSK link snaps, and why a KSK rollover without updating the parent DS silently takes your site offline for 30% of users.

en/networking/04-dns-resolution/05-encry.title: Encrypted DNS: DoH, DoT, DoQ, and cache poisoning
en/networking/04-dns-resolution/05-encry.summary: Why plaintext UDP/53 is a surveillance and attack surface, how DoH/DoT/DoQ address it, what EDNS Client Subnet leaks, and how Kaminsky''''s attack and SAD DNS shaped modern defences.

en/networking/04-dns-resolution/project.title: DNS: run a signed zone through a migration and a rollover
en/networking/04-dns-resolution/project.summary: Hands-on project — stand up a signed, encrypted-resolved zone, instrument the resolution path, then run a zero-downtime IP migration and deliberately break and recover the DNSSEC chain, proving each step with dig.

en/networking/04-dns-resolution/quiz-cho.title: DNS: multiple-choice review
en/networking/04-dns-resolution/quiz-cho.summary: Multiple-choice synthesis across the DNS unit — the resolver walk, glue, TTL and propagation, negative caching, DNSSEC failure modes, and encrypted transport.

en/networking/04-dns-resolution/quiz-cod.title: DNS: dig and zone-file reading
en/networking/04-dns-resolution/quiz-cod.summary: Read real dig output, a zone file, and a resolver config, predict the DNS behaviour, and pick the diagnosis or fix a senior engineer would reach for first.

en/networking/04-dns-resolution/quiz-sho.title: DNS: free-recall review
en/networking/04-dns-resolution/quiz-sho.summary: Free-recall prompts across the DNS unit — the resolver walk, glue, TTL semantics, negative caching, DNSSEC, and what encryption does and does not add. Answer first, then reveal.

en/networking/05-tls-handshake/01-what-t.title: What TLS does and why it exists
en/networking/05-tls-handshake/01-what-t.summary: TLS builds a sealed channel over an untrusted network — before TLS 1.3 that took two round-trips; understanding why sets up everything that follows.

en/networking/05-tls-handshake/02-the-1r.title: The 1-RTT handshake: key shares and ECDHE
en/networking/05-tls-handshake/02-the-1r.summary: How ClientHello key shares, ECDHE ephemeral keys, and the transcript hash collapse TLS 1.2''''s two-RTT negotiation into one — and why Perfect Forward Secrecy follows automatically.

en/networking/05-tls-handshake/03-sessio.title: Session resumption and 0-RTT
en/networking/05-tls-handshake/03-sessio.summary: PSK tickets let warm connections skip certificate validation; 0-RTT early data eliminates the handshake RTT for read-only requests — but replay attacks constrain what can safely go in early data.

en/networking/05-tls-handshake/04-key-sc.title: Key schedule, SNI, ALPN, and extensions
en/networking/05-tls-handshake/04-key-sc.summary: How HKDF derives every traffic key from the shared secret, why SNI leaks which hostname you visit, and how ALPN, HelloRetryRequest, and OCSP stapling work inside the handshake.

en/networking/05-tls-handshake/05-0rtt-d.title: 0-RTT defenses, ECH, hybrid PQ, and production TLS
en/networking/05-tls-handshake/05-0rtt-d.summary: Production 0-RTT replay defenses, STEK rotation at CDN scale, Encrypted ClientHello, hybrid post-quantum key exchange, kernel TLS offload, and the observability metrics every TLS-serving service should track.

en/networking/06-http-versions/02-http2-.title: HTTP/2: streams, frames, and HPACK
en/networking/06-http-versions/02-http2-.summary: HTTP/2 replaced HTTP/1.1''''s parallel-connections workaround with multiplexed streams on one TCP connection — HPACK compresses headers, and server push proved a dead end.

en/networking/06-http-versions/03-http3-.title: HTTP/3 and QUIC: stream-level loss isolation
en/networking/06-http-versions/03-http3-.summary: HTTP/3 replaces TCP with QUIC — a UDP-based transport that gives each stream its own loss recovery, adds connection migration for mobile, and integrates TLS into the handshake.

en/networking/06-http-versions/04-header.title: HTTP headers, caching, and CORS
en/networking/06-http-versions/04-header.summary: The HTTP header layer — methods, status codes, Cache-Control, ETags, cookies, CORS — is where most operational bugs live and most security wins or losses happen.

en/networking/06-http-versions/05-stream.title: HTTP streaming, SSE, WebSockets, and gRPC
en/networking/06-http-versions/05-stream.summary: HTTP is not just request-response — chunked transfer, SSE, WebSockets, and gRPC each punch a hole in the single-response model for real-time and bidirectional communication.

en/networking/06-http-versions/06-http3-.title: HTTP/3 in production: QUIC internals, fallback, and observability
en/networking/06-http-versions/06-http3-.summary: Running HTTP/3 in production means understanding QUIC congestion control in userspace, ALPN-based version negotiation, silent fallback mechanics, and the metrics that reveal when UDP is being blocked.

en/networking/06-http-versions/07-http-d.title: HTTP design: priorities, WebTransport, and semantic correctness
en/networking/06-http-versions/07-http-d.summary: RFC 9218 extensible priorities replace HTTP/2''''s broken dependency trees; MASQUE and WebTransport extend QUIC beyond request-response; semantic correctness — right status codes, right Vary, right CORS — is where CDN and caching bugs hide.

en/networking/07-cdn-edge/01-cdn-what-an.title: CDN: putting content next door
en/networking/07-cdn-edge/01-cdn-what-an.summary: A CDN moves copies of your content to hundreds of edge servers worldwide so each user fetches from a server 20 ms away instead of 200 ms.

en/networking/07-cdn-edge/02-anycast-and.title: Anycast and GeoDNS: routing to the nearest edge
en/networking/07-cdn-edge/02-anycast-and.summary: How the same IP address advertised from 300 cities and geography-aware DNS cooperate to send every user to their closest CDN edge server.

en/networking/07-cdn-edge/03-tiered-cach.title: Tiered cache and Cache-Control
en/networking/07-cdn-edge/03-tiered-cach.summary: How edge cache, origin shield, and Cache-Control directives cooperate so 90%+ of requests never touch origin — and what to set per content type.

en/networking/07-cdn-edge/04-vary-header.title: Vary header and cache keys
en/networking/07-cdn-edge/04-vary-header.summary: How CDN cache keys are built, why Vary: User-Agent destroys hit rates, and why a missing Vary: Cookie can serve one user''''s account page to another.

en/networking/07-cdn-edge/05-stale-while.title: Stale-while-revalidate and cache stampede
en/networking/07-cdn-edge/05-stale-while.summary: How stale-while-revalidate defeats cache stampedes, when stale-if-error saves you during origin outages, and the four strategies to prevent thundering herds.

en/networking/07-cdn-edge/06-edge-worker.title: Edge workers and edge-side composition
en/networking/07-cdn-edge/06-edge-worker.summary: How V8 isolates at the CDN edge run custom logic in 2–5 ms cold starts, and how ESI and HTMLRewriter compose responses from independently-cached fragments.

en/networking/07-cdn-edge/07-cdn-operati.title: CDN operations and observability

en/networking/08-websocket-realtime/01-u.summary: How a normal HTTP request becomes a persistent bidirectional message pipe in one round-trip — and what each header in the upgrade does.

en/networking/08-websocket-realtime/02-f.title: WebSocket frame format: opcodes, masking, fragmentation
en/networking/08-websocket-realtime/02-f.summary: The 2-byte header that carries every WebSocket message — what FIN, opcode, MASK, and the three-tier length encoding mean, and why client frames must be masked.

en/networking/08-websocket-realtime/03-t.summary: Latency, overhead, and proxy compatibility compared across WebSocket, Server-Sent Events, and long-polling — so you pick the right tool before you build.

en/networking/08-websocket-realtime/04-b.title: WebSocket backpressure: when clients can''''t keep up
en/networking/08-websocket-realtime/04-b.summary: How slow clients fill TCP windows, bloat application send queues, and crash servers — and the high-water-mark pattern that prevents it.

en/networking/08-websocket-realtime/05-r.title: Reconnection: jittered backoff, thundering herd, message resumption
en/networking/08-websocket-realtime/05-r.summary: How to reconnect without crashing your own server — jittered exponential backoff, message IDs, and the at-least-once delivery guarantee with deduplication.

en/networking/08-websocket-realtime/06-s.title: WebSocket at scale: HTTP/2 multiplexing, permessage-deflate, C10M
en/networking/08-websocket-realtime/06-s.summary: The three ceilings that gate WebSocket scale — RAM per idle connection, file descriptors, and NIC bandwidth — and how HTTP/2 extended CONNECT and compression tuning shift those limits.

en/networking/08-websocket-realtime/07-p.summary: How to configure Nginx and ALB for long-lived upgrades, harden against DoS and cache-poisoning, and scale WebSocket clusters with pub/sub and sticky sessions.

en/networking/09-proxy-load-balancing/01.title: What reverse proxies do
en/networking/09-proxy-load-balancing/01.summary: A reverse proxy sits invisibly between clients and backends — it completes the client connection, picks a backend, and forwards the request, decoupling scaling from client visibility.

en/networking/09-proxy-load-balancing/02.title: Balancing algorithms: round-robin to power-of-two-choices
en/networking/09-proxy-load-balancing/02.summary: Round-robin ignores real load; least-connections causes herding; power-of-two-choices is O(1) and ~12% imbalance — the modern default and why.

en/networking/09-proxy-load-balancing/03.title: L4 vs L7 load balancing and client-IP preservation
en/networking/09-proxy-load-balancing/03.summary: L4 routes on IP:port at 1–5 µs with 10–40 Gbps throughput; L7 parses HTTP at 100–500 µs for content routing — and X-Forwarded-For, RFC 7239, and PROXY protocol each preserve the client IP differently.

en/networking/09-proxy-load-balancing/04.title: Health checks, connection draining, and slow start
en/networking/09-proxy-load-balancing/04.summary: Active probes catch total failures; passive outlier detection catches silent 5xx degradation; connection draining lets in-flight requests finish before a backend is removed; slow start prevents a cold backend from drowning under full load.

en/networking/09-proxy-load-balancing/05.title: Session affinity, consistent hashing, and the right fix
en/networking/09-proxy-load-balancing/05.summary: Sticky sessions pin clients to one backend and cause 1.5–2.5x load imbalance and session loss on failure; consistent hashing maps keys to backends with minimal remapping on membership changes; the right fix is externalizing session state to Redis.

en/networking/09-proxy-load-balancing/06.title: Retry storms, circuit breakers, and load shedding
en/networking/09-proxy-load-balancing/06.summary: Automatic retries amplify load 2^K× across K microservice layers; circuit breakers stop the cascade with fast 503s; retry budgets and exponential backoff with jitter are the minimum production mitigations.

en/networking/09-proxy-load-balancing/07.title: Resilient LB architecture: anycast, zone-aware routing, and observability
en/networking/09-proxy-load-balancing/07.summary: A single LB is a SPOF — anycast + BGP ECMP eliminates it; zone-aware routing cuts cross-zone egress cost; TLS terminates at the edge; RED metrics and circuit-breaker state are the minimum observability for safe operation.

en/networking/09-proxy-load-balancing/pr.title: Proxy and load balancing: survive a failing backend
en/networking/09-proxy-load-balancing/pr.summary: Hands-on project — front a backend pool with a real load balancer, drive it into a retry storm, then apply the unit's resilience ladder until the cluster survives a failing node, proven with before/after metrics.

en/networking/10-quic-internals/01-why-q.title: Why QUIC and not TCP+TLS
en/networking/10-quic-internals/01-why-q.summary: QUIC moves transport logic out of the kernel and onto UDP so the protocol can evolve freely — trading CPU overhead for faster handshakes and independent streams.

en/networking/10-quic-internals/02-quic-.title: QUIC streams and head-of-line blocking
en/networking/10-quic-internals/02-quic-.summary: QUIC multiplexes independent streams over one UDP connection so a lost packet blocks only the stream carrying it, not every other stream — a 575x improvement on lossy paths.

en/networking/10-quic-internals/03-hands.title: Integrated handshake and 1-RTT
en/networking/10-quic-internals/03-hands.summary: QUIC fuses the transport and TLS layers into one exchange — the client sends TLS ClientHello in the first packet and application data flows after just one round trip.

en/networking/10-quic-internals/04-conne.title: Connection IDs and network migration
en/networking/10-quic-internals/04-conne.summary: QUIC identifies connections by an opaque Connection ID rather than the 4-tuple, so connections survive IP address changes — WiFi to cellular — without reconnecting.

en/networking/10-quic-internals/05-loss-.title: Loss detection and congestion control
en/networking/10-quic-internals/05-loss-.summary: QUIC uses monotonically increasing packet numbers and pluggable congestion control — NewReno, CUBIC, BBR — eliminating Karn''''s algorithm ambiguity and enabling per-application CC upgrades.

en/networking/10-quic-internals/06-0rtt-.title: 0-RTT resumption and packet encryption
en/networking/10-quic-internals/06-0rtt-.summary: QUIC''''s 0-RTT resumption lets clients piggyback data on the first packet — but without replay protection. Almost-full packet encryption eliminates passive sniffing and RST injection at the cost of operational opacity.

en/networking/10-quic-internals/07-deplo.title: Deployment tradeoffs and CPU cost
en/networking/10-quic-internals/07-deplo.summary: QUIC''''s user-space packet processing costs 15–30% more CPU per byte than kernel TCP, drops up to 45% goodput on fast links, and requires mandatory HTTP/2 fallback for the 3–5% of networks that block UDP.

en/networking/10-quic-internals/project.title: QUIC internals: prove it on the wire
en/networking/10-quic-internals/project.summary: Hands-on project — stand up an HTTP/3 server, prove its 1-RTT handshake, stream independence, and migration on the wire, then measure the CPU cost against TCP and decide where QUIC belongs.

en/networking/11-network-security/01-ddo.title: DDoS: what it is and why it works
en/networking/11-network-security/01-ddo.summary: A DDoS attack overwhelms a service with traffic from many sources simultaneously — making it unavailable to real users without stealing data or breaking code.

en/networking/11-network-security/02-amp.title: Amplification attacks and state exhaustion
en/networking/11-network-security/02-amp.summary: Amplification attacks exploit open third-party servers to multiply attacker bandwidth 50–1280x; state-exhaustion attacks fill TCP backlog tables to drop legitimate connections.

en/networking/11-network-security/03-rat.title: Rate limiting: algorithms and architecture
en/networking/11-network-security/03-rat.summary: Token bucket, leaky bucket, fixed window, and sliding window counter each make a different tradeoff between accuracy, memory, burst tolerance, and implementation complexity.

en/networking/11-network-security/04-waf.title: WAFs, firewalls, mTLS, and HSTS
en/networking/11-network-security/04-waf.summary: Firewalls block L3/L4 nonsense; WAFs inspect HTTP content against attack patterns; mTLS authenticates service-to-service identity; HSTS preload prevents TLS downgrade attacks.

en/networking/11-network-security/05-dns.title: DNS cache poisoning and BGP hijacking
en/networking/11-network-security/05-dns.summary: The Kaminsky attack poisons DNS caches via transaction ID brute-force; BGP hijacking redirects traffic at the routing level — DNSSEC and RPKI/ROV are the respective defenses, both with partial deployment.

en/networking/11-network-security/06-def.title: Defense-in-depth architecture and attack economics
en/networking/11-network-security/06-def.summary: No single defense stops all DDoS vectors — anycast edge absorption, rate limiting, WAF, mTLS, and adaptive load shedding form the layers; attack economics favor the attacker only if you defend alone.

en/networking/11-network-security/projec.title: Network security: survive a layered DDoS
en/networking/11-network-security/projec.summary: Hands-on project — build a small service, drive it into an L7 cache-busting overload, then layer rate limiting, WAF tuning, and adaptive concurrency until it survives, proving each step with before/after numbers.

en/networking/11-network-security/quiz-c.summary: Multiple-choice synthesis across the network-security unit: attack vectors, amplification economics, rate-limiting tradeoffs, WAF tuning, mTLS identity, and RPKI/ROV.

en/networking/12-putting-it-together/01-.title: The twelve layers: one URL, seven actors
en/networking/12-putting-it-together/01-.summary: When you type a URL, seven actors — browser, resolver, router, origin, CA, CDN edge, and render engine — execute twelve phases in sequence. This lesson maps the whole journey.

en/networking/12-putting-it-together/02-.title: DNS, TCP, TLS in sequence: where the milliseconds go
en/networking/12-putting-it-together/02-.summary: Seven concrete phases from cold DNS to first encrypted byte, with timing numbers and the optimisation levers (TLS resumption, 0-RTT, connection coalescing) that eliminate round-trips instead of shortening them.

en/networking/12-putting-it-together/03-.title: Critical render path and Core Web Vitals
en/networking/12-putting-it-together/03-.summary: How the browser turns bytes into pixels — the DOM/CSSOM merge, CSS render-blocking, the preload scanner, JavaScript deferral — and how LCP, INP, and CLS measure the user''''s experience of that pipeline.

en/networking/12-putting-it-together/04-.title: Proxy intercepts and security gates: rate limiters, WAF, mTLS
en/networking/12-putting-it-together/04-.summary: Before a request reaches origin processing, it passes through reverse proxy health-routing, token-bucket rate limiters, WAF signature matching, and optional mTLS service-mesh auth — each adding latency budgets and operational complexity.

en/networking/12-putting-it-together/05-.title: Alternate paths: QUIC 0-RTT, WebSocket upgrade, connection migration
en/networking/12-putting-it-together/05-.summary: When the standard HTTP/1.1 request-response path is too slow or too static, two alternate transports take over: HTTP/3 over QUIC (0-RTT, HoL-free streams, mobile migration) and WebSocket upgrade (persistent full-duplex). Both have specific failure modes you must handle.

en/networking/12-putting-it-together/06-.title: Observability: distributed traces, USE/RED, and sampling
en/networking/12-putting-it-together/06-.summary: OpenTelemetry W3C Trace Context propagation reveals which hop ate the 500 ms; USE and RED methods discipline instrumentation; head-based vs tail-based sampling controls the cost of capturing traces at 1M req/s.

en/networking/12-putting-it-together/07-.title: Resilience: cascading retries, circuit breakers, and error budgets
en/networking/12-putting-it-together/07-.summary: A single slow dependency triggers client retries across all twelve layers simultaneously — amplifying 1 error into 10× load. Circuit breakers, exponential backoff with jitter, bulkheads, and error-budget-driven release cadence are the layered defenses against cascade failures.

en/networking/12-putting-it-together/pro.title: Putting it together: trace and optimise a full page load
en/networking/12-putting-it-together/pro.summary: Capstone — trace one real page load end-to-end across DNS, TCP/QUIC, TLS, HTTP, and CDN, then optimise each layer and prove the wins with before/after numbers.

en/networking/12-putting-it-together/qui.title: Putting it together: multiple-choice review
en/networking/12-putting-it-together/qui.summary: Cross-track multiple-choice synthesis for the networking capstone — one URL through DNS, TCP/QUIC, TLS, proxy gates, render, and the cascade defenses that keep it standing.

en/networking/12-putting-it-together/qui.summary: Read real tooling output — a tcpdump capture, a dig trace, a curl TLS handshake, and an Alt-Svc HTTP/3 negotiation — and diagnose what the bytes actually say.

en/networking/12-putting-it-together/qui.title: Putting it together: free-recall review
en/networking/12-putting-it-together/qui.summary: Free-recall prompts spanning the whole networking track — the phase chain, round-trip elimination, the render pipeline, tracing, cascades, and QUIC migration. Answer from memory, then compare.

en/nextjs/01-rendering-strategies/01-ssr.title: SSG, SSR, ISR: who builds the HTML, and when
en/nextjs/01-rendering-strategies/01-ssr.summary: SSG builds HTML at deploy, SSR per request, ISR serves stale and rebuilds in the background after a revalidate window. The axis: TTFB vs freshness vs infra cost; classic failures — stale pages surviving a deploy and a thundering herd of simultaneous revalidations.

en/nextjs/01-rendering-strategies/02-ser.title: React Server Components: the boundary, the payload, and what crosses it
en/nextjs/01-rendering-strategies/02-ser.summary: RSC run only on the server and ship zero JS — the client receives a serialized tree (the RSC payload), not a bundle. "use client" marks a boundary, not a component; only serializable props cross it. Hooks are impossible server-side: the component has no client lifetime.

en/nextjs/01-rendering-strategies/03-hyd.title: Hydration: matching the server's HTML, and paying for the JS you ship
en/nextjs/01-rendering-strategies/03-hyd.summary: Hydration attaches listeners to server HTML — markup must match the client render, or React recovers with a costly full client re-render. Date.now, locale, browser-only branches cause mismatches; Suspense enables selective hydration; less shipped JS = better INP/TBT.

en/nextjs/02-app-router-and-data/01-app-.title: App Router architecture: layouts that persist and files that mean things
en/nextjs/02-app-router-and-data/01-app-.summary: Folders are routes, special files are UI: layout wraps and persists across navigation (it never re-renders, state survives), page is the leaf, loading is a Suspense boundary, error a client boundary. Route groups, parallel and intercepting routes shape the tree.

en/nextjs/02-app-router-and-data/02-cach.title: The four Next.js caches — and why your data doesn't update
en/nextjs/02-app-router-and-data/02-cach.summary: Four caches: Request Memoization (one render pass), Data Cache (server, survives deploys), Full Route Cache (static HTML+RSC, cleared on deploy), Router Cache (client). Diagnose stale data layer by layer; revalidatePath/Tag invalidate; Next 15 stops caching fetch by default.

en/nextjs/02-app-router-and-data/03-serv.title: Server actions: RPC over POST that you must treat as public endpoints
en/nextjs/02-app-router-and-data/03-serv.summary: A server action is RPC over POST: 'use server' gives the function an id clients invoke. Forms work pre-hydration; args must be React-serializable. Every action is a public endpoint — validate and authorize inside, revalidate after mutation; external callers get route handlers.

en/nextjs/03-route-handlers-and-middlewa.title: Route handlers: route.ts as your HTTP surface — verbs, params, and the Next 15 caching flip
en/nextjs/03-route-handlers-and-middlewa.summary: route.ts exports GET/POST and friends as functions over web Request/Response. Dynamic segments arrive as awaited params. Next 15 flipped GET caching to dynamic-by-default — force-static is opt-in. Handlers are your public HTTP surface; server actions are internal mutations.

en/nextjs/03-route-handlers-and-middlewa.title: Middleware and the edge of trust: matchers, rewrites, and CVE-2025-29927
en/nextjs/03-route-handlers-and-middlewa.summary: middleware.ts runs before every matched request: matcher config, rewrite/redirect/headers. It is for routing decisions — locale, A/B, redirects — not heavy auth or DB calls. CVE-2025-29927 let one header skip middleware entirely: the definitive case for defense in depth.

en/nextjs/03-route-handlers-and-middlewa.title: Node vs Edge runtime: cold starts, missing APIs, and why compute must live near data
en/nextjs/03-route-handlers-and-middlewa.summary: Edge runtime trades Node APIs (native modules, fs, long CPU) for near-zero cold starts and natural streaming. The catch is placement: edge compute next to the user with a central DB pays cross-region RTT per query. Choose runtime and region per route — code belongs near its data.

en/nextjs/03-route-handlers-and-middlewa.title: Streaming responses: ReadableStream, SSE for LLM UIs, and the proxies that buffer them
en/nextjs/03-route-handlers-and-middlewa.summary: Route handlers stream via ReadableStream and SSE — the transport of LLM token UIs. Backpressure is pull-based: produce as the consumer drains. Suspense streams HTML; handlers stream data. Both break silently behind buffering proxies and compression — send no-transform.

en/nextjs/04-auth-patterns/01-sessions-v.title: Sessions vs JWT: revocation, rotation, and where the state lives on serverless
en/nextjs/04-auth-patterns/01-sessions-v.summary: Opaque session ids in an HttpOnly __Host- cookie plus a KV/DB store buy instant revocation at ~1-2 ms per request; JWTs verify locally but cannot be recalled before exp. Rotation, cookie attributes, and where the store lives on serverless decide which one you can operate.

en/nextjs/04-auth-patterns/02-auth-bound.title: Auth boundaries: why middleware and layouts cannot protect, and the Data Access Layer that can
en/nextjs/04-auth-patterns/02-auth-bound.summary: Middleware is an optimistic redirect, not a guard — CVE-2025-29927 skipped it with one header. Layouts render independently and do not re-run on navigation, so a layout check protects nothing. The authoritative boundary is a Data Access Layer: verify the session at every read.

en/nextjs/04-auth-patterns/03-server-onl.title: server-only and secrets: the module graph, NEXT_PUBLIC_, and what taint APIs actually catch
en/nextjs/04-auth-patterns/03-server-onl.summary: Secrets leak through the client module graph and serialized props, not just the network. import server-only turns a wrong import into a build error; NEXT_PUBLIC_ vars are inlined into the bundle forever; taint APIs are an experimental tripwire, not a security boundary.

en/nextjs/04-auth-patterns/04-csrf-and-a.title: CSRF and action security: every server action is a public POST endpoint
en/nextjs/04-auth-patterns/04-csrf-and-a.summary: Every exported server action is a public POST endpoint. Next compares Origin to Host — that stops cross-site forgery and nothing else, and route handlers get no such check. Authentication, per-row authorization, zod validation, and rate limiting belong inside every action.

en/nextjs/05-assets-and-images/01-next-i.title: next/image: the resize pipeline, srcset, and what every variant costs
en/nextjs/05-assets-and-images/01-next-i.summary: next/image renders an img with a srcset of on-demand AVIF/WebP variants from /_next/image, lazy-loads below the fold, and requires dimensions so layout never shifts. priority marks the LCP image; remotePatterns gates the optimizer; every variant costs CPU or per-image billing.

en/nextjs/05-assets-and-images/02-fonts-.title: next/font and CSS strategies: self-hosted fonts, zero-shift swaps, zero-runtime styles
en/nextjs/05-assets-and-images/02-fonts-.summary: next/font downloads Google fonts at build and self-hosts them — no runtime request to Google — with a size-adjusted fallback so the swap shifts nothing. Subsets and variable fonts set the byte budget; Tailwind and CSS Modules stay zero-runtime, CSS-in-JS drags a client bundle.

en/nextjs/05-assets-and-images/03-bundle.title: Bundle analysis and budgets: first-load JS, barrel-file bloat, and CI gates
en/nextjs/05-assets-and-images/03-bundle.summary: First-load JS is the number to own: barrel imports and use-client creep inflate shared chunks invisibly. Read the analyzer treemap, know the KB→main-thread-ms→INP/LCP chain, and gate per-route budgets in CI so a +300 KB icon import fails the PR, not the field data.

en/nextjs/06-deployment-and-edge/01-self.title: Self-host vs Vercel: standalone anatomy, build-time env baking, and what the platform actually sells
en/nextjs/06-deployment-and-edge/01-self.summary: output standalone emits server.js plus a file-traced node_modules subset, but .next/static, public and sharp are yours to ship. NEXT_PUBLIC_ vars are inlined into client bundles at build time, and the honest cost math is per-request metering versus a flat VM plus CDN.

en/nextjs/06-deployment-and-edge/02-edge.title: Edge vs Node in production: isolates, cold starts, and the data-locality trap
en/nextjs/06-deployment-and-edge/02-edge.summary: Edge runtime is V8 isolates: near-zero cold start versus 200-800 ms for Node lambdas, paid with no Node APIs, no native deps, code-size caps. Edge wins when compute is data-free or data is replicated; edge plus a single-region DB pays cross-continent RTT per query.

en/nextjs/06-deployment-and-edge/03-isr-.title: ISR and CDN layers: stale-while-revalidate at origin, per-pod caches, and purge ordering
en/nextjs/06-deployment-and-edge/03-isr-.summary: revalidate serves stale, regenerates in the background and swaps atomically — per pod. Past one pod the default disk cache diverges: you need a shared cacheHandler and pub/sub fan-out for revalidatePath. On top, the CDN layer orders as regenerate first, purge second.

en/nextjs/07-observability-and-errors/01.title: error.tsx hierarchy: what each boundary actually catches, digests, and when reset() lies
en/nextjs/07-observability-and-errors/01.summary: error.tsx wraps its segment page, not its layout: layout errors bubble to the parent boundary, and a root crash reaches only global-error.tsx. Production redacts server errors to a digest; reset() heals only transient failures. Place boundaries by blast radius.

en/nextjs/07-observability-and-errors/02.title: instrumentation.ts and tracing: one register() per process, one trace per request, and the sampling bill
en/nextjs/07-observability-and-errors/02.summary: instrumentation.ts register() runs once per server process before any request — the only safe OTel init point, with a runtime guard for edge. Next emits render and fetch spans and propagates traceparent to backends. Sampling strategy and attribute cardinality decide the bill.

en/nextjs/07-observability-and-errors/03.title: Server logging and Web Vitals: structured logs with request ids, and beacons that name the bad deploy
en/nextjs/07-observability-and-errors/03.summary: Server component logs go to server stdout only — teams lose evidence after migrating from pages. Structured pino JSON with a middleware-minted request id on every line restores it; useReportWebVitals beacons field LCP and INP tagged with the deploy id that caused them.

en/nextjs/08-architecture-at-scale/01-ro.title: Route groups as module boundaries: per-domain shells, colocation, and the full-reload tax
en/nextjs/08-architecture-at-scale/01-ro.summary: Route groups partition app/ into domain modules that vanish from the URL: per-group root layouts give marketing and app separate shells at the cost of a full reload when crossing. Private folders keep code colocated; lint, not the router, enforces dependency direction.

en/nextjs/08-architecture-at-scale/02-mo.title: Monorepo mechanics: pnpm workspaces, the Turborepo task graph, and packages that earn their boundary
en/nextjs/08-architecture-at-scale/02-mo.summary: pnpm workspaces link internal packages; Turborepo hashes task inputs and replays cached outputs — 38-minute cold CI becomes single-digit warm builds. transpilePackages ships source-TSX ui packages; changesets only matter when publishing. A god utils package erases every win.

en/nextjs/08-architecture-at-scale/03-pa.title: pages/ to app/ migration: coexistence, the translation map, and a quarters-not-sprints timeline
en/nextjs/08-architecture-at-scale/03-pa.summary: Both routers run side by side, so migration is route-by-route: getServerSideProps becomes an awaited fetch in an RSC, _app becomes the root layout, and router.events has no routeChangeStart replacement. Leaf pages move first; a 100-page app takes quarters, not sprints.

en/nextjs/09-data-layer/01-orm-and-sql-i.title: ORM and SQL in server components: the data layer owns queries, memoization, and the tree-shaped N+1
en/nextjs/09-data-layer/01-orm-and-sql-i.summary: RSC query the database directly, so discipline moves to the data layer: queries live in lib/data next to the auth check, React cache() dedupes one render pass, Promise.all and preload kill waterfalls, and the tree-shaped N+1 — 50 cards, 50 queries — gets hoisted or batched.

en/nextjs/09-data-layer/02-pooling-on-se.title: Pooling on serverless: the multiplication problem, pgbouncer transaction mode, and per-lambda sizing
en/nextjs/09-data-layer/02-pooling-on-se.summary: Every lambda owns a pool: 100 invocations times pool 5 is 500 connections against max_connections 100 — FATAL: too many clients. Per-instance pools shrink to 1-2; the fix ladder: pgbouncer transaction mode with its costs, RDS Proxy, HTTP drivers. Cold starts dial in herds.

en/nextjs/09-data-layer/03-cache-tags-by.title: Cache tags by domain: invalidation taxonomy, webhook wiring, and the over-invalidation storm
en/nextjs/09-data-layer/03-cache-tags-by.summary: revalidateTag is only as strong as your tag taxonomy: entity tags, collection tags, prefixes per bounded context. One global tag turns every CMS edit into a site-wide purge storm; a missing collection tag leaves stale prices for hours. The webhook-to-tags mapping table is code.

en/nextjs/10-production-nextjs/01-cache-.title: Cache poisoning incidents: when one user becomes everyone
en/nextjs/10-production-nextjs/01-cache-.summary: A cache key that omits something the response depends on serves one user to everyone: an unstable_cache closure, a CDN storing Set-Cookie, a missing Vary, X-Forwarded-Host in cached HTML. The invariant: everything the response reads is in the key, or the route is dynamic.

en/nextjs/10-production-nextjs/02-isr-st.title: ISR storms and cold starts: the self-DDoS you schedule for yourself
en/nextjs/10-production-nextjs/02-isr-st.summary: A deploy that resets the ISR cache turns the catalog into one synchronized re-render against your own origin. Mitigations with mechanics: persistent cacheHandler, jittered windows, capped regeneration queues — plus cold-start anatomy and why p99 spikes at deploy hour.

en/nextjs/10-production-nextjs/03-cost-e.title: Cost engineering: the five line items and the patterns that 10x them
en/nextjs/10-production-nextjs/03-cost-e.summary: Decompose the bill into GB-hours, image transformations, egress, ISR ops and edge invocations — then hunt the multipliers: the resize-farm optimizer, middleware on every asset, revalidate:1 on a long tail, the accidental-dynamic tax. Per-route math plus guardrails.

en/node/00-start-here/01-what-node-is.title: What Node.js actually is
en/node/00-start-here/01-what-node-is.summary: Node.js is JavaScript outside the browser: V8 runs your code, libuv gives it a single-threaded event loop with non-blocking I/O, and a built-in library exposes files, networking, and the process. Great at I/O, poor at heavy CPU.

en/node/01-modules-and-runtime/01-cjs-vs.title: CommonJS vs ESM
en/node/01-modules-and-runtime/01-cjs-vs.summary: CommonJS resolves require() synchronously at runtime with value-copy exports; ESM is a static, hoisted, async graph with live read-only bindings and top-level await. Node picks one per file, and the interop seam is where teams bleed time.

en/node/01-modules-and-runtime/02-packag.title: package.json, npm, semver and lockfiles
en/node/01-modules-and-runtime/02-packag.summary: package.json declares intent with semver ranges; the lockfile pins the exact resolved tree. npm install may rewrite the lock, npm ci installs strictly from it — so commit the lockfile and use npm ci in CI.

en/node/01-modules-and-runtime/03-module.title: The module cache: identity, singletons, and duplicate copies
en/node/01-modules-and-runtime/03-module.summary: A Node module is a singleton keyed by its resolved absolute path: the first require evaluates it once and every later require returns the same object. Two install locations of one package resolve to two keys — two instances — so instanceof and shared state silently break.

en/node/01-modules-and-runtime/04-runtim.title: Runtime bootstrap and the event loop
en/node/01-modules-and-runtime/04-runtim.summary: Node runs your JS on one thread driven by libuv's phase-ordered event loop; microtasks (nextTick > Promise) drain between callbacks, fs/crypto use a 4-slot threadpool, and any sync work blocks every concurrent request.

en/node/01-modules-and-runtime/05-proces.title: Process lifecycle and graceful shutdown
en/node/01-modules-and-runtime/05-proces.summary: A process exits when the event loop drains or you force it; the senior skill is dying cleanly — catch SIGTERM, flip readiness off, stop accepting connections, drain in-flight work under a hard timeout, then exit, so deploys cost zero 502s.

en/node/02-async-and-streams/01-async-pa.title: Async patterns and error handling
en/node/02-async-and-streams/01-async-pa.summary: Callbacks, promises, and async/await are three faces of one model. Compose with Promise.all, propagate rejections instead of swallowing them, cancel with AbortController, and know that microtasks drain before the next macrotask.

en/node/02-async-and-streams/02-streams-.title: Streams, pipes and backpressure
en/node/02-async-and-streams/02-streams-.summary: Streams move data chunk-by-chunk so a 4GB file never lands in RAM. When a fast producer outruns a slow consumer, backpressure — write() returning false until drain — is the brake. Wire it with pipeline(), never a manual pipe.

en/node/02-async-and-streams/03-concurre.title: Concurrency control: combinators, bounded fan-out, and cancellation
en/node/02-async-and-streams/03-concurre.summary: Promise.all rejects on first failure but never cancels its siblings; an unbounded fan-out DoSes your own DB. The senior answer is a bounded worker pool plus AbortController, which actually cancels the loser instead of leaking it.

en/node/02-async-and-streams/04-async-it.title: Async iterators and generators: pull-based streams without the buffer
en/node/02-async-and-streams/04-async-it.summary: Async iterators are pull-based: the consumer pulls each value, so the producer is suspended at yield and backpressure is structural. break/throw runs the generator's finally so cursors close. Chain generators for a lazy O(1)-memory pipeline.

en/node/02-async-and-streams/05-stream-p.title: Stream pipelines, transforms, and the .pipe() error trap
en/node/02-async-and-streams/05-stream-p.summary: .pipe() does not forward errors or destroy the chain, so one mid-stream failure leaks fds until EMFILE. stream.pipeline() wires errors and cleanup; write Transforms with _transform, and bridge Node and Web streams at the edges.

en/node/03-errors-and-diagnostics/01-err.title: Error handling: throw, reject, and never swallow
en/node/03-errors-and-diagnostics/01-err.summary: An error is an object with a stack and a code, not a string. Match throw, reject, or an error-first callback to the call style, chain the original with cause, and never swallow a rejection — an unhandled one crashes the process by default.

en/node/03-errors-and-diagnostics/02-deb.title: Debugging Node with --inspect and DevTools
en/node/03-errors-and-diagnostics/02-deb.summary: `node --inspect` opens a V8 Inspector WebSocket on 127.0.0.1:9229 that DevTools and VS Code attach to; `--inspect-brk` breaks before line one. Keep it on localhost — that port is remote code execution. For cheap logs use util.debuglog gated by NODE_DEBUG.

en/node/03-errors-and-diagnostics/03-dia.title: Diagnostics: channels, async context, and profiles
en/node/03-errors-and-diagnostics/03-dia.summary: diagnostics_channel is in-process pub/sub that costs nothing unless subscribed, AsyncLocalStorage carries a request id across await without threading args, and --cpu-prof writes a profile on exit — instrument without monkey-patching.

en/node/04-performance/01-event-loop-mon.title: Monitoring event-loop lag
en/node/04-performance/01-event-loop-mon.summary: Node runs JS on one thread, so one slow synchronous call stalls every queued timer and I/O callback. Measure event-loop lag with monitorEventLoopDelay, watch the p99 not the mean, and move CPU work off the loop.

en/node/04-performance/02-cpu-and-memory.title: CPU profiles and the heap-snapshot leak hunt
en/node/04-performance/02-cpu-and-memory.summary: A CPU profile shows where time goes — wide flame frames are hot. A leak is old space that climbs across GCs and never drops; find it with three heap snapshots, chase retained size and the retainer path, then bound the cache or remove the listener.

en/node/04-performance/03-worker-threads.title: Worker threads and clustering
en/node/04-performance/03-worker-threads.summary: On one thread, async I/O scales but CPU-bound work blocks the event loop and starves every request. Offload CPU work to a worker_threads pool sized to your cores; spread a stateless network server across cores with cluster or replicas. Neither fixes pure I/O.

en/node/05-http-and-frameworks/01-http-m.title: The http module: servers, clients, and streams
en/node/05-http-and-frameworks/01-http-m.summary: In raw http, req is an IncomingMessage (a Readable body + headers) and res is a ServerResponse (a Writable). Stream the body, respect backpressure, reuse sockets with keep-alive, and add the timeouts and body cap that http omits — or a slow client exhausts your sockets.

en/node/05-http-and-frameworks/02-expres.title: Express vs Fastify: middleware and throughput
en/node/05-http-and-frameworks/02-expres.summary: Express is a linear (req, res, next) middleware chain — minimal and unopinionated with the largest ecosystem. Fastify trades that for a plugin model with JSON-Schema validation and fast-json-stringify serialization, the real throughput win. Both are production-grade.

en/node/05-http-and-frameworks/03-middle.title: Middleware, error boundaries, and graceful shutdown
en/node/05-http-and-frameworks/03-middle.summary: Middleware is an ordered pipeline ending in one 4-arg error boundary that maps typed errors to status codes and a safe body. Async throws need forwarding in Express 4, and SIGTERM must drain in-flight requests via server.close() before exit.

en/node/06-testing/01-unit-testing.title: Unit testing with node:test and Vitest
en/node/06-testing/01-unit-testing.summary: Node ships a stable test runner (node:test) plus node:assert; Vitest adds Vite speed and rich matchers. Test behavior not implementation, keep each test independent, and fake the clock so time-dependent tests are fast and deterministic.

en/node/06-testing/02-integration-and-su.title: Integration testing an HTTP API
en/node/06-testing/02-integration-and-su.summary: An integration test drives routing, middleware, handler and a real DB through the HTTP surface. supertest boots your app on an ephemeral port; isolation and a real engine decide whether the suite catches bugs or invents flakes.

en/node/06-testing/03-test-doubles-and-m.title: Test doubles and mocking: seams, not sledgehammers
en/node/06-testing/03-test-doubles-and-m.summary: A test double substitutes a collaborator at a seam. Know the five kinds, prefer injected seams over module mocks, fake timers to make a 30s backoff test run in 5ms — and never mock the thing you are actually testing, or the suite goes green while prod 500s.

en/node/06-testing/04-test-isolation-and.title: Test isolation and flakiness: making tests deterministic
en/node/06-testing/04-test-isolation-and.summary: A flaky test is a hidden race, not bad luck. Kill non-determinism at the source — pin the clock, seed randomness, freeze TZ — isolate state cheaply with beforeEach resets or transaction rollback, and quarantine flakes instead of letting retries mask a real failure rate.

en/node/06-testing/05-coverage-and-mutat.title: Coverage, mutation testing, and what's worth testing
en/node/06-testing/05-coverage-and-mutat.summary: Coverage measures execution, not verification — a suite at 94% line coverage can assert nothing. Branch coverage finds untested paths; mutation testing finds untested behavior. Chase mutation score on critical code, not a 100% coverage mandate.

en/node/07-security/01-input-and-secrets.title: Input validation and handling secrets
en/node/07-security/01-input-and-secrets.summary: Every external input is hostile until a schema at the boundary turns it into a typed value. Each injection class has one defense: parameterized queries, an argument array instead of a shell, a base-dir check for paths, bounded input for ReDoS. Secrets stay in env and out of git.

en/node/07-security/02-dependencies-and-.title: Dependencies and supply-chain risk
en/node/07-security/02-dependencies-and-.summary: Installing a package runs its code. Pin and verify the tree with a committed lockfile and `npm ci`, gate known CVEs with `npm audit`, block lifecycle scripts on untrusted installs, validate merge keys, and never treat `vm` as a sandbox.

en/node/07-security/03-authentication-an.title: Authentication and sessions: cookies, JWTs, and password hashing
en/node/07-security/03-authentication-an.summary: A server session is an opaque id in an HttpOnly cookie with state in a store; a JWT is signed claims verified statelessly. For browsers default to cookie sessions, hash passwords with scrypt + timingSafeEqual, and pin the JWT algorithm or one forged header owns every account.

en/node/07-security/04-security-headers-.title: Security headers, CORS, and TLS posture
en/node/07-security/04-security-headers-.summary: Security headers are the browser-side perimeter: CSP cuts XSS, HSTS kills SSL-strip, nosniff stops MIME guessing. CORS is the server opting in to cross-origin reads — reflecting the Origin with credentials hands any site your users' cookies. Terminate TLS 1.2+ with a full chain.

en/node/07-security/05-ssrf-redos-path-t.title: SSRF, ReDoS, and path traversal: the server attack surface
en/node/07-security/05-ssrf-redos-path-t.summary: Three server-side Node vulns: SSRF turns a URL fetcher into a probe of cloud metadata; ReDoS freezes the single event loop with one crafted string; path traversal escapes a dir via `../`. Fixes: pin the IP, bound the regex, contain the path.

en/node/08-packaging-and-deploy/01-bundl.title: Bundling and publishing: ESM, CJS, and exports
en/node/08-packaging-and-deploy/01-bundl.summary: Publishing is package.json design. The exports map is the modern entry point: it picks ESM vs CJS vs types by condition and encapsulates internals. Dual-publish risks the dual-package hazard; ESM-only is often simpler.

en/node/08-packaging-and-deploy/02-conta.title: Containerizing Node: PID 1, signals, and slim images
en/node/08-packaging-and-deploy/02-conta.summary: A Node process running as PID 1 ignores SIGTERM by default, so deploys hang the full grace period then hard-kill. Run node in exec form behind an init, build a multi-stage slim non-root image, and add a healthcheck and .dockerignore.

en/node/08-packaging-and-deploy/03-confi.title: Configuration and runtime flags: env, fail-fast, and heap limits
en/node/08-packaging-and-deploy/03-confi.summary: Read config once at boot into a frozen, schema-validated object and crash on a bad var before serving — and size the V8 old-space heap to ~75% of the container limit, because a non-cgroup-aware Node grows past the cap and gets OOMKilled at 137 with no JS stack.

en/node/08-packaging-and-deploy/04-zero-.title: Zero-downtime deploys: health probes, draining, and rollouts
en/node/08-packaging-and-deploy/04-zero-.summary: A deploy 502 is a race: SIGTERM closes the server before the load balancer de-registers it, so new requests hit a dying pod. Fix the order — fail readiness first, then close and exit — and pick a rollout (rolling, blue-green, canary) with backward-compatible migrations.

en/node/08-packaging-and-deploy/05-relea.title: The release pipeline: versioning, dist-tags, and npm provenance
en/node/08-packaging-and-deploy/05-relea.summary: A release is a tarball plus a contract. The `files` allow-list and a dry-run decide what ships; semver and dist-tags decide who resolves it; provenance proves who built it. You cannot unpublish after 72h, so deprecate and ship a fix.

en/node/09-putting-it-together/01-capsto.title: Capstone: designing and hardening a production Node service
en/node/09-putting-it-together/01-capsto.summary: A production Node service is the whole track composed at once: typed errors behind one boundary, an unblocked loop, an ordered middleware stack with timeouts and graceful shutdown, validated input, env config, and observability. Each skipped concern is a named incident.

en/node/10-networking-deep/01-tcp-and-ne.title: TCP and the net module: sockets, lifecycle, and backpressure
en/node/10-networking-deep/01-tcp-and-ne.summary: The net module gives you the raw TCP stream under http: a duplex socket with data/end/error/close, half-open semantics, Nagle batching you can disable with setNoDelay, and a write() boolean that is your socket-level backpressure signal.

en/node/10-networking-deep/02-udp-and-dg.title: UDP and dgram: datagrams, message boundaries, and when to drop reliability
en/node/10-networking-deep/02-udp-and-dg.summary: UDP via dgram sends independent datagrams with no connection, no ordering, and no delivery guarantee. Each send is one packet bounded by the MTU; you trade reliability for latency, and it wins for metrics, discovery, games, and DNS.

en/node/10-networking-deep/03-sockets-in.title: Sockets in production: timeouts, limits, and fd exhaustion
en/node/10-networking-deep/03-sockets-in.summary: Production socket failures are predictable: idle sockets without timeouts pin file descriptors, ECONNRESET/EPIPE crash unhardened handlers, and an unbounded accept rate exhausts fds. Add timeouts, limits, and a graceful drain.

en/node/11-tls-and-http2/01-tls-and-http.title: TLS and HTTPS in Node: ship the whole chain
en/node/11-tls-and-http2/01-tls-and-http.summary: TLS in Node hinges on shipping the full certificate chain, not just the leaf. Learn the handshake, SNI, session resumption, secureContext, and the cert errors you actually hit — and why you fix the chain instead of disabling verification.

en/node/11-tls-and-http2/02-http2-and-al.title: HTTP/2 and ALPN: one connection, many streams, one failure mode
en/node/11-tls-and-http2/02-http2-and-al.summary: HTTP/2 multiplexes many streams over one TCP connection and negotiates h2 via ALPN in the TLS handshake — but one connection means transport HoL still bites under loss.

en/node/11-tls-and-http2/03-http-client-.title: The HTTP client deep dive: undici, pools, timeouts, and leaked sockets
en/node/11-tls-and-http2/03-http-client-.summary: undici is the modern Node HTTP client and what global fetch runs on. Reuse connections with a pool, set timeouts, retry only idempotent requests, and always drain bodies or you leak sockets.

en/node/12-native-and-ffi/01-native-addo.title: Native addons with Node-API: the stable ABI and the boundary
en/node/12-native-and-ffi/01-native-addo.summary: Node-API is a stable C ABI: an addon built once keeps loading across Node majors, unlike raw-V8/NAN addons that must be rebuilt. You trade JS handles across an opaque boundary, run blocking work off-thread, and pay a real per-call cost.

en/node/12-native-and-ffi/02-build-and-w.title: Building native addons, prebuilds, and when not to: WASM and the alternatives
en/node/12-native-and-ffi/02-build-and-w.summary: Native addons build with node-gyp from a binding.gyp, which means a compiler at install time unless you ship prebuilds. WebAssembly, a child process, or plain JS often dodge that entirely — so the senior move is usually NOT to write one.

en/node/12-native-and-ffi/03-ffi-and-dlo.title: FFI: calling a prebuilt shared library from JS with koffi — and who owns the memory
en/node/12-native-and-ffi/03-ffi-and-dlo.summary: FFI calls an already-compiled shared library from JS — no C glue, no compiler — by declaring the C prototype and letting libffi build the call at runtime. You cross into native memory the GC cannot see, so a wrong signature or an unfreed pointer segfaults the process.

en/node/13-modules-deep/01-module-resolu.title: The module resolution algorithm: how Node finds your code
en/node/13-modules-deep/01-module-resolu.summary: CJS require() runs a synchronous algorithm — resolve the specifier kind, probe file then directory then index, walk node_modules up the tree — while ESM resolves URLs with mandatory extensions. Knowing the exact steps turns MODULE_NOT_FOUND from a mystery into a checklist.

en/node/13-modules-deep/02-package-expor.title: Package exports and conditions: the public API contract
en/node/13-modules-deep/02-package-expor.summary: The exports field is your package's public API contract: it overrides main, blocks every path it does not list, and routes import vs require to different files via conditions — which is also how you create, and avoid, the dual-package hazard of two divergent module instances.

en/node/13-modules-deep/03-module-custom.title: Module customization hooks: intercepting resolve and load
en/node/13-modules-deep/03-module-custom.summary: Customization hooks intercept resolve and load for every module. Registered via module.register on a separate thread, they chain through next… hooks. Great for dev transpilation and mocking — but they tax startup and a hook that drops source maps wrecks every stack trace.

en/node/13-modules-deep/04-cjs-esm-inter.title: CJS/ESM interop, deeply: require(esm), named exports, and TLA
en/node/13-modules-deep/04-cjs-esm-inter.summary: require() can now load an ESM module synchronously — but only if its graph has no top-level await, else ERR_REQUIRE_ASYNC_MODULE. The CJS<->ESM seam has traps: a static lexer misses dynamic named exports, esModuleInterop reshapes defaults, one package can load twice.

en/node/13-modules-deep/05-module-load-p.title: Module load performance: cold start, compile cache, and snapshots
en/node/13-modules-deep/05-module-load-p.summary: Cold start is dominated by resolution I/O (thousands of stat() per boot), V8 parse+compile, and top-level eval. Cut it by bundling to one file, caching bytecode with NODE_COMPILE_CACHE, deferring heavy deps with lazy require, and snapshotting init for CLIs and serverless.

en/node/14-v8-and-crypto/01-v8-optimizat.title: V8 optimization: hidden classes, inline caches, and the JIT tiers
en/node/14-v8-and-crypto/01-v8-optimizat.summary: V8 makes type-stable code fast by giving same-shaped objects one hidden class, caching property lookups monomorphically, and tiering hot functions up to TurboFan. Shape churn, deletes, and type-mixing trigger deopts and slow dictionary mode.

en/node/14-v8-and-crypto/02-crypto-deep.title: Node crypto, used right: KDFs, HMAC, signatures, and constant-time compares
en/node/14-v8-and-crypto/02-crypto-deep.summary: Node's crypto is correct only if you pick the right primitive: scrypt for passwords, HMAC for authenticated integrity, randomBytes for secrets, timingSafeEqual to compare them. Fast hashes and === are the bugs.

en/node/14-v8-and-crypto/03-heap-snapsho.title: Heap snapshots and flame graphs: finding leaks and hot paths in production Node
en/node/14-v8-and-crypto/03-heap-snapsho.summary: Heap snapshots and flame graphs are the two lenses on a hot Node process: retained size and the three-snapshot diff find a leak, the V8 profiler and flame graph find where CPU goes — and you must tell a true leak from harmless churn.

en/observability/00-start-here/01-overvi.title: Start from zero: what observability actually is
en/observability/00-start-here/01-overvi.summary: Observability is the ability to ask "what is my running system doing and why" from the outside. This is the from-zero map and the eight words the rest of the track assumes you already know.

en/observability/01-three-pillars/01-wha.title: What the three signals are: logs, metrics, and traces
en/observability/01-three-pillars/01-wha.summary: The three telemetry shapes production systems emit, why each exists, and how a five-minute triage works by picking the right one.

en/observability/01-three-pillars/02-met.title: Metrics and cardinality: the cost model of a time-series database
en/observability/01-three-pillars/02-met.summary: How Prometheus-model metrics work, why cardinality is the central cost driver, and what happens when a single label explodes series count.

en/observability/01-three-pillars/03-log.title: Logs and volume: the cost model of structured logging
en/observability/01-three-pillars/03-log.summary: How structured logs work, why ingestion bytes dominate the bill, and how level discipline and tiered retention control the cost.

en/observability/01-three-pillars/04-tra.title: Traces and sampling: the cost model of distributed tracing
en/observability/01-three-pillars/04-tra.summary: How a distributed trace is built, why sampling is mandatory, and the engineering tradeoffs between head-based and tail-based strategies.

en/observability/01-three-pillars/05-joi.title: Join keys and exemplars: making the three signals compose
en/observability/01-three-pillars/05-joi.summary: How shared attribute names connect metrics, logs, and traces into a navigable surface, and how exemplars bridge aggregate metrics to individual traces.

en/observability/01-three-pillars/06-obs.title: Observability 2.0: wide events and the cost shift
en/observability/01-three-pillars/06-obs.summary: Why Charity Majors and the Honeycomb team argue that three pillars are a 1990s storage artifact, how wide events collapse them, and when the 1.0 split is still cost-optimal.

en/observability/01-three-pillars/07-fai.title: Failure modes and engineering practice: cardinality budgets, PII, and sampling
en/observability/01-three-pillars/07-fai.summary: Real production failure modes per signal, cardinality budgets as engineering culture, PII leaks on metric and log surfaces, and OTel sampling configuration in practice.

en/observability/01-three-pillars/projec.title: Three pillars: build a navigable observability surface
en/observability/01-three-pillars/projec.summary: Hands-on project — instrument one service with all three signals, wire join keys and exemplars, then prove a sub-30-second metric-to-log-to-trace triage and a cardinality guardrail.

en/observability/02-structured-logging/0.title: Why structured logs exist: the diary vs the spreadsheet
en/observability/02-structured-logging/0.summary: Free-text logs look readable and become un-queryable at scale. Structured logs are a spreadsheet — every line is a record with addressable fields.

en/observability/02-structured-logging/0.title: The production log schema: fields every line must carry
en/observability/02-structured-logging/0.summary: What a production-grade structured log line contains in 2026 — the OTel Logs Data Model fields, resource attributes, and why the schema is the API your on-call tooling expects.

en/observability/02-structured-logging/0.title: Log levels and alert routing
en/observability/02-structured-logging/0.summary: The TRACE–FATAL ladder controls what gets stored and who gets paged. Misclassified levels pollute either the alert or the bill.

en/observability/02-structured-logging/0.title: Sampling strategies and log cost
en/observability/02-structured-logging/0.summary: Success-path, pattern-based, and tail sampling are the three levers that keep the log bill proportional to incidents, not to traffic.

en/observability/02-structured-logging/0.title: PII redaction and log injection
en/observability/02-structured-logging/0.summary: Logs are the easiest signal to leak sensitive data into and the hardest to clean up. Redact at the source, defend in depth at the collector, and never interpolate user input into log messages.

en/observability/02-structured-logging/0.title: Trace context propagation in logs
en/observability/02-structured-logging/0.summary: Every log line emitted inside a traced request must carry trace_id and span_id. Without them, the log-to-trace pivot fails and observability degrades to guesswork.

en/observability/02-structured-logging/0.title: OTel Logs Data Model and audit logs as a subsystem
en/observability/02-structured-logging/0.summary: The OTel Logs Data Model is the cross-vendor schema converging point for 2026. Audit logs share the JSON format but differ on retention, immutability, and access — mixing them with operational logs is a compliance failure.

en/observability/02-structured-logging/p.title: Structured logging: build a production logging pipeline
en/observability/02-structured-logging/p.summary: Hands-on project — instrument a service with an OTel-shaped log schema, route levels, sample at the collector, redact PII, correlate by trace_id, and separate audit logs, proving each property with evidence.

en/observability/02-structured-logging/q.summary: Multiple-choice synthesis across the structured-logging unit — schema contracts, level routing, sampling economics, PII and injection defence, trace correlation, and audit separation.

en/observability/03-otel/01-what-is-otel.title: What is OpenTelemetry: API, SDK, Collector, OTLP
en/observability/03-otel/01-what-is-otel.summary: OTel is four pieces stacked: an API your code calls, an SDK that builds telemetry, a Collector that routes it, and OTLP that carries it — together they let you instrument once and swap backends without rewriting code.

en/observability/03-otel/02-signals-and-.title: OTel signals, Semantic Conventions, and the OTLP wire format
en/observability/03-otel/02-signals-and-.summary: Traces, metrics, and logs each have their own SDK pipeline and OTLP message shape but share the Resource and trace context. OTLP/gRPC is 50-70% smaller than JSON and is the vendor-neutral edge contract.

en/observability/03-otel/03-auto-and-man.title: Auto-instrumentation and manual spans: the 80/20 of OTel
en/observability/03-otel/03-auto-and-man.summary: Auto-instrumentation covers 70-80% of production traffic for free — HTTP, DB, queues. The remaining 20-30% is manual spans with business attributes, and that is where the real diagnostic value lives.

en/observability/03-otel/04-collector-pi.title: The OTel Collector: receivers, processors, exporters, and deployment patterns
en/observability/03-otel/04-collector-pi.summary: The Collector is a YAML-configured pipeline — receivers accept telemetry, processors transform it in-flight, exporters ship it to backends. Three deployment patterns dominate: agent, gateway, and agent-to-gateway.

en/observability/03-otel/05-sampling-str.title: Sampling strategies: head, tail, and parent-based
en/observability/03-otel/05-sampling-str.summary: Head sampling is cheap and predictable; tail sampling is expensive but curated. ParentBased(TraceIdRatioBased(0.2)) at the SDK plus tail sampling on the gateway — 100% errors and slow tails, 1% baseline — is the textbook production combination.

en/observability/03-otel/06-vendor-neutr.title: Vendor neutrality, eBPF instrumentation, the Operator, and browser/serverless OTel
en/observability/03-otel/06-vendor-neutr.summary: True vendor neutrality lives at the application edge, not the Collector. eBPF covers breadth; SDK instrumentation covers depth. The OTel Operator turns instrumentation into a platform-team concern. Browser and serverless have OTLP/HTTP constraints.

en/observability/03-otel/07-collector-op.title: Operating the OTel Collector: reliability, version skew, failure modes, and governance
en/observability/03-otel/07-collector-op.summary: The Collector is critical-path observability infrastructure. HA gateway (3+ replicas), persistent queue, meta-monitoring, conservative version upgrades, and Semantic Convention governance — these are the disciplines that prevent silent telemetry loss.

en/observability/03-otel/project.title: OTel: build a vendor-neutral pipeline
en/observability/03-otel/project.summary: Hands-on project — instrument a multi-service app with OTel, stand up an agent-to-gateway Collector pipeline with tail sampling, and prove vendor-neutrality and self-monitoring with evidence.

en/observability/03-otel/quiz-choice.summary: Multiple-choice synthesis across the OTel unit — the four-piece architecture, signals and OTLP, Collector pipeline, sampling, vendor-neutrality, and operations.
