en/observability/03-otel/quiz-code.summary: Read real Collector YAML, a tail-sampling config, a gctrace-style log line, and a manual-span snippet — then pick the behaviour or the highest-leverage fix.

en/observability/04-red-use/01-red-and-u.title: RED and USE: two checklists, one triage discipline
en/observability/04-red-use/01-red-and-u.summary: RED (Rate, Errors, Duration) describes what the user felt. USE (Utilization, Saturation, Errors) describes which resource caused it. Running both in sequence is the senior engineer''''s first reflex when the pager fires.

en/observability/04-red-use/02-red-instr.title: Instrumenting RED in Prometheus: counters, histograms, and cardinality discipline
en/observability/04-red-use/02-red-instr.summary: The three canonical Prometheus metrics for RED, why Duration must be a histogram (never an average), how histogram_quantile works, and the iron label discipline that keeps cardinality under control.

en/observability/04-red-use/03-use-on-li.title: USE on Linux: CPU, memory, disk, network, and PSI
en/observability/04-red-use/03-use-on-li.summary: How to collect utilization, saturation, and error signals for every Linux resource — and why Pressure Stall Information (PSI, kernel 4.20+) is the modern saturation signal that replaces load averages.

en/observability/04-red-use/04-golden-si.title: Golden signals, dashboard layout, and service mesh auto-RED
en/observability/04-red-use/04-golden-si.summary: How Google''''s four golden signals extend RED, what a senior RED+USE dashboard looks like, how service meshes emit RED without application code, and how RED transfers to non-HTTP protocols.

en/observability/04-red-use/05-cardinali.title: Cardinality as a cost driver: labels, PII, exemplars, and sampling
en/observability/04-red-use/05-cardinali.summary: Every unique label combination is a separate time series charged separately in RAM and in hosted billing. The discipline is iron: only bounded, actionable labels go on metrics — everything else lives in logs or traces, joined by exemplars.

en/observability/04-red-use/06-histogram.title: Native histograms, SLO tie-in, and production failure patterns
en/observability/04-red-use/06-histogram.summary: Native (exponential) histograms eliminate manual bucket tuning. RED''''s Duration and Errors feed the SLO error budget. Real production failures — Cloudflare, GitHub, Stripe, Discord — each trace to a specific RED+USE gap.

en/observability/04-red-use/project.title: RED and USE: build the dashboard and triage an incident
en/observability/04-red-use/project.summary: Hands-on project — instrument a service with bounded RED, wire USE/PSI for its hosts, build the layered dashboard, then drive an incident and triage it RED-first, USE-second with evidence.

en/observability/04-red-use/quiz-choice.summary: Multiple-choice synthesis across the RED+USE unit — symptom vs cause triage, saturation, histogram aggregation, cardinality, and alert-severity discipline.

en/observability/05-slo-budgets/01-sli-s.title: SLI, SLO, and the error budget: reliability by the numbers
en/observability/05-slo-budgets/01-sli-s.summary: An SLO is a promise about how reliable your service will be, and an error budget is the leftover failure allowance you can spend before that promise breaks — together they end arguments about ''''how reliable is reliable enough?

en/observability/05-slo-budgets/02-sli-s.title: Choosing SLIs and SLO targets: ratios, not feelings
en/observability/05-slo-budgets/02-sli-s.summary: A good SLI is a ratio in [0%, 100%] that correlates with user pain — not CPU usage or queue depth — and the right SLO target is the lowest number users tolerate, because each extra nine multiplies engineering cost by 3–10x.

en/observability/05-slo-budgets/03-mwmbr.title: Multi-window multi-burn-rate alerting: why AND beats OR
en/observability/05-slo-budgets/03-mwmbr.summary: Single-window SLO alerts are either too noisy (short window) or too slow to clear (long window) — the MWMBR pattern''''s AND between a long and a short window gets both fast detection and fast reset.

en/observability/05-slo-budgets/04-budge.title: Error budget policy, latency SLOs, and composite journeys
en/observability/05-slo-budgets/04-budge.summary: A signed error budget policy turns alert burns into organisational action. Latency SLOs require histogram bucket boundaries at the threshold. Composite journeys multiply SLO failures — 5 services at 99.9% give a ~99.5% journey ceiling.

en/observability/05-slo-budgets/05-slo-p.title: SLO platforms and the 90-day rollout
en/observability/05-slo-budgets/05-slo-p.summary: Hand-rolling MWMBR PromQL per service is error-prone — Sloth, Pyrra, OpenSLO, Nobl9, and Datadog SLOs generate it declaratively. Adoption is the bottleneck: a structured 90-day rollout turns SLO-as-arithmetic into SLO-as-culture.

en/observability/05-slo-budgets/06-low-t.title: Low-traffic SLOs and burn-rate math from first principles
en/observability/05-slo-budgets/06-low-t.summary: Low-traffic services break naive SLO arithmetic — solutions include synthetic probes, aggregation, and longer windows. The six SLO alerting approaches from the Google SRE Workbook show exactly why five fail. Every canonical burn-rate threshold is derivable from one equation.

en/observability/05-slo-budgets/07-icebe.title: Iceberg SLIs, composite SLO math, and SLA vs SLO
en/observability/05-slo-budgets/07-icebe.summary: A 2xx-only SLI misses correctness errors, 4xx bugs, and high-latency successes — the iceberg. Composite SLO math for N services in series is a product; parallel hedging and idempotent retries are architectural levers. SLA is contractual and tighter than SLO by design.

en/observability/05-slo-budgets/08-produ.title: Production SLO failures, self-observability, security, and the big picture
en/observability/05-slo-budgets/08-produ.summary: Stripe, GitHub, Coinbase, and Netflix incidents reveal SLO failure modes. SLO self-observability — NaN denominators, burn rate drift, policy gaps — is the meta-layer. Security intersects SLIs. The framework survives tool migrations because it is a contract, not a config.

en/observability/05-slo-budgets/project.summary: Hands-on project — define a journey SLI, generate MWMBR alerts with a platform, prove them with a fire drill, and write a signed error budget policy for a multi-service journey.

en/observability/05-slo-budgets/quiz-cho.summary: Multiple-choice synthesis across the SLO unit — budget arithmetic, burn-rate derivation, MWMBR AND logic, composite ceilings, and the organisational failure modes.

en/observability/05-slo-budgets/quiz-cod.summary: Read real PromQL recording rules, MWMBR alert expressions, a latency-bucket SLI, and a Sloth YAML, then predict the behaviour and pick the highest-leverage fix.

en/observability/05-slo-budgets/quiz-sho.title: SLO and error budgets: free-recall review
en/observability/05-slo-budgets/quiz-sho.summary: Free-recall prompts across the SLO unit. Answer each from memory first, then reveal the model answer and compare — budget math, burn derivation, MWMBR, composites, policy.

en/observability/06-trace-propagation/01.title: What is trace propagation and why broken propagation is worse than none
en/observability/06-trace-propagation/01.summary: Trace propagation passes one shared identifier across every service a request touches — miss a single hop and the trace silently splits into orphan fragments that look fine on dashboards but hide the real bottleneck.

en/observability/06-trace-propagation/02.title: traceparent and tracestate: the W3C header format in full
en/observability/06-trace-propagation/02.summary: The traceparent header is exactly 55 bytes — four fixed-width fields encoding version, trace-id, parent-id, and trace-flags. tracestate is the vendor escape hatch. Knowing the bit-level layout is what lets you validate, debug, and safely ignore malformed input.

en/observability/06-trace-propagation/03.title: Baggage and async boundaries: carrying context across queues and callbacks
en/observability/06-trace-propagation/03.summary: W3C baggage propagates key-value pairs alongside the trace, but its unbounded size and semi-public visibility make it a PII trap. Async boundaries — setTimeout, Kafka, workers — silently drop context unless bound with context.with() or message-level inject/extract.

en/observability/06-trace-propagation/04.title: Head sampling and tail sampling: deciding which traces survive
en/observability/06-trace-propagation/04.summary: Head sampling is cheap but blind — it makes the keep/drop decision at trace start without seeing the outcome. Tail sampling sees the whole trace before deciding, catching errors and slow requests that head sampling drops, at the cost of collector RAM and routing discipline.

en/observability/06-trace-propagation/05.title: Sampling consistency and the tail-sampling Collector tier
en/observability/06-trace-propagation/05.summary: Consistent sampling uses deterministic trace-id hashing so all services agree on keep/drop without coordination. The tail-sampling Collector tier requires a load-balancing exporter, a RAM budget model, and an explicit cap to prevent OOMs from long-running traces.

en/observability/06-trace-propagation/06.title: Async context per language, service mesh, B3 migration, and security
en/observability/06-trace-propagation/06.summary: Every runtime has a context substrate — Node AsyncLocalStorage, Python contextvars, Java thread-local, Go context.Context — each with distinct failure modes. Mesh propagates headers for HTTP not queues. traceparent in browsers is a privacy risk unless scope-limited.

en/observability/06-trace-propagation/07.title: Production propagation failures, span links, and platform design
en/observability/06-trace-propagation/07.summary: Propagation bugs are silent: Uber, GitHub, Slack, Datadog all had dashboards showing traces, just not the right ones. Span links solve fan-in and async follow-ups. Orphan rate and invalid-traceparent count are the meta-layer that catches regressions before customers notice.

en/observability/06-trace-propagation/pr.title: Trace propagation: stitch a broken system into one trace
en/observability/06-trace-propagation/pr.summary: Hands-on project — build a polyglot multi-service system, deliberately break propagation across HTTP, async, and Kafka boundaries, then make every user request one connected trace and prove it with an orphan-rate metric.

en/observability/06-trace-propagation/qu.title: Trace propagation: multiple-choice review
en/observability/06-trace-propagation/qu.summary: Multiple-choice synthesis across the trace-propagation unit — the W3C header, consistent sampling, tail-sampling collector limits, async boundaries, and silent production failures.

en/observability/06-trace-propagation/qu.title: Trace propagation: code and header reading
en/observability/06-trace-propagation/qu.summary: Read a traceparent header, a broken async-propagation snippet, a producer/consumer inject pair, and a tail-sampling config — then pick the behaviour and the highest-leverage fix.

en/observability/06-trace-propagation/qu.title: Trace propagation: free-recall review
en/observability/06-trace-propagation/qu.summary: Free-recall prompts across the trace-propagation unit. Answer each in your own words first, then reveal the model answer and compare.

en/observability/07-profiling/01-flame-g.title: Flame graphs: reading the picture that shows where time goes
en/observability/07-profiling/01-flame-g.summary: A profiler samples your call stack 100 times per second and draws a flame graph — the widest frame at any level is the function eating the most CPU, discoverable in one glance.

en/observability/07-profiling/02-samplin.title: Sampling vs instrumentation profiling: why 99 Hz wins in production
en/observability/07-profiling/02-samplin.summary: Instrumentation wraps every function call for exact data but collapses under production load; sampling captures one stack every 10 ms at bounded overhead, making it the only viable production profiling strategy.

en/observability/07-profiling/03-profile.title: Profile types: CPU, memory, off-CPU, mutex — which one to reach for
en/observability/07-profiling/03-profile.summary: CPU profiling only sees code that is running; off-CPU, block, and mutex profiles cover the 96% of a request that can be spent waiting — you need all four to diagnose any slow service.

en/observability/07-profiling/04-continu.title: Continuous profiling: always-on flame graphs with eBPF and trace-id correlation
en/observability/07-profiling/04-continu.summary: Continuous profiling runs always at 2-5% overhead — when an SLO burns the flame graph is already saved. eBPF captures polyglot stacks without language hooks; trace-id correlation drills any slow span to the exact function in 30 seconds.

en/observability/07-profiling/05-reading.title: How flame graphs are built from samples, and the production workflows that use them
en/observability/07-profiling/05-reading.summary: Identical stacks collapse, alphabetical sorting groups parents with children, and width is sample count — once you know the algorithm you never misread the x-axis as time again. Profiling integrates with SLO burn, deploy diff, and capacity planning.

en/observability/07-profiling/06-advance.title: Linux perf, eBPF internals, PGO, and the limits of sampling
en/observability/07-profiling/06-advance.summary: perf_event_open is the kernel foundation under every profiler; BPF programs filter and aggregate in-kernel; PGO feeds profiles back to the compiler for 2-7% speedups; and sampling has blind spots engineers must know.

en/observability/07-profiling/07-profili.title: Profiling in production: security, war stories, OTel profiles, and the infrastructure design
en/observability/07-profiling/07-profili.summary: Profiles expose function names and call patterns — treat them like debugger output. Five war stories show what continuous profiling catches and what dashboards miss. OTel profile signal is the fourth pillar closing the SLO → trace → profile loop.

en/observability/07-profiling/project.title: Profiling: from SLO to flame graph
en/observability/07-profiling/project.summary: Hands-on project — stand up continuous profiling on a small polyglot service, drill a planted slow path from SLO to flame graph in under 30 seconds, and catch a deploy regression with a differential profile.

en/observability/07-profiling/quiz-choic.summary: Multiple-choice synthesis across the profiling unit — sampling economics, profile-type selection, flame-graph reading, eBPF symbolization, and production discipline.

en/observability/07-profiling/quiz-code.summary: Read real pprof output, a collapsed flame graph, an allocation profile, and a profiler config — predict the behaviour and pick the highest-leverage diagnosis.

en/observability/07-profiling/quiz-short.title: Profiling: free-recall review
en/observability/07-profiling/quiz-short.summary: Free-recall prompts across the profiling unit. Answer each in your own words first, then reveal the model answer and compare.

en/observability/08-putting-it-together/.title: The debugging funnel: SLO → RED → trace → profile
en/observability/08-putting-it-together/.summary: A fixed funnel order — SLO burn, then RED, then trace, then profile, then git blame — cuts MTTR by 50–80% by eliminating random dashboard navigation.

en/observability/08-putting-it-together/.title: OTel architecture: one SDK, four signals, one wire format
en/observability/08-putting-it-together/.summary: How OpenTelemetry unifies logs, metrics, traces, and profiles through one collector pipeline — and how the trace-id becomes the join key that lets all four signals answer one query.

en/observability/08-putting-it-together/.title: Cost discipline: keeping observability under 5% of infra spend
en/observability/08-putting-it-together/.summary: Three levers — cardinality limits on metrics, tail sampling on traces, and tiered log retention — keep observability cost at $1–5/million requests even as traffic grows 10x.

en/observability/08-putting-it-together/.title: The incident loop: from pager to postmortem to prevention
en/observability/08-putting-it-together/.summary: The full production incident loop — T+0 to T+1 week — plus the cultural mechanisms (blameless postmortem, runbooks, game days, error budget policy) that compound MTTR improvement over time.

en/observability/08-putting-it-together/.title: Scale, security, and the ROI of observable systems
en/observability/08-putting-it-together/.summary: Storage tiering, semantic conventions as ABI, PII leakage through signals, real org-scale failures, and the arithmetic that proves a mature observability stack returns 10–30x in prevented outage cost.

en/observability/08-putting-it-together/.title: Observability capstone: instrument a service and debug an incident
en/observability/08-putting-it-together/.summary: Capstone — instrument a multi-service system end-to-end with correlated logs, metrics, traces, and profiles, add an SLO burn-rate alert, then debug a real incident through the funnel.

en/observability/08-putting-it-together/.title: Observability capstone: multiple-choice synthesis
en/observability/08-putting-it-together/.summary: Cross-track synthesis MCQs spanning the whole observability chapter — funnel order, the trace-id join, tail sampling, cardinality cost, MTTD vs MTTR, and ROI.

en/observability/08-putting-it-together/.title: Observability capstone: reading signals and queries
en/observability/08-putting-it-together/.summary: Read a PromQL burn-rate expression, a traceparent header, a flame graph, and a correlated log line — predict the behaviour and pick the senior-level read.

en/observability/08-putting-it-together/.title: Observability capstone: free-recall review
en/observability/08-putting-it-together/.summary: Free-recall prompts spanning the whole observability track — funnel, three-pillar join, OTel architecture, sampling, burn-rate alerting, and ROI.

en/performance/00-start-here/01-overview.title: Start from zero: what performance work actually is
en/performance/00-start-here/01-overview.summary: Performance engineering is one discipline with one rule — measure first, fix the proven bottleneck. This is the from-zero map and the eight words every senior performance unit assumes you already know.

en/performance/01-profile-first/01-why-p.title: Why profile first: measure where time actually goes
en/performance/01-profile-first/01-why-p.summary: Engineers who skip profiling optimise the wrong code more than half the time. A profiler is the infrared camera that names the real bottleneck in 30 seconds.

en/performance/01-profile-first/02-amdah.title: Amdahl''''s law and self-time: the ceiling on every speedup you can ship
en/performance/01-profile-first/02-amdah.summary: Amdahl''''s law converts ''''should I optimise this?'''' into a number. Self-time vs cum-time tells you whether to fix a function or walk down to what it calls.

en/performance/01-profile-first/03-measu.title: The measurement loop: microbench, macrobench, prod profile, observer effect
en/performance/01-profile-first/03-measu.summary: Three measurement scopes each answer different questions and each lie when misapplied. The observer effect means your profiler perturbs what it measures — know by how much.

en/performance/01-profile-first/04-readi.title: Reading flame graphs: shapes, per-language profilers, and the 60-second scan
en/performance/01-profile-first/04-readi.summary: Flame graphs have five recognisable shapes that a senior engineer reads before zooming into names. Per-language profiler picks ensure representative measurements, not debug-build artefacts.

en/performance/01-profile-first/05-stati.title: Statistical baselines: why one run is not a measurement
en/performance/01-profile-first/05-stati.summary: A single benchmark run cannot distinguish a real 15% speedup from natural noise. Report median, p95, p99 across multiple runs with confidence intervals — anything less is a guess wearing a number.

en/performance/01-profile-first/06-profi.title: Profiler history and microbenchmark pitfalls: Knuth to GWP
en/performance/01-profile-first/06-profi.summary: From Amdahl 1967 to Google-Wide Profiling 2010, the intellectual lineage explains why modern profiling works the way it does. Naive microbenchmarks are wrong by default — JIT warmup, dead-code elimination, and constant folding all corrupt the measurement.

en/performance/01-profile-first/07-hardw.title: Hardware counters, cold-start profiles, and profile security
en/performance/01-profile-first/07-hardw.summary: A flame graph names a hot function. Hardware performance counters tell you why it is hot: memory-stalled at 0.5 IPC or compute-bound at 3.0 IPC. Cold-start profiles drive different fixes than steady-state ones. Profiles leak code structure and must be RBAC-gated.

en/performance/01-profile-first/08-conti.title: Continuous profiling at scale: costs, CI gates, trace correlation, and anti-patterns
en/performance/01-profile-first/08-conti.summary: Always-on profiling at 2-5% overhead is standard, but the storage compounds across a fleet. Profile-trace correlation turns incident triage from guessing into a 30-second drill. Profile-diff CI gates catch regressions before merge.

en/performance/01-profile-first/project.title: Profile first: run the loop on a misleading service
en/performance/01-profile-first/project.summary: Hands-on project — run the full profile-first loop on a deliberately misleading slow service: quantify, profile, predict with Amdahl, fix the real hotspot, and prove the win with statistically valid before/after numbers.

en/performance/01-profile-first/quiz-cho.title: Profile first: multiple-choice review
en/performance/01-profile-first/quiz-cho.summary: Multiple-choice synthesis across the profile-first unit — Amdahl ceilings, self vs cum-time, measurement scopes, the observer effect, statistical baselines, and flame-graph shape reading.

en/performance/01-profile-first/quiz-cod.title: Profile first: code and trace reading
en/performance/01-profile-first/quiz-cod.summary: Read a microbenchmark, a profiler diff, a perf hardware-counter readout, and an Amdahl calculation, then predict the behaviour and pick the highest-leverage fix.

en/performance/01-profile-first/quiz-sho.title: Profile first: free-recall review
en/performance/01-profile-first/quiz-sho.summary: Free-recall prompts across the profile-first unit. Answer each in your own words first, then reveal the model answer and compare.

en/performance/02-hot-paths/01-what-make.title: What makes a hot path: symptom vs cause
en/performance/02-hot-paths/01-what-make.summary: A wide flame-graph frame names where time accumulates, not why. The same leaf can hide five different bottlenecks — each demanding a different fix.

en/performance/02-hot-paths/02-five-shap.title: Five shapes of hotspot: CPU, alloc, cache, lock, syscall
en/performance/02-hot-paths/02-five-shap.summary: Each of the five hotspot categories has a tell-tale signature in the profile and a categorical fix. Picking the wrong fix family wastes the entire engineering effort.

en/performance/02-hot-paths/03-reading-p.title: Reading parent and child chains: where to apply the fix
en/performance/02-hot-paths/03-reading-p.summary: A wide leaf with one parent means fix the caller. A wide leaf with twenty parents means fix the leaf. Self-time vs cum-time boundary locates the work vs dispatch split.

en/performance/02-hot-paths/04-jit-deopt.title: JIT deopt, the fix-and-verify loop, and PR-time profiling
en/performance/02-hot-paths/04-jit-deopt.summary: JIT deopt loops silently multiply hot-path cost 10–100x. The fix-and-verify loop is the discipline that proves a fix landed. PR-time profiling catches regressions before production.

en/performance/02-hot-paths/05-hardware-.title: Hardware counters and Intel TMA: sub-category diagnosis
en/performance/02-hot-paths/05-hardware-.summary: Hardware performance counters distinguish compute-bound from memory-bound when both appear equally wide. Intel''''s TMA framework pins each CPU cycle to a specific microarchitectural resource.

en/performance/02-hot-paths/06-false-sha.title: False sharing and native-bridge hot paths
en/performance/02-hot-paths/06-false-sha.summary: Two classes of hot path that defeat naive fixes: false sharing (lock-free code that performs worse than locked) and native-bridge overhead (stub wider than the native function it calls). Both need hardware counters or cross-language profilers to see.

en/performance/02-hot-paths/07-security-.title: Hot paths in production: security, tail latency, and tooling lineage
en/performance/02-hot-paths/07-security-.summary: Why optimising security-sensitive hot paths requires a security-review gate, how hot paths hide in tail latency rather than mean, and the 50-year lineage of profiling tools that produced the methodology.

en/performance/02-hot-paths/project.title: Hot paths: diagnose and fix two shapes
en/performance/02-hot-paths/project.summary: Hands-on project — seed a service with two different-shaped hotspots, diagnose each from the right profile, apply the matching fix, and prove the wins with before/after numbers under identical load.

en/performance/02-hot-paths/quiz-choice.title: Hot paths: multiple-choice review
en/performance/02-hot-paths/quiz-choice.summary: Multiple-choice synthesis across the hot-paths unit — the five shapes, symptom-vs-cause reading, parent/child chains, IPC and TMA, false sharing, and the security gate.

en/performance/02-hot-paths/quiz-code.summary: Read real Go snippets, a perf stat block, and an N-API hot path; predict the hotspot shape from the evidence and pick the highest-leverage fix.

en/performance/02-hot-paths/quiz-short.title: Hot paths: free-recall review
en/performance/02-hot-paths/quiz-short.summary: Free-recall prompts across the hot-paths unit. Answer each in your own words first, then reveal the model answer and compare.

en/performance/03-cache-vs-bigo/01-memor.title: Memory hierarchy: why the same O(N) loop can be 17x slower
en/performance/03-cache-vs-bigo/01-memor.summary: Modern CPUs have five storage levels separated by 100x latency gaps — the level where your data lives decides wall-clock cost more than operation count does.

en/performance/03-cache-vs-bigo/02-row-m.title: Row-major vs column-major: access order and the 9x gap
en/performance/03-cache-vs-bigo/02-row-m.summary: Changing loop order on the same matrix can produce a 9x wall-clock difference — because the step from row to column flips every access from a cache hit to a cache miss.

en/performance/03-cache-vs-bigo/03-cache.title: Cache lines, struct layout, and false sharing
en/performance/03-cache-vs-bigo/03-cache.summary: A 64-byte cache line is the atom of memory transfer — misaligned structs, over-packed fields, and threads sharing a line all pay the same 100x penalty despite appearing unrelated.

en/performance/03-cache-vs-bigo/04-branc.title: Branch prediction and branchless code
en/performance/03-cache-vs-bigo/04-branc.summary: Modern CPUs predict every branch before executing it — a miss flushes the pipeline at 10–30 cycles. Unpredictable branches in hot loops are the branch equivalent of a cache miss.

en/performance/03-cache-vs-bigo/05-simd-.title: SIMD, SoA vs AoS, and memory bandwidth
en/performance/03-cache-vs-bigo/05-simd-.summary: Array-of-Structures (AoS) prevents SIMD; Structure-of-Arrays (SoA) enables it. Memory bandwidth and NUMA are the two constraints that profiling cache-miss rate misses.

en/performance/03-cache-vs-bigo/06-hardw.title: Hardware prefetcher, TLB, and memory-level parallelism
en/performance/03-cache-vs-bigo/06-hardw.summary: The hardware prefetcher is a lubricant — it helps predictable patterns but cannot infer pointer-chasing. TLB misses add 5–50 cycles before any cache check. MLP lets the CPU stack multiple outstanding misses.

en/performance/03-cache-vs-bigo/07-cache.title: Cache-oblivious algorithms, PGO, and production failures
en/performance/03-cache-vs-bigo/07-cache.summary: Cache-oblivious recursion, profile-guided optimisation, real regressions from Discord/Mojang/Bun, and the full perf-stat observability toolkit that ties it all together.

en/performance/03-cache-vs-bigo/project.title: Cache vs big-O: beat the textbook
en/performance/03-cache-vs-bigo/project.summary: Hands-on project — take a benchmark where an O(N) layout beats an O(log N) one, profile the constant-factor causes with perf, and drive a 3–5x speedup through layout, branch, and locality fixes with before/after numbers.

en/performance/03-cache-vs-bigo/quiz-cho.title: Cache vs big-O: multiple-choice review
en/performance/03-cache-vs-bigo/quiz-cho.summary: Multiple-choice synthesis across the cache-vs-big-O unit — memory hierarchy, cache lines, false sharing, branch prediction, data layout, and reading a perf profile.

en/performance/03-cache-vs-bigo/quiz-cod.title: Cache vs big-O: code and layout reading
en/performance/03-cache-vs-bigo/quiz-cod.summary: Read real snippets — a strided loop, an AoS struct, a padded counter, and a pointer chain — predict the cache and pipeline behaviour, then pick the highest-leverage fix.

en/performance/03-cache-vs-bigo/quiz-sho.title: Cache vs big-O: free-recall review
en/performance/03-cache-vs-bigo/quiz-sho.summary: Free-recall prompts across the cache-vs-big-O unit. Answer each from memory first, then reveal the model answer and compare.

en/performance/04-gc/01-gc-basics.title: GC basics: what the runtime taxes you for
en/performance/04-gc/01-gc-basics.summary: Garbage collection frees heap memory automatically — but the work shows up as pauses and CPU. Allocation rate, not heap size, drives GC-driven tail latency.

en/performance/04-gc/02-gc-algorithms.title: GC algorithms: generational, concurrent, and per-runtime
en/performance/04-gc/02-gc-algorithms.summary: The generational hypothesis (most objects die young) shapes every major production GC. Knowing which algorithm your runtime ships — and why it makes different tradeoffs than others — is the prerequisite for diagnosing any pause.

en/performance/04-gc/03-gc-tradeoffs.title: GC tradeoffs: pause, throughput, heap — and object pooling
en/performance/04-gc/03-gc-tradeoffs.summary: Every collector picks two of three: short pauses, high throughput, or low memory. Allocation pressure is the upstream cause of all three; reducing it is more durable than tuning the collector. Object pooling works only when the profile says so.

en/performance/04-gc/04-gc-tuning.title: GC tuning: pacing, heap shape, and allocation observability
en/performance/04-gc/04-gc-tuning.summary: Pacing controls when the GC fires, heap shape distinguishes live data from overhead, and allocation-rate dashboards are the leading indicator every on-call needs. Know the knobs before you touch them.

en/performance/04-gc/05-gc-internals.title: GC internals: tri-color invariant, write barriers, and per-runtime deep-dives
en/performance/04-gc/05-gc-internals.summary: Tri-color marking is the formal core of every concurrent GC. Write barriers maintain the invariant. Go''''s pacer, ZGC''''s colored pointers, and V8 Orinoco each implement the same ideas differently — knowing the implementation shapes how you write allocation-safe hot paths.

en/performance/04-gc/06-gc-production.title: GC in production: observability, security, edge cases, and fleet governance
en/performance/04-gc/06-gc-production.summary: GC pressure shows up in production as SLO burns before it shows up as OOMs. Building alloc-rate dashboards, finalizer-safe code, and a one-page runbook accessible to on-call SREs is what separates teams that chase GC fires from teams that prevent them.

en/performance/04-gc/project.title: GC: tame a death-spiral
en/performance/04-gc/project.summary: Hands-on project — instrument, diagnose, and tame a GC death-spiral in a small allocation-heavy service, then prove the fix with before/after numbers.

en/performance/04-gc/quiz-choice.summary: Multiple-choice synthesis across the GC unit — allocation pressure, pacing, collector tradeoffs, barriers, and production failure modes.

en/performance/04-gc/quiz-short.summary: Free-recall prompts across the GC unit. Answer each in your own words first, then reveal the model answer and compare.

en/performance/05-n-plus-one/01-what-is-.title: N+1: one logical operation, many round-trips
en/performance/05-n-plus-one/01-what-is-.summary: One screen renders into 50 database queries because the ORM loads each related row on demand. The fix is not a faster query — it is fewer queries.

en/performance/05-n-plus-one/02-fix-fami.title: Fix families: JOIN, IN, preload, and DataLoader
en/performance/05-n-plus-one/02-fix-fami.summary: The four structural fixes for N+1 — JOIN, IN-based batching, ORM eager loading, and DataLoader — and how to pick the right one by relationship cardinality and data shape.

en/performance/05-n-plus-one/03-detectin.title: Detecting N+1: query logs, APM traces, and CI gates
en/performance/05-n-plus-one/03-detectin.summary: N+1 hides from CPU profilers because the cost is off-CPU wait time, not compute. Query logs, APM waterfalls, and per-request counters surface it — and a CI gate prevents regressions.

en/performance/05-n-plus-one/04-dataload.title: DataLoader: batching across resolver trees
en/performance/05-n-plus-one/04-dataload.summary: DataLoader queues lookup IDs across an entire request and fires one batched query per type when the event loop yields — the canonical fix for GraphQL N+1 and multi-source fan-out.

en/performance/05-n-plus-one/05-fan-out-.title: Cross-protocol N+1: HTTP fan-out and Redis MGET
en/performance/05-n-plus-one/05-fan-out-.summary: The N+1 shape appears in HTTP microservice fan-out, Redis key lookups, and gRPC streaming — the fix family is the same: collect, batch, send once.

en/performance/05-n-plus-one/06-nplus1-s.title: N+1 at scale: pool exhaustion, plan changes, and denormalisation
en/performance/05-n-plus-one/06-nplus1-s.summary: How N+1 cascades into connection pool exhaustion, why fix strategies change query plans in surprising ways, how N+1 paths become DoS vectors, and when denormalisation is the right answer.

en/performance/05-n-plus-one/project.title: N+1: diagnose, batch, and gate
en/performance/05-n-plus-one/project.summary: Hands-on project — diagnose and eliminate N+1 across an ORM list page, a GraphQL resolver tree, and a service fan-out, then lock it in with a CI query-count gate.

en/performance/05-n-plus-one/quiz-choice.title: N+1: multiple-choice review
en/performance/05-n-plus-one/quiz-choice.summary: Multiple-choice synthesis across the N+1 unit — round-trip cost, fix-family choice by cardinality, DataLoader, off-CPU detection, pool exhaustion, and DoS amplification.

en/performance/05-n-plus-one/quiz-code.title: N+1: code and log reading
en/performance/05-n-plus-one/quiz-code.summary: Read real ORM loops, a DataLoader batch function, a query log, and a fan-out handler — predict the round-trip count and pick the highest-leverage fix.

en/performance/05-n-plus-one/quiz-short.summary: Free-recall prompts across the N+1 unit. Answer each in your own words first, then reveal the model answer and compare.

en/performance/06-batching/01-basics.title: Batching: amortize fixed cost per operation
en/performance/06-batching/01-basics.summary: When per-operation price is mostly fixed (syscall, network round-trip, ACK, log flush), grouping operations amortizes it. The window — size plus max-wait — decides where throughput meets tail latency.

en/performance/06-batching/02-window.title: The batching window: size and wait time
en/performance/06-batching/02-window.summary: Every batching system has two knobs: max-size (bytes or records) and max-wait (time). Whichever fires first sends the batch — and which one fires tells you whether you''''re throughput-bound or latency-bound.

en/performance/06-batching/03-kafka-post.title: Batching in Kafka and Postgres
en/performance/06-batching/03-kafka-post.summary: Kafka producer batching (batch.size, linger.ms) and Postgres COPY vs INSERT for efficient bulk writes; why compression needs batching first.

en/performance/06-batching/04-syscall-ob.title: io_uring and observability of batching
en/performance/06-batching/04-syscall-ob.summary: Syscalls cost 1-5µs each; at 100k ops/s that''''s 100-500ms/s burned in transitions. io_uring''''s shared rings remove per-op cost. Then four metrics — batch size, wait, depth, drops — tell you if the batcher is healthy or quietly dropping data.

en/performance/06-batching/05-nagle-io-u.title: From Nagle to io_uring: evolution of batching
en/performance/06-batching/05-nagle-io-u.summary: One pattern runs from Nagle (1984) through Kafka linger.ms to io_uring: amortize a fixed per-op cost over N ops. The lever is the same; only the fixed cost (TCP header, round-trip, syscall) and the window-tuning move change.

en/performance/06-batching/06-backpressu.title: Backpressure, failure isolation, and batch security in production
en/performance/06-batching/06-backpressu.summary: Poison messages, partial-batch failure, bounded queues (block/drop/spill), compression bombs, adaptive windowing — the operational edge cases that crash batched systems.

en/performance/06-batching/project.title: Batching: build and harden an ingest pipeline
en/performance/06-batching/project.summary: Hands-on project — build a batching ingest pipeline, tune its window against an SLO, then harden it with backpressure, poison-message isolation, and observability, proving each step with before/after numbers.

en/performance/06-batching/quiz-choice.title: Batching: multiple-choice review
en/performance/06-batching/quiz-choice.summary: Multiple-choice synthesis across the batching unit — the fixed-cost model, the size/wait window, break-even math, backpressure policies, and production failure modes.

en/performance/06-batching/quiz-code.title: Batching: code and config reading
en/performance/06-batching/quiz-code.summary: Read real producer configs, a Go buffered-writer window, a split-and-retry loop, and a batcher metrics line; predict the behaviour and pick the highest-leverage fix.

en/performance/06-batching/quiz-short.title: Batching: free-recall review
en/performance/06-batching/quiz-short.summary: Free-recall prompts across the batching unit. Answer each in your own words first, then reveal the model answer and compare.

en/performance/07-bundle-budgets/01-what.title: What a bundle actually costs: download, parse, compile, execute
en/performance/07-bundle-budgets/01-what.summary: A 1 MB JS bundle is not a 1 MB cost — it is four chained CPU phases that hit mid-range mobile 4-8x harder than your laptop.

en/performance/07-bundle-budgets/02-core.title: Core Web Vitals: LCP, INP, and CLS
en/performance/07-bundle-budgets/02-core.summary: Google''''s three field metrics quantify what users feel. Bundle size is the dominant lever for LCP and INP — this lesson maps bytes to thresholds.

en/performance/07-bundle-budgets/03-code.title: Code splitting: route-level, component-level, vendor splitting
en/performance/07-bundle-budgets/03-code.summary: Code splitting is the highest-leverage bundle reduction: each route downloads only what it needs, components load when triggered, vendor chunks cache separately across deploys.

en/performance/07-bundle-budgets/04-tree.title: Tree shaking and compression: removing what you don''''t use
en/performance/07-bundle-budgets/04-tree.summary: Tree shaking strips unused exports at build time — but four common pitfalls silently defeat it. Brotli and gzip reduce wire bytes without touching parse cost.

en/performance/07-bundle-budgets/05-thir.title: Third-party scripts: the silent budget killer
en/performance/07-bundle-budgets/05-thir.summary: Analytics, ads, chat widgets, and A/B testing tools routinely add 500 KB to 1 MB across a page — outside your control but inside the user''''s cost. Three patterns mitigate them.

en/performance/07-bundle-budgets/06-ci-e.title: CI enforcement and RUM: making budgets stick
en/performance/07-bundle-budgets/06-ci-e.summary: Without a CI gate, a bundle budget is an aspiration. With size-limit in CI and RUM in production, every PR that blows the budget fails, and every production regression pages the owning team.

en/performance/07-bundle-budgets/07-v8-p.title: V8 JIT pipeline, HTTP priorities, and bundle security
en/performance/07-bundle-budgets/07-v8-p.summary: V8''''s four compilation tiers, HTTP/3 Extensible Priorities (RFC 9218), 103 Early Hints, and Subresource Integrity form the senior layer of bundle delivery — the mechanisms that explain why a smaller bundle still varies by 2-3x depending on how it is served.

en/performance/07-bundle-budgets/project.title: Bundle budgets: cut a route under budget and keep it there
en/performance/07-bundle-budgets/project.summary: Hands-on project — analyze, split, and govern a bloated route bundle down under a per-route budget, then lock the win with a CI gate and a RUM dashboard, proving each step with before/after numbers.

en/performance/07-bundle-budgets/quiz-ch.title: Bundle budgets: multiple-choice review
en/performance/07-bundle-budgets/quiz-ch.summary: Multiple-choice synthesis across the bundle-budgets unit — the four-phase cost model, Core Web Vitals levers, splitting vs compression, third-party tax, and CI enforcement.

en/performance/07-bundle-budgets/quiz-co.title: Bundle budgets: config and output reading
en/performance/07-bundle-budgets/quiz-co.summary: Read real bundler config, import patterns, a size-limit CI snippet, and a Priority header, predict the effect on shipped bytes, and pick the highest-leverage fix.

en/performance/07-bundle-budgets/quiz-sh.title: Bundle budgets: free-recall review
en/performance/07-bundle-budgets/quiz-sh.summary: Free-recall prompts across the bundle-budgets unit. Answer each in your own words first, then reveal the model answer and compare.

en/performance/08-putting-it-together-pe.title: Performance capstone: a full investigation, end-to-end
en/performance/08-putting-it-together-pe.summary: Capstone — run a full performance investigation on a real slow path end-to-end: measure first, find the one dominant cost, fix it at the right layer, verify under identical load, and enforce the gain in CI.

en/performance/08-putting-it-together-pe.title: Performance capstone: multiple-choice synthesis
en/performance/08-putting-it-together-pe.summary: Cross-track synthesis MCQs — pick the dominant cost, the right layer to fix, and the verification step across profiling, hot paths, cache, GC, N+1, batching, and bundles.

en/performance/08-putting-it-together-pe.title: Performance capstone: reading profiles, traces, and stats
en/performance/08-putting-it-together-pe.summary: Read real artifacts from across the track — a pprof profile, a hot-path snippet, an N+1 query log, and a bundle report — predict the dominant cost, and pick the highest-leverage fix.

en/performance/08-putting-it-together-pe.title: Performance capstone: free-recall synthesis
en/performance/08-putting-it-together-pe.summary: Free-recall prompts spanning the whole track — the measurement loop, Amdahl's cap, the five cost shapes, fixing at the right layer, and verify-then-enforce.

en/performance/08-putting-it-together-pe.title: The performance loop: discipline, not a project
en/performance/08-putting-it-together-pe.summary: Performance regresses by default. The eight-step loop — observe, profile, classify, predict, fix, verify, enforce, repeat — is the discipline that keeps a service fast year over year.

en/performance/08-putting-it-together-pe.title: Classify and fix: matching bottleneck families to remedies
en/performance/08-putting-it-together-pe.summary: Each bottleneck belongs to one of eight families. Naming the family takes seconds from the profile; picking the wrong family wastes days. Amdahl sets the ceiling on any fix before you write a line of code.

en/performance/08-putting-it-together-pe.title: Observability stack and CI gates: catching regressions before they ship
en/performance/08-putting-it-together-pe.summary: Five integrated data streams — metrics, logs, traces, profiles, RUM — plus pre-merge CI gates that fail regressions before they reach users. The cheapest fix is the one that never ships.

en/performance/08-putting-it-together-pe.title: Incident to enforcement: SLO burn to verified fix in 35 minutes
en/performance/08-putting-it-together-pe.summary: A complete worked example: an /checkout p99 SLO burn, diagnosed via continuous profiling and distributed traces, fixed in 35 minutes, and armoured with enforcement gates so the class of regression cannot return.

en/performance/08-putting-it-together-pe.title: Culture, economics, and org-scale performance
en/performance/08-putting-it-together-pe.summary: Error budgets quantify the tradeoff between performance and feature velocity. 2x throughput halves the AWS bill. Cultural mechanics — PR criteria, EM OKRs, blameless retros — compound indefinitely.

en/python/00-start-here/01-why-python-fo.title: Why Python for JS/TS developers
en/python/00-start-here/01-why-python-fo.summary: You already think in a dynamic, REPL-driven, function-first language — Python is the second one worth knowing because it owns data, ML/AI, and glue work. The mental model transfers; the idioms (indentation, None, pip/venv) do not.

en/python/01-language-core/01-syntax-and.title: Syntax and types: Python through a JS/TS lens
en/python/01-language-core/01-syntax-and.summary: Python blocks are whitespace, names are just references, ints are arbitrary-precision, and type hints never run — coming from JS/TS the gotchas are == vs is and that None is the only nullish.

en/python/01-language-core/02-data-struc.title: Lists, dicts, sets, tuples
en/python/01-language-core/02-data-struc.summary: Python ships four core containers — list, dict, set, tuple. Picking the right one is a question of mutability and hashability, and the wrong pick costs O(n) where O(1) was free.

en/python/01-language-core/03-comprehens.title: Comprehensions and functions
en/python/01-language-core/03-comprehens.summary: Comprehensions are Pythonic map/filter; generator expressions stream lazily over huge inputs. Functions add a sharp trap — default args are evaluated once at def time — plus *args/**kwargs and LEGB closures unlike JS.

en/python/02-scripting-and-io/01-files-a.title: Files and CLI arguments
en/python/02-scripting-and-io/01-files-a.summary: A real Python script reads CLI arguments, opens files under a with-block that closes them even on exception, streams large files line by line, and exits with a status code the shell can branch on.

en/python/02-scripting-and-io/02-http-an.title: HTTP requests, venv and packaging
en/python/02-scripting-and-io/02-http-an.summary: A useful Python tool is two skills: HTTP calls with requests (always a timeout, raise_for_status, env-var keys) and venv isolation that keeps one project deps from breaking another.

en/python/02-scripting-and-io/03-subproc.title: subprocess and shell-injection safety
en/python/02-scripting-and-io/03-subproc.summary: Run external commands with subprocess.run and a list of args so no shell parses your input — the one change that turns shell injection into an inert string argument. Then bound every call with check=True and timeout= so failures and hangs surface instead of passing silently.

en/python/02-scripting-and-io/04-concurr.title: Concurrency for I/O-bound scripts: threads, async, processes
en/python/02-scripting-and-io/04-concurr.summary: The GIL lets one thread run Python bytecode at a time but releases on blocking I/O, so threads and asyncio make I/O-bound scripts fast while CPU-bound work needs separate processes. Match the tool to the bottleneck: waiting vs burning CPU.

en/python/02-scripting-and-io/05-robust-.title: Robust CLI scripts: exit codes, logging, retries, signals
en/python/02-scripting-and-io/05-robust-.summary: A script that runs unattended in cron or CI lives or dies by four contracts: a non-zero exit on failure, logs to stderr instead of print, bounded backoff retries for transient I/O, and signal-safe atomic writes so a kill never ships a truncated file.

en/python/03-data-model/01-dunder-protoc.title: Dunder protocols: __repr__, the eq/hash contract, truthiness, and NotImplemented
en/python/03-data-model/01-dunder-protoc.summary: Dunders are how objects plug into Python syntax: __repr__ for debugging, the __eq__/__hash__ contract (define eq, lose hash), the __bool__/__len__ truthiness chain, and operator dunders that return NotImplemented so the other operand gets a turn. Protocols beat inheritance.

en/python/03-data-model/02-attributes-an.title: Attribute lookup and descriptors: why the instance dict does not always win
en/python/03-data-model/02-attributes-an.summary: Attribute lookup is not instance-first: data descriptors on the type beat the instance __dict__, which beats non-data descriptors. __getattribute__ runs on every access, __getattr__ only on misses. property is a data descriptor; __set_name__ lets ORM fields learn their names.

en/python/03-data-model/03-classes-datac.title: Classes, dataclasses, and __slots__: generated boilerplate and the per-instance dict
en/python/03-data-model/03-classes-datac.summary: @dataclass generates __init__/__repr__/__eq__ from annotations; eq without frozen sets __hash__ = None; mutable defaults need default_factory. __slots__ drops the instance __dict__: ~100 B saved per object, faster access, but no dynamic attrs and tricky multiple inheritance.

en/python/03-data-model/04-iterators-and.title: Iterators and generators: paused frames, lazy pipelines, and the file handle that never closed
en/python/03-data-model/04-iterators-and.summary: for calls __iter__, then __next__ until StopIteration. A generator is a paused frame: send/throw/close drive it, yield from delegates. Lazy pipelines process gigabytes in constant memory — but a paused frame holds its resources, so a generator can hold a file open for hours.

en/python/04-typing-and-tooling/01-type-.title: Type hints as a system: unions, TypedDict, Literal, and typing the boundaries first
en/python/04-typing-and-tooling/01-type-.summary: Python hints are erased at runtime — only a checker enforces them. X | Y unions, collection generics, TypedDict, Literal and Annotated turn dicts and string flags into contracts. In legacy code, type the boundaries first: a checked hint is documentation that cannot go stale.

en/python/04-typing-and-tooling/02-gener.title: Generics and Protocols: PEP 695 syntax, variance without hand-waving, structural typing
en/python/04-typing-and-tooling/02-gener.summary: PEP 695 makes generics first-class: class Stack[T] without TypeVar ceremony. Variance explains why list[Dog] is not list[Animal] but Sequence[Dog] is a Sequence[Animal]. Protocol brings Go-style structural typing; runtime_checkable checks names only. overload shapes APIs.

en/python/04-typing-and-tooling/03-check.title: Type checkers in anger: narrowing, strictness, Any contagion, and mypy vs pyright
en/python/04-typing-and-tooling/03-check.summary: A checker verifies what your code proves: isinstance and TypeGuard/TypeIs narrowing, strict flags, no implicit Optional. Any spreads silently and erases checking. mypy and pyright differ in inference and speed; reveal_type shows what the checker believes. Run one in CI.

en/python/04-typing-and-tooling/04-uv-ru.title: The 2025 toolchain: uv for environments and locking, ruff for lint and format, one pyproject.toml
en/python/04-typing-and-tooling/04-uv-ru.summary: uv collapses pip, venv, pipx and pip-tools into one Rust binary: a fast resolver, a universal lockfile, uv run and uvx. ruff replaces flake8, isort and black with one pass. pyproject.toml holds every config, and migration from legacy setups is incremental, not a rewrite.

en/python/05-concurrency/01-gil-honestly.title: The GIL, honestly: what it serializes, why refcounting needs it, and what 3.13 free-threading changes
en/python/05-concurrency/01-gil-honestly.summary: The GIL serializes bytecode execution, not I/O or GIL-releasing C code; it exists because refcount updates are not atomic. Threads swap every ~5 ms (sys.setswitchinterval). Free-threaded 3.13+ (PEP 703) removes it for a single-thread tax and an extension-compatibility catch.

en/python/05-concurrency/02-threads-and-.title: Threads vs processes: choosing by workload, races under the GIL, and the fork+threads deadlock
en/python/05-concurrency/02-threads-and-.summary: ThreadPoolExecutor for I/O-bound, ProcessPoolExecutor for CPU-bound — minus the pickling tax. The GIL does not prevent races: check-then-act and += still need locks. fork copies locks but not the threads holding them, so fork+threads deadlocks; spawn is the safe default.

en/python/05-concurrency/03-asyncio-fund.title: asyncio honestly: suspendable frames, await as the only switch point, and the blocking call that freezes everyone
en/python/05-concurrency/03-asyncio-fund.summary: The event loop runs one coroutine at a time; await points are the only switch points. A coroutine does nothing until awaited or wrapped in a Task; gather runs them concurrently. One blocking call freezes every request — run_in_executor and to_thread are the escape hatch.

en/python/05-concurrency/04-structured-c.title: Structured concurrency: TaskGroup, except*, asyncio.timeout, and why bare create_task is a leak
en/python/05-concurrency/04-structured-c.summary: TaskGroup (3.11+) scopes task lifetimes: one child fails, siblings cancel, errors arrive as ExceptionGroup for except*. asyncio.timeout converts cancellation to TimeoutError at the boundary. Discipline: re-raise CancelledError, clean up in finally, shield only what must commit.

en/python/06-web-services/01-asgi-and-fa.title: ASGI and FastAPI: the scope/receive/send contract and the one blocking call that stalls a worker
en/python/06-web-services/01-asgi-and-fa.summary: ASGI hands your app a scope dict plus receive/send awaitables; uvicorn runs one event loop per worker. async def runs on that loop — a single blocking call stalls every in-flight request; plain def is dispatched to a ~40-thread anyio pool. Worker math and honest req/s included.

en/python/06-web-services/02-pydantic-va.title: Pydantic v2: parse at the boundary, trust inside — coercion, validators, and response_model filtering
en/python/06-web-services/02-pydantic-va.summary: BaseModel turns input dicts into typed objects or a 422 — parse, do not validate. The Rust core costs ns–µs per field (visible on 10k-item lists). Lax coercion masks contract drift, field/model validators carry cross-field rules, response_model stops internal-field leaks.

en/python/06-web-services/03-request-lif.title: The request lifecycle: middleware onion, dependency resolution, lifespan, and where errors surface
en/python/06-web-services/03-request-lif.summary: uvicorn accepts, middleware wraps inward (last added runs first), the router matches, dependencies resolve with per-request caching, yield teardown after send. Pools live in lifespan, BackgroundTasks occupy the worker, 422/500 surface at fixed layers.

en/python/07-testing/01-pytest-idioms.title: pytest idioms: assertion rewriting, discovery, markers, and the debug loop
en/python/07-testing/01-pytest-idioms.summary: pytest rewrites assert via an AST import hook, but only in collected files — helpers need register_assert_rewrite. Discovery imports every test module, so one import-time singleton kills the whole suite. raises(match=), strict xfail, -k/-x/--lf and exit codes shape the CI loop.

en/python/07-testing/02-fixtures-and-par.title: Fixtures and parametrize: dependency injection, scopes, and teardown order
en/python/07-testing/02-fixtures-and-par.summary: Fixtures resolve by name and cache per scope: session scope amortizes expensive setup but shares mutable state — the order-dependent failure class. yield puts teardown beside setup and unwinds in reverse. parametrize stacks cartesian; indirect=True routes params through fixtures.

en/python/07-testing/03-property-based-h.title: Property-based testing with Hypothesis: invariants, shrinking, and the example database
en/python/07-testing/03-property-based-h.summary: Hypothesis generates inputs against declared invariants — roundtrip, idempotence, oracle — shrinks each failure to a minimal case and replays it from the .hypothesis database. Budget max_examples against suite time, relax deadline on noisy CI, aim at roundtrips, not CRUD glue.

en/python/08-performance/01-profiling-cp.title: Profiling with cProfile and py-spy: measure the production shape before touching code
en/python/08-performance/01-profiling-cp.summary: cProfile hooks every call: 1.3-2x overhead that inflates tiny hot functions and cannot see inside C. py-spy samples stacks from outside via ptrace at ~1%: top, record flamegraphs, dump for stuck processes. timeit flatters. Profile prod-shaped workloads and re-measure p99 after.

en/python/08-performance/02-memory-and-o.title: Memory and objects: why an int costs 28 bytes and where the leak actually lives
en/python/08-performance/02-memory-and-o.summary: Every object pays a 16-byte header: int 28 B, empty dict 64 B. getsizeof is shallow — containers count pointers, not contents. Refcounting frees instantly; cycles need generational GC. tracemalloc snapshot diffs find growth sites; most leaks are reachable unbounded caches.

en/python/08-performance/03-c-extensions.title: C extensions, honestly: the options ladder, the GIL boundary, and the marshalling tax
en/python/08-performance/03-c-extensions.summary: Interpreter time goes to dispatch, boxing, refcounting; C skips all three. The ladder: numpy vectorization, Cython types, cffi/ctypes, raw C-API last. Extensions can release the GIL; crossing the boundary per element erases the win. Wheels and manylinux are the distribution bill.

en/python/08-performance/04-when-python-.title: When Python is the wrong tool: the decision tree and the salary-versus-servers arithmetic
en/python/08-performance/04-when-python-.summary: Triage the bottleneck: I/O-bound and C-library-bound workloads keep Python; interpreter-bound hot loops at scale cost 10-50x per core. Free-threaded 3.13 changes thread math, not single-thread speed. Strangler-extract the hot path; keep Python where dev speed beats compute.

en/python/09-data-work/01-pandas-polars-.title: pandas and Polars, pragmatically: columnar blocks, eager vs lazy, and the pitfalls that bite in production
en/python/09-data-work/01-pandas-polars-.summary: A DataFrame is columnar arrays: pandas wraps numpy blocks with object-pointer string columns; polars is Arrow-backed with a lazy optimizer. Covers predicate/projection pushdown, SettingWithCopyWarning and Copy-on-Write, silent int-to-float promotion, and when each wins.

en/python/09-data-work/02-file-formats.title: File formats: CSV at the edges, Parquet inside — row groups, statistics, Arrow, and compression tradeoffs
en/python/09-data-work/02-file-formats.summary: The format ladder with mechanisms: CSV re-parses and re-guesses types on every read; Parquet adds a typed schema, row groups with stats, column pruning and compression; Arrow is the zero-copy in-memory standard. Plus partitioning, the small-files failure, and schema evolution.

en/python/09-data-work/03-pipelines-and-.title: Pipelines and validation: contracts at boundaries, idempotent writes, and the rows that silently vanish
en/python/09-data-work/03-pipelines-and-.summary: A pipeline is stages with contracts: validate at boundaries with pandera-style schemas, write idempotently (overwrite partitions, never blind append), process incrementally with watermarks, and log row counts per stage — the cheap detector for silently vanishing rows.

en/python/10-packaging-and-distribution/.title: Modules and imports deep: sys.modules, finders and loaders, and the circular-import trap
en/python/10-packaging-and-distribution/.summary: After the first exec, import is a sys.modules lookup — modules are process-global singletons. Finders on sys.meta_path locate code, loaders run it once; the script dir shadows stdlib names; circular from-imports hit half-initialized modules; python -m runs with package context.

en/python/10-packaging-and-distribution/.title: pyproject.toml and entry points: build backends, src layout, and console-script shims
en/python/10-packaging-and-distribution/.summary: pyproject.toml [project] declares metadata; the build backend turns source into a wheel. src layout forces tests onto the installed package; editable installs are a .pth redirect; [project.scripts] generates PATH shims; plugins discover via entry-point groups.

en/python/10-packaging-and-distribution/.title: Publishing and lockfiles: wheels vs sdists, pinning by consumer, and trusted publishing
en/python/10-packaging-and-distribution/.summary: Wheels unpack; sdists build — platform tags decide which you get. Libraries declare ranges, applications lock the resolved graph with hashes; --require-hashes survives a hijacked release. Publish via build then uv/twine; trusted publishing uses short-lived OIDC.

en/python/11-async-deep/01-event-loop-in.title: One loop iteration, dissected: ready queue, selector poll, timer heap, and which awaits actually yield
en/python/11-async-deep/01-event-loop-in.summary: A loop iteration drains ready callbacks, polls the selector until the nearest timer, pops due timers. await yields only on real suspension — completed futures chain synchronously. One blocking call freezes the poll; debug mode flags callbacks over 100 ms.

en/python/11-async-deep/02-cancellation-.title: Cancellation semantics: an injected CancelledError, the bare-except immortality bug, and cleanup that must re-raise
en/python/11-async-deep/02-cancellation-.summary: task.cancel() throws CancelledError at the next suspending await; between awaits code is uninterruptible. except Exception misses it, bare except swallows it — immortal tasks. Clean up in finally, bound cleanup awaits, re-raise. TaskGroup cancels siblings on first failure.

en/python/11-async-deep/03-timeouts-and-.title: Timeouts and shielding: scoped cancel with TimeoutError conversion, deadline propagation, and shield as half a tool
en/python/11-async-deep/03-timeouts-and-.summary: asyncio.timeout cancels its body at expiry and converts CancelledError to TimeoutError at the boundary; cancel-count bookkeeping makes nesting compose. Propagate deadlines, not per-hop timeouts. shield blocks outer cancel but inner work runs detached — pair it with a timeout.

en/python/11-async-deep/04-bridging-sync.title: Bridging sync and async: to_thread and executors one way, a long-lived loop and run_coroutine_threadsafe the other
en/python/11-async-deep/04-bridging-sync.summary: Async to sync: to_thread moves blocking work off the loop — threads unblock I/O, the GIL still serializes CPU, processes pay pickling. Sync to async: asyncio.run for scripts, run_coroutine_threadsafe into one long-lived loop for servers — per-call loops rebuild every pool.

en/python/12-production-python/01-loggin.title: Logging and config: the dot-name logger tree, JSON output, and settings that fail at boot
en/python/12-production-python/01-loggin.summary: Loggers form a dot-name tree: configure the root once via dictConfig; libraries call getLogger(__name__) and add nothing. JSON logs plus contextvars request ids are queryable; lazy %s args skip work unless emitted; typed settings fail at boot, SecretStr hides secrets.

en/python/12-production-python/02-contai.title: Containerizing Python: slim plus multi-stage uv builds, cache-ordered layers, and signals that reach PID 1
en/python/12-production-python/02-contai.summary: python:3.x-slim over alpine (musl breaks manylinux wheels); multi-stage: uv sync a venv in the builder, copy into slim — ~1GB to ~80MB. Lockfile COPY before code keeps deps cached. PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1 or logs go silent; exec-form CMD or PID 1 is a shell and SIGTERM dies there.

en/python/12-production-python/03-worker.title: Workers and lifecycle: gunicorn process math, preload and fork safety, graceful shutdown
en/python/12-production-python/03-worker.summary: Sync workers for blocking apps, uvicorn for async; ~cores CPU-bound, 1-2x cores I/O — the GIL makes processes the unit. preload_app saves memory but shares pre-fork sockets: init clients post_fork. max_requests+jitter mitigates leaks; SIGTERM drains within graceful_timeout.

en/python/12-production-python/04-incide.title: Incident postmortems: the leak, the hang, the thundering restart — and the craft of blameless analysis
en/python/12-production-python/04-incide.summary: Three dissected incidents: an unbounded lru_cache leaks 40MB/h to OOMKill (tracemalloc diff finds it); a sync requests.get freezes the event loop (py-spy shows socket.recv); a 2-minute model load plus liveness probe equals CrashLoopBackOff. Blameless postmortems fix systems.

en/queues/00-start-here/01-overview.title: Start from zero: what a message queue actually is
en/queues/00-start-here/01-overview.summary: A message queue is a buffer that lets one service hand work to another without waiting. This is the from-zero map and the eight words the delivery-guarantees unit assumes you already know.

en/queues/01-delivery-guarantees/01-thre.title: At-most-once, at-least-once, exactly-once: the three delivery contracts
en/queues/01-delivery-guarantees/01-thre.summary: What the three delivery guarantees mean, why exactly-once delivery is impossible, and why at-least-once is the production default.

en/queues/01-delivery-guarantees/02-fail.title: The three failure legs — where duplicates and losses actually happen
en/queues/01-delivery-guarantees/02-fail.summary: How producer-to-broker, broker durability, and broker-to-consumer failures each produce duplicates or loss, traced through a real double-charge incident.

en/queues/01-delivery-guarantees/03-cons.title: Consumer-side dedup: the cheapest path to exactly-once processing
en/queues/01-delivery-guarantees/03-cons.summary: How to wrap side effects and dedup inserts in one DB transaction, why INSERT must come before the side effect, and the Stripe Idempotency-Key pattern for external APIs.

en/queues/01-delivery-guarantees/04-kafk.title: Kafka exactly-once semantics: idempotent producer and transactions
en/queues/01-delivery-guarantees/04-kafk.summary: How Kafka''''s idempotent producer eliminates producer-retry duplicates at 3% cost, and how transactions extend exactly-once across multi-partition writes and offset commits at 20–30% cost.

en/queues/01-delivery-guarantees/05-sqs-.title: SQS visibility timeout, DLQ, and the outbox pattern
en/queues/01-delivery-guarantees/05-sqs-.summary: How SQS visibility timeout works per-message, the heartbeat pattern for long-running consumers, DLQ redrive discipline, and the outbox pattern for reliable producer-side publishing.

en/queues/01-delivery-guarantees/06-exac.title: Exactly-once in production: impossibility proof, hybrid patterns, and real incidents
en/queues/01-delivery-guarantees/06-exac.summary: The Two Generals proof of why exactly-once delivery is impossible, the hybrid Kafka+DB pattern that achieves effectively-once at scale, observability metrics, and real production failures from Stripe, AWS, and Slack.

en/queues/01-delivery-guarantees/project.title: Delivery guarantees: build a crash-proof payment consumer
en/queues/01-delivery-guarantees/project.summary: Hands-on project — build a payment consumer that survives crashes with zero double-charges, then prove effectively-once under injected failures with before/after duplicate counts.

en/queues/01-delivery-guarantees/quiz-ch.title: Delivery guarantees: multiple-choice review
en/queues/01-delivery-guarantees/quiz-ch.summary: Multiple-choice synthesis across the delivery-guarantees unit — the impossibility proof, the three failure legs, idempotent consumers, Kafka EOS, SQS timeouts, and the outbox.

en/queues/01-delivery-guarantees/quiz-co.title: Delivery guarantees: code and log reading
en/queues/01-delivery-guarantees/quiz-co.summary: Read real consumer code, SQL, and a metrics line, predict the delivery-guarantee behaviour, and pick the highest-leverage fix a senior engineer makes first.

en/queues/01-delivery-guarantees/quiz-sh.title: Delivery guarantees: free-recall review
en/queues/01-delivery-guarantees/quiz-sh.summary: Free-recall prompts across the delivery-guarantees unit. Answer each from memory first, then reveal the model answer and compare.

en/queues/02-kafka-partitions/01-overvie.title: Kafka partitions: the unit of parallelism, ordering, and a one-way door
en/queues/02-kafka-partitions/01-overvie.summary: A topic splits into N partitions; the key''''s hash picks one; ordering holds only within a partition; one consumer per partition caps your parallelism. Partition count is a decision you can''''t take back.

en/queues/02-kafka-partitions/project.title: Kafka partitions: break and fix per-key ordering
en/queues/02-kafka-partitions/project.summary: Hands-on project — build a keyed order pipeline, prove per-key ordering, break it with an in-place partition increase, then migrate to a larger topic the safe way with evidence at every step.

en/queues/02-kafka-partitions/quiz-choic.title: Kafka partitions: multiple-choice review
en/queues/02-kafka-partitions/quiz-choic.summary: Multiple-choice synthesis across the Kafka partitions unit — key hashing, consumer-group assignment, the one-way door of partition count, skew, and rebalancing.

en/queues/02-kafka-partitions/quiz-code.title: Kafka partitions: code and config reading
en/queues/02-kafka-partitions/quiz-code.summary: Read real producer code, consumer config, partition math, and a rebalance log, predict the behaviour, and pick the highest-leverage fix.

en/queues/02-kafka-partitions/quiz-short.title: Kafka partitions: free-recall review
en/queues/02-kafka-partitions/quiz-short.summary: Free-recall prompts across the Kafka partitions unit. Answer each in your own words first, then reveal the model answer and compare.

en/queues/03-rabbit-exchanges/01-overvie.title: RabbitMQ exchanges: the routing layer that decides who gets a copy
en/queues/03-rabbit-exchanges/01-overvie.summary: Producers never publish to a queue — they publish to an exchange, and bindings plus routing keys decide which queues get a copy. Pick the wrong exchange type and messages either fan out everywhere or vanish silently.

en/queues/04-ordering/01-overview.title: Message ordering: total order is a throughput tax, partial order is the deal
en/queues/04-ordering/01-overview.summary: Global total order needs a single serialization point that caps throughput at one consumer. The real-world model is partial order — per-key FIFO — and the senior skill is knowing where it silently breaks.

en/queues/05-outbox/01-overview.title: The transactional outbox: ending the dual-write between DB and broker
en/queues/05-outbox/01-overview.summary: You cannot atomically write your database and publish to a broker. The outbox writes the business row and an event row in one local transaction, then a relay ships the event — at-least-once, so consumers must be idempotent.

en/queues/05-outbox/project.summary: Hands-on project — build an order service that eliminates the dual write with a transactional outbox, ship events with a polling relay, and prove no event is lost or double-applied under injected crashes.

en/queues/06-cdc/01-overview.title: Change-Data Capture: streaming the write-ahead log without filling the disk
en/queues/06-cdc/01-overview.summary: CDC tails the database''''s replication log so every committed insert/update/delete becomes an event — lower latency than polling, no app changes, but the replication slot can grow WAL until the primary halts.

en/queues/07-eventual-ux/01-overview.title: Designing UX over async backends: optimistic UI, pending states, read-your-writes
en/queues/07-eventual-ux/01-overview.summary: When a write goes through a queue, the result is not immediately readable. Naive UIs either lie (''''done!'''' before the pipeline finished) or show stale data. This is the frontend half of event-driven systems.

en/queues/07-eventual-ux/project.title: Eventual-consistency UX: make an async backend feel instant

en/react-patterns/00-start-here/01-what-.title: What is a React pattern?
en/react-patterns/00-start-here/01-what-.summary: A React pattern is a reusable, named solution to a recurring component-design problem. This track assumes you can already build with React and teaches the patterns that keep components simple as an app scales — composition, state, boundaries.

en/react-patterns/01-composition/01-chil.title: Children and slots
en/react-patterns/01-composition/01-chil.summary: The children prop and named JSX slots let callers compose content while the component owns structure — inverting control to kill prop explosion and keep components open, as long as the shape is actually variable.

en/react-patterns/01-composition/02-comp.title: Composition over inheritance
en/react-patterns/01-composition/02-comp.summary: React has no component inheritance — you specialize a base component by rendering it with preset props and children, not by extending it. Ask "does X contain/use Y", and watch for wrapper chains where a single variant prop would do.

en/react-patterns/01-composition/03-prop.title: Prop drilling, and when it's fine
en/react-patterns/01-composition/03-prop.summary: Prop drilling is passing a prop through components that do not use it. Two or three levels is often fine — explicit and greppable; reach for passing children, then context, only once drilling actually hurts.

en/react-patterns/02-compound-components.title: The compound component pattern
en/react-patterns/02-compound-components.summary: Compound components are a parent plus sub-components sharing implicit state via context: the parent owns behavior, the consumer arranges the pieces. They pay off for rearrangeable design-system widgets, and are pure overhead for a fixed two-element component.

en/react-patterns/02-compound-components.title: Sharing state with component context
en/react-patterns/02-compound-components.summary: Compound components share state through a context private to the component module — sub-components read the active value with no prop drilling and the consumer never sees it; leaking it app-wide or an unstable value object is the failure mode.

en/react-patterns/02-compound-components.title: Controlled vs uncontrolled
en/react-patterns/02-compound-components.summary: A reusable widget should support both controlled (parent owns state via value/onChange) and uncontrolled (component owns state via defaultValue) modes — built once with a useControllableState hook that prefers the prop when present and falls back to internal state.

en/react-patterns/03-render-props-headle.title: Render props
en/react-patterns/03-render-props-headle.summary: A render prop is a prop whose value returns JSX, sharing behavior while the caller owns the markup — mostly superseded by custom hooks for pure logic, but still right when you must inject something at render time.

en/react-patterns/03-render-props-headle.title: Headless components
en/react-patterns/03-render-props-headle.summary: Headless components give you behavior, state, accessibility, and keyboard handling with zero styling or markup — you supply the UI — so you get fully custom looks without fighting a library; the failure mode is abstracting a one-look in-app widget.

en/react-patterns/03-render-props-headle.title: Hooks as the headless pattern
en/react-patterns/03-render-props-headle.summary: A custom hook is the most ergonomic headless pattern: useX() returns state, handlers, and prop-getters the caller spreads onto its own markup — logic reuse with no wrapper, no nesting, full markup freedom. The failure mode is a hook that returns JSX.

en/react-patterns/04-custom-hooks/01-ext.title: Extracting a custom hook
en/react-patterns/04-custom-hooks/01-ext.summary: A custom hook names and isolates a slice of stateful logic so it is reusable and independently testable. Extract when the same state+effect sequence repeats, or has a clear nameable purpose — not for a single-caller useState wearing a new name.

en/react-patterns/04-custom-hooks/02-hoo.title: Hook design and dependencies
en/react-patterns/04-custom-hooks/02-hoo.summary: A custom hook is an API: clear inputs, a stable return shape, an honest dependency array, and cleanup. The classic hook bugs are stale closures and missing cleanup — a hook's deps and cleanup ARE its contract.

en/react-patterns/04-custom-hooks/03-whe.title: When not to extract a hook
en/react-patterns/04-custom-hooks/03-whe.summary: Extracting a custom hook has a carrying cost; do not pay it for a single caller, a one-line wrapper, or to share a file across unrelated state — inline code is often the senior choice, and a codebase of one-use hooks is unnavigable.

en/react-patterns/05-state-colocation/01.title: Colocation and lifting
en/react-patterns/05-state-colocation/01.summary: Put state as low as it can go — in the only component that reads it — and lift it only to the nearest common ancestor of two components that genuinely share it. Location is your primary lever for re-render width and clarity.

en/react-patterns/05-state-colocation/02.title: Derive, don't store
en/react-patterns/05-state-colocation/02.summary: Anything you can compute from existing props or state is derived, not state — calculate it during render instead of mirroring it into another useState with an effect, which creates two sources of truth that drift out of sync.

en/react-patterns/05-state-colocation/03.title: URL as state
en/react-patterns/05-state-colocation/03.summary: Put shareable, navigational state — filters, active tab, page, search query — in the URL via search params instead of useState, so it survives refresh, is linkable, and gets back/forward for free; keep transient high-frequency UI state out of it.

en/react-patterns/06-context/01-context-.title: Context for low-frequency state
en/react-patterns/06-context/01-context-.summary: Context broadcasts to every consumer whenever its value changes, so it fits low-frequency, widely-read state like theme, auth user, and locale — and turns fast-changing state into a tree-wide re-render storm.

en/react-patterns/06-context/02-splittin.title: Splitting contexts
en/react-patterns/06-context/02-splittin.summary: Context granularity sets the re-render blast radius: one fat context re-renders every consumer on any change. Split by concern, separate state from setters, and stabilize the value with useMemo — without sliding into provider hell.

en/react-patterns/06-context/03-context-.title: Context with a reducer
en/react-patterns/06-context/03-context-.summary: Context + useReducer is the built-in store for moderate cross-cutting state with non-trivial transitions; split state and dispatch into two contexts so dispatch — whose identity is stable — never re-renders consumers; fails for server state or huge/high-frequency state.

en/react-patterns/07-external-state/01-w.title: When to reach for a store
en/react-patterns/07-external-state/01-w.summary: An external store earns its place only when lifting state and context stop scaling — distant consumers, high-frequency updates that storm context, or persistence across routes. Otherwise it is over-engineering or duplicated server state.

en/react-patterns/07-external-state/02-s.title: Selectors and tearing
