en/react-patterns/07-external-state/02-s.summary: A selector subscribes a component to only the store slice it reads, so unrelated changes skip its render; read through the store hook to avoid tearing, and give shallow equality to any selector that builds a fresh object/array — or it re-renders on every change.

en/react-patterns/07-external-state/03-u.title: useSyncExternalStore
en/react-patterns/07-external-state/03-u.summary: useSyncExternalStore is Reacts blessed primitive for subscribing to any external store safely under concurrent rendering — subscribe + getSnapshot + getServerSnapshot. Stable snapshots avoid render loops; getServerSnapshot avoids SSR crashes.

en/react-patterns/08-effects/01-effects-.title: Effects are for synchronization
en/react-patterns/08-effects/01-effects-.summary: useEffect synchronizes React with an external system — subscriptions, browser APIs, non-React widgets, connections — and cleans them up; it is not a react-to-state hook for computing derived data, which is the source of most effect bugs.

en/react-patterns/08-effects/02-you-migh.title: You might not need an effect
en/react-patterns/08-effects/02-you-migh.summary: Most effects in real codebases are unnecessary and buggy. Learn the catalog of effects to delete — derived state, display transforms, prop-driven resets, caching, parent notifications, chained updates — and the one effect you must never delete by mistake.

en/react-patterns/08-effects/03-cleanup-.title: Cleanup and stale closures
en/react-patterns/08-effects/03-cleanup-.summary: Every subscription, interval, listener, and fetch an effect starts must be torn down in its return, and effects capture the render that created them — so fix stale closures with correct deps plus functional updates or a ref, never by silencing the lint rule.

en/react-patterns/09-render-performance/.title: When to memoize
en/react-patterns/09-render-performance/.summary: Default to NOT memoizing. Reach for memo/useMemo/useCallback only when identity feeds a memoized child, when a value is another hook's dependency, or when a computation is measurably expensive — and profile before, not by reflex.

en/react-patterns/09-render-performance/.title: memo, useMemo, useCallback
en/react-patterns/09-render-performance/.summary: memo, useMemo and useCallback only pay off as one system: memo skips a child whose props are shallow-equal, and useMemo/useCallback supply the stable object/function identities that let that equality hold — any link missing makes the whole chain a no-op.

en/react-patterns/09-render-performance/.title: Keys and lists
en/react-patterns/09-render-performance/.summary: Keys are React's identity mechanism for list items: stable unique keys let state follow the right row, index keys corrupt state on reorder/insert/delete, and a changing key intentionally forces a remount.

en/react-patterns/10-server-client-bound.title: Server vs client components
en/react-patterns/10-server-client-bound.summary: In the App Router, Server Components are the default — no client JS, direct data access — and Client Components opt in with 'use client' only for interactivity; default to server and push the boundary down to the interactive leaves.

en/react-patterns/10-server-client-bound.title: 'use client' and serializable props
en/react-patterns/10-server-client-bound.summary: 'use client' marks a module and its whole import subtree as client; Server-to-Client props must be serializable, so data crosses downward as serializable props while server content is composed into client shells via children — not by importing across.

en/react-patterns/10-server-client-bound.title: server-only and data flowing down
en/react-patterns/10-server-client-bound.summary: The server/client boundary is also a security boundary: mark secret and data-access modules with import "server-only" so a client import fails the build, fetch on the server, and pass only plain serializable data down to interactive client leaves.

en/react-patterns/11-suspense-and-bounda.title: Suspense placement
en/react-patterns/11-suspense-and-bounda.summary: Suspense shows a fallback while a child loads; placing boundaries close to where data is needed lets already-loaded content reveal progressively, whereas one root boundary blanks the whole page when any small part is pending.

en/react-patterns/11-suspense-and-bounda.title: Error boundaries
en/react-patterns/11-suspense-and-bounda.summary: Suspense handles the loading state; an Error Boundary above it handles the failed state by catching errors thrown during render and showing a fallback — a real async UI needs both, and a Suspense with no boundary lets a failed fetch crash to a blank screen.

en/react-patterns/11-suspense-and-bounda.title: Transitions and deferred values
en/react-patterns/11-suspense-and-bounda.summary: useTransition marks a state update non-urgent so typing stays responsive; useDeferredValue lags a derived value behind input — both keep the UI snappy under heavy renders and let Suspense show stale content instead of a fallback.

en/react-patterns/12-forms-and-actions/0.title: Controlled vs uncontrolled forms
en/react-patterns/12-forms-and-actions/0.summary: Controlled inputs let React own each value (value + onChange) for live validation or value-driven UI; uncontrolled inputs let the DOM own them, read once via FormData or a ref — fewer re-renders, less code. Default to uncontrolled for plain submit-only forms.

en/react-patterns/12-forms-and-actions/0.title: Form actions and useActionState
en/react-patterns/12-forms-and-actions/0.summary: React 19 form actions run a function with FormData on submit; useActionState gives you pending, result, and error state for free, and useFormStatus reads submit state inside a child — so stop hand-rolling onSubmit + isSubmitting, and validate the action on the server.

en/react-patterns/12-forms-and-actions/0.title: Optimistic UI with useOptimistic
en/react-patterns/12-forms-and-actions/0.summary: useOptimistic shows a result immediately while an action is pending and reverts automatically on failure — the safe shape is snapshot, apply optimistic, then reconcile or roll back with visible error feedback, and never for operations the user must not believe are done.

en/react-patterns/13-data-fetching/01-rs.title: RSC fetch vs client cache
en/react-patterns/13-data-fetching/01-rs.summary: In the App Router, await data in a Server Component for initial per-request fetches with no client cache; reach for a query library (TanStack Query/SWR) only when you need client cache semantics — refetch, dedupe, mutate, optimistic, polling.

en/react-patterns/13-data-fetching/02-qu.title: Query libraries and dedupe
en/react-patterns/13-data-fetching/02-qu.summary: A query library turns server state into a cached, self-revalidating resource — caching, request dedupe, background revalidation, retries, and mutation-with-invalidation — so you stop copying server data into useState/Redux and manually syncing it.

en/react-patterns/13-data-fetching/03-av.title: Avoiding request waterfalls
en/react-patterns/13-data-fetching/03-av.summary: A request waterfall is independent data fetched serially — invisible until real latency hits; fix it by running independent requests in parallel and prefetching likely-next data, without serializing requests that genuinely depend on each other.

en/react-patterns/14-antipatterns/01-pro.title: God components & prop drilling
en/react-patterns/14-antipatterns/01-pro.summary: God components and deep prop drilling are React's forms of low cohesion and high coupling; cure them with composition, custom hooks, and state colocation — and resist over-correcting drilling with an app-wide context or global store when passing children was the lighter fix.

en/react-patterns/14-antipatterns/02-eff.title: Effect-as-derived-state
en/react-patterns/14-antipatterns/02-eff.summary: The most common React anti-pattern: a useEffect whose only job is setState-from-props-or-state. It costs an extra render and shows a stale value for one tick. Delete it — derive in render, or reset with a key — but not if it syncs an external system.

en/react-patterns/14-antipatterns/03-con.title: Context misuse & key-as-index
en/react-patterns/14-antipatterns/03-con.summary: Two anti-patterns that pass a demo and fail in production: high-frequency or local state in context (tree-wide re-render storms) and key-as-index (list state corrupting on reorder/insert) — plus their fixes and the over-correction traps.

en/react-patterns/15-capstone/01-feature.title: Capstone I: the pattern-smell inventory
en/react-patterns/15-capstone/01-feature.summary: Before refactoring a messy React feature, diagnose it: name each anti-pattern with the track's vocabulary, locate it, and rank by impact (wasted renders, latent bugs, change-cost) so every later edit can prove it improved something.

en/react-patterns/15-capstone/02-increme.title: Capstone II: the incremental refactor
en/react-patterns/15-capstone/02-increme.summary: Execute the part-1 inventory one change at a time: fix the P0 bugs first (derived-state effect, keys), then split context and stabilize its value, decompose via composition + custom hooks, and wrap async parts in Suspense + an Error Boundary — never a big-bang rewrite.

en/react-patterns/15-capstone/03-measure.title: Capstone III: measure before and after
en/react-patterns/15-capstone/03-measure.summary: Close the capstone by measuring the refactor: prove fewer re-renders (Profiler), shallower drilling, the staleness bug gone, and the target change now a single local edit — then stop, because good enough beats perfect.

en/react/01-rendering-model/01-render-an.title: Render and commit: why React calls your component more often than it paints
en/react/01-rendering-model/01-render-an.summary: Render is React calling your components as pure functions to produce an element tree; commit is the only phase that mutates the DOM. Concurrent React can repeat or discard a render, so a side effect in render fires an unpredictable number of times — keep render pure.

en/react/01-rendering-model/02-reconcili.title: Reconciliation and keys: where your state actually lives
en/react/01-rendering-model/02-reconcili.summary: React diffs by element type and key, not by your component instances: same type at the same position keeps the fiber and its state, a type change unmounts the subtree. Index-as-key pins state to positions, so a reorder silently hands one row's state to another.

en/react/01-rendering-model/03-state-and.title: setState is a request: snapshots, update queues, and automatic batching
en/react/01-rendering-model/03-state-and.summary: setState is a request queued on the fiber, not an assignment: state is a per-render snapshot, so two setCount(count+1) calls increment once. React 18 batches everywhere — promises, timeouts, native handlers — one render per batch; flushSync forces a sync flush at real cost.

en/react/02-hooks-and-state/01-effect-li.title: useEffect is synchronization, not lifecycle
en/react/02-hooks-and-state/01-effect-li.summary: useEffect synchronizes a component with an external system — not lifecycle. Deps compare per element with Object.is; cleanup runs before every re-run and on unmount. StrictMode double-mounts to expose missing cleanup; fetch races need an ignore flag or AbortController.

en/react/02-hooks-and-state/02-memoizati.title: Memoization: referential equality is the contract
en/react/02-hooks-and-state/02-memoizati.summary: useMemo caches a value, useCallback a function identity, React.memo skips re-renders on shallow-equal props — all contracts over referential equality. Inline objects and children defeat memo; cheap or always-changing deps make memoization a net loss. Profile first, then memoize.

en/react/02-hooks-and-state/03-context-a.title: Context, value identity, and the re-render storm
en/react/02-hooks-and-state/03-context-a.summary: Context re-renders every consumer when the provider value changes identity — an inline value object means a storm on each provider render, and memo ancestors cannot block it. Fixes: memoized value, split state/dispatch contexts, or an external store with per-slice subscriptions.

en/react/03-data-fetching/01-fetching-in.title: Fetching in effects: races, waterfalls, and why the baseline is worth knowing
en/react/03-data-fetching/01-fetching-in.summary: Fetching in useEffect is the honest baseline: an effect keyed on params, three states of boilerplate, and two structural bugs — races, because responses return out of order, and waterfalls, because the component tree serializes requests. Data libraries exist to fix exactly these.

en/react/03-data-fetching/02-suspense-fo.title: Suspense for data: the throw-a-promise contract, use(), and boundaries as UX design
en/react/03-data-fetching/02-suspense-fo.summary: Suspense inverts data loading: a component reads a promise with use(), React suspends to the nearest boundary, and resolve retries the render. Boundary placement is UX design, rejected promises route to error boundaries — and without a cache, raw fetch in render suspends forever.

en/react/03-data-fetching/03-query-libra.title: Query libraries: queryKey identity, the two clocks, and what TanStack Query actually saves you
en/react/03-data-fetching/03-query-libra.summary: TanStack Query treats server data as a cache, not state: queryKey is cache identity (dedup, sharing), staleTime and gcTime are two independent clocks (refetch vs memory), refetch-on-focus keeps data live, and mutations plus invalidateQueries close the write loop.

en/react/03-data-fetching/04-cache-inval.title: Cache invalidation patterns: invalidate vs write-through, optimistic rollback, and live sync
en/react/03-data-fetching/04-cache-inval.summary: After a write, the cache lies until you reconcile it. Invalidate buys server truth for an extra request; setQueryData is instant but replicates server logic; optimistic updates need cancel + snapshot + rollback. Plus infinite-query refetch costs and websocket sync.

en/react/04-forms-and-mutations/01-contr.title: Controlled vs uncontrolled inputs: who owns the value, and what it costs
en/react/04-forms-and-mutations/01-contr.summary: Controlled inputs put the value in React state and re-render per keystroke; uncontrolled inputs leave it in the DOM, read via refs or FormData on submit. Each wins in different forms — and a value prop without onChange, or switching modes mid-life, produces production bugs.

en/react/04-forms-and-mutations/02-form-.title: Form state and validation: values, errors, touched — and when to run the check
en/react/04-forms-and-mutations/02-form-.summary: A form is three maps — values, errors, touched — plus a timing policy: validate on blur, re-validate on change once touched, gate on submit. One zod schema serves client and server; errors need aria-describedby and focus management, or some users never find them.

en/react/04-forms-and-mutations/03-actio.title: Form actions and useActionState: mutations as a first-class React primitive
en/react/04-forms-and-mutations/03-actio.summary: React 19 forms take action={fn}: submission runs as an async transition, FormData in, new state out. useActionState gives state, a wrapped action, isPending; useFormStatus reads pending from inside. With server functions the form submits before hydration — enhancement built in.

en/react/04-forms-and-mutations/04-optim.title: Optimistic UI with useOptimistic: lying to the user honestly
en/react/04-forms-and-mutations/04-optim.summary: useOptimistic renders the hoped-for state while the mutation flies and reverts to canonical state when the transition settles — rollback is free. Reconciliation, idempotency keys against double-submit, and knowing when optimism is wrong (payments, deletes) stay on you.

en/react/05-performance/01-profiler-and-.title: Profiler and measurement: find the 600 ms commit before touching React.memo
en/react/05-performance/01-profiler-and-.summary: Profile before optimizing: the React DevTools flamegraph shows which commits cost what, the Profiler API turns that into numbers you can ship, and INP — not the 16 ms frame myth — is the budget users actually feel. A team that memoized for two sprints fixed 4 ms and missed 620.

en/react/05-performance/02-rendering-cos.title: Rendering cost and virtualization: the 10,000-row table that renders 30 rows
en/react/05-performance/02-rendering-cos.summary: Render volume kills: a 10k-row table is 300k DOM nodes and a second per keystroke. Virtualization renders only the viewport plus overscan (TanStack Virtual: estimateSize, measureElement, translate); content-visibility is the CSS cousin for static content. Keys must be item ids.

en/react/05-performance/03-transitions-a.title: Transitions and useDeferredValue: making slow renders interruptible, not faster
en/react/05-performance/03-transitions-a.summary: Transitions put updates in urgent and background lanes: the urgent commit lands first, the heavy render is interruptible per keystroke. useDeferredValue mirrors it for received values; with Suspense old UI holds, no fallback flash. One giant component cannot be interrupted.

en/react/05-performance/04-code-splittin.title: Code splitting with React.lazy: ship the screen, not the application
en/react/05-performance/04-code-splittin.summary: React.lazy turns a dynamic import into a component that suspends until its chunk loads. Split at routes first, then heavy conditional components; preload on hover/viewport; never chain lazy inside lazy — each hop is a full round trip. Measure chunks, not vibes.

en/react/06-state-architecture/01-liftin.title: Lifting and colocation: state lives at the lowest common owner
en/react/06-state-architecture/01-liftin.summary: State belongs to the lowest component that needs it. Lift it only to the nearest common owner of its readers; every extra level widens the re-render blast radius. Global-by-default turns each keystroke into an app-wide render; composition via children isolates state instead.

en/react/06-state-architecture/02-reduce.title: Reducers and context: turning scattered setState into testable transitions
en/react/06-state-architecture/02-reduce.summary: useReducer models multi-field updates as named transitions in one pure, unit-testable function instead of scattered setState calls. Split state and dispatch into two contexts — dispatch is stable, so write-only components never re-render. Often this replaces a state library.

en/react/06-state-architecture/03-extern.title: External stores: useSyncExternalStore, selector subscriptions, and tearing
en/react/06-state-architecture/03-extern.summary: useSyncExternalStore is the contract for reading state React does not own: subscribe + cached getSnapshot, with tearing checks. Stores like zustand build selectors on it — no provider, re-render only when your slice changes — and beat context for write-heavy, cross-tree state.

en/react/06-state-architecture/04-server.title: Server state vs client state: deciding who owns which truth
en/react/06-state-architecture/04-server.summary: Server state is a cache of truth the server owns — async, shared, stale by default; a query library manages its lifecycle. Client state is UI truth you own. Copying server data into useState forks the truth; form drafts are the one deliberate fork, committed explicitly on submit.

en/react/07-testing/01-rtl-and-user-even.title: RTL and user-event: test the contract the user sees
en/react/07-testing/01-rtl-and-user-even.summary: Testing Library queries the accessibility tree — role over label over text over testid — so tests fail when UX breaks, not when markup moves. user-event replays real event sequences where fireEvent dispatches one synthetic event. act warnings flag updates your test never awaited.

en/react/07-testing/02-async-tests-and-m.title: Async tests and MSW: mock the network, not the fetch
en/react/07-testing/02-async-tests-and-m.summary: findBy is getBy plus waitFor — 1 s timeout, 50 ms polls — so async UI is awaited, not slept for. MSW 2.x intercepts at the network seam: http.get plus HttpResponse, server.use for per-test overrides. Fetch mocks couple tests to the client; MSW survives client refactors.

en/react/07-testing/03-testing-hooks-and.title: Testing hooks and context: renderHook, fake timers, stale snapshots
en/react/07-testing/03-testing-hooks-and.summary: renderHook mounts a throwaway host component around your hook; result.current is a live property — re-read it after every act, a destructured copy is one render frozen. wrapper injects providers. Fake timers deadlock user-event unless setup wires advanceTimers.

en/react/07-testing/04-test-suites-that-.title: Test suites that scale: contracts, flake taxonomy, budgets
en/react/07-testing/04-test-suites-that-.summary: Each component tier has a public contract — test that, not internals. Whole-DOM snapshots assert everything and thus nothing. Flakes split into timing, order-dependence, and shared state; retry masks all three. MSW: happy-path defaults, per-test overrides. Unit slice under 10 s.

en/react/08-concurrent-react/01-suspense.title: Suspense boundaries: designing what disappears together
en/react/08-concurrent-react/01-suspense.summary: A Suspense boundary decides what disappears together: the nearest boundary above a suspender shows its fallback. Nesting controls reveal order, fallbacks must reserve space or cause CLS, and startTransition keeps shown content on screen instead of swapping it for a spinner.

en/react/08-concurrent-react/02-deferred.title: useDeferredValue and transitions: priority is a second render
en/react/08-concurrent-react/02-deferred.summary: useDeferredValue re-renders urgently with the old value, then runs an interruptible background render with the new one — two renders by design. Without memo downstream the deferral buys nothing. Unlike debounce there is no fixed delay: it adapts to device speed.

en/react/08-concurrent-react/03-streamin.title: Streaming SSR and selective hydration: HTML in waves
en/react/08-concurrent-react/03-streamin.summary: renderToPipeableStream sends the shell first; suspended subtrees stream later as hidden chunks plus inline scripts that swap them in. Hydration is per boundary and a click reprioritizes it, replaying the event. One slow await in the shell blocks everything.

en/react/08-concurrent-react/04-react-co.title: React Compiler, honestly: automated memo with silent bailouts
en/react/08-concurrent-react/04-react-co.summary: The React Compiler memoizes at build time by proving the Rules of React hold. Where it cannot prove them it bails out silently — code just stays unmemoized. The eslint plugin is the contract surface, manual memo keeps narrow jobs, and wins are measured in the Profiler.

en/react/09-error-handling/01-error-boun.title: Error boundaries: the class-only net and its four blind spots
en/react/09-error-handling/01-error-boun.summary: A render crash with no boundary unmounts the whole tree. Boundaries are class-only: getDerivedStateFromError swaps in fallback state, componentDidCatch reports componentStack. Handlers, async, SSR and the boundary itself escape — cover the gaps with route and widget tiers.

en/react/09-error-handling/02-recovery-a.title: Recovery and degradation: evict state, back off on retry, fail honestly
en/react/09-error-handling/02-recovery-a.summary: Recovery is state eviction: resetKeys or reset() remount the crashed subtree so corrupted state dies. Retry transient failures with exponential backoff and jitter, never in a tight loop. Degrade per widget so the page lives; fail the whole page only when integrity is at stake.

en/react/09-error-handling/03-errors-out.title: Errors outside render: the global net and the React 19 reporting pipeline
en/react/09-error-handling/03-errors-out.summary: Handlers, async code and timers never reach boundaries: catch them via window error and unhandledrejection, then route reports through React 19 root callbacks. Dedupe StrictMode doubles, upload source maps, tag releases — and treat hydration mismatches as recoverable, not fatal.

en/react/10-accessibility/01-semantics-a.title: Semantics and roles: the accessibility tree does not see your divs
en/react/10-accessibility/01-semantics-a.summary: A clickable div has no role, no name, no keyboard path — assistive tech cannot operate it. Native elements ship the contract free; the accname ladder (labelledby beats label beats content beats title) decides the announced name; landmarks and headings are the navigation surface.

en/react/10-accessibility/02-focus-manag.title: Focus management: focus is application state you own
en/react/10-accessibility/02-focus-manag.summary: SPAs decouple focus from navigation: a route change announces nothing until you focus the new heading (tabIndex -1); dialogs trap focus, inert the background, restore to the trigger; flushSync beats focus-after-render races; deleting the focused node strands users at body.

en/react/10-accessibility/03-aria-compos.title: ARIA composite widgets: APG patterns are keyboard contracts
en/react/10-accessibility/03-aria-compos.summary: One Tab stop per composite; arrows move inside — roving tabindex (real focus, the 0/-1 dance) or aria-activedescendant (DOM focus stays on the input). ARIA state must derive from the same state as the pixels or the widget lies to AT. For combobox-grade widgets, buy headless.

en/react/10-accessibility/04-testing-acc.title: Testing accessibility: layers that catch what axe cannot
en/react/10-accessibility/04-testing-acc.summary: getByRole makes every test an a11y smoke test; axe catches roughly a third of WCAG issues — focus order, name quality, announcement timing need a manual screen-reader pass. CI: jsx-a11y lint, role queries, axe on key pages; every a11y bug gets a failing test first.

en/react/11-react-server-components/01-t.title: The RSC model: two environments, one tree
en/react/11-react-server-components/01-t.summary: Server components run once per request — async, direct data access, zero bundle weight. Client components hydrate and live. The Flight payload is a serialized element tree with module-reference holes, not HTML, and it composes with SSR instead of replacing it.

en/react/11-react-server-components/02-s.title: The serialization boundary: use client splits the module graph
en/react/11-react-server-components/02-s.summary: use client marks a module-graph cut: everything a client file imports joins the bundle. Props crossing must serialize — plain data, Date, Map yes; functions and class instances no. Children put server output inside a client shell; use server is the reverse channel.

en/react/11-react-server-components/03-r.title: RSC outside Next.js: the framework is the bundler
en/react/11-react-server-components/03-r.summary: RSC is React infrastructure, not a Next.js feature: react-server-dom bindings speak Flight, a bundler plugin splits the module graph and emits the client manifest, a client runtime consumes the stream, a router refetches payloads. The discipline transfers everywhere.

en/react/12-design-systems/01-compositio.title: Composition patterns: compound components over boolean props
en/react/12-design-systems/01-compositio.summary: Boolean props explode into a 2^n matrix nobody tests. Composition moves variation into JSX: compound components share state via context with dev-time guards and controlled/uncontrolled duality; children inspection is fragile; render props win when the library owns the loop.

en/react/12-design-systems/02-headless-c.title: Headless components: buy the state machine, own the skin
en/react/12-design-systems/02-headless-c.summary: A widget is 80% state machine, keyboard contract, ARIA and focus — headless libraries ship that and zero pixels; you own skin, motion, density. Choose headless when brand is strong, a styled kit when speed wins; wrapping a styled kit means fighting its specificity forever.

en/react/12-design-systems/03-polymorphi.title: Polymorphic components: the as prop versus asChild and Slot
en/react/12-design-systems/03-polymorphi.summary: Polymorphism two ways: the as prop swaps the rendered element and pays in polymorphic ref types and type-instantiation blowup; asChild merges props onto the existing child via Slot — className concat, handler chaining, ref composition. as suits primitives; asChild suits behavior.

en/react/12-design-systems/04-tokens-and.title: Design tokens and theming: the contract between design and code
en/react/12-design-systems/04-tokens-and.summary: Tokens are a three-tier contract: primitive palette, semantic intent, component bindings. Themes re-declare the semantic tier — data-theme flips custom properties, zero re-render. Ship tokens as a versioned package, alias renames, lint raw hex; a rebrand takes days, not months.

en/react/13-animations-and-interaction/0.title: The compositor and the frame budget: which properties are free
en/react/13-animations-and-interaction/0.summary: transform and opacity animate on the compositor thread and survive a blocked main thread; width or top re-run layout and paint per frame. Budget: ~10 ms of your code at 60 Hz. setState per frame burns it on render plus reconcile — use rAF + ref or CSS. will-change costs memory.

en/react/13-animations-and-interaction/0.title: FLIP: layout animation without paying layout every frame
en/react/13-animations-and-interaction/0.summary: Animating top or height re-runs layout for every item on every frame. FLIP pays layout once: measure First, apply Last, Invert with transform, Play to identity. Batch reads before writes to avoid thrashing; Framer Motion layoutId is FLIP with automated measurement.

en/react/13-animations-and-interaction/0.title: View Transitions and gestures: snapshots, springs, and seizing values mid-flight
en/react/13-animations-and-interaction/0.summary: document.startViewTransition snapshots the old state, your callback mutates the DOM (flushSync for React), and ::view-transition pseudo-elements animate old to new. Gestures: pointer capture, rAF-batched transforms, no layout reads in move handlers, seize values mid-flight.

en/react/14-production-react/01-version-.title: React version migrations: the dependency audit is the project
en/react/14-production-react/01-version-.summary: React majors are dependency projects: createRoot flips automatic batching everywhere, StrictMode double-invoke exposes effects that were already wrong, 19 deletes legacy APIs. Audit deps first, codemod the mechanical part, canary-ramp with RUM. Weeks to months at scale.

en/react/14-production-react/02-rum-and-.title: RUM and field profiling: lab lies, the field decides
en/react/14-production-react/02-rum-and-.summary: Wire onLCP, onINP, onCLS to a beacon carrying route, release, and device class — without those dimensions field data answers nothing. INP attribution splits input delay, processing, presentation. Sample the React Profiler at 1 percent, alert on p75 per release ring, keep PII out.

en/react/14-production-react/03-performa.title: Performance regressions: the slow creep nobody ships on purpose
en/react/14-production-react/03-performa.summary: Bundle creep, hydration growth, and memo decay degrade p75 without one bad release. Defense in layers: hard-fail CI byte budgets, synthetic checks on a fixed device, RUM percentiles per release. Bisect with release diffs plus profile diffs; give every route an owned budget.

en/react/14-production-react/04-incident.title: Incident postmortems: three production React failures, dissected
en/react/14-production-react/04-incident.summary: Three dissected React incidents: an async render loop pinning CPU without exceptions, a hydration mismatch storm from timezone-dependent render, and a subscription leak crashing 8-hour sessions. Blameless format: detection, impact, root cause, mitigation, prevention.

en/security-cloud/00-start-here/01-the-s.title: The shared-responsibility model
en/security-cloud/00-start-here/01-the-s.summary: The cloud provider secures the platform; you secure how you use it — and the line moves with IaaS, PaaS, and SaaS. The dominant failure isn't a 0-day, it's a misconfiguration on your side of the line. Identity is the new perimeter; blast radius is the metric.

en/security-cloud/01-cloud-iam/01-cloud-.title: The cloud identity model
en/security-cloud/01-cloud-iam/01-cloud-.summary: Cloud authz is not one ACL but several policy documents evaluated together: a request is allowed only if some policy explicitly allows it and none denies it. Get the principal, the policy types, and the deny-by-default evaluation order right and most access mysteries dissolve.

en/security-cloud/01-cloud-iam/02-least-.title: Least-privilege policies
en/security-cloud/01-cloud-iam/02-least-.summary: A tight policy grants exactly the actions and resources a role needs and nothing more. Wildcards (`Action:*`, `Resource:*`) feel convenient and quietly become the blast radius. Permission boundaries cap what a role can ever grant — the guardrail least privilege needs at scale.

en/security-cloud/01-cloud-iam/03-role-a.title: Role assumption and federation
en/security-cloud/01-cloud-iam/03-role-a.summary: Long-lived access keys are the credential that leaks. Assume-role mints short-lived STS credentials for a scoped task; cross-account uses a trust policy with an external id; CI and pods federate via OIDC, so there are no keys to steal at all.

en/security-cloud/01-cloud-iam/04-iam-mi.title: IAM misconfigurations
en/security-cloud/01-cloud-iam/04-iam-mi.summary: The IAM misconfigs that turn one foothold into account takeover: iam:PassRole + a service that assumes any role is a privilege-escalation ladder, and a third party you let assume your role with no ExternalId is a confused deputy. Both are grants, not bugs.

en/security-cloud/02-container-and-kuber.title: Container image security
en/security-cloud/02-container-and-kuber.summary: An image is a tarball of someone else's code plus yours, and `:latest` is a moving target you do not control. Pin by digest, build on a minimal base, scan and rebuild for CVEs, run non-root, and verify the signature so the image you run is the one you meant to run.

en/security-cloud/02-container-and-kuber.title: Container runtime security
en/security-cloud/02-container-and-kuber.summary: A container is a process, not a VM — it shares the host kernel. Drop Linux capabilities, add a seccomp profile, and run read-only so one process bug stays a process bug instead of becoming a host compromise.

en/security-cloud/02-container-and-kuber.title: Kubernetes RBAC
en/security-cloud/02-container-and-kuber.summary: Kubernetes RBAC is deny-by-default, but the foot-guns are in the grants: a wildcard verb, a Role that can create pods, or a stray cluster-admin binding quietly equals full-cluster takeover. Least privilege here is a verb-by-verb discipline, not a checkbox.

en/security-cloud/02-container-and-kuber.title: Network Policy and Pod Security
en/security-cloud/02-container-and-kuber.summary: A fresh Kubernetes pod is wide open: any pod can reach any other on the flat network, and without a SecurityContext it can run as root with host access. NetworkPolicy and Pod Security Standards are the two opt-in gates that turn that default-allow posture into default-deny.

en/security-cloud/02-container-and-kuber.title: Secrets in Kubernetes
en/security-cloud/02-container-and-kuber.summary: A Kubernetes Secret is base64, not encryption — plaintext to anyone with etcd, a node, or RBAC read. Why that matters and how to manage secrets without copies sprawling across namespaces and CI logs.

en/security-cloud/03-iac-and-supply-chai.title: IaC scanning
en/security-cloud/03-iac-and-supply-chai.summary: Cloud breaches are usually misconfigurations, not exploits — a bucket left public, a security group open to 0.0.0.0/0. IaC scanning reads the Terraform plan and fails the pipeline before apply, so the bad config never reaches the cloud.

en/security-cloud/03-iac-and-supply-chai.title: Image and dependency scanning
en/security-cloud/03-iac-and-supply-chai.summary: Scanners flag every CVE in your dependencies and base images, but most don't reach exploitable code. Reachability, severity, and fix-availability are how seniors turn a wall of red into a short, ranked list of things that actually matter.

en/security-cloud/03-iac-and-supply-chai.title: SLSA and SBOM in delivery
en/security-cloud/03-iac-and-supply-chai.summary: SolarWinds and the XZ backdoor shipped through trusted build pipelines, not exploits. SLSA provenance plus signing proves how an artifact was built and that it is the one you reviewed; an SBOM lists what is inside so you can answer 'am I affected' in minutes.

en/security-cloud/03-iac-and-supply-chai.title: Pipeline hardening
en/security-cloud/03-iac-and-supply-chai.summary: CI runs attacker-influenced code with production credentials. The poisoned-pipeline and over-privileged-runner are how that turns into a breach — and least-privilege, trust boundaries, and pinned actions are how you stop it.

en/security-cloud/04-cloud-detection-and.title: CSPM and posture management
en/security-cloud/04-cloud-detection-and.summary: IaC scanning stops bad config before apply, but consoles, runtime, and 10 other teams keep drifting prod. CSPM is the read-only API sweep across every account that finds the public bucket nobody filed a ticket for.

en/security-cloud/04-cloud-detection-and.title: Cloud logging and trails
en/security-cloud/04-cloud-detection-and.summary: The control-plane audit trail is the one record of who did what in your cloud — and the first thing an attacker deletes. If they can edit it, you have a log, not evidence. Tamper-resistance is what turns one into the other.

en/security-cloud/04-cloud-detection-and.title: Misconfiguration detection
en/security-cloud/04-cloud-detection-and.summary: The public bucket and the open Postgres port are the two breaches that keep happening. Detection finds them after the fact; preventive guardrails make the misconfig structurally impossible. Seniors build both, and lead with prevention.

en/security-cloud/04-cloud-detection-and.title: Data security and KMS
en/security-cloud/04-cloud-detection-and.summary: Encryption at rest is only as strong as who can call Decrypt. KMS-backed envelope encryption and a deny-by-default key policy are what actually protect data — not the AES box being ticked.

en/security-defensive/00-start-here/01-t.title: The defender's job: turning attacks into signals
en/security-defensive/00-start-here/01-t.summary: Defense is asymmetric: the attacker needs one working path, you must cover all of them. So you assume breach, layer controls, and turn every attacker action into a signal you can detect, triage, and respond to. This is the defender's job.

en/security-defensive/01-logging-monitor.title: What to log
en/security-defensive/01-logging-monitor.summary: You cannot detect, investigate, or prove an incident you never logged. Capture every auth, access, and admin event with enough context to reconstruct who-did-what-to-what — and make sure secrets, tokens, and full PII never land in the log.

en/security-defensive/01-logging-monitor.title: SIEM fundamentals
en/security-defensive/01-logging-monitor.summary: A SIEM ingests logs from every host, normalizes them into one schema, and correlates that firehose into a handful of alerts. The hard part isn't storage — it's turning millions of events an hour into the three that mean something.

en/security-defensive/01-logging-monitor.title: MITRE ATT&CK for detection
en/security-defensive/01-logging-monitor.summary: ATT&CK is the shared catalog of how real adversaries operate. Map each detection rule to a technique and your coverage stops being a feeling and becomes a grid — one that names exactly which attacker moves you would never see.

en/security-defensive/01-logging-monitor.title: Detection engineering
en/security-defensive/01-logging-monitor.summary: A rule clicked into a SIEM console has no history, no test, no reviewer. Detection engineering treats detections as code — Sigma rules in Git, tested against sample logs, reviewed in a PR — so tuning becomes an auditable diff, not a click no one remembers.

en/security-defensive/01-logging-monitor.title: Alert quality and tuning
en/security-defensive/01-logging-monitor.summary: Most alerts are noise, and a wall of noise hides the one real intrusion. Senior tuning raises precision — killing low-value rules, scoping the rest — without quietly dropping the true positive you exist to catch.

en/security-defensive/02-incident-respon.title: The IR lifecycle
en/security-defensive/02-incident-respon.summary: NIST splits incident response into four phases, but the one nobody is watching during an outage — Preparation — quietly decides the outcome of the other three. This is why the work you do before the pager fires is the work that saves you.

en/security-defensive/02-incident-respon.title: Triage and containment
en/security-defensive/02-incident-respon.summary: The first hour decides everything. Scope the blast radius before you act, then contain in a way that cuts the attacker's access without nuking the volatile evidence you'll need to prove what they did and when.

en/security-defensive/02-incident-respon.title: Forensics basics
en/security-defensive/02-incident-respon.summary: Evidence is only as good as how you handled it. Collect volatile data before it evaporates, hash and log every artifact for chain of custody, extract IOCs, and stitch a timeline that turns scattered logs into a defensible story.

en/security-defensive/02-incident-respon.title: Postmortems and learning
en/security-defensive/02-incident-respon.summary: A blameless postmortem trades the name of who fumbled for the name of the system that let them. It exists to ship corrective actions with owners and dates — not a verdict. If it produces blame, it produced nothing.

en/security-defensive/03-hardening-defen.title: OS and host hardening
en/security-defensive/03-hardening-defen.summary: Every running service, open port, and shipped default is attack surface. Hardening shrinks a host to the job it actually does, swaps permissive defaults for safe ones, and pins a measurable baseline so drift becomes visible.

en/security-defensive/03-hardening-defen.title: Network hardening
en/security-defensive/03-hardening-defen.summary: Default-deny networking blocks everything and allows only named flows — including egress, the direction most teams forget. Combined with segmentation and killing plaintext protocols, it turns one compromised box from a launchpad into a dead end.

en/security-defensive/03-hardening-defen.title: CIS benchmarks and baselines
en/security-defensive/03-hardening-defen.summary: CIS Benchmarks give you a vetted hardening baseline so you do not invent one. The senior work is the loop after: capture that baseline as code, then detect and close configuration drift before an attacker finds the gap.

en/security-defensive/03-hardening-defen.title: Patch and vulnerability management
en/security-defensive/03-hardening-defen.summary: A new scan drops 4,000 findings and you have time for forty. CVSS alone is a trap — it ranks severity in a vacuum. Real prioritization multiplies severity by exposure: is it reachable, exploited in the wild, and on a box that touches your data?

en/security-defensive/04-secops-and-gove.title: Vulnerability management
en/security-defensive/04-secops-and-gove.summary: Vulnerability management is a closed loop — discover, prioritize, remediate, verify — not a quarterly scan you email to nobody. The senior skill is ranking by exploitability and exposure, then closing findings inside an SLA you can defend.

en/security-defensive/04-secops-and-gove.title: SBOM and supply chain
en/security-defensive/04-secops-and-gove.summary: A new dependency CVE drops and the first question is "are we affected?" An SBOM — the per-build inventory of everything you ship — is what lets you answer in minutes instead of days. Provenance and SLSA add the missing half: trusting that inventory.

en/security-defensive/04-secops-and-gove.title: Security programs
en/security-defensive/04-secops-and-gove.summary: A security program is the standing machinery — owners, risk acceptance, and metrics — that decides which of a thousand findings gets fixed. As an engineer you plug into it by owning risk for your service and feeding it real numbers, not by chasing a green dashboard.

en/security-defensive/04-secops-and-gove.title: Compliance overview
en/security-defensive/04-secops-and-gove.summary: SOC 2, ISO 27001, and GDPR are control sets, not paperwork. SOC 2 audits whether you do what you say; ISO 27001 certifies a management system; GDPR is law with teeth. Learn what each actually demands of your code before sales promises a date.

en/security-foundations/00-start-here/01.title: Why every engineer needs a security foundation
en/security-foundations/00-start-here/01.summary: Security is a way of thinking, not a checklist. This lesson frames the whole cybersecurity cluster around Shostack's four questions, pins down threat vs vulnerability vs risk, and maps how foundations, red, blue, and cloud feed the appsec track you already know.

en/security-foundations/01-threat-modeli.title: What threat modeling is: the four questions
en/security-foundations/01-threat-modeli.summary: Threat modeling is four questions asked at design time, before code exists — what are we building, what can go wrong, what do we do about it, did we do a good enough job. It catches the flaws a pentest finds too late to cheaply fix.

en/security-foundations/01-threat-modeli.title: STRIDE: a vocabulary for what can go wrong
en/security-foundations/01-threat-modeli.summary: STRIDE is six prompts — Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information disclosure, Denial of service, Elevation of privilege — each the negation of one security property. It is a vocabulary for completeness, not a checklist, applied element by element.

en/security-foundations/01-threat-modeli.title: Data-flow diagrams and trust boundaries
en/security-foundations/01-threat-modeli.summary: A data-flow diagram turns a system into elements and the lines data crosses between them. Trust boundaries are those lines where ownership or privilege changes — and where threats concentrate. The DFD is what makes STRIDE-per-element systematic instead of guesswork.

en/security-foundations/01-threat-modeli.title: Attack trees and abuse cases: thinking like an attacker
en/security-foundations/01-threat-modeli.summary: Attack trees decompose one attacker goal into AND/OR sub-goals down to costed leaf attacks, and abuse cases write the evil user story beside the real one. Goal-centric where STRIDE is element-centric — reach for trees when you need to reason about the cheapest path.

en/security-foundations/01-threat-modeli.title: From threats to priorities: ranking risk and choosing mitigations
en/security-foundations/01-threat-modeli.summary: A threat list is a backlog, not a plan. This lesson turns enumerated threats into priorities with likelihood x impact, explains why DREAD lost the room, and walks the four mitigation responses — mitigate, eliminate, transfer, accept — down to residual risk.

en/security-foundations/02-cryptography-.title: Hashing vs encryption vs signing
en/security-foundations/02-cryptography-.summary: Hashing, encryption, and signing are three different primitives engineers constantly confuse. Each guarantees something distinct — and using the wrong one is how passwords leak, sessions get forged, and "it's encrypted" turns out to mean nothing.

en/security-foundations/02-cryptography-.title: Symmetric encryption and AEAD
en/security-foundations/02-cryptography-.summary: Raw block-cipher modes leak structure and say nothing about tampering. AEAD (AES-GCM, ChaCha20-Poly1305) gives you confidentiality and integrity in one primitive — but a single reused nonce can leak the keystream and forge messages.

en/security-foundations/02-cryptography-.title: Asymmetric crypto and key exchange
en/security-foundations/02-cryptography-.summary: Public-key crypto solves the key-distribution problem symmetric ciphers can't, but it's 1000x slower — so you use it only to agree a symmetric key. This lesson covers RSA vs ECC, Diffie-Hellman key exchange, and why ephemeral DH gives forward secrecy.

en/security-foundations/02-cryptography-.title: TLS and PKI
en/security-foundations/02-cryptography-.summary: TLS 1.3 builds an encrypted channel in one round trip and proves who you are talking to with a certificate chain anchored in a trusted CA. This is how the browser decides the green padlock is honest — and how it goes wrong.

en/security-foundations/02-cryptography-.title: Key management and crypto misuse
en/security-foundations/02-cryptography-.summary: Algorithms almost never break in production — key management does. Where keys live, how they rotate, and a handful of misuse patterns (hardcoded keys, ECB, roll-your-own crypto) cause far more breaches than weak ciphers.

en/security-foundations/03-authenticatio.title: From passwords to MFA
en/security-foundations/03-authenticatio.summary: Passwords fail at scale: people reuse them, dumps fuel credential stuffing, and storage mistakes turn one breach into millions of cracked accounts. MFA helps but is routinely phished; only phishing-resistant factors like passkeys actually hold.

en/security-foundations/03-authenticatio.title: Sessions vs tokens
en/security-foundations/03-authenticatio.summary: Server sessions are stateful and instantly revocable; bearer tokens are stateless and fast but live until they expire. The real tradeoff is revocation latency vs lookup cost — and where each one breaks in production.

en/security-foundations/03-authenticatio.title: Passkeys and WebAuthn
en/security-foundations/03-authenticatio.summary: Passkeys are origin-bound public-key credentials; the browser signs over the page's true origin so a phished or relayed login is rejected. But WebAuthn only secures the login event — session and recovery stay your problem.

en/security-foundations/03-authenticatio.title: SSO and federation
en/security-foundations/03-authenticatio.summary: SSO federates login to an IdP, but the SP still owns verification on the way in (signature, issuer, audience, expiry) and session teardown on the way out — and revocation across a federation is only ever eventually consistent.

en/security-foundations/04-network-secur.title: TLS in depth
en/security-foundations/04-network-secur.summary: A valid padlock only proves the channel is encrypted and the server authenticated right now. Whether that protection survives a stolen key, an active downgrade, or a plaintext first hop depends on forward secrecy, a minimum protocol version, and HSTS.

en/security-foundations/04-network-secur.title: mTLS and service identity
en/security-foundations/04-network-secur.summary: Ordinary TLS proves the server to the client. mTLS makes both peers present certificates, turning a cryptographic identity into the unit of authorization between services — and making short-lived certs and automated rotation the hard part.

en/security-foundations/04-network-secur.title: Segmentation and firewalls
en/security-foundations/04-network-secur.summary: One compromised web box should not reach your database, your secrets store, and your CI runner. Segmentation, firewalls, security groups, and microsegmentation are how you bound that blast radius — and where flat networks quietly fail.

en/security-foundations/04-network-secur.title: DNS security and zero-trust networking
en/security-foundations/04-network-secur.summary: DNS resolves trust before TLS ever proves it, which makes the lookup an attack surface most teams forget. This lesson covers cache poisoning, DNSSEC and DoH, and why the industry traded the network perimeter for per-request identity.

en/security-foundations/05-access-contro.title: Role-Based Access Control (RBAC)
en/security-foundations/05-access-contro.summary: RBAC grants permissions to roles and users to roles, so every authorization question is a join. Clean until the org needs exceptions, then roles multiply faster than people and you drown in near-duplicates. This is where roles stop scaling.

en/security-foundations/05-access-contro.title: ABAC and ReBAC
en/security-foundations/05-access-contro.summary: RBAC asks who you are; ABAC adds context; ReBAC asks how you are connected. Google's Zanzibar made relationship checks fast and consistent at billions of objects. This is when roles run out of road and what replaces them.

en/security-foundations/05-access-contro.title: Least privilege in practice
en/security-foundations/05-access-contro.summary: Least privilege is the principle everyone cites and almost nobody holds. The decay is privilege creep — grants accumulate, nothing is ever revoked. The cure is operational: deny by default, just-in-time elevation, and a revocation loop.

en/security-foundations/05-access-contro.title: Policy engines and authz at scale
en/security-foundations/05-access-contro.summary: Once authz logic is scattered across 40 services, every team reinvents it and nobody can answer "who can do what." A policy engine externalizes the decision — policy-as-code, evaluated as a sidecar — but it is a latency and consistency problem.

en/security-offensive/00-start-here/01-e.title: Ethics, scope, and the attacker mindset
en/security-offensive/00-start-here/01-e.summary: Before any technique, the rule is authorization. This track teaches the attacker mindset as a defensive tool — goals, attack surface, and the kill chain — with nothing aimed at systems you do not own or are not authorized to test.

en/security-offensive/01-recon-and-enume.title: OSINT and footprinting
en/security-offensive/01-recon-and-enume.summary: Before a single packet hits your target, an authorized attacker has already mapped your subdomains, your tech stack, your employees, and your leaked secrets — all from public data. This is footprinting, and it decides the whole engagement.

en/security-offensive/01-recon-and-enume.title: Attack surface mapping
en/security-offensive/01-recon-and-enume.summary: Your real attack surface is what is actually reachable, not your architecture diagram. Enumerate assets, subdomains, and shadow IT against authorized, in-scope targets to see what an attacker sees — the forgotten host is the one that gets owned.

en/security-offensive/01-recon-and-enume.title: Port and service scanning
en/security-offensive/01-recon-and-enume.summary: A port scan finds which services are listening; fingerprinting names their versions. Both are reconnaissance against authorized targets only — and every probe also leaves a line in the defender's log, which is what makes scanning a two-sided story.

en/security-offensive/01-recon-and-enume.title: Enumeration techniques
en/security-offensive/01-recon-and-enume.summary: Enumeration turns an unknown attack surface into a concrete target list — hidden endpoints, valid users, undocumented API objects. The same probing is exactly what rate limits and monitoring are built to slow down and surface.

en/security-offensive/02-web-exploitatio.title: Injection attacks
en/security-offensive/02-web-exploitatio.summary: Injection is one bug with many faces — SQL, OS command, NoSQL, LDAP — and all of them are the same mistake, attacker data crossing into an interpreter as code. See how an attacker reasons about it, and why parameterization is the only fix that closes the class.

en/security-offensive/02-web-exploitatio.title: XSS in practice
en/security-offensive/02-web-exploitatio.summary: XSS comes in three shapes — reflected, stored, and DOM-based — and all three end the same way: attacker JavaScript running in your origin. This is how each one works and why CSP plus context-correct encoding is the fix, not input filtering.

en/security-offensive/02-web-exploitatio.title: SSRF and IDOR
en/security-offensive/02-web-exploitatio.summary: SSRF and IDOR are the modern high-impact pair — one makes your server fetch an attacker-chosen URL, the other returns a record by id with no owner check. Both are the same root error: a trust boundary the server never enforced. See how each works and the reflex that kills both.

en/security-offensive/02-web-exploitatio.title: Auth bypass and session attacks
en/security-offensive/02-web-exploitatio.summary: Authentication proves who you are once; the session carries that proof on every later request. Attackers rarely guess the password — they steal, forge, or replay the proof. See how, and why each control is the structural fix.

en/security-offensive/02-web-exploitatio.title: Finding and proving bugs
en/security-offensive/02-web-exploitatio.summary: A vulnerability you can't prove to someone else doesn't exist yet — to the triager it's noise. This lesson is the craft of turning a hunch into a report that survives a stranger's machine — a reproducible PoC, an honest impact statement, and disclosure that stays inside scope.

en/security-offensive/03-network-and-inf.title: MITM and interception
en/security-offensive/03-network-and-inf.summary: Interception only works when the attacker sits on the traffic path. ARP spoofing and TLS stripping put them there; authenticated TLS plus integrity collapses that position into a useless, detected link.

en/security-offensive/03-network-and-inf.title: Privilege escalation
en/security-offensive/03-network-and-inf.summary: Privilege escalation turns a low-priv foothold into root or SYSTEM by abusing a misconfig the host already shipped — a SUID binary, a sudo gap, a writable service, a stale kernel. Learn the escalation path the attacker enumerates, so you close the rung first.

en/security-offensive/03-network-and-inf.title: Password attacks and cracking
en/security-offensive/03-network-and-inf.summary: Offline cracking is an economics problem: a fast unsalted hash turns a stolen dump into a free wordlist, while a slow salted hash makes the same dump worthless. See the guesses-per-second math behind why work factor and per-user salt decide who wins.

en/security-offensive/03-network-and-inf.title: Pivoting and lateral movement
en/security-offensive/03-network-and-inf.summary: One host gets popped; the breach happens when the attacker turns it into a stepping stone. Pivoting routes traffic through it, lateral movement reuses identity. Segmentation plus identity hygiene break both.

en/security-offensive/04-exploitation-an.title: From vulnerability to exploit
en/security-offensive/04-exploitation-an.summary: A memory-safety bug is not yet an exploit. The bridge is hijacking control flow — and ASLR, DEP, and stack canaries each remove one girder, so a modern exploit must defeat several mitigations at once, not one bug.

en/security-offensive/04-exploitation-an.title: Payloads and shells
en/security-offensive/04-exploitation-an.summary: A shell is the code that runs once an exploit lands. Reverse vs bind is a question of who dials whom — and that single choice is exactly what egress filtering and EDR are built to catch. Learn the mechanism so you can break the channel.

en/security-offensive/04-exploitation-an.title: Command and control
en/security-offensive/04-exploitation-an.summary: Once code runs on a target, the operator needs a channel back. C2 beaconing solves the firewall problem by calling out, not in — and that regular outbound rhythm is exactly the signal a defender hunts.

en/security-offensive/04-exploitation-an.title: Persistence and post-exploitation
en/security-offensive/04-exploitation-an.summary: Code execution is the start, not the win. Attackers spend most of their dwell time on persistence, lateral movement, and exfiltration — each a noisy step a defender can catch.

en/security-offensive/05-tooling-and-met.title: The pentest toolkit
en/security-offensive/05-tooling-and-met.summary: Pentest tools split into a few categories — proxy, scanner, fuzzer, recon — each built for a different bug class. Knowing what each is for, where it lies to you, and the one rule that gates all of it (authorization) is the toolkit.

en/security-offensive/05-tooling-and-met.title: Pentest methodology
en/security-offensive/05-tooling-and-met.summary: A pentest without a methodology is luck — you find what you happened to poke at. PTES and OWASP WSTG turn it into coverage you can prove, scope you can defend, and a report a defender can act on.

en/security-offensive/05-tooling-and-met.title: Writing findings
en/security-offensive/05-tooling-and-met.summary: A finding only earns its place in the report when an engineer can reproduce it, sees the real impact, and knows the fix. Repro + impact + severity + remediation is the unit of work — a bare severity label is noise.

en/security-offensive/05-tooling-and-met.title: The pentest report
en/security-offensive/05-tooling-and-met.summary: A pentest report has two readers — an exec deciding whether the risk is acceptable and an engineer applying the fix. A single document has to serve both, plus a defender who reads it as a roadmap. Structure it so each gets what they need on the first page they open.

en/security/00-start-here/01-overview.title: Start from zero: what web security actually is
en/security/00-start-here/01-overview.summary: Web security is designing so a hostile stranger can send anything and your system still holds. This is the from-zero map and the eight words the security track assumes you already know.

en/security/01-owasp-modern/01-overview.title: The OWASP Top 10 (2021): what changed and why it matters
en/security/01-owasp-modern/01-overview.summary: The 2021 list moved Broken Access Control to #1 (found in 94% of tested apps) and shifted the whole field from ''''filter bad input'''' to ''''design for least privilege and deny by default.'''' This is the map of how web apps actually break.

en/security/01-owasp-modern/project.title: OWASP Top 10: audit and harden a vulnerable service
en/security/01-owasp-modern/project.summary: Hands-on project — audit a deliberately vulnerable web service against the OWASP Top 10 (2021), exploit and then remediate the findings, and prove each fix with a before/after test.

en/security/01-owasp-modern/quiz-choice.title: OWASP Top 10: multiple-choice review
en/security/01-owasp-modern/quiz-choice.summary: Multiple-choice synthesis across the OWASP Top 10 (2021) — access control, crypto, injection, insecure design, SSRF, and misconfiguration as decisions you make in a real review.

en/security/01-owasp-modern/quiz-code.title: OWASP Top 10: code and config reading
en/security/01-owasp-modern/quiz-code.summary: Read real code, config, and log snippets — an access-control check, an SSRF fetch, a CORS config — name the OWASP category, and pick the fix a senior makes first.

en/security/01-owasp-modern/quiz-short.title: OWASP Top 10: free-recall review
en/security/01-owasp-modern/quiz-short.summary: Free-recall prompts across the OWASP Top 10 (2021). Answer each in your own words first, then reveal the model answer and compare.

en/security/02-oauth-oidc/01-what-is-oau.title: What OAuth is and why passwords are not the answer
en/security/02-oauth-oidc/01-what-is-oau.summary: OAuth delegates access without sharing passwords. Three parties, two tokens, one trust model — explained through the dog-walker metaphor.

en/security/02-oauth-oidc/02-auth-code-p.title: Authorization code flow with PKCE
en/security/02-oauth-oidc/02-auth-code-p.summary: How OAuth 2.1''''s mandatory PKCE prevents code interception, why exact-match redirect URIs block open-redirect exfiltration, and what state and nonce defend against.

en/security/02-oauth-oidc/03-id-token-va.title: ID token validation and JWKS cache management
en/security/02-oauth-oidc/03-id-token-va.summary: The eight mandatory checks every OIDC client must perform on id_tokens, why JWKS cache staleness causes auth outages, and the on-cache-miss refresh pattern.

en/security/02-oauth-oidc/04-refresh-tok.title: Refresh token rotation and scope-based least privilege
en/security/02-oauth-oidc/04-refresh-tok.summary: How OAuth 2.1 refresh token rotation detects stolen tokens via replay, why granular scopes limit breach radius, and the difference between introspection and local JWT validation.

en/security/02-oauth-oidc/05-sender-cons.title: Sender-constrained tokens: DPoP and mTLS
en/security/02-oauth-oidc/05-sender-cons.summary: Why bearer tokens fail under XSS or supply-chain attack, how DPoP binds a token to a client-held key, and when to use mTLS-bound tokens instead — with FAPI 2.0 requirements.

en/security/02-oauth-oidc/06-oauth-produ.title: OAuth in production: audience attacks, observability, and real failures
en/security/02-oauth-oidc/06-oauth-produ.summary: Audience confusion attacks, token storage by client type, the observability metrics that detect compromise, and the four real-world OAuth failures that cost millions.

en/security/02-oauth-oidc/project.title: OAuth/OIDC: build and audit a hardened login
en/security/02-oauth-oidc/project.summary: Hands-on project — build a hardened OIDC login plus a sender-constrained API, then audit it against the unit's complete-set checklist and prove each mandatory check with an adversarial test.

en/security/02-oauth-oidc/quiz-choice.title: OAuth/OIDC: multiple-choice review
en/security/02-oauth-oidc/quiz-choice.summary: Multiple-choice synthesis across the OAuth/OIDC unit — PKCE, exact redirect match, id_token checks, refresh rotation, sender-constrained tokens, and audience attacks.

en/security/02-oauth-oidc/quiz-code.title: OAuth/OIDC: code review
en/security/02-oauth-oidc/quiz-code.summary: Read real OAuth/OIDC code — PKCE exchange, id_token validation, refresh rotation, and DPoP binding — spot the mandatory check that is missing or inverted, and pick the fix.

en/security/02-oauth-oidc/quiz-short.title: OAuth/OIDC: free-recall review
en/security/02-oauth-oidc/quiz-short.summary: Free-recall prompts across the OAuth/OIDC unit. Answer each in your own words first, then reveal the model answer and compare.

en/security/03-jwt-pitfalls/01-overview.title: JWT security pitfalls: alg confusion, no revocation, and where tokens leak
en/security/03-jwt-pitfalls/01-overview.summary: A JWT is only as safe as how you verify it. The classic failures — accepting alg:none, RS256→HS256 confusion, no revocation, and tokens in localStorage — all come from trusting the token instead of pinning what the server expects.

en/security/03-jwt-pitfalls/project.title: JWT pitfalls: break and harden an auth flow
en/security/03-jwt-pitfalls/project.summary: Hands-on project — build a JWT auth flow, attack it with alg:none, algorithm confusion, and kid injection, then harden it and prove each exploit is closed.

en/security/03-jwt-pitfalls/quiz-choice.title: JWT pitfalls: multiple-choice review
en/security/03-jwt-pitfalls/quiz-choice.summary: Multiple-choice synthesis across the JWT-pitfalls unit — alg:none, RS256-to-HS256 confusion, claim validation, revocation, and token storage tradeoffs.

en/security/03-jwt-pitfalls/quiz-code.title: JWT pitfalls: code and token reading
en/security/03-jwt-pitfalls/quiz-code.summary: Read real JWT verification snippets and a forged token, spot the vulnerability, and pick the highest-leverage fix a security-minded senior makes first.

en/security/03-jwt-pitfalls/quiz-short.title: JWT pitfalls: free-recall review
en/security/03-jwt-pitfalls/quiz-short.summary: Free-recall prompts across the JWT-pitfalls unit. Answer each in your own words first, then reveal the model answer and compare.

en/security/04-csrf/01-overview.title: CSRF in the SameSite era: why the default helped but didn''''t kill it
en/security/04-csrf/01-overview.summary: The browser auto-attaches cookies to cross-site requests, so a malicious page can trigger authenticated state changes. SameSite=Lax (Chrome''''s 2020 default) shrank the surface — but GET state-changes, SameSite=None, and the top-level-navigation gap keep CSRF alive.

en/security/04-csrf/project.title: CSRF: build the exploit, then the defense
en/security/04-csrf/project.summary: Hands-on project — build a vulnerable cookie-session app, prove CSRF end-to-end with a real attacker page, then layer SameSite, a token defense, and an Origin check until every exploit fails.

en/security/04-csrf/quiz-choice.title: CSRF: multiple-choice review
en/security/04-csrf/quiz-choice.summary: Multiple-choice synthesis across the CSRF unit — ambient authority, SameSite gaps, GET side effects, token patterns, Origin checks, and why CORS is not CSRF protection.

en/security/04-csrf/quiz-code.title: CSRF: code and config reading
en/security/04-csrf/quiz-code.summary: Read real cookie configs and route handlers, predict the CSRF behaviour, and pick the highest-leverage fix a senior reviewer would make first.

en/security/04-csrf/quiz-short.title: CSRF: free-recall review
en/security/04-csrf/quiz-short.summary: Free-recall prompts across the CSRF unit. Answer each in your own words first, then reveal the model answer and compare.

en/security/05-password-hashing/01-overv.title: Password storage: why a slow, salted, memory-hard KDF is the only safe choice
en/security/05-password-hashing/01-overv.summary: A general-purpose fast hash like SHA-256 is the wrong tool for passwords — a GPU does ~22 billion of them per second, so a leaked DB is cracked in hours. The fix is a deliberately slow, per-user-salted, memory-hard KDF: Argon2id, scrypt, or bcrypt.

en/security/05-password-hashing/project.title: Password hashing: build a migration-safe auth store
en/security/05-password-hashing/project.summary: Hands-on project — build a password-storage layer on Argon2id with rehash-on-login migration, an external pepper, and timing-safe verify, then prove each property with tests and a benchmark.

en/security/05-password-hashing/quiz-cho.title: Password hashing: multiple-choice review
en/security/05-password-hashing/quiz-cho.summary: Multiple-choice synthesis across the password-hashing unit — fast-hash failure, salt vs pepper, Argon2id/bcrypt/scrypt parameters, the 72-byte trap, work-factor migration, and timing-safe compare.

en/security/05-password-hashing/quiz-cod.title: Password hashing: code review
en/security/05-password-hashing/quiz-cod.summary: Read real auth snippets — Argon2id parameters, a naive SHA-256 store, a timing-unsafe compare, and a missing rehash-on-login — and pick the fix a senior would make first.

en/security/05-password-hashing/quiz-sho.title: Password hashing: free-recall review
en/security/05-password-hashing/quiz-sho.summary: Free-recall prompts across the password-hashing unit. Answer each in your own words first, then reveal the model answer and compare.

en/security/06-secrets/01-overview.title: Secrets management: why a key in git is already a breach
en/security/06-secrets/01-overview.summary: A credential in source code is a leaked credential. Git history keeps it after you delete it, scanners find public keys in about a minute, and the only real fix is rotation, not removal. The maturity ladder runs from hardcoded keys to a managed, audited, short-lived secret.

en/security/06-secrets/project.title: Secrets management: climb the maturity ladder
en/security/06-secrets/project.summary: Hands-on project — take a service with a leaked hardcoded secret and climb the maturity ladder to a managed, scanned, short-lived setup, proving each rung with evidence.

en/security/06-secrets/quiz-choice.title: Secrets management: multiple-choice review
en/security/06-secrets/quiz-choice.summary: Multiple-choice synthesis across the secrets unit — leak remediation, the maturity ladder, dynamic short-lived credentials, envelope encryption, and least privilege under real incident pressure.

en/security/06-secrets/quiz-code.title: Secrets management: code and config reading
en/security/06-secrets/quiz-code.summary: Read real config and code snippets — a committed .env, a Vault dynamic-secret fetch, a KMS envelope-encryption helper, and a leaky log line — predict the failure and pick the highest-leverage fix.

en/security/06-secrets/quiz-short.title: Secrets management: free-recall review
en/security/06-secrets/quiz-short.summary: Free-recall prompts across the secrets unit — answer each in your own words first, then reveal the model answer and compare leak remediation, the ladder, dynamic creds, and envelope encryption.

en/security/07-supply-chain/01-overview.title: Supply-chain security: your real attack surface is your dependencies
en/security/07-supply-chain/01-overview.summary: You ship far more third-party code than your own, so the modern attack surface is the install step. Lockfiles, pinned versions, provenance, and registry precedence are the defenses against xz-style backdoors and dependency confusion.

en/security/07-supply-chain/project.summary: Hands-on project — harden a real service's supply chain end to end: enforce the lockfile, kill confusion, generate an SBOM, and sign with verifiable provenance, proving each control catches a planted attack.

en/security/08-putting-it-together/01-ov.summary: No single security control is sufficient. Each layer — TLS, auth, authz, input handling, secrets, dependencies — can be individually correct and the system still falls, because the breach lives in the seam where two correct controls meet.

en/security/08-putting-it-together/quiz-.summary: Free-recall prompts spanning the whole security track. Answer each in your own words first, then reveal the model answer and compare against the full threat model.

en/sql-postgres/00-start-here/01-why-sql.title: Why SQL still runs everything
en/sql-postgres/00-start-here/01-why-sql.summary: SQL is declarative — you describe the result set you want, and the engine decides how to fetch it. That one separation is why it survived 50 years and every NoSQL wave.

en/sql-postgres/00-start-here/02-how-pos.title: How Postgres executes a query
en/sql-postgres/00-start-here/02-how-pos.summary: A query passes through five stages — parse, analyze, rewrite, plan, execute — before a single row comes back. Knowing the pipeline tells you where time goes and which problems live at which stage.

en/sql-postgres/01-sql-foundations/01-se.title: The SELECT mental model: logical processing order
en/sql-postgres/01-sql-foundations/01-se.summary: You write SELECT … FROM … WHERE …, but Postgres evaluates FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → ORDER BY. That gap explains why an alias works in ORDER BY but not WHERE.

en/sql-postgres/01-sql-foundations/02-fi.title: Filtering rows: WHERE, precedence, and sargability
en/sql-postgres/01-sql-foundations/02-fi.summary: WHERE decides which rows survive — and, quietly, whether the planner can use an index. Wrapping a column in a function or a leading wildcard kills the index and turns a 2 ms lookup into a full scan.

en/sql-postgres/01-sql-foundations/03-nu.title: NULL and three-valued logic
en/sql-postgres/01-sql-foundations/03-nu.summary: NULL means 'unknown', not 'empty'. That turns SQL's logic three-valued (TRUE/FALSE/UNKNOWN) and produces the silent NOT IN bug that returns zero rows the day one NULL appears.

en/sql-postgres/01-sql-foundations/04-di.title: DISTINCT, DISTINCT ON, and set operations
en/sql-postgres/01-sql-foundations/04-di.summary: DISTINCT and UNION dedup by sorting or hashing the whole result — real cost. UNION ALL skips it. And DISTINCT ON is Postgres's idiomatic 'latest row per group'.

en/sql-postgres/01-sql-foundations/05-so.title: Sorting and limiting: ORDER BY, LIMIT, and keyset pagination
en/sql-postgres/01-sql-foundations/05-so.summary: ORDER BY + LIMIT can be answered by an index with no sort. But OFFSET 100000 still reads 100000 rows first — the deep-pagination cliff. Keyset pagination fixes it.

en/sql-postgres/02-joins-deep/01-join-as.title: A join is a filtered product
en/sql-postgres/02-joins-deep/01-join-as.summary: Every join starts as the Cartesian product of two tables — every row of A paired with every row of B — and the ON predicate is just a filter on that product. Internalize this and join behavior stops being magic.

en/sql-postgres/02-joins-deep/02-inner-v.title: Inner vs outer joins
en/sql-postgres/02-joins-deep/02-inner-v.summary: INNER keeps only matched pairs; LEFT/RIGHT/FULL OUTER also keep unmatched rows, NULL-extended. The classic prod bug: a predicate on the outer table in WHERE silently demotes a LEFT JOIN to an INNER JOIN.

en/sql-postgres/02-joins-deep/03-semi-an.title: Semi and anti joins
en/sql-postgres/02-joins-deep/03-semi-an.summary: EXISTS/IN return left rows that have a match without fanning out (a semi-join); NOT EXISTS/NOT IN return left rows with no match (an anti-join). NOT IN breaks silently when the subquery yields a NULL — prefer NOT EXISTS.

en/sql-postgres/02-joins-deep/04-self-an.title: Self and cross joins
en/sql-postgres/02-joins-deep/04-self-an.summary: A self-join joins a table to itself to walk hierarchies or compare rows pairwise; dedup pairs with a.id < b.id. An explicit CROSS JOIN builds deliberate products — calendar grids, gap-fills, all-combinations — distinct from an accidental comma join.

en/sql-postgres/02-joins-deep/05-lateral.title: LATERAL joins
en/sql-postgres/02-joins-deep/05-lateral.summary: LATERAL lets a subquery in FROM reference earlier FROM items, so it runs once per outer row. It's the clean way to do top-N-per-group and to unnest set-returning functions — usually one pass, beating correlated scalar subqueries.

en/sql-postgres/02-joins-deep/06-join-tr.title: Join traps and row explosions
en/sql-postgres/02-joins-deep/06-join-tr.summary: Joining two one-to-many children to a parent multiplies rows and silently doubles your SUM and COUNT — the fan-out bug. The fix is to aggregate each child separately first. Plus missing conditions, duplicate keys, and join order.

en/sql-postgres/03-aggregation/01-group-.title: The GROUP BY model: rows into buckets
en/sql-postgres/03-aggregation/01-group-.summary: GROUP BY collapses many rows into one row per distinct key. The iron rule follows from that collapse: every SELECT expression must be in GROUP BY or wrapped in an aggregate.

en/sql-postgres/03-aggregation/02-having.title: HAVING vs WHERE: filter before or after grouping
en/sql-postgres/03-aggregation/02-having.summary: WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters whole groups after aggregation. You can't aggregate in WHERE, and pushing row filters into WHERE is a real performance lever.

en/sql-postgres/03-aggregation/03-aggreg.title: Aggregate functions: COUNT, SUM, FILTER, and the traps
en/sql-postgres/03-aggregation/03-aggreg.summary: COUNT(*) counts rows, COUNT(col) skips NULLs, COUNT(DISTINCT) dedupes. FILTER beats CASE for conditional aggregates, and integer AVG plus SUM overflow are the silent bugs.

en/sql-postgres/03-aggregation/04-groupi.title: GROUPING SETS, ROLLUP, CUBE: many groupings, one pass
en/sql-postgres/03-aggregation/04-groupi.summary: GROUPING SETS computes several groupings in one query; ROLLUP adds hierarchical subtotals, CUBE all combinations. GROUPING() tells a subtotal NULL from a real one.

en/sql-postgres/03-aggregation/05-condit.title: Conditional aggregation: pivot long rows into wide columns
en/sql-postgres/03-aggregation/05-condit.summary: SUM(CASE WHEN …) and COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE …) turn one row-per-category into one column-per-category — pivoting reports without crosstab, combinable with GROUP BY.

en/sql-postgres/04-window-functions/01-w.title: Windows vs GROUP BY
