en/sql-postgres/04-window-functions/01-w.summary: A window function computes an aggregate-like value per row without collapsing the result set. GROUP BY collapses; OVER() keeps every row. Reach for a window when you need detail rows and an aggregate in the same query.

en/sql-postgres/04-window-functions/02-p.title: PARTITION BY and ORDER BY
en/sql-postgres/04-window-functions/02-p.summary: PARTITION BY splits rows into independent windows; ORDER BY inside OVER orders rows within each one. The twist: adding ORDER BY silently changes the default frame from the whole partition to a running range.

en/sql-postgres/04-window-functions/03-w.title: Window frames: ROWS vs RANGE vs GROUPS
en/sql-postgres/04-window-functions/03-w.summary: The frame is the slice of rows a window function actually aggregates. The default is RANGE UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW — which includes all peer rows tied on the ORDER BY value, quietly overcounting running totals on ties. ROWS does not.

en/sql-postgres/04-window-functions/04-r.title: Ranking functions and top-N-per-group
en/sql-postgres/04-window-functions/04-r.summary: ROW_NUMBER, RANK, and DENSE_RANK differ only in how they treat ties. ROW_NUMBER is the workhorse for top-N-per-group and dedup: rank inside a subquery, then filter rn <= N — the pattern that replaces a dozen correlated subqueries.

en/sql-postgres/04-window-functions/05-r.title: Running totals, moving averages, LAG/LEAD
en/sql-postgres/04-window-functions/05-r.summary: Cumulative SUM, moving averages with ROWS BETWEEN n PRECEDING, and LAG/LEAD for period-over-period deltas — plus the classic LAST_VALUE trap, where the default frame ends at CURRENT ROW so LAST_VALUE returns the current row, not the partition's last.

en/sql-postgres/04-window-functions/06-w.title: Real-world window patterns: gaps, islands, sessions
en/sql-postgres/04-window-functions/06-w.summary: Gaps-and-islands detects consecutive runs via the row_number difference trick; sessionization flags a new session when LAG on the timestamp shows a gap over threshold, then SUMs the flags. Each distinct window ORDER BY adds a Sort/WindowAgg node — order windows to share sorts.

en/sql-postgres/05-cte-and-recursion/01-.title: CTE basics: naming a subquery
en/sql-postgres/05-cte-and-recursion/01-.summary: A WITH clause names a subquery so a tangled, nested query becomes a top-down pipeline of named steps — and each step is referenceable by every step that follows it.

en/sql-postgres/05-cte-and-recursion/02-.title: CTE vs subquery vs view
en/sql-postgres/05-cte-and-recursion/02-.summary: A CTE, an inline subquery, and a view express the same logic in different places with different lifetimes — and a CTE once carried a quiet optimization caveat that a subquery never did.

en/sql-postgres/05-cte-and-recursion/03-.title: CTE materialization: the fence that moved
en/sql-postgres/05-cte-and-recursion/03-.summary: Postgres 12 turned the old unconditional CTE optimization fence into smart inlining — and gave you MATERIALIZED / NOT MATERIALIZED to force either when the planner guesses wrong.

en/sql-postgres/05-cte-and-recursion/04-.title: Recursive CTEs: anchor, iterate, stop
en/sql-postgres/05-cte-and-recursion/04-.summary: WITH RECURSIVE is an anchor term UNION a recursive term that re-reads the CTE — Postgres runs it as an iterative working-table loop until the recursive term yields nothing, so termination and cycle protection are on you.

en/sql-postgres/05-cte-and-recursion/05-.title: Walking graphs in SQL
en/sql-postgres/05-cte-and-recursion/05-.summary: Recursive CTEs traverse trees, DAGs, and graphs — org charts, bills of materials, reachability — by accumulating a path array; but path explosion and per-hop joins mean SQL is the wrong tool past a few million edges.

en/sql-postgres/06-types-and-modeling/01.title: Core types: money, text, time, identity
en/sql-postgres/06-types-and-modeling/01.summary: Postgres has a precise type system. Pick numeric (not float) for money, timestamptz (never timestamp) for time, and the right uuid version — the defaults bite you in production.

en/sql-postgres/06-types-and-modeling/02.title: Constraints: integrity the engine enforces
en/sql-postgres/06-types-and-modeling/02.summary: NOT NULL, CHECK, UNIQUE, foreign keys with ON DELETE actions, DEFERRABLE checks, and EXCLUDE constraints push data integrity into the engine — where the app can't forget it.

en/sql-postgres/06-types-and-modeling/03.title: JSONB, deeply: operators, GIN, and the boundary
en/sql-postgres/06-types-and-modeling/03.summary: jsonb is binary, dedups keys, and is indexable; json is text. Master the operators and GIN containment, and learn the real boundary — typed columns for hot filters, jsonb for the sparse tail.

en/sql-postgres/06-types-and-modeling/04.title: Arrays and enums: when each beats a string
en/sql-postgres/06-types-and-modeling/04.summary: Native arrays (ANY, unnest, @> with GIN) and enums (ordered, compact) are powerful at the right boundary — but the enum ALTER pain and array's join-hostility decide when a lookup table wins.

en/sql-postgres/06-types-and-modeling/05.title: Generated and identity columns
en/sql-postgres/06-types-and-modeling/05.summary: GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY is the standard, cleaner replacement for serial; STORED generated columns compute from other columns; and sequences are non-transactional — gaps are normal, never rely on gapless ids.

en/sql-postgres/06-types-and-modeling/06.title: Schema design: normalize, then denormalize on purpose
en/sql-postgres/06-types-and-modeling/06.summary: Normalize so a fact lives in one place, model with real Postgres types instead of stringly-typed columns, pick surrogate vs natural keys deliberately, and denormalize only for read performance — kept consistent by the engine.

en/sql-postgres/07-transactions-concurre.title: ACID in practice
en/sql-postgres/07-transactions-concurre.summary: A transaction is a fence: BEGIN…COMMIT makes a group of writes all-or-nothing, and SAVEPOINT carves rollback points inside it. But ACID is not concurrency control — by default it does not serialize.

en/sql-postgres/07-transactions-concurre.title: Isolation levels in Postgres
en/sql-postgres/07-transactions-concurre.summary: READ COMMITTED, REPEATABLE READ, and SERIALIZABLE are escalating promises about which anomalies concurrent transactions can see. Only SERIALIZABLE stops write skew — and it makes you write retry logic.

en/sql-postgres/07-transactions-concurre.title: SELECT FOR UPDATE and the job queue
en/sql-postgres/07-transactions-concurre.summary: Pessimistic row locks fix the lost-update race: FOR UPDATE locks rows you read so the next write is safe. FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED turns one table into a contention-free concurrent job queue.

en/sql-postgres/07-transactions-concurre.title: Advisory locks
en/sql-postgres/07-transactions-concurre.summary: Advisory locks are application-defined mutexes keyed by an integer, not tied to any row. They are perfect for leader election and cron dedup — and session-level ones silently leak through a transaction pooler.

en/sql-postgres/07-transactions-concurre.title: Deadlocks
en/sql-postgres/07-transactions-concurre.summary: A deadlock is a lock cycle: two transactions each hold a row the other needs. Postgres detects the cycle, kills a victim with error 40P01, and you retry — but consistent lock ordering prevents it entirely.

en/sql-postgres/08-internals-and-tuning/.title: Reading EXPLAIN ANALYZE
en/sql-postgres/08-internals-and-tuning/.summary: EXPLAIN ANALYZE prints a plan tree annotated with estimate vs actual. The gap between estimated rows and actual rows is the signal that tells you the planner was lied to.

en/sql-postgres/08-internals-and-tuning/.title: The cost-based planner
en/sql-postgres/08-internals-and-tuning/.summary: The planner prices every candidate scan and join by an estimated cost and picks the cheapest. Postgres ships no query hints on purpose — you tune the inputs, not the output.

en/sql-postgres/08-internals-and-tuning/.title: Statistics and the misestimate
en/sql-postgres/08-internals-and-tuning/.summary: The planner estimates rows from pg_statistic — n_distinct, MCV lists, histograms. Correlated columns break the independence assumption; CREATE STATISTICS is the fix before the misestimate cascades into a bad join.

en/sql-postgres/08-internals-and-tuning/.title: VACUUM and table bloat
en/sql-postgres/08-internals-and-tuning/.summary: MVCC leaves dead tuples behind every UPDATE and DELETE; autovacuum reclaims them. When it falls behind, bloat inflates every scan — and VACUUM FULL's exclusive lock is the wrong cure in production.

en/sql-postgres/08-internals-and-tuning/.title: WAL and durability
en/sql-postgres/08-internals-and-tuning/.summary: The write-ahead log records every change before the data page is touched. fsync and synchronous_commit are the durability-vs-throughput knob; checkpoints bound recovery time; the same WAL powers replication and PITR.

en/sql-postgres/08-internals-and-tuning/.title: The tuning workflow
en/sql-postgres/08-internals-and-tuning/.summary: The systematic loop: find the slow query with pg_stat_statements, reproduce with EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS), diagnose the real cause, apply the smallest fix, verify, repeat. Measure, don't guess.

en/sql-postgres/09-putting-it-together/0.title: Capstone: an analytics query system end to end
en/sql-postgres/09-putting-it-together/0.summary: Design and tune a per-tenant analytics API: timestamptz + jsonb schema, FILTER metrics, windowed top-N, keyset pages, fan-out-free joins, a SKIP LOCKED rollup worker, and an EXPLAIN-driven index fix — every unit of the track in one query system.

en/system-design-cases/01-foundational/0.title: Design a distributed key-value store
en/system-design-cases/01-foundational/0.summary: A Dynamo-style key-value store: a hash ring for partitioning, sloppy quorums (R+W>N) for tunable consistency, vector clocks vs last-write-wins for conflicts, and gossip for membership. Availability bought with eventual consistency.

en/system-design-cases/01-foundational/0.title: Design a URL shortener
en/system-design-cases/01-foundational/0.summary: Design TinyURL: a read-heavy 100:1 system where the whole game is the redirect path. Compare counter+base62, hashing, and a key-generation service for short codes; cache aggressively; serve a 301/302 in single-digit milliseconds.

en/system-design-cases/01-foundational/0.title: Design a web crawler
en/system-design-cases/01-foundational/0.summary: Design a distributed web crawler: a polite URL frontier, robots.txt and per-host rate limits, dedup with bloom filters plus content hashing, DNS at scale, freshness-driven recrawl, and the traps that make a naive crawler loop forever.

en/system-design-cases/01-foundational/0.title: Design a distributed message queue
en/system-design-cases/01-foundational/0.summary: Design a Kafka-like log: topics split into partitions for parallelism, replicated via an ISR for durability, consumer offsets for replay, and the delivery-semantics trade — at-most-once, at-least-once, exactly-once — that every async system must pick.

en/system-design-cases/01-foundational/p.title: Foundational cases: write a full design doc
en/system-design-cases/01-foundational/p.summary: Hands-on project: pick one of the four foundational cases and produce a complete design document — requirements, back-of-envelope estimate, high-level architecture diagram, two deep-dive components, and a bottlenecks-and-tradeoffs section a senior engineer would sign off.

en/system-design-cases/01-foundational/q.title: Foundational cases: multiple-choice review
en/system-design-cases/01-foundational/q.summary: Multiple-choice synthesis across the foundational case studies: the KV store's quorum, the shortener's read:write ratio and redirect status, the crawler's frontier and dedup, and the message queue's ordering and delivery semantics.

en/system-design-cases/01-foundational/q.title: Foundational cases: numbers and config reading
en/system-design-cases/01-foundational/q.summary: Read real capacity math and config from the four cases, then do the arithmetic: a quorum overlap check, a shortener QPS/keyspace estimate, a crawler bloom-filter sizing, and a Kafka partition-count calculation.

en/system-design-cases/01-foundational/q.title: Foundational cases: free-recall review
en/system-design-cases/01-foundational/q.summary: Free-recall prompts across the foundational case studies. Reconstruct each design from memory — the KV store's three blocks, the shortener's read path, the crawler's frontier and dedup, the queue's log — before revealing the model answer.

en/system-design-cases/02-social-feed/01.title: Design a notification system
en/system-design-cases/02-social-feed/01.summary: Design push, SMS, and email notifications: fan-out from one event to millions of devices, provider integration (APNs/FCM), per-channel rate limiting, dedup, user preferences, retries with a dead-letter queue, and delivery tracking — the parts forgotten until the dup-push storm.

en/system-design-cases/02-social-feed/02.title: Design a news feed
en/system-design-cases/02-social-feed/02.summary: Design a news feed: fan-out-on-write vs fan-out-on-read, the celebrity problem and the hybrid that fixes it, ranking, the feed cache, cursor pagination, and how timelines are actually stored — the canonical read-heavy social system.

en/system-design-cases/02-social-feed/03.title: Design a chat system
en/system-design-cases/02-social-feed/03.summary: Design WhatsApp/Messenger: persistent WebSocket connections vs long-poll, a connection registry for routing, message delivery with per-conversation ordering and the three delivery ticks (sent/delivered/read), presence at scale, offline queues, group fan-out, and message storage.

en/system-design-cases/02-social-feed/04.title: Design search autocomplete
en/system-design-cases/02-social-feed/04.summary: Design typeahead with a sub-100ms budget: a trie of prefixes, precomputed top-k completions per node, an offline aggregation pipeline that ranks queries by frequency, edge caching, and why suggestions are served from precomputed structures, never queried live per keystroke.

en/system-design-cases/02-social-feed/pr.title: Social-feed cases: design and defend a feed-backed app
en/system-design-cases/02-social-feed/pr.summary: Hands-on project: produce a design doc for a social app with a news feed, notifications, and presence — choosing fan-out strategies, the celebrity hybrid, delivery guarantees, and ordering — then justify each threshold with a number and validate the riskiest with a prototype.

en/system-design-cases/02-social-feed/qu.title: Social-feed cases: multiple-choice review
en/system-design-cases/02-social-feed/qu.summary: Multiple-choice synthesis across the social-feed cases: notification fan-out and the retry storm, the feed's fan-out tradeoff and the celebrity hybrid, chat's server-push and per-conversation ordering, and autocomplete's precompute-offline rule.

en/system-design-cases/02-social-feed/qu.title: Social-feed cases: reading config and code
en/system-design-cases/02-social-feed/qu.summary: Read real config and code from the four cases, then pick the senior fix: a retry loop missing dedup, an offset-paginated feed, a chat handler that acks before persisting, and an autocomplete that ranks on the read path.

en/system-design-cases/02-social-feed/qu.title: Social-feed cases: free-recall review
en/system-design-cases/02-social-feed/qu.summary: Free-recall prompts across the social-feed cases. Reconstruct each design from memory — notification pipeline, feed fan-out hybrid, chat push/ordering, autocomplete precompute — before revealing the model answer.

en/system-design-cases/03-media-storage/.title: Design YouTube
en/system-design-cases/03-media-storage/.summary: Design YouTube: a write path that ingests and transcodes one upload into many renditions, and a read path that serves billions of views from a CDN. The bytes never touch the app servers, the metadata DB never holds a video, and view counts are eventually consistent on purpose.

en/system-design-cases/03-media-storage/.title: Design Google Drive / Dropbox
en/system-design-cases/03-media-storage/.summary: Design a file-sync service: split files into content-hashed chunks for dedup and delta sync, separate the metadata DB from the blob store, sync changes to every device with versioning and conflict resolution, and push notifications so clients pull only what changed.

en/system-design-cases/03-media-storage/.title: Design an object store (S3-like)
en/system-design-cases/03-media-storage/.summary: Design S3: a flat key→bytes namespace where the metadata service maps keys to data locations and the data plane stores bytes durably. Erasure coding buys eleven nines of durability at ~1.5× overhead instead of 3× replication, and multipart upload makes huge objects reliable.

en/system-design-cases/03-media-storage/.title: Design Gmail-scale email
en/system-design-cases/03-media-storage/.summary: Design distributed email: SMTP ingest with spam filtering, mailboxes sharded per user, attachments deduplicated in object storage, a per-user inverted index for search, labels as a many-to-many overlay (not folders), and IMAP-style incremental sync via a per-mailbox change log.

en/system-design-cases/03-media-storage/.title: Media & storage: build a chunked, deduplicated upload-and-sync service
en/system-design-cases/03-media-storage/.summary: Hands-on project: build a small file service that uploads bytes direct to object storage, splits files into content-addressed chunks for delta sync and dedup, stores metadata separately, and resolves conflicts via a version chain — the spine of every design in this unit.

en/system-design-cases/03-media-storage/.title: Media & storage: multiple-choice review
en/system-design-cases/03-media-storage/.summary: Multiple-choice synthesis across the media-storage cases: the control-path/data-path split, transcoding ladders and adaptive bitrate, content-addressed chunking and delta sync, erasure coding for durability, and per-user partitioning for email.

en/system-design-cases/03-media-storage/.title: Media & storage: code and config reading
en/system-design-cases/03-media-storage/.summary: Read real upload handlers, storage configs, sync logic, and counters, then pick the senior fix: a direct-to-object-store upload, an erasure-coding overhead calc, a delta-sync chunk comparison, and an eventually-consistent view counter.

en/system-design-cases/03-media-storage/.title: Media & storage: free-recall review
en/system-design-cases/03-media-storage/.summary: Free-recall prompts across the media-storage cases. Reconstruct each design in your own words first — the bytes/metadata split, the transcoding pipeline, chunking and conflict resolution, durability via erasure coding, and email at scale — then reveal and compare.

en/system-design-cases/04-location-realt.title: Design a proximity service
en/system-design-cases/04-location-realt.summary: Design a find-nearby service (Yelp-style): index the world with geohash, quadtree, or S2/H3, query by cell instead of scanning, handle the cell-boundary problem, and cache the read-heavy answers per cell while ranking the survivors.

en/system-design-cases/04-location-realt.title: Design nearby friends
en/system-design-cases/04-location-realt.summary: Design real-time nearby-friends: ingest a flood of location pings (write-heavy), route updates through region-keyed pub/sub to subscribers over WebSockets, fan out only to people who care, and make privacy and TTL first-class so stale or unwanted locations expire.

en/system-design-cases/04-location-realt.title: Design Google Maps
en/system-design-cases/04-location-realt.summary: Design Maps: serve map tiles from a CDN, route over a road graph with Dijkstra/A* and contraction hierarchies, compute ETA from live traffic ingestion, and geocode addresses — anchored on partitioning a continent-sized road graph so routing stays fast.

en/system-design-cases/04-location-realt.title: Design a realtime leaderboard
en/system-design-cases/04-location-realt.summary: Design a realtime leaderboard: back it with a Redis sorted set (ZSET) for O(log n) score updates and top-k reads, answer 'my rank among millions' via ZRANK, break ties deterministically, and shard by score range when one node can't hold the whole board.

en/system-design-cases/04-location-realt.title: Location & realtime: build a live proximity + leaderboard service
en/system-design-cases/04-location-realt.summary: Hands-on project: build a working find-nearby service over a spatial index (querying neighbor cells), add a realtime push channel for moving entities by region, and back a leaderboard with a sorted set — then prove rank and proximity correctness with a small test harness.

en/system-design-cases/04-location-realt.title: Location & realtime: multiple-choice review
en/system-design-cases/04-location-realt.summary: Multiple-choice synthesis across the location-and-realtime cases: spatial indexing and the cell-boundary trap, write-heavy location fan-out, contraction hierarchies for routing, and the sorted set behind a leaderboard's rank query.

en/system-design-cases/04-location-realt.title: Location & realtime: reading the code and config
en/system-design-cases/04-location-realt.summary: Read real geo-query code, a pub/sub routing config, a routing-engine setup, and Redis sorted-set commands, then do the reasoning: spot the single-cell bug, the broadcast blow-up, the re-contraction trap, and the O(n) rank query.

en/system-design-cases/04-location-realt.title: Location & realtime: free-recall review
en/system-design-cases/04-location-realt.summary: Free-recall prompts across the location-and-realtime cases. Answer each from memory first — the index choice, the boundary fix, the fan-out layer, the routing preprocessing, the rank structure — then reveal the model answer and compare.

en/system-design-cases/05-data-money/01-.title: Design a metrics & alerting system
en/system-design-cases/05-data-money/01-.summary: Design a metrics and alerting platform: time-series ingest at scale, push vs pull collection, downsampling and retention tiers, the cardinality explosion that kills the database, alert-rule evaluation, and dashboards that stay cheap at read time.

en/system-design-cases/05-data-money/02-.title: Design ad-click aggregation
en/system-design-cases/05-data-money/02-.summary: Design a system that counts ad clicks for billing: stream processing with Kafka and Flink, exactly-once via idempotency, windowed aggregation, late events and watermarks, deduplication, and a batch reconciliation layer that corrects the fast path.

en/system-design-cases/05-data-money/03-.title: Design a payment system
en/system-design-cases/05-data-money/03-.summary: Design a payment system: idempotency keys against the double-charge problem, a double-entry ledger as the source of truth, reconciliation against the PSP, saga orchestration for the distributed transaction, and an immutable audit trail.

en/system-design-cases/05-data-money/04-.title: Design a digital wallet
en/system-design-cases/05-data-money/04-.summary: Design a digital wallet: balance correctness under concurrency, transfers as ACID vs distributed transactions, idempotency, the lost-update problem and how to avoid it, sharded balances, an event-sourced ledger, and the consistency the money demands.

en/system-design-cases/05-data-money/05-.title: Design a stock exchange
en/system-design-cases/05-data-money/05-.summary: Design a matching engine: the order book, price-time priority matching, a single sequencer for total order, low-latency in-memory design, durability via an event log, deterministic replay, and market-data fan-out to participants.

en/system-design-cases/05-data-money/06-.title: Design a hotel reservation system
en/system-design-cases/05-data-money/06-.summary: Design hotel booking: the double-booking problem, inventory as a counter per room-type per night, reservation holds with expiry, concurrency control, deliberate overbooking, availability search, and payment integration on the booking path.

en/system-design-cases/05-data-money/pro.title: Data & money: build a correct money mover
en/system-design-cases/05-data-money/pro.summary: Hands-on project: build a small wallet/ledger service that survives retries and concurrency — a double-entry ledger, client idempotency keys, an atomic transfer that defeats the lost update, and a reconciliation pass — proven with adversarial tests.

en/system-design-cases/05-data-money/qui.title: Data & money: multiple-choice review
en/system-design-cases/05-data-money/qui.summary: Multiple-choice synthesis across the data-and-money cases: cardinality, exactly-once and watermarks, idempotency and the double-entry ledger, the lost update, exchange determinism, and the double-booking race.

en/system-design-cases/05-data-money/qui.title: Data & money: code and config reading
en/system-design-cases/05-data-money/qui.summary: Read real code and config from the data-and-money cases, then pick the senior fix: a metric label, an idempotent charge, a lost-update wallet debit, and an atomic multi-night reservation.

en/system-design-cases/05-data-money/qui.title: Data & money: free-recall review
en/system-design-cases/05-data-money/qui.summary: Free-recall prompts across the data-and-money cases. Reconstruct each design from memory — cardinality, exactly-once and reconciliation, idempotency and the ledger, the lost update, exchange determinism, double-booking — then reveal and compare.

en/system-design/00-start-here/01-what-i.title: What system design is
en/system-design/00-start-here/01-what-i.summary: System design is not trivia about famous architectures — it is the discipline of reasoning from requirements to bottlenecks to tradeoffs under scale and failure. There is rarely one right answer, only defensible ones. This is what coding stops teaching you.

en/system-design/00-start-here/02-the-in.title: The design frame
en/system-design/00-start-here/02-the-in.summary: A repeatable thinking frame you carry into every design problem: clarify requirements, estimate scale, sketch a high-level design, deep-dive the hard parts, find the bottleneck, and state every tradeoff out loud. It is scaffolding for reasoning under pressure, not a script.

en/system-design/01-scalability/01-laten.title: Latency vs throughput
en/system-design/01-scalability/01-laten.summary: Latency is time per request; throughput is requests per second. They are not opposites — Little's Law binds them through concurrency, and queueing theory explains why latency explodes long before throughput maxes out. Confuse them and you optimize the wrong number.

en/system-design/01-scalability/02-verti.title: Vertical vs horizontal scaling
en/system-design/01-scalability/02-verti.summary: Scaling up means a bigger machine; scaling out means more machines. Up is simple but hits a hardware ceiling and stays a SPOF; out is elastic and fault-tolerant but forces statelessness and pays a coordination tax the Universal Scalability Law makes concrete.

en/system-design/01-scalability/03-back-.title: Back-of-the-envelope estimation
en/system-design/01-scalability/03-back-.summary: Before you choose a design, estimate it: QPS, storage over 5 years, bandwidth, cache size. A two-minute calculation rounded to one significant figure rejects the wrong architecture cheaply — and tells you which resource will break first.

en/system-design/01-scalability/04-numbe.title: Numbers every engineer should know
en/system-design/01-scalability/04-numbe.summary: The latency hierarchy — L1 ~1ns, RAM ~100ns, SSD ~16µs, datacenter RTT ~0.5ms, disk seek ~10ms, cross-region ~150ms — spans eight orders of magnitude. Memorize the ratios and you can reject a design in your head before building it.

en/system-design/01-scalability/project.title: Scalability: a capacity plan from scratch
en/system-design/01-scalability/project.summary: Hands-on project: take a product brief, produce a full back-of-the-envelope capacity plan (QPS, storage, bandwidth, memory), then validate the Little's Law and queueing predictions with a tiny load test.

en/system-design/01-scalability/quiz-cho.title: Scalability: multiple-choice review
en/system-design/01-scalability/quiz-cho.summary: Multiple-choice synthesis across the scalability unit: Little's Law and the queueing curve, vertical vs horizontal tradeoffs and the USL, back-of-envelope arithmetic, and the latency numbers used to reject designs.

en/system-design/01-scalability/quiz-cod.title: Scalability: numbers and config reading
en/system-design/01-scalability/quiz-cod.summary: Read real capacity math, config, and code, then do the arithmetic: a Little's Law ceiling, a queueing budget, an estimation helper, and a latency check that rejects a design.

en/system-design/01-scalability/quiz-sho.title: Scalability: free-recall review
en/system-design/01-scalability/quiz-sho.summary: Free-recall prompts across the scalability unit. Answer each in your own words first — including the arithmetic — then reveal the model answer and compare.

en/system-design/02-availability/01-sla-.title: SLA, SLO, SLI
en/system-design/02-availability/01-sla-.summary: An SLI is the number you measure, an SLO is the target you hold it to, and an SLA is the contract you pay out on if you miss. Set the SLO below the SLA, spend the gap as an error budget, and measure the SLI users actually feel — not the one that's easy to graph.

en/system-design/02-availability/02-redu.title: Redundancy & single points of failure
en/system-design/02-availability/02-redu.summary: A single point of failure is any component whose death takes the whole system down. Redundancy removes it — N+1, N+2, active-active, active-passive — but only if the copies fail independently. Shared dependencies turn 'redundant' designs into one big blast radius.

en/system-design/02-availability/03-fail.title: Failover & fault tolerance
en/system-design/02-availability/03-fail.summary: Failover moves traffic off a dead component onto a healthy one. Fault tolerance survives a fault with no visible interruption at all. Get detection, split-brain, and the retry/timeout interaction wrong and your failover causes the outage it was meant to prevent.

en/system-design/02-availability/project.title: Availability: an SLO and failover plan from scratch
en/system-design/02-availability/project.summary: Hands-on project: take a product brief, derive its SLIs/SLOs and error budget, hunt every single point of failure and design the redundancy and failover to remove them, then prove your failover and degradation work with a small chaos test that injects failures.

en/system-design/02-availability/quiz-ch.title: Availability: multiple-choice review
en/system-design/02-availability/quiz-ch.summary: Multiple-choice synthesis across the availability unit: SLI/SLO/SLA and the nines, error budgets, redundancy sizing and correlated failure, and the failover/split-brain/retry-storm traps that turn recovery into outage.

en/system-design/02-availability/quiz-co.title: Availability: numbers and config reading
en/system-design/02-availability/quiz-co.summary: Read real availability math, config, and code, then do the arithmetic: an error-budget calculation, a serial-availability composition, a redundancy-sizing check, and a retry config that turns a slow dependency into an outage.

en/system-design/02-availability/quiz-sh.title: Availability: free-recall review
en/system-design/02-availability/quiz-sh.summary: Free-recall prompts across the availability unit. Answer each in your own words first — including the arithmetic — then reveal the model answer and compare: SLO/SLA, the nines and error budgets, redundancy and correlated failure, failover and split-brain.

en/system-design/03-traffic/01-load-bala.title: Load balancing
en/system-design/03-traffic/01-load-bala.summary: A load balancer spreads requests across a pool of servers. The choice between L4 and L7, and between round-robin and load-aware algorithms, decides your tail latency — and a naive health-check on failover can stampede the survivors into a second outage.

en/system-design/03-traffic/02-reverse-p.title: Reverse proxy and API gateway
en/system-design/03-traffic/02-reverse-p.summary: A reverse proxy fronts your servers; an API gateway adds cross-cutting concerns — auth, rate limiting, routing, aggregation, TLS termination. Both centralize control, but both can become the bottleneck and the SPOF. Know when a gateway earns its keep and when it's overkill.

en/system-design/03-traffic/03-cdn.title: Content delivery networks (CDN)
en/system-design/03-traffic/03-cdn.summary: A CDN caches content at edge nodes near users, cutting latency and offloading the origin. Levers: cache-control/TTL, hit ratio, push vs pull, origin shielding, purge. Knowing what NOT to cache, and how invalidation works, beats a stale-data incident.

en/system-design/03-traffic/project.title: Traffic & edge: a load balancer and edge plan
en/system-design/03-traffic/project.summary: Hands-on project: stand up a real load balancer in front of a small pool, prove that a load-aware algorithm beats round-robin under an uneven node, then design and measure a CDN cache policy — hit ratio, TTL, and what must never hit the shared edge.

en/system-design/03-traffic/quiz-choice.title: Traffic & edge: multiple-choice review
en/system-design/03-traffic/quiz-choice.summary: Multiple-choice synthesis across the traffic unit: L4 vs L7 and load-balancing algorithms, reverse proxy vs gateway and the SPOF it concentrates, the mesh split, and CDN hit-ratio, TTL, and what not to cache.

en/system-design/03-traffic/quiz-code.title: Traffic & edge: config and code reading
en/system-design/03-traffic/quiz-code.summary: Read real load-balancer, gateway, and CDN config, then make the call: a health-check that lies, an algorithm mismatch, a single-instance gateway, and a cache header that leaks or goes stale.

en/system-design/03-traffic/quiz-short.title: Traffic & edge: free-recall review
en/system-design/03-traffic/quiz-short.summary: Free-recall prompts across the traffic unit. Answer each in your own words first — including the tradeoffs and the arithmetic — then reveal the model answer and compare.

en/system-design/04-data-distribution/01.title: Replication
en/system-design/04-data-distribution/01.summary: Copy data to many nodes for reads, locality, and survival — but every copy is a lie until it catches up. Leader-follower, multi-leader, and leaderless each trade write availability against the chance of silently losing an acknowledged write.

en/system-design/04-data-distribution/02.title: Sharding & partitioning
en/system-design/04-data-distribution/02.summary: When one node can't hold the data or absorb the writes, split it. Range, hash, and directory partitioning each balance differently — and all of them can produce a hot shard, a painful resharding, and queries that no longer fit on one node.

en/system-design/04-data-distribution/03.title: Consistent hashing
en/system-design/04-data-distribution/03.summary: hash(key) mod N remaps almost every key when N changes — a reshard from hell. Consistent hashing places nodes and keys on a ring so adding or removing one node moves only ~1/N of the keys, with virtual nodes for balance.

en/system-design/04-data-distribution/04.title: CAP & PACELC
en/system-design/04-data-distribution/04.summary: CAP is narrow: only during a network partition must you choose consistency or availability. PACELC completes it — else, with no partition, you still trade latency against consistency. Pick per use case along the linearizable-to-eventual spectrum.

en/system-design/04-data-distribution/pr.title: Data distribution: shard, replicate, and break it
en/system-design/04-data-distribution/pr.summary: Hands-on project: take a dataset, design its partition key and replication, build a tiny sharded + consistent-hashed store, then deliberately trigger a hot shard, a lost write on failover, and a quorum-staleness read — and prove the mitigations work.

en/system-design/04-data-distribution/qu.title: Data distribution: multiple-choice review
en/system-design/04-data-distribution/qu.summary: Multiple-choice synthesis across the data-distribution unit: replication lag and lost writes, partitioning strategies and the hot shard, consistent hashing vs mod-N, and the CAP/PACELC choice per use case.

en/system-design/04-data-distribution/qu.title: Data distribution: config and code reading
en/system-design/04-data-distribution/qu.summary: Read real replication config, a partition-key choice, a routing function, and a quorum setting, then do the reasoning: spot the lost-write risk, the hot shard, the mod-N reshard trap, and whether a quorum guarantees a fresh read.

en/system-design/04-data-distribution/qu.title: Data distribution: free-recall review
en/system-design/04-data-distribution/qu.summary: Free-recall prompts across the data-distribution unit. Answer each in your own words first — replication modes, the hot shard, the hash ring, the quorum inequality, CAP and PACELC — then reveal the model answer and compare.

en/system-design/05-caching-at-scale/01-.title: Caching strategies
en/system-design/05-caching-at-scale/01-.summary: Cache-aside, read-through, write-through, write-back, and write-around are not interchangeable: each wires the read and write paths differently, and each makes a specific promise — and breaks a specific one — about freshness, miss cost, and what happens when the cache dies.

en/system-design/05-caching-at-scale/02-.title: Eviction policies and TTL
en/system-design/05-caching-at-scale/02-.summary: A cache is finite, so it must throw things away. Eviction policy (LRU, LFU, FIFO, random) decides what leaves when memory fills; TTL decides when a value goes stale. Both exist to keep the working set hot — and your hit ratio, not your cache size, is the number that matters.

en/system-design/05-caching-at-scale/03-.title: Distributed caches
en/system-design/05-caching-at-scale/03-.summary: One cache node is not enough memory and is a single point of failure. Sharding (via consistent hashing) spreads keys across nodes; replication survives node death. But scaling out the cache invites cache stampedes, hot keys, and cold starts — failures that only appear at scale.

en/system-design/05-caching-at-scale/04-.title: Cache invalidation
en/system-design/05-caching-at-scale/04-.summary: Keeping the cache honest is the genuinely hard part. TTL, explicit invalidation, and versioned keys each trade staleness against complexity, write-time races produce stale reads, and the deepest trap is treating the cache as the source of truth instead of a disposable copy of it.

en/system-design/05-caching-at-scale/pro.title: Caching at scale: build and break a cache
en/system-design/05-caching-at-scale/pro.summary: Hands-on project: put a cache in front of a slow store with a chosen strategy, measure its hit ratio and the DB load behind it, then deliberately trigger and fix a stampede, a stale read, and a synchronized-expiry storm.

en/system-design/05-caching-at-scale/qui.title: Caching at scale: multiple-choice review
en/system-design/05-caching-at-scale/qui.summary: Multiple-choice synthesis across the caching unit: read/write strategies and their consistency, eviction and TTL, hit-ratio arithmetic, sharding with consistent hashing, the stampede, and the source-of-truth anti-pattern.

en/system-design/05-caching-at-scale/qui.title: Caching at scale: code and config reading
en/system-design/05-caching-at-scale/qui.summary: Read real caching code and config, then reason about behavior: a stale-read race, a miss-rate-to-DB-load calculation, a noeviction misconfiguration, and a hot-key stampede in a read path.

en/system-design/05-caching-at-scale/qui.title: Caching at scale: free-recall review
en/system-design/05-caching-at-scale/qui.summary: Free-recall prompts across the caching unit. Answer each in your own words first — strategy and consistency, eviction and hit-ratio math, sharding and the stampede, invalidation and the source-of-truth rule — then reveal the model answer and compare.

en/system-design/06-async-messaging/01-m.title: Message queues
en/system-design/06-async-messaging/01-m.summary: A point-to-point queue decouples producer from consumer in time, so a slow or dead downstream can't take the caller with it. The cost is delivery semantics: at-least-once and at-most-once are the only honest options, and 'exactly-once' is really effectively-once via idempotency.

en/system-design/06-async-messaging/02-p.title: Publish/subscribe
en/system-design/06-async-messaging/02-p.summary: Pub/sub replaces one-to-one delivery with topic-based fan-out: a publisher emits to a topic and every interested consumer gets a copy. The deepest split is broker queues that delete on consume versus log systems that keep an append-only log with per-consumer offsets and replay.

en/system-design/06-async-messaging/03-e.title: Event-driven architecture
en/system-design/06-async-messaging/03-e.summary: Event-driven systems coordinate via facts, not calls — choreography vs orchestration. The load-bearing pattern is the outbox: it makes 'write the DB and publish the event' atomic, defeating the dual-write problem at the cost of eventual consistency you must show in the UX.

en/system-design/06-async-messaging/04-b.title: Backpressure
en/system-design/06-async-messaging/04-b.summary: Backpressure is the signal a slow consumer sends upstream so producers slow instead of piling work into a growing buffer. An unbounded queue is a latent disaster: it absorbs an incident, then a backlog built in minutes takes hours to drain. Bound it, shed load, flow-control.

en/system-design/06-async-messaging/proj.title: Async & messaging: an event-driven order pipeline
en/system-design/06-async-messaging/proj.summary: Hands-on project: build a small event-driven order pipeline with an idempotent at-least-once consumer, a transactional outbox, and a bounded queue, then break it on purpose — kill the relay, redeliver, and overload it — to prove your guarantees hold.

en/system-design/06-async-messaging/quiz.title: Async & messaging: multiple-choice review
en/system-design/06-async-messaging/quiz.summary: Multiple-choice synthesis across the async unit: delivery semantics and effectively-once, queue vs log and replay, choreography vs orchestration, the outbox against dual writes, and the unbounded-queue backlog trap.

en/system-design/06-async-messaging/quiz.title: Async & messaging: code and config reading
en/system-design/06-async-messaging/quiz.summary: Read real consumer code, broker config, and an outbox handler, then pick the answer a senior would commit to: an ack-order bug, a visibility-timeout duplicate, an inline-publish dual write, and an unbounded buffer.

en/system-design/06-async-messaging/quiz.title: Async & messaging: free-recall review
en/system-design/06-async-messaging/quiz.summary: Free-recall prompts across the async unit. Answer each in your own words first — including the mechanism and the failure mode — then reveal the model answer and compare.

en/system-design/07-storage-choices/01-s.title: SQL vs NoSQL
en/system-design/07-storage-choices/01-s.summary: Relational stores enforce relationships with ACID and a schema; NoSQL families (document, key-value, wide-column, graph) trade joins and strong consistency for an access-pattern-first layout that scales out. The senior call is which costs you can pay, not which is modern.

en/system-design/07-storage-choices/02-b.title: Blob & object storage
en/system-design/07-storage-choices/02-b.summary: Object storage (S3) keeps bytes by key behind HTTP; block and file storage attach to a machine. The durable pattern is metadata-in-DB, bytes-in-object via presigned URLs — never blobs in the DB. Durability and availability are separate numbers; lifecycle tiering controls cost.

en/system-design/07-storage-choices/03-t.title: Time-series & search stores
en/system-design/07-storage-choices/03-t.summary: Time-series stores are write-optimized (LSM, downsampling, retention) for append-only metrics; search engines invert text into a term index so full-text is fast where SQL LIKE collapses. A specialized store means owning the dual-write problem — add it only when the primary can't.

en/system-design/07-storage-choices/proj.title: Storage choices: a polyglot media service
en/system-design/07-storage-choices/proj.summary: Hands-on project: build a small media-sharing backend that puts each workload on the right store — relational metadata, object-storage bytes with presigned URLs, a search index — and then deliberately solve the dual-write consistency between the database and the search index.

en/system-design/07-storage-choices/quiz.title: Storage choices: multiple-choice review
en/system-design/07-storage-choices/quiz.summary: Multiple-choice synthesis across the storage unit: SQL vs NoSQL and the ACID/BASE trade, access-pattern-first design, blobs vs object storage with presigned URLs, durability vs availability, specialized stores, and the dual-write problem.

en/system-design/07-storage-choices/quiz.title: Storage choices: code and config reading
en/system-design/07-storage-choices/quiz.summary: Read real schema, config, and code, then make the call: a blob-in-DB anti-pattern, a LIKE-vs-inverted-index query, a best-effort dual write, and a presigned-URL upload path. Pick the change a senior engineer would commit to.

en/system-design/07-storage-choices/quiz.title: Storage choices: free-recall review
en/system-design/07-storage-choices/quiz.summary: Free-recall prompts across the storage unit. Answer each in your own words first — the SQL/NoSQL trade, access-pattern design, the metadata/bytes split, durability vs availability, time-series and search internals, and the dual-write fix — then reveal and compare.

en/system-design/08-building-blocks/01-r.title: Rate limiter
en/system-design/08-building-blocks/01-r.summary: A rate limiter caps how fast a client may hit you. Token bucket and leaky bucket smooth bursts; fixed windows are simple but spike on the boundary; sliding windows fix that. At scale the counter lives in shared storage, and the read-modify-write race is the whole problem.

en/system-design/08-building-blocks/02-u.title: Unique ID generation
en/system-design/08-building-blocks/02-u.summary: At scale you can't ask one database for the next number. UUIDv4 is random and decentralized but fragments indexes; Snowflake and UUIDv7 are time-ordered (timestamp + machine + sequence), keeping IDs sortable and index-friendly — at the cost of leaking time and trusting the clock.

en/system-design/08-building-blocks/03-b.title: Bloom filters
en/system-design/08-building-blocks/03-b.summary: A bloom filter answers 'maybe present, or definitely absent?' in a tiny bit-array with no false negatives. It trades a tunable false-positive rate for huge space savings, letting a cache or DB skip lookups that would certainly miss — at the cost of an occasional empty lookup.

en/system-design/08-building-blocks/04-g.title: Geohashing
en/system-design/08-building-blocks/04-g.summary: Geohashing encodes lat/lng into a short sortable string where a shared prefix means proximity — turning 'find things near me' into an indexed prefix range scan. S2 and H3 refine the idea; all share one trap: neighbours can sit just across a cell boundary with a different code.

en/system-design/08-building-blocks/05-l.title: Leader election
en/system-design/08-building-blocks/05-l.summary: Some jobs need exactly one coordinator. Leader election picks it — via a consensus protocol (Raft/ZAB) or a lease/lock in ZooKeeper, etcd, or Redis. The deep trap is split-brain: a paused leader that thinks it's still in charge. The fix is a fencing token, not a longer timeout.

en/system-design/08-building-blocks/proj.title: Building blocks: a distributed rate limiter, end to end
en/system-design/08-building-blocks/proj.summary: Hands-on project: build a correct distributed token-bucket rate limiter — shared counter, atomic increment, 429 + Retry-After, fail-open — then prove the race is gone under concurrent load and reason about how the unit's other blocks would compose into the same service.

en/system-design/08-building-blocks/quiz.title: Building blocks: multiple-choice review
en/system-design/08-building-blocks/quiz.summary: Multiple-choice synthesis across the building-blocks unit: the rate-limiter race, time-ordered vs random IDs, the bloom filter's one-sided guarantee, the geohash boundary problem, and the split-brain that fencing tokens defeat.

en/system-design/08-building-blocks/quiz.title: Building blocks: code and config reading
en/system-design/08-building-blocks/quiz.summary: Read real limiter code, an ID config, a bloom-filter sizing call, and a geohash query, then pick the answer a senior engineer would commit to: the lost-update race, the index-fragmenting key, the saturated filter, and the missed boundary neighbour.

en/system-design/08-building-blocks/quiz.title: Building blocks: free-recall review
en/system-design/08-building-blocks/quiz.summary: Free-recall prompts across the building-blocks unit. Answer each in your own words first — including the mechanism and the failure mode — then reveal the model answer and compare.

en/system-design/09-interview-framework/.title: Clarifying requirements
en/system-design/09-interview-framework/.summary: The interview starts with the design you don't draw. Split functional from non-functional requirements, name the core entities and read/write access patterns, and pin consistency, latency, and availability targets — those constraints, not the boxes, decide the architecture.

en/system-design/09-interview-framework/.title: Estimation in the interview
en/system-design/09-interview-framework/.summary: Estimation earns its keep in the interview only when a number changes the design. Estimate the scale that matters, read whether the interviewer wants the math or the conclusion, and convert estimates into capacity — servers, storage, bandwidth — forced by arithmetic.

en/system-design/09-interview-framework/.title: High-level design & the deep-dive
en/system-design/09-interview-framework/.summary: Draw the high-level design first — client to load balancer to service to data — then pick the one or two genuinely hard components and go deep. The HLD shows you can compose; the deep-dive shows you can engineer. Justify every box; sketch the API and data model first.

en/system-design/09-interview-framework/.title: Bottlenecks & tradeoffs
en/system-design/09-interview-framework/.summary: Find the bottleneck — the one resource that breaks first — and state every tradeoff: consistency vs availability, latency vs cost, simplicity vs scale. Handle 'what if 10x?' by naming which resource breaks and why. Acknowledging the tradeoff separates a mid answer from senior.

en/system-design/09-interview-framework/.title: Interview framework: a full design, end to end
en/system-design/09-interview-framework/.summary: Hands-on project: take a product prompt and run the entire framework as a written design doc — clarify requirements, estimate, draw the HLD, deep-dive the hard component, and find the bottleneck while naming every tradeoff — then defend it against a 10x growth scenario.

en/system-design/09-interview-framework/.title: Interview framework: multiple-choice review
en/system-design/09-interview-framework/.summary: Multiple-choice synthesis across the interview-framework unit: clarifying requirements and access patterns, estimation that changes the design, the HLD-and-deep-dive split, and finding the bottleneck while naming tradeoffs.

en/system-design/09-interview-framework/.title: Interview framework: applied numbers and config
en/system-design/09-interview-framework/.summary: Read the artifacts of a real interview — an estimation helper, a requirements note, a capacity calc, a config that encodes a tradeoff — and do the reasoning a senior engineer would: which number changes the design, what the config gives up, where the bottleneck moves.

en/system-design/09-interview-framework/.title: Interview framework: free-recall review
en/system-design/09-interview-framework/.summary: Free-recall prompts across the interview-framework unit. Reconstruct each step of the procedure in your own words — requirements, estimation, HLD and deep-dive, bottlenecks and tradeoffs — before revealing the model answer.

en/typescript/00-start-here/01-why-types.title: Why types, deeply
en/typescript/00-start-here/01-why-types.summary: TypeScript types are a compile-time proof about the shape of runtime values that erases entirely before the code runs — a type error is a counterexample the checker found before your users did, not a runtime guard.

en/typescript/00-start-here/02-type-vs-v.title: Type space vs value space
en/typescript/00-start-here/02-type-vs-v.summary: Every TypeScript identifier lives in value space, type space, or both; `typeof` bridges value-to-type and `keyof` stays type-to-type, and the classic "only refers to a type / a value" errors come from crossing the worlds.

en/typescript/01-foundations/01-structur.title: Structural typing: shape is the only thing the checker compares
en/typescript/01-foundations/01-structur.summary: TypeScript compares types by shape, not by name. Two unrelated interfaces with the same members are interchangeable. Excess-property checks on object literals are the one place it feels nominal — and branded types let you fake nominal safety on purpose.

en/typescript/01-foundations/02-inferenc.title: Inference basics: how the checker fills in the types you didn't write
en/typescript/01-foundations/02-inferenc.summary: TypeScript infers most types so you don't annotate them. The rules — initializer typing, const-vs-let widening, contextual typing of callbacks, and best-common-type for arrays — are predictable once you see them. Annotate boundaries; infer locals.

en/typescript/01-foundations/03-any-unkn.title: any, unknown, never: the top, the bottom, and the escape hatch
en/typescript/01-foundations/03-any-unkn.summary: any opts out of checking and silently spreads; unknown is the safe top type you must narrow before use; never is the empty bottom type that powers exhaustiveness checks. Knowing where each sits on the assignability lattice is core type-system fluency.

en/typescript/01-foundations/04-literal-.title: Literal types: single values as types, and the as const that keeps them
en/typescript/01-foundations/04-literal-.summary: A literal type is a single value as a type: "GET", 200, true. Unions of literals are lightweight enums. const keeps literals, let widens them, and as const locks deep readonly literals on objects, arrays, and tuples — the trick that powers config-as-types.

en/typescript/02-everyday-types/01-union.title: Unions and intersections
en/typescript/02-everyday-types/01-union.summary: Unions mean one-of and only expose common members; intersections mean all-of and merge object members. Mix incompatible primitives and you get never.

en/typescript/02-everyday-types/02-narro.title: Narrowing and control-flow analysis
en/typescript/02-everyday-types/02-narro.summary: Control-flow analysis tracks the type of a variable at each program point. typeof, truthiness, in, instanceof and assignment narrow a union — but a closure or await can re-widen it.

en/typescript/02-everyday-types/03-type-.title: User-defined type guards
en/typescript/02-everyday-types/03-type-.summary: User-defined type guards return `x is T`. The checker trusts the predicate unsoundly — a lying guard compiles and corrupts every narrowing downstream.

en/typescript/02-everyday-types/04-discr.title: Discriminated unions
en/typescript/02-everyday-types/04-discr.summary: A shared literal tag turns a union into a discriminated union: switch on the tag narrows each branch, and an assertNever default makes adding a variant a compile error everywhere it is unhandled.

en/typescript/02-everyday-types/05-index.title: keyof and indexed access types
en/typescript/02-everyday-types/05-index.summary: keyof gives the union of a type's keys; T[K] indexes into a type. Index with a union of keys to get a union of value types, and Arr[number] to get an array's element type.

en/typescript/03-generics/01-generic-fun.title: Generic functions
en/typescript/03-generics/01-generic-fun.summary: A generic function is a function over types. The checker reads the call arguments and solves for each type parameter — but a parameter used only once is just `any` wearing a costume.

en/typescript/03-generics/02-constraints.title: Generic constraints
en/typescript/03-generics/02-constraints.summary: A constraint `T extends C` is a two-way contract — it restricts which arguments callers may pass, and in exchange lets the body touch the members C guarantees. The classic trap is returning C instead of T and erasing specificity.

en/typescript/03-generics/03-defaults-an.title: Defaults and inference
en/typescript/03-generics/03-defaults-an.summary: Default type parameters fill the tail when inference finds nothing, but inference always wins where it can. `NoInfer<T>` (TS 5.4) blocks inference at a position so one argument can decide T for the rest.

en/typescript/03-generics/04-generic-cla.title: Generic classes
en/typescript/03-generics/04-generic-cla.summary: A class type parameter is scoped to the instance, never the static side. Typed containers like Stack<T> and Result<T, E> show why — and structural compatibility of instances foreshadows variance.

en/typescript/03-generics/05-variance-in.title: Variance intuition
en/typescript/03-generics/05-variance-in.summary: Variance is the direction subtyping flows through a type constructor. Function parameters are contravariant, arrays are unsoundly covariant, and method parameters stay bivariant even under strictFunctionTypes — the gotcha that lets a too-loose callback slip through.

en/typescript/04-type-system-deep/01-con.title: Conditional types: a type-level ternary keyed on assignability
en/typescript/04-type-system-deep/01-con.summary: Conditional types pick a branch by asking 'is T assignable to U?' — not by JS class inheritance. A naked type parameter distributes the check over each union member, and a generic T defers resolution until instantiation.

en/typescript/04-type-system-deep/02-the.title: The infer keyword: pattern-match a type and capture a piece of it
en/typescript/04-type-system-deep/02-the.summary: `infer` declares a fresh type variable in a conditional's extends clause, bound to whatever fills that slot — the engine behind ReturnType, Awaited, and tuple head/tail. One infer name across several positions unions covariant candidates but intersects contravariant ones.

en/typescript/04-type-system-deep/03-map.title: Mapped types: iterate a type's keys to build a new one
en/typescript/04-type-system-deep/03-map.summary: A mapped type `{ [K in keyof T]: ... }` iterates T's keys to transform values, with `?`/`-?` and `readonly`/`-readonly` modifiers. The crucial subtlety is homomorphism: mapping over `keyof T` preserves modifiers and array/tuple-ness; mapping a separate key union does not.

en/typescript/04-type-system-deep/04-key.title: Key remapping via as: rename and filter keys in a mapped type
en/typescript/04-type-system-deep/04-key.summary: Key remapping (`as` in a mapped type, TS 4.1) computes a new key per iteration. Rename with template literals and `Capitalize`, or remap a key to `never` to delete it — how you filter properties by value type. Keys must be string|number|symbol, and `as` breaks homomorphism.

en/typescript/04-type-system-deep/05-tem.title: Template literal types: compute, expand, and parse string types
en/typescript/04-type-system-deep/05-tem.summary: Template literal types build string types by interpolation. Interpolating unions yields the full cross product — a combinatorial blowup. Intrinsics transform case, and `infer` inside a pattern parses strings. Pattern inference is non-greedy at the first delimiter.

en/typescript/05-type-level-programming/.title: Recursion in types
en/typescript/05-type-level-programming/.summary: A recursive conditional type peels one element off a tuple, recurses on the rest, and stops at a base case — like a runtime recursion, but the compiler is the interpreter and depth is finite.

en/typescript/05-type-level-programming/.title: Distributive conditionals
en/typescript/05-type-level-programming/.summary: A naked type parameter in a conditional distributes over each member of a union; wrapping it in a tuple opts out — and a conditional over never yields never because never is the empty union.

en/typescript/05-type-level-programming/.title: Utility types from scratch
en/typescript/05-type-level-programming/.summary: Every standard utility type is a one-line mapped or conditional type — reimplementing Partial, Pick, Omit, ReturnType, Awaited and friends demystifies them and reveals why stdlib Omit is non-distributive.

en/typescript/05-type-level-programming/.title: Type-level arithmetic
en/typescript/05-type-level-programming/.summary: TypeScript has no type-level numbers, so you encode N as a tuple of length N — concatenate to add, infer-off the front to subtract, and compare lengths to order — bounded and slow by construction.

en/typescript/05-type-level-programming/.title: Limits and type performance
en/typescript/05-type-level-programming/.summary: Clever type-level code has a real compile-time cost — instantiation depth and count limits, union cross-product blowup, editor lag — and a senior knows how to measure it and when to stop and validate at runtime instead.

en/typescript/06-functions-this/01-overl.title: Function overloads
en/typescript/06-functions-this/01-overl.summary: How overloads expose multiple call signatures over one hidden implementation, how the compiler resolves a call top-to-bottom and picks the first match, and when a single generic or conditional return beats overloads.

en/typescript/06-functions-this/02-typin.title: Typing this
en/typescript/06-functions-this/02-typin.summary: How TypeScript types the hidden first parameter with `this: T` (erased at emit), why a method loses its `this` when passed as a callback, and how ThisType, polymorphic `this`, and this-based guards model fluent and stateful APIs.

en/typescript/06-functions-this/03-asser.title: Assertion functions
en/typescript/06-functions-this/03-asser.summary: Assertion functions (`asserts x is T`, `asserts cond`) narrow the rest of the scope by throwing — how they differ from type predicates, why the return-type annotation is mandatory, and the unsoundness traps.

en/typescript/06-functions-this/04-the-s.title: The satisfies operator
en/typescript/06-functions-this/04-the-s.summary: How `satisfies` validates a value against a type without widening it — keeping the precise inferred type that an annotation would discard — contrasted with annotation and `as`, plus where you still need a contextual type.

en/typescript/07-config-modules-build/01.title: tsconfig strictness: what `strict` actually flips, and the flags it leaves out
en/typescript/07-config-modules-build/01.summary: `strict: true` flips eight flags at once; `strictNullChecks` retypes every value by splitting null/undefined from `T`. The biggest wins are flags NOT in the bundle — `noUncheckedIndexedAccess`, `exactOptionalPropertyTypes` — plus migrating a loose codebase incrementally.

en/typescript/07-config-modules-build/02.title: module & moduleResolution: how an import string becomes a file
en/typescript/07-config-modules-build/02.summary: `module` and `moduleResolution` decide how import strings become files — the classic 'works in the editor, fails at runtime' bug. `node16`/`nodenext` enforce real Node ESM rules; `bundler` (TS 5.0) relaxes them. `tsc` never rewrites `paths` — the bundler must.

en/typescript/07-config-modules-build/03.title: .d.ts files: ambient declarations, augmentation, and the public type surface
en/typescript/07-config-modules-build/03.summary: `.d.ts` files describe shapes with no implementation: ambient declarations, `declare module`, `declare global`, and module augmentation. The traps: augmentation that silently fails to merge, accidental global pollution, and emitting types that reference private paths.

en/typescript/07-config-modules-build/04.title: Project references: tsc --build, composite, and the incremental build graph
en/typescript/07-config-modules-build/04.summary: Project references split a monorepo into `tsconfig` projects that `tsc --build` compiles in dependency order. `composite` (which forces `declaration`) enables referencing and `.tsbuildinfo` caching. Traps: stale buildinfo, circular references, the 'must have composite' error.

en/typescript/07-config-modules-build/05.title: Type-checking vs transpilation: why your bundler doesn't catch type errors
en/typescript/07-config-modules-build/05.summary: esbuild/swc/babel transpile file-by-file and DO NOT type-check — a type error never stops the bundle. That model needs `isolatedModules` (no cross-file const enums, demands `export type`). The pattern: the bundler builds, and `tsc --noEmit` is the separate CI type gate.

en/typescript/08-real-world/01-typing-ap.title: Typing APIs: a fetch type is a promise, not a proof
en/typescript/08-real-world/01-typing-ap.summary: A type annotation on a fetch response is a promise about the server's shape, not a proof; `as User` checks nothing. Model responses as discriminated unions and Result types, and treat the network edge as where static types end and runtime validation begins.

en/typescript/08-real-world/02-zod-and-v.title: zod: one schema, the static type and the runtime guard
en/typescript/08-real-world/02-zod-and-v.summary: zod is schema-first validation: write one schema, derive the static type with `z.infer`, and `.parse`/`.safeParse` check bytes at runtime and narrow. The type and the guard come from one definition, so they can't drift — never hand-write both a type and a schema.

en/typescript/08-real-world/03-trpc-end-.title: tRPC: end-to-end types with no codegen, and what that costs
en/typescript/08-real-world/03-trpc-end-.summary: tRPC gives end-to-end type safety with no codegen: the client infers its whole API type from `typeof appRouter`, so types flow across the wire at compile time. 'No codegen' means client and server share the type (`import type`); the cost is inference time and editor lag.

en/typescript/08-real-world/04-library-g.title: Library generics: APIs that infer beautifully (and the ones that don't)
en/typescript/08-real-world/04-library-g.summary: Designing generic library APIs that infer well: order type params so inference flows, use constraints and defaults, block inference with `NoInfer`, and return precise types not the constraint. The failure mode: an API that forces callers to write type args.

en/typescript/08-real-world/05-common-pi.title: Common pitfalls: traps that compile clean and bite later
en/typescript/08-real-world/05-common-pi.summary: The senior pitfalls roundup: `as`/`!` hiding bugs, `any` leaks, structural typing letting wrong objects through, `Object.keys` returning `string[]`, array covariance, mutation invalidating narrowing, forgotten `as const`. For each: the symptom, why it compiles, the fix.

en/typescript/09-putting-it-together/01-.title: Capstone: ship one feature, typed end-to-end
en/typescript/09-putting-it-together/01-.summary: The finale: ship a 'create + list paginated comments' feature end-to-end. One zod schema derives every layer; a discriminated Result is handled exhaustively; the boundary is validated not cast; the client type is inferred — each move naming the earlier unit it came from.

ru/ai-llm/00-start-here/01-overview.title: С нуля: что такое интеграция LLM на самом деле
ru/ai-llm/00-start-here/01-overview.summary: Интегрировать LLM — значит вызывать вероятностную текстовую модель как сервис и проектировать код с учётом её ограничений — конечного контекстного окна, оплаты за токены и галлюцинаций. Это карта и слова, которые остальной трек считает знакомыми.

ru/ai-llm/01-prompt-caching/01-overview.title: Кэширование промпта: как стабильный префикс режет стоимость входа в 10 раз
ru/ai-llm/01-prompt-caching/01-overview.summary: Кэш переиспользует точный префикс токен-в-токен по цене ~0.1x от входа. Любой байт, сдвигающий префикс — таймстамп, переставленный tool — инвалидирует весь кэш и тихо умножает счёт на 10.

ru/ai-llm/01-prompt-caching/project.title: Prompt caching: измерь экономию
ru/ai-llm/01-prompt-caching/project.summary: Практический проект — добавь prompt caching в реальный LLM-сервис, инструментируй hit rate и стоимость, и докажи экономию до/после по тратам на вход и TTFT.

ru/ai-llm/01-prompt-caching/quiz-choice.title: Prompt caching: тест с множественным выбором
ru/ai-llm/01-prompt-caching/quiz-choice.summary: Синтез по всему юниту prompt caching в формате выбора: сопоставление префикса, экономика записи/чтения, выбор TTL, правила порядка и тихое отравление префикса.

ru/ai-llm/01-prompt-caching/quiz-code.title: Prompt caching: чтение запроса и usage
ru/ai-llm/01-prompt-caching/quiz-code.summary: Читай реальные тела запросов Anthropic SDK и блоки usage, предсказывай, где встаёт cache breakpoint и попадёт ли он, и выбирай фикс наибольшего рычага.

ru/ai-llm/01-prompt-caching/quiz-short.title: Prompt caching: тест на свободное припоминание
ru/ai-llm/01-prompt-caching/quiz-short.summary: Промпты на свободное припоминание по всему юниту prompt caching. Сначала ответь своими словами, затем раскрой модельный ответ и сравни.

ru/ai-llm/02-tool-calls/01-overview.title: Вызовы инструментов: цикл round-trip, валидация схемы и защита от зацикливания агента
ru/ai-llm/02-tool-calls/01-overview.summary: Вызов инструментов превращает модель в вызывающего функцию, но модель лишь шлёт запрос — выполняешь его ты. Каждый вызов — лишний round trip, аргументы бывают галлюцинацией, а цикл без защиты будет жечь токены вечно.

ru/ai-llm/02-tool-calls/project.title: Tool calls: построй устойчивый цикл tool calling
ru/ai-llm/02-tool-calls/project.summary: Практический проект — построй устойчивый цикл tool calling с валидацией JSON schema, авторизацией, per-tool timeout, ограниченными ретраями и защитой от runaway, и докажи, что он выживает против tools, которые лгут, виснут и падают.

ru/ai-llm/02-tool-calls/quiz-choice.title: Tool calls: тест с выбором ответа
ru/ai-llm/02-tool-calls/quiz-choice.summary: Тест с выбором на синтез по всему юниту — цикл round-trip, валидация JSON schema как граница доверия, защита от runaway-цикла, parallel tool use и tool_choice.

ru/ai-llm/02-tool-calls/quiz-code.title: Tool calls: чтение кода и схем
ru/ai-llm/02-tool-calls/quiz-code.summary: Читай реальные сниппеты tool calling — JSON schema tool, диспетчер parallel-вызовов, цикл с timeout/обработкой ошибок и валидатор аргументов — и выбирай фикс с наибольшим рычагом.

ru/ai-llm/02-tool-calls/quiz-short.title: Tool calls: тест на воспроизведение
ru/ai-llm/02-tool-calls/quiz-short.summary: Промпты на свободное воспроизведение по всему юниту tool calls. Сначала ответь своими словами, затем открой эталонный ответ и сравни.

ru/ai-llm/03-rag-architecture/01-overvie.title: Архитектура RAG: пайплайн, который ломается на ретривале, а не на генерации
ru/ai-llm/03-rag-architecture/01-overvie.summary: RAG — это задача ретривала в костюме генерации. Размер чанка, top-k, реранкинг и порядок контекста двигают recall и стоимость, а промах ретривала заставляет модель уверенно выдумывать ответ вместо признания «не знаю».

ru/ai-llm/03-rag-architecture/project.title: RAG architecture: соберите и оцените retrieval-pipeline
ru/ai-llm/03-rag-architecture/project.summary: Практический проект — собрать RAG-pipeline на реальном корпусе, затем измерить качество retrieval, grounding и latency/cost и доказать каждое улучшение числами до/после на отложенном eval-наборе.

ru/ai-llm/03-rag-architecture/quiz-choic.title: RAG architecture: тест с множественным выбором
ru/ai-llm/03-rag-architecture/quiz-choic.summary: Синтез по всему юниту RAG в формате выбора — chunking, стоимость embedding, retrieval по схеме wide-then-narrow, lost-in-the-middle и режим уверенной галлюцинации.

ru/ai-llm/03-rag-architecture/quiz-code.title: RAG architecture: чтение кода и pipeline
ru/ai-llm/03-rag-architecture/quiz-code.summary: Чтение реального кода RAG-pipeline — chunker, поиск по cosine similarity, стадия retrieve-then-rerank и сборщик контекста — с выбором исправления наибольшего рычага.

ru/ai-llm/03-rag-architecture/quiz-short.title: RAG architecture: тест со свободным воспроизведением
ru/ai-llm/03-rag-architecture/quiz-short.summary: Промпты на свободное воспроизведение по юниту RAG — компромиссы chunking, стоимость embedding, retrieval wide-then-narrow, lost-in-the-middle и abstain-gate. Сначала ответьте, потом откройте.

ru/ai-llm/04-streaming/01-overview.title: Стриминг ответов LLM: SSE, частичные токены и прокси, который их съедает
ru/ai-llm/04-streaming/01-overview.summary: Стриминг меняет общее время генерации на time-to-first-token. SSE шлёт delta-события, которые ты накапливаешь; аргументы tool-call приходят как частичный JSON, его нельзя парсить до конца. Классика прода: буферизующий прокси держит весь ответ — и стриминг тихо умирает.

ru/ai-llm/04-streaming/project.title: Streaming: собери устойчивый streaming-эндпоинт и клиент
ru/ai-llm/04-streaming/project.summary: Практический проект — собрать устойчивый streaming-эндпоинт и клиент целиком: SSE-реле, измерение TTFT/TPOT, отмена посреди потока, восстановление после ошибок и проверка на буферизующем прокси.

ru/ai-llm/04-streaming/quiz-choice.title: Streaming: тест с множественным выбором
ru/ai-llm/04-streaming/quiz-choice.summary: Синтез всего юнита в формате выбора — TTFT против общего времени, жизненный цикл событий SSE, накопление delta, частичный JSON в аргументах tool, reconnect и буферизующий прокси.

ru/ai-llm/04-streaming/quiz-code.title: Streaming: чтение кода и потока
ru/ai-llm/04-streaming/quiz-code.summary: Читай реальные сниппеты парсинга SSE и streaming-клиента, предсказывай поведение и выбирай фикс с наибольшим рычагом — фрейминг событий, накопление delta, client abort и частичный JSON в аргументах tool.

ru/ai-llm/04-streaming/quiz-short.title: Streaming: повторение на припоминание
ru/ai-llm/04-streaming/quiz-short.summary: Промпты на свободное припоминание по всему юниту streaming. Сначала ответь своими словами, затем открой модельный ответ и сравни.

ru/ai-llm/05-cost-budgets/01-overview.title: Бюджеты на LLM: асимметрия токенов, роутинг и kill switch
ru/ai-llm/05-cost-budgets/01-overview.summary: Output-токены стоят ~5x от input, а system prompt + история + RAG-контекст пересылаются каждый ход — поэтому зацикленный агент сжигает тысячи за ночь. Роутинг, кэширование и жёсткие лимиты бюджета на запрос держат трату в рамках.

ru/ai-llm/05-cost-budgets/project.title: LLM cost budgets: построй cost observability и гардрейлы
ru/ai-llm/05-cost-budgets/project.summary: Практический проект — добавь cost observability и budget-гардрейлы к LLM-фиче, затем сократи расход caching и routing и докажи это числами before/after.

ru/ai-llm/05-cost-budgets/quiz-choice.title: LLM cost budgets: тест с множественным выбором
ru/ai-llm/05-cost-budgets/quiz-choice.summary: Синтез с множественным выбором по юниту cost budgets — асимметрия цен на token, повторно отправляемый context, model routing, prompt caching и in-process budget-гардрейлы.

ru/ai-llm/05-cost-budgets/quiz-code.title: LLM cost budgets: код и cost-арифметика
ru/ai-llm/05-cost-budgets/quiz-code.summary: Читай реальный код учёта token и ценовую арифметику, предсказывай расход и выбирай фикс с наибольшим рычагом — cost-арифметика, per-tenant budget, routing и cache savings.

ru/ai-llm/05-cost-budgets/quiz-short.title: LLM cost budgets: тест на свободное воспроизведение
ru/ai-llm/05-cost-budgets/quiz-short.summary: Промпты на свободное воспроизведение по юниту cost budgets. Ответь сначала своими словами, затем открой эталонный ответ и сравни.

ru/ai-llm/06-agents/01-overview.title: Цикл агента: ReAct, неуправляемые шаги и контекст, растущий каждый ход
ru/ai-llm/06-agents/01-overview.summary: LLM-агент — это while-цикл: вызвать модель, выполнить инструмент, добавить результат, снова вызвать модель. Опасность — цикл, который не останавливается, и история, которая не перестаёт расти; за оба платишь по токенам.

ru/ai-llm/06-agents/project.title: Агенты: собрать ограниченного, наблюдаемого агента
ru/ai-llm/06-agents/project.summary: Практический проект — собрать ограниченного, наблюдаемого ReAct-агента с реальными guardrails, затем загнать его в runaway-цикл и доказать, что защиты держат, измеряя успешность задачи.

ru/ai-llm/06-agents/quiz-choice.title: Агенты: тест с множественным выбором
ru/ai-llm/06-agents/quiz-choice.summary: Синтез по всему юниту в формате выбора — цикл ReAct, квадратичная стоимость контекста, выходы из цикла (termination), ловушки error recovery и когда писать скрипт вместо agent.

ru/ai-llm/06-agents/quiz-code.title: Агенты: чтение кода и цикла
ru/ai-llm/06-agents/quiz-code.summary: Чтение реальных сниппетов agent-цикла — диспетч инструментов, лимиты шагов, обрезка контекста, error recovery — предскажите поведение и выберите фикс с наибольшим рычагом.

ru/ai-llm/06-agents/quiz-short.title: Агенты: тест на свободное воспроизведение
ru/ai-llm/06-agents/quiz-short.summary: Запросы на свободное воспроизведение по всему юниту. Сначала ответьте своими словами, затем раскройте модельный ответ и сверьтесь.

ru/ai-llm/07-evals/01-overview.title: LLM-evals: регрессионный тест для недетерминированной фичи
ru/ai-llm/07-evals/01-overview.summary: LLM-фичу нельзя выкатывать без evals: один и тот же ввод даёт разный вывод, а смена модели или промпта тихо роняет качество. Golden-набор, программные проверки и откалиброванный judge — то, чем ловят регрессию раньше пользователей.

ru/ai-llm/07-evals/project.title: LLM-evals: собери eval-набор и CI-гейт
ru/ai-llm/07-evals/project.summary: Практический проект — собери eval-набор на golden set плюс откалиброванный judge и CI regression gate для одной реальной LLM-фичи с измеримыми критериями прохождения и online-проверкой дрейфа.

ru/ai-llm/07-evals/quiz-choice.title: LLM-evals: тест с множественным выбором
ru/ai-llm/07-evals/quiz-choice.summary: Тест с множественным выбором на синтез по всему юниту evals — golden set, программные проверки против judge, калибровка judge, offline-гейт против online-семплинга и режимы, когда зелёный набор лжёт.

ru/ai-llm/07-evals/quiz-code.title: LLM-evals: чтение кода и харнесса
ru/ai-llm/07-evals/quiz-code.summary: Читаем реальный код eval-харнесса, judge-промпт и его скоринг, diff golden set и CI regression gate — затем выбираем поведение или самый рычажный фикс, который senior-инженер сделает первым.

ru/ai-llm/07-evals/quiz-short.title: LLM-evals: тест на свободное воспроизведение
ru/ai-llm/07-evals/quiz-short.summary: Промпты на свободное воспроизведение по всему юниту evals. Ответь на каждый своими словами, затем открой модельный ответ и сравни.

ru/ai-llm/08-putting-it-together/01-over.title: Сборка production LLM-приложения: баг живёт в шве
ru/ai-llm/08-putting-it-together/01-over.summary: Кэширование, RAG, стриминг, тулзы, агенты и evals проходят каждый свой тест, а вместе падают. Трассируй один запрос насквозь: баг живёт в шве между двумя корректными слоями, а не внутри одного из них.

ru/ai-llm/08-putting-it-together/project.title: Капстоун: выкати собранную LLM-фичу, держащую на швах
